->**<term>Hermetic Philosophy<note>original: "Philosophia Hermetica." A branch of spiritual and occult philosophy based on writings attributed to the legendary Hermes Trismegistus, traditionally associated with alchemy and hidden wisdom.</note></term>**<-

<note>The bookplate depicts a "pelican in her piety," a mother bird feeding her young with blood from her own breast. While originally a Christian symbol of sacrifice, in alchemical contexts it represents the "multiplication" stage of the Great Work, where the elixir is nourished. The bird perches on a cubic pedestal featuring a coat of arms—a shield with a red saltire (X-shaped cross) and four roses—beneath a radiant sun, signifying enlightenment and successful transformation.</note>

# JOHN
### REUCHLIN OF PFORZHEIM,
### DOCTOR OF LAWS.
## ON THE
### <term>ART OF KABBALAH</term><note>Kabbalah (historically spelled Cabala) is an ancient tradition of Jewish mysticism. Reuchlin, a pioneering German scholar, was the first major Christian thinker to study these texts deeply, believing they held keys to understanding divine philosophy.</note>

### AND ACCURATE-

<note>The image shows a woodcut heraldic device belonging to Reuchlin. The shield is inscribed with the word "ARACAPNION" (original: "ARACAP-NIONIS"), which is a Greek-styled pseudonym meaning "without smoke." This is a clever scholarly pun on his German name, Reuchlin, which is derived from the word for "smoke" (*Rauch*). The device features a tilting helmet and a crest showing a cross within a wheel.</note>

<summary>This is the title page of Johannes Reuchlin's seminal 1517 work on Jewish mysticism, marking a pivotal moment in the Northern Renaissance where Christian scholars began to engage directly with Hebrew texts. The page features Reuchlin’s personal heraldic device and ownership marks from previous collectors.</summary>

# JOHN
## REUCHLIN OF PFORZ-

<image-desc>
A detailed woodcut coat of arms belonging to the author. The central element is a shield containing a tall, tapered vessel or altar bound with ropes. Inscribed on this vessel are the words "ALTAR" and "OF CAPNIO" <note>original: "ARACAP NIONIS", referring to Ara Capnionis. "Capnio" was Reuchlin's scholarly pseudonym—a Greek translation of his German name, which relates to the word for "smoke."</note>. Above the shield sits a closed helmet in profile, decorated with a small cross. The crest atop the helmet consists of a spiked breaking wheel <note>The symbol of Saint Catherine, the patron saint of philosophers and scholars</note>, which contains within it a smaller wheel or circle with a cross. The entire shield and helmet are surrounded by ornate, flourishing leaf-like mantling.
</image-desc>

The page features Reuchlin's personal coat of arms and handwritten notes indicating it once belonged to the prominent library of Jean de Lapoussie.</summary>

<meta>This page begins the formal dedication of the work to Pope Leo X. It transitions from the technical index of Kabbalistic terms to a rhetorical praise of the Medici family's role in the Renaissance revival of ancient learning.</meta>

# TO THE MOST HOLY
## LEO THE TENTH, SUPREME PONTIFF,
### Johannes Reuchlin, humbly
### commends himself.

<image-desc>A large historiated initial 'I' set within a decorated square frame. The design features two winged putti or cherubs climbing or supporting the letter 'I' amidst floral or foliate ornamentation.</image-desc>

ITALIAN PHILOSOPHY <note>original: "ITALICA PHILOSOPHIA" — referring to the Pythagorean tradition which flourished in southern Italy, or Magna Graecia</note>, MOST BLESSED LEO the Tenth, Supreme Pontiff of the Christian religion—first brought forth by Pythagoras, the father of that name, and once passed down to the highest men endowed with excellent talents—had for many years perished under the immense barking of the Sophists. It lay buried in darkness and thick night for so long, until the sun of every kind of noble study, the most illustrious Lorenzo de' Medici, your father, a descendant of the Great Cosimo and prince of the Florentine city, arose by the favor of God. Although we know him to have been so masterly in spirit and in the science of governing the Republic, and in conducting all affairs of home and war with counsel and prudence, that no one in his age seemed more worthy of praise in civil practice, yet we must confess it was even more beneficial for us that he was born—as if sent down from heaven—so that, after the disciplines of eloquence and the arts of fine speaking had been handed down to the Florentine youth by Petrarch, Philelphus, and the Aretine <note>Referring to Leonardo Bruni, a famous humanist from Arezzo</note> rhetoricians, the citizens might (beyond controversy) be more distinguished than all foreign nations by a more polished pen and a greater purity of tongue. He finally brought into his homeland that wisdom which expels vices and that method of investigating secrets which had lain hidden in the books and monuments of the ancients until his own times.

For this task, he diligently summoned from everywhere the most learned men and those most skilled in the ancient authors, who possessed sufficient eloquence alongside their knowledge of things: Demetrius Chalcondyles, Marsilio Ficino, Giorgio Vespucci, Cristoforo Landino, Valori, Angelo Poliziano, Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, and other most erudite men of the world, through whom the skill of the ancients and the secret antiquity—obliterated by the malice of chance—might return to the light. These great men labored in competition; for one taught, another commented, this one read, that one interpreted and translated languages into other languages. Marsilio [Ficino] led Greece into Latium <note>meaning he translated Greek works into Latin</note>. Poliziano brought the Romans back to Greece. All pressed on with the work, everyone bringing the highest praise to the Medici. Upon these heroes, Most Blessed LEO, your divine "birth-wand" <note>original: "natalis uirgula" — a metaphorical reference to a lucky or divine influence present at birth</note>, as they say, happily fell by the grace of the Gods; certainly so that there would remain no kind of more elegant learning in which you did not...

<summary>In this dedication to Pope Leo X, Johannes Reuchlin praises the Medici family, specifically Lorenzo the Magnificent, for patronizing the scholars who rediscovered ancient Greek and Latin wisdom, setting the stage for Reuchlin's own work.</summary>
<keywords>Johannes Reuchlin, Pope Leo X, Lorenzo de' Medici, Renaissance Humanism, Pythagoras, Marsilio Ficino, Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, Florence, Classical scholarship</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Reuchlin’s dedication to Pope Leo X (Giovanni de' Medici). Reuchlin is currently describing the intellectual climate of Florence under the Pope’s father, Lorenzo the Magnificent, and recounting his own personal visit to the Medici palace in 1482.</meta>

...you emerged more skilled, indeed as a boy having embraced the sweetness of the most polished Poliziano <note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494), a brilliant Renaissance humanist and tutor to the Medici children</note>. Why use many words? In that age, nothing was more flourishing than Florence. Within it, the best of the arts—all of which had previously fallen into decay—were being reborn; nothing of languages and letters remained untouched that the noble Florentines did not practice. I was then strongly moved by that fame, seized by a desire for that place—not only for the magnificent architecture of your ancestral home (unusual to us from the Hercynian <note>Referring to the Hercynian Forest, a classical term for the wooded mountains of central and southern Germany</note> regions), which they named for the Great Cosimo, but also by a longing to see your father, from whom such great benefits have come to our century.

Therefore, having set out for Italy with the illustrious Eberhard the Bearded <note>Eberhard I (1445–1496), the first Duke of Württemberg, whom Reuchlin served as a counselor</note>, the first Duke of the Swabians in our time, to whom I served as Secretary, I entered Florence around the 21st of March <note>original: "xii. Kalend. Apriles"</note>, in the Year of Christ 1482. And when I had commended the distinguished nobility of the Medici family to that Duke, as indeed I was bound to do by the truth of the matter, he desired to have a conversation with that man [Lorenzo]. When Lorenzo noticed this (revealed by I know not whom), he took the foreigner’s right hand most graciously and led us all to his home, showing us every single thing worthy of sight. First, the most skillfully built stables for horses; then the armory filled with every preparation for war; then each chamber decorated with most precious hangings and beautiful carpets; and, on the high roof of the building, a grove planted with trees, like the Gardens of the Hesperides with golden apples. When I praised his Library to the heavens with my words, that sweetest man responded most graciously (as was his custom) that he possessed a greater treasure in his children than in his books.

I beg you, Most Holy Pope, allow me, a man from the lowest rank of the common people, to speak somewhat more freely with you. With what great admiration and joy do you think I was seized when, amid universal applause, I heard that you—the best son of the best and wisest Prince, the divine Lorenzo de' Medici—had ascended to the highest peak of affairs? I suddenly remembered, like some hierophant <note>A priest or interpreter of sacred mysteries</note>, that paternal prediction which was truly like a prophecy. What could sprout from this Laurel <note>A pun on "Laurentius" (Lorenzo) and "Laurus" (Laurel)</note> that would be more precious, not only to the people of Laurentum but to the whole world? What greater treasure could be imagined than your ineffable reign, from which all riches flow to us as if from the depths of the Pactolus <note>A river in modern-day Turkey, famous in antiquity for being the source of King Croesus's gold</note>, <margin>◦</margin> along with all graces, all ornaments of the best literature, and everything that is good in human affairs? 

Your father sowed the seeds of all ancient philosophy, which now, with you as his son, rise into stalks, so that during your reign we may reap the ears of grain in all languages: Greek, Latin, Hebrew, Arabic, and Aramaic <note>original: "Chaldaïca & Chaldiaca" — referring to the languages of the Near East</note>, in which these books are now offered to your Majesty. Everything begun so prudently by your father is being brought to a more fruitful completion under your rule. Therefore, considering that only the Pythagorean teachings were missing for scholars—which nevertheless are found scattered in the aca... <note>catchword: "demia" (academy)</note>

He frames Pope Leo X’s papacy as the fulfillment of a "prophecy" and the harvest of the intellectual seeds sown by his father.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes the formal dedication to Pope Leo X and transitions into the narrative of the dialogue. Reuchlin (as Capnion) positions himself as the German counterpart to the great Italian and French humanists, using the "Cabalistic art" to recover the lost wisdom of Pythagoras.</meta>

# BOOK ONE.

<margin>A</margin>...hidden in the Laurentian Academy <note>The library of the Medici family in Florence</note>, I believed it would not be unwelcome to you if I also brought into the public forum those things which Pythagoras and the noble Pythagoreans are said to have thought, so that they might be read under your auspicious favor, having been unknown to the Latin world until now. For the Italians, Marsilio Ficino published Plato; for the French, Jacques Lefèvre d’Étaples restored Aristotle. I, Capnion <note>Reuchlin’s humanist name, a Greek translation of his German name "Reuchlin," meaning "little smoke"</note>, will complete the number, and I shall present to the Germans Pythagoras, reborn through me and dedicated to your name. However, this could not be done without the Cabala of the Hebrews, because the philosophy of Pythagoras
<margin>B</margin>took its beginnings from the precepts of the Cabalists; when it departed from the memory of the fathers in Great Greece <note>Magna Graecia, the Greek-settled areas of Southern Italy</note>, it rested again in the volumes of the Cabalists. Therefore, almost everything had to be unearthed from there. For this reason, I have written *On the Cabalistic Art*, which is a symbolic philosophy, so that the dogmas of the Pythagoreans might become better known to students. In all these things I affirm nothing, but merely recount the opinions of the non-believers <note>original: "infideles." Reuchlin uses this term for the three non-Christian characters of his dialogue</note> who, arriving from different journeys, meet in an inn in Frankfurt to hear Simon the Jew, an expert in Cabala: Philolaus the younger, a Pythagorean, and Marranus the Muslim. Now indeed, having dropped their small packs at the inn, the travelers, desiring to ward off hunger, are repelled by the tumultuous crowd of banqueters; but after those people leave the tavern after their feast, it began thus:

<margin>C</margin>**MARRANUS.** I restrained myself from many words amidst such a murmur of the local fellow-diners, who, having enjoyed too much lunch, are now leaving. I feared I would be ill-regarded if I, a foreigner, had interrupted the shouting of those whom I know to be weighed down by destructive drunkenness. But after they have departed, and we alone meet in this tavern as before—both of us, as can be seen, travelers and not a little tired from the journey—I pray you, if you agree with me, ask the innkeeper to bring the second course and sweets—not at all Sybaritic <note>Luxurious or decadent, after the ancient city of Sybaris</note>—since we may now live and talk more freely. But look, the servers are approaching, bringing I know not what treats with nuts and cheese—would that it were Bithynian <note>A type of cheese from Turkey praised by ancient writers like Pliny</note>—and a vessel, uncertain whether for beer or wine, though we have suggested nothing of all this. Then **PHILOLAUS**, with no small skill, says: This merchant plays the innkeeper like one who sets snares everywhere for coins; he even provides "long-eared" service <note>meaning attentive or spying</note> to the guests so that he might sell more wine to those eager to guzzle. For as soon as the talk turns to sweets, the dishes are ready. Now indeed, amidst respectable cups, I hope we shall have a more relaxed fellowship. For in my opinion, my fellow guest, each of us must take on a new countenance, and rest must be provided for our weary limbs—especially for me, after a road too long and rough, and the hard paths I have measured out until now. What remains for you, I know not, since I have not yet been informed about your pilgrimage...

“...from how far away? Or who are you, or where have you come from?” “From Byzantium,” he replied, “the city of Constantine, which many call the New Rome. For I am
<margin>A</margin> a Byzantine by birth, varied in my studies—whether you prefer Greek, or Hebrew, or rather Latin—yet being more skilled in the doctrine of the Arabs. And unless it is a bother, do not refuse in turn to indicate who you yourself are.” “They call me Philolaus,” the other said, “an Alan by nationality <note>The Alans were an Iranian nomadic people; here, Philolaus represents the "outsider" seeking ancient wisdom</note>, a Pythagorean by training, and perhaps a talkative fellow not unlike yourself. But what, I ask, is your name?”
<margin>B <gloss>g/ concise [unclear: Jufsans] prepuce +</gloss></margin> “The people of Constantinople call me Marranus,” he said, “a name known to scholars from Cerinthus and Ebion <note>Cerinthus and Ebion were early Christian figures often labeled as heretics for maintaining Jewish practices; Reuchlin uses them to explain Marranus’s hybrid identity</note>, because I am both dipped in water <note>baptized</note> and circumcised <note>original: recutitus - a Latin term for circumcision</note>. In other respects, I have been initiated into both the laws of Moses and the doctrine of the Christians. You mention scholars?” Philolaus replied to this, “I ask then: are there schools of humanity <note>the liberal arts</note> in Constantinople now, among those most cruel and savage Turks?” “Very many,” he said, “to which men of the most excellent talents have dedicated themselves. For there are more than ten thousand students there, from Persia, Greece, Latium <note>Italy</note>, and Judaism, all within one set of walls. Since I have been a student of many arts there for eighteen years, I finally decided to travel elsewhere, to see if perhaps even across the Alps I might find those endowed with a zeal for wisdom who are able to discourse copiously and plausibly on the greatest questions.” Then Philolaus asked what kind of philosophy he sought. Marranus replied, “Any kind, since I am bound by the laws of no single discipline; thus, I am not prohibited from defending whatever I feel, even within a sect of faith.” “Certainly you have a desire for exploration equal to my own,” Philolaus said, “as I see. For I joined myself as a companion to merchants migrating from Thrace to this
<margin>C <gloss>The Cabalistic art</gloss></margin> noble German market-town of Frankfurt, because I heard there was a Jew here of great fame in Cabalistic work and of enormous reputation. Many most learned men in my presence have judged this single faculty—overflowing as it is with sweet leisure and the richest counsels—to be more closely related than all others to the Pythagorean philosophy, as if nothing were more similar. For they say that Pythagoras fished out almost all his dogmas from that source. They say that Jew’s name is Simon, the son of Eleazar, from the ancient lineage of the Yochaites <note>Refers to the family of Shimon bar Yochai, the traditional author of the Zohar</note>, whom I am now determined to approach once the tables are cleared <note>i.e., after the meal</note>.” “Indeed,” said Marranus, “if you permit it, I will approach the man with you, even though I am little instructed in Pythagorean matters. For the Arabs have always been more held in veneration by me: Al-Ghazali, Al-Farabi, Abu-Katen, Hali, Abu-Maron, Ibn Sina—whom the Latins call Avicenna—and Ibn Rushd—whom they call Averroes—and the rest of the similar Peripatetics <note>Aristotelian philosophers</note>. Although in my time in Constantinople, no one was ever denied the opportunity to pursue any kind of philosophy of almost all languages and sects, especially...”

...with teachers from different nations teaching publicly every day. Then Philolaus said, “Have confidence, for he easily becomes a Pythagorean who both willingly believes the word, and knows how to be silent for a time <note>Silence was a core requirement for students in the Pythagorean tradition</note>, and understands all precepts intellectually.” But the other <note>Marranus</note> replied, “I will at least stand by where you allow me, like some Pythagorean, and I will listen to what the talk between you is about. Thus you will make me drenched in inexpressible joy, when I shall have esteemed it a great thing to have been in the company of wise men.” And Alanus said: <margin>Alanus</margin> “Let us go, for he is said to be walking alone now in the orchard of his house where he lives; and certainly he is in this place, and the door is open. Do you not see him coming from the garden toward us? Come, let us enter more quickly. Greetings, teacher.” To whom Simon, according to the custom of his people, replied: <margin>Simon</margin> “The Lord be with you.” <note>original: "Dominus uobiscum," a Latin rendering of the Hebrew greeting "Shalom Aleichem"</note> “Are you that Simon the Jew?” the newcomers ask. Then he said, “Both, for I am both a Jew and Simon. But what names shall I take for both of you, so that I may address you more correctly?” <margin>Marranus</margin> Each replied to this. “I am Philolaus,” and “I am Marranus,” they answered. “And traveling by different routes, each unaware of the other, we have finally come together here after a long pilgrimage. It was not this marketplace <note>referring to Frankfurt</note>, looming so widely with such great commerce, celebrated throughout nearly all of Europe, nor the famous fairs with so many precious goods, nor the beautiful gathering of so many different nations that drew us to its contemplation. Rather, the fame of you alone led us here, <margin>Kabbalah</margin> with such a desire that you might briefly and conveniently open up your noble thoughts—highly praised in Scythia as well as Thracia <note>Ancient names for regions in Eastern Europe and the Balkans</note>—concerning the whole system of Kabbalah <term>Kabbalah: derived from the Hebrew word for 'received tradition,' referring to Jewish mystical and esoteric philosophy</term>, which, as it seems to the learned, is both to be greatly cultivated and sought after.” To this, he said: “Is there, Simon, a memory of us even among the Scythians and Thracians, such distant peoples?” “There is indeed,” he said, “among both, and it is very great. For about three years ago, about twenty years <note>original: "quatuor lustra," a lustrum being a five-year period</note> after your people <margin>B</margin> reckoned five thousand two hundred and thirty-eight years from the beginning of the world <note>The year 5238 in the Hebrew calendar corresponds to 1478 CE; adding the "four lustra" brings the narrative setting to roughly 1498–1500 CE</note>, one hundred and twenty-four thousand Jews were expelled from Spain. From there, the greatest part of them, as exiles, set out for our regions in various ways. They spoke much of you—a man very well known to them, as they affirm—noting your mastery of the arts, your great learning, your incredible sharpness of wit, and the ready integrity of your philosophical speech. <margin>D Kabbalah</margin> They especially praised your divine skill in Kabbalistic speculation, which they declare is admirable to all listeners; so much so that in the eyes of all who are eager to learn, you shine even beyond the Sarmatians <note>Ancient nomadic peoples of the northern Black Sea region</note> and the frozen Ocean.” At this, he replied: “Such a great estimation of me, you Pythagorean men, brings me no small blush of shame. I fear that if I frustrate or fail this judgment of yours, which was conceived from popular rumor—however much that might happen through my own fragility—I myself would seem to have committed a regrettable injury against such a divine study of Kabbalah through my own laziness...”

For they say that Pythagoras fished out almost all his dogmas from that source <note>Reuchlin’s central thesis was that Greek philosophy originated from ancient Hebrew wisdom</note>."

'I, indeed,' said Marranus, 'if you permit, will go with you to the man myself, although I am little schooled in Pythagorean matters; for the Arabs have always been more held in veneration by me: al-Ghazali, al-Farabi, Abucaten, Hali, Abumaron, Ibn Sina (whom the Latins call Avicenna) and Ibn Rushd (whom they call Averroes), and the rest of the similar Peripatetics <note>Philosophers following the tradition of Aristotle</note>. Although in my time it was never denied to anyone in Constantinople to pursue any kind of philosophy of almost every language and sect, especially...

Therefore, man was born for this, and nature shaped and formed him for this: so that he might walk upon the earth with his feet like the beasts, yet alone of all living things, he might converse in heaven with the angels with his head held high. Furthermore, his two hands, placed between his feet and his head, he may either fix upon the earth for necessary sustenance through labor, or lift toward heaven for eternal life through contemplation. For the protection of these hands, the orbs of the eyes—the only instruments of the senses given to man that are movable—were granted, so that they might look toward the earth for the health of the body, and toward heaven for the health of the soul. Such is the aptitude and power of man, this faculty, this potential, which neither God nor nature would have implanted unless the faculty were intended for use and the potential eventually brought into action, especially in a diligent man <margin>L</margin> preparing himself for this purpose. For if that grasp of divinity were not possible for man, nature would have implanted that desire in vain; for an agile and capable man is never satisfied by the senses of the body or the crude touch of materials, but is carried forward by every thought toward the purity of separate things and the knowledge of the highest matters. This is clearly the restlessness of all scholars, in whom a powerful application of the mind arises through moral, natural, and mathematical truths toward the arrangement of supernatural things, and finally a faithful ascent to the first being is granted.

</margin>
For example: you see a most bright fire burning in the distance; its form is projected through the clear medium—which the Greeks call the **transparent medium** <note>original Greek: diaphanon</note>—all the way to the physical eye. Within, the spiritual vision waits and perceives the form of the object presented to be its own; therefore, it gladly receives it as a relative and neighbor, and through the medium of appearance—which you call **imagination** <note>original: phantasia</note>—presents it spiritually to the sensory and animal judgment. This image is then brought up to human judgment, and a little higher, the whole matter is promoted to reason itself. Then, at last, after a swift discourse, reason transfers that abstraction of physical fire—now so refined and sifted—to the **intellect** <margin>M</margin>. In this ascent, therefore, three regions are found, and in each one, a state of abstraction. In the first region: the object, the transparent medium, the external sense—and there it stops. In the second: the internal sense, imagination, animal judgment—and it stops a second time. In the third: human judgment, reason, intellect—and it stops a third time. The mind, mistress of all these, having received the higher light, illuminates and perfects the human intellect. What else should we think the Cabalists were teaching regarding the **Intellect, Sandalphon, and Metatron**? <note>original: Sechel (Intellect), Sandalphon, and Mettattron. ### BOOK ONE. V

...the soul <note>Latin: *anima*, referring here to the basic life force shared with animals</note> ceases, and reason begins, from which he is named "man." In the third stage, the intellectual power ceases and the **mind** <note>Latin: *mens*, the highest spiritual faculty</note> begins, which alone, without controversy, <margin>N</margin> arrives from the outside, by which he is named "God," according to the oracle: *I have said, you are gods.* <note>Psalm 82:6</note> Therefore, the names of the static states are sense, judgment, and intellect. However, the mediums in the intervals that carry the species <note>The "forms" or mental images of things</note> are the transparent medium, imagination, and reason. Regarding this matter, the Cabalists of the **Merkabah** <note>original: *Merçaua*; the "Chariot" tradition of Jewish mysticism</note> put forward something not dissimilar: the three fathers, who are **Abraham** the superior, **Isaac** <note>original: *Is-hac*</note> the inferior, and **Jacob** the middle. Therefore, since the two intervals of the three regions—sense and judgment—are doubled according to the lower and the upper, and both are reduced to two boundaries, <margin>O</margin> there remain ten steps of the scale through which we can ascend from the bottom to the highest toward the knowledge of all things that truly exist, whether by sense, science, or faith. Concerning this, Abraham the Cabalist <note>The patriarch Abraham was traditionally credited with writing the *Sefer Yetzirah*</note> says thus in that marvelous book, **Yetzirah** <note>original: *Ietzira*; The "Book of Formation," a foundational Cabalistic text</note>:

**Ten sefirot of nothingness, ten and not nine, ten and not eleven. Understand with wisdom and be wise with understanding; examine them and investigate them, and set the matter upon its clarity, and restore the Creator to His throne.** <note>original Hebrew: *Eser sephirot belimah, velo tesha velo achad-asar...*</note> 

This means there are ten numerations beyond the "what," <note>Referring to the *Sefirot* as metaphysical categories rather than physical things</note> ten and not nine, ten and not eleven. Understand in wisdom and be wise in understanding, investigate them, and prove from them, and establish the matter upon its purities, and replace the Creator upon his throne; thus far the text. For the human intellect understands those things which are above in wisdom, and is wise in those things which are below in understanding. And the exterior sense establishes the matter offered by the object through its "species," and the interior sense establishes the matter upon its purities—that is, the abstractions of the species which were previously peculiar to the transparent medium and finally to the imagination. Then judgment, between imagination and reason, should investigate from those same appearances, and reason, through various discourse and conclusion, proves within them. Then I believe at the beginning, and I say that the intellect restores the Creator, as the first cause of all causes, upon His throne, which is the mind itself, the **Active Intellect** <note>original Hebrew: *Sekhel HaPoel*; the Aristotelian concept of the "intellect that acts" to make knowledge possible</note>. You have therefore, most skillful men, the ten numerations by which the apprehension of things happens to man: which are the object, the transparent medium, the exterior sense, the interior sense, the imagination, the lower judgment, the upper judgment, reason, and intellect; and all these <margin>P</margin> are not so much a "what" as a "by what." 

But the supreme **mind** in man is something else entirely. Wherefore, just as God is in the world, so the mind in man bears the **Diadem** <note>The crown</note> among the ten **Sefirot** <note>original: *Sephiroth*</note> of the kingdom; and it is rightly named **Keter** <note>original Hebrew: *Keter*</note>, that is, the **Crown**, which, as **Aristotle** asserts in the second book of *The Generation of Animals*, is alone divine and alone enters man from the outside. From its received light, the lower virtues are directed and governed **until the intellect, the one who understands, and the thing understood are one and the same.** <note>original Hebrew: *Ad she-ha-sekhel ve-ha-maskil ve-ha-mushal echad*; a famous philosophical formula used by Maimonides to describe divine consciousness</note> Thus the Commentator on the Tree of the Ten Sefirot writes that the masters, regarding the words of the Prophet, *In your light we shall see light,* judged it so: **For by the flow of the intellect which overflowed...** <note>original Hebrew fragment: *Ki be-shefa ha-sekhel asher shafa...*</note>

### BOOK ONE. SECTION V

<margin>P</margin> “From you we understand and are set right.” <note>original Hebrew: *Mimcha naskil ve-nivaser*</note> That is: it is through the influence of the mind which flows from you that we understand and are corrected. I believe it has already been made clear to everyone who has carefully examined the condition of human nature: first, that we are led by a natural desire—or if it is better said, we are drawn—to apprehend the highest and divine things. Second, that we are able to grasp them, so far as is sufficient for our happiness, through diligent effort and according to our own measure and capacity. Nature inclines us toward the one; divinity toward the other. Both are demonstrated artistically by the Cabalists through the figure of **fire**, which tends upward and in a certain way encompasses and laps up everything. Regarding this, Rabbi Joseph Gikatilla <note>original: *Ioseph Castilien.*, a 13th-century Spanish Cabalist</note> says among other things in these words in the second book of the *Garden of the Nut* <term>Hortus Nucis<gloss>*Ginnat Egoz*, a foundational work by Gikatilla exploring the names of God and the nature of the soul</gloss></term>: “Know this: that the intellectual soul infused into man, which represents the supreme form within him, is itself called **fire**.” <note>original Hebrew: *Teda lecha ki nefesh ha-maskilit...*</note> To this they apply that saying of Solomon: *The spirit of man is the lamp of God.* <note>Proverbs 20:27</note>

To speak plainly, however, as both reason proves and the experience of practice confirms, a man must first be instructed in many arts and no small number of human sciences. He must possess industry, readiness, and talent so that his mind becomes accustomed to the contemplation of the separate and simple forms of the higher, intelligible world, until he almost creeps into the very inner sanctuaries of God. Above all, it is proper for us to be educated in ethics and the good morals of prudent men, so that we may avoid the base and follow the honorable. This is what Ecclesiastes warned: *Watch your foot when you go to the house of God.* <note>Ecclesiastes 5:1</note> For Ethan the Ezrahite <note>Traditionally identified as the author of Psalm 89</note> sings thus regarding instruction: *Justice and judgment are the preparation of his throne.* <note>Psalm 89:14</note> In this song, he encompasses not only the works of men, which must be perfected by justice, but also the thoughts of the heart and the words of the mouth, which must be established by right judgment. For this reason, the Cabalists teach with one voice and a similar sentiment: <margin>Q</margin> “Because by following after heart’s desire like fools, the desires for contemplation are brought to nothing.” <note>original Hebrew: *Ki be-himashek achar ha-ta'avah...*</note> That is: by indulging only in lust and desire, as fools do, the desires for speculation are corrupted. 

Therefore, after morals are settled and the mind is purged—to say nothing of the nearly infinite rules of speaking well, whether correctly or truly <margin>R</margin> (which are merely the vestibules and doors of the sciences, but not the sciences themselves)—there will then be a need for mathematics and physics. These encompass innumerable things found everywhere in the volumes of the Arabs, Greeks, and Latins, whether concerning universal number, weight, and measure, or concerning all motion and rest essentially inherent in things, which they call **nature**. For nature is, as Rabbi Judah ben Levi <note>Judah Halevi (c. 1075–1141), author of the Kuzari</note> writes in the book *Al-Khazari* <term>Alcozer<gloss>*The Kuzari*, a famous defense of Judaism written as a dialogue between a rabbi and the King of the Khazars</gloss></term>: <margin>S</margin> “The principle and the cause by which the thing in which it exists rests and moves essentially and not by accident.” <note>original Hebrew: *Hatachala ve-hasiba asher bah yanuach ve-yanua ha-davar...*</note>

That is: **A principle and a cause** through which a thing, in which it resides inherently and not by accident, rests and is moved. <note>Simon is quoting Aristotle’s classic definition of "Nature" from his *Physics*.</note> In this definition, you see how great and of what kind, how many and how unmeasured are the things gathered together, such that nearly everything must be undertaken by us who investigate nature—from the highest heaven to the lowest center of the earth. Whether things stand and subsist by their own strength, or in whatever way they lean upon or happen to things as accidents, the span of a man's life would not suffice to even discover the names of each individual thing, let alone their properties, conditions, powers, behaviors, and operations. This is due to the near infinity of those things we desire to know, the capacity of our rational power, the difficulty of the subjects to be investigated, the fragility of human power, and the multifaceted distraction of our desires. For what? Was it not said to Abraham <margin>Abraham was a distinguished astrologer</margin>: *Look up at the heaven and count the stars if you can*? <note>Genesis 15:5</note> And he himself could not, although in his own time, according to Rambam <note>Rabbi Moses ben Maimon, or Maimonides, the preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher</note>, he was a distinguished astrologer.

<margin>V</margin>
Whence the Cabalists teach: **Everything that is in the heavens, man knows nothing of it** <note>original Hebrew: *Kol mah she-bashamayim lo yada ha-adam davar mimmenno*</note>, except for a very small amount according to the manner of the mathematical sciences or disciplines. By this saying, I am reminded that the ancients erred in many things regarding Mathematics, even those to which they devoted almost their entire lives, as is the custom of scholars. The ancient Abubacher <note>Likely referring to the philosopher Avempace (Ibn Bajja), active in 12th-century Spain</note> records this in his writings, testifying to us, his successors, that even in that age following the time of Aristotle, the mathematical sciences were not fully known. For he says thus: **The mathematical sciences were not perfect in his time.** <note>original Hebrew: *Ki kol limmudim lo nishlemu bi-zemanno*</note> Therefore, since—as Solomon says—*all things are difficult* <note>Ecclesiastes 1:8</note>, and even in natural things (the principles of which are at least known to us, or can be), such as **Matter, Form, and Privation** <note>original Hebrew: *Ha-chomer, ha-tzurah, ha-he-der*. These are the three principles used in Aristotelian physics to explain how things change.</note>, there resides in men such a slowness of apprehension, what shall we think will become of us as we seek to gaze upon those highest types of spiritual causes? For this, there will be a need for abstractions from all lower things, for discourse, reason, and logical speculations, which could easily occupy a man's whole life. For example, it is a matter of no small weight to learn **The Categories** <note>original Hebrew: *Ha-ma'amarot*</note> which we call the *predicaments*, and to speak according to their custom, the "most general genera," which are:

**Substance, quantity, quality, relation, when, where, position, state, action, and passion.** <note>original Hebrew: *Etzem, kammah, eichut, ha-yechas, matay, anah, matzav, lo, po’el, yitpa’el*. <meta>This page continues the discourse of Simon the Jew on the hierarchy of knowledge. # BOOK IV: ON THE ART OF THE KABBALAH

...and they conduct investigations through each of the causes of any given thing, which are: **the Matter, the Form, the Efficient Cause, and the Final Purpose** <note>original Hebrew: *ha-chomer, ha-tzurah, ha-po’el, ve-ha-tachlit*</note>, that is: Matter, form, the agent, and the end. From these, as we gently flatter ourselves, we might hunt the truth of every matter through a certain "evident demonstration," as they say, which they call **a proof** <note>original Hebrew: *mofet*</note>. This involves running from one point to the ultimate other, like racing from the starting gates to the goal, by means of a certain artifice to which they have given the name **syllogism** <note>original Hebrew: *hekkish*, meaning comparison or logical deduction</note>. 

But indeed, our sages have taught us with what cleverness and through what windings the sophisms <note>Arguments that seem true but are actually false or misleading</note> of those men are built—men who usually show off these things more than they actually perform them. They say: **Every syllogism and demonstration is joined together from two premises, the Major and the Minor, in three parts; these are called "terms." One of them is the subject of the inquiry, which is called the Minor Term; the second is the shared part, which is called the Middle Term; and the third is the predicate of the inquiry, which is called the Major Term.** <note>Simon is quoting a standard Hebrew definition of Aristotelian logic</note>

<margin>On the syllogism</margin>
From these comes the **conclusion** <note>original Hebrew: *toledah*, literally "offspring" or "result"</note>. That is: every syllogism and demonstration is composed of two propositions or premises, the major and the minor, according to three small parts which are called "terms." One of these is the subject of the thing sought, and is called the minor extremity. The second part is the participant, and is called the middle term. The third is the predicate of the thing sought, which is named the major extremity. And from these comes the conclusion. 

This is that net, this that hook, the birdlime and the lure, this the bond by which—in their opinion—truth is captured freely. They use it indistinctly, and sometimes in vain, whether concerning things subject to nature (such as **physics**), or things accompanying nature (such as **mathematics**), or things that in a certain way strip away nature (such as **metaphysics** <note>original Greek: *meta ta physika*, literally "after the physics"</note>). 

However, those things which are essentially absolute and separated from nature entirely, and from all matter and motion, we call **theological**. Indeed, these are not subject to those "talkativenesses" and syllogistic whispers. Properly speaking, there is no "science" of these things—as they are immediate truths—but rather a firmer and more powerful knowledge. Aristotle suggests this to us more absolutely in the first volume of those illustrious books he wrote *after* the natural ones [the *Metaphysics*]. He hints that the possession of such knowledge is not human. We see this because it happens rarely, and scarcely to one in thousands; it seems to glide in from the divine rather than being acquired by human effort. Furthermore, it is established in the greatest difficulty because of, I believe, the thin and meager instinct of our intellect from the start. 

Zophar hints at this through a certain figure of speech in the Book of Job: *A man is born as a wild donkey’s colt* <note>Job 11:12; suggesting man is born ignorant and wild</note>. Then there is the lack and defect of natural aptitude, even when aided by convenient instruction. This is because for a long time now, deluded by bad teachers, boys who are not yet prudent are compelled toward "filthy sophisms" at a tender age—having abandoned the study of the best literature. They do this at the persuasion of those whose ears admit nothing except "whether it is this" or "whether it is that," along with their propositions and corollaries. Added to this cause is the over-hasty promotion of students...

# BOOK ONE. VII

...to the higher levels, for those to whom such lofty things should not yet be entrusted, since they have consumed too little "midnight oil" in the study of the liberal arts. For this reason, they often retreat, exhausted by the troublesome labor among so many thorns and thickets, before they have reached the years of venerable old age—indeed, while they are still in the prime of their manhood. Listen, I pray you, to the words of Job:

> Wisdom is found among the ancient, and understanding in a long life. <note>Job 12:12</note>

This is why Rabbi Eleazar was once moved to respond to his master, Yohanan, who had kindly said to him, "Come, I will teach you the **Work of the Chariot** <note>original Latin: *Opus de Mercaua*; Hebrew: *Ma'aseh Merkabah*. This refers to the highest and most secret form of Jewish mysticism, based on Ezekiel’s vision of the Divine Chariot.</note>," that is, concerning the most sublime contemplations. 
<margin>What the Merkabah is</margin>
He replied: **"I have not yet grown old,"** <note>original Hebrew: *Lo zakanti*</note> meaning he had not yet reached a sufficient age. For that wise disciple, a youth of precocious talent, knew that no one is fit or suitable for such sublime and high wisdom except those whose fires of desire have already been stilled and extinguished, and whose youthful heat has cooled; those who, being advanced in years, grow old with a certain natural integrity. For what benefit would old age bring here, unless it added probity and a constant integrity of life? 
<margin>D</margin>
Therefore, I would wish that no one believes those men to be true Theologians—however old they may be or however much they are gifted with contentious talkativeness—who are defiled by any kind of vice: pride, hypocrisy, greed, hatred, envy, and (often hidden under a religious cloak) lust. Such men follow their animal passions and neglect the light of the mind. Solomon agrees with this opinion of mine when he says:

> The perverse man is himself an abomination to God. <note>Proverbs 3:32</note>

This is the man who, turned away from the heights, sinks toward the depths, no matter how much nature may have raised him toward the high things. Your Algazel <note>Abu Hamid al-Ghazali (1058–1111), a major Persian theologian and philosopher.</note>, O Marrano <note>The text addresses "Marrane," likely referring to a specific interlocutor or a "New Christian" of Jewish descent.</note>, that follower of Muhammad, was not ignorant of how these contrary movements of the soul—upward and downward—are most unhappy for a learned man. In his *Book of Divine Science*, he demonstrates that from the conflict of these opposing impressions, the most powerful and fearful torments are created in the soul. Thus, besides vices, secular business also perverts and turns us away: perhaps parents, a wife, children, family property, friends, enemies, accidents, events, and any of the needs of those close to us, which do not allow the strengths of men to ascend to the highest steps of understanding. 

But suppose that for any of you, there is nothing within us to hinder us; imagine our natural talent is happy and favored, and there is not even a shadow of madness or foolishness. Let everything be ready to assist in undertaking the highest matters, so that no one can rightly complain of our fragility. Even so, would not many be deterred from contemplation by that "obscurity of divine things"? It is higher than heaven and deeper than the underworld <note>original Latin: *Tartarus*</note>; it cannot be tracked down by sense or reason. Unlike other sciences, it does not receive light from our studies, but rather brings light with it. It radiates and shines upon worthy men as if from its own storehouse. Yet, it does not prostitute itself everywhere of its own accord as if it were cheap, nor does it offer itself uninvited; rather, it is sought by our will through the human sciences...

### ON THE ART OF THE KABBALAH

...be believed. I return to the point from which I digressed: by the prompting of nature alone, when both [Adam and Eve] were in the world, the man felt that his wife belonged to him; this was not yet **Kabbalah** <note>The speaker is distinguishing between natural instinct/reason and the received mystical tradition known as Kabbalah.</note>. Moreover, it was a mark of singular and sharp intelligence that the **first-formed man** <note>original Latin: *protoplastus*, referring to Adam as the first created human</note> himself, now lord of the world, added a name to each thing by a spontaneous act, so we may know it was a matter of will, not of nature. 

Nor was it without reason that, after the transgression of the law, he dreaded the penalty of death threatened in the warning—which by the guidance of reason he judged would not be corporeal, since he did not feel himself die as soon as he had eaten from the tree. Therefore, according to **Ramban** <note>Rabbi Moses ben Nachman, also known as Nachmanides (1194–1270), a leading medieval Jewish scholar and Kabbalist.</note>, he understood it as "dying in sin," just as we Kabbalists understand it. Now, in all this, what I pray must we think was of divine revelation? Certainly we have found nothing so far that everyone would not hesitate to attribute either to the counsel of reason or the movement of the senses. 

But that so pernicious transgression of the law, such a great insult to God, the Best and Greatest, such hostile rashness, such contagious lust, such a foul, such a poisonous toxic plague and loathsome pestilence, the corrupter of the human race, sitting in the tunnels of the veins and creeping with the very flow of the seed into posterity in a continuous passage—no presumed thought of human fragility could conceive by what path or in what way it could be expiated and turned away. 

<margin>P</margin> Here, I say, here at the point of imminent despair (a disease than which nothing is more destructive), there was need for the effective aid of **divine revelation**. And even then, God the Creator <note>original Latin: *fictor*, literally "the fashioner" or "molder"</note> did not entirely desert His creation, but instilled a certain hope that this very crime, however monstrous and committed against infinite majesty, could nevertheless be abolished, removed, and extinguished over a finite span of time.

<margin>o</margin> He said therefore to the angels in Adam’s hearing: **"And now, lest he put forth his hand, and take also of the tree of life, and live forever"** <note>Genesis 3:22</note>, and the Lord God sent him forth from the **paradise of pleasure**. This was the last voice the wretched man heard from the mouth of God as he was being driven from the garden; yet amidst such sorrows and griefs, he received from it that firm hope toward his Creator that so horrible a sentence might, in the course of time, be made revocable by God’s mercy. 

The words of the oracle indicated this to him, for He said: **"Now"** or **"Already, lest he put forth his hand and take from the tree of life."** <margin>Q</margin> Truly, it was not in vain that God added the word **"now"** or **"already"** <note>original Latin: *nunc uel iam*</note>, by which the present time is designated, suggesting that the sentence would not be perpetual, but that an abolition of it could be obtained in a future time, if ever a man should come destined to eat from the tree of life. 

This was so, although at that time, as long as his spirit ruled his limbs, he suspected he was irrevocably paying the penalty, because God would not be with him the day after next as He was accustomed to speak face to face—which was a clear sign of indignation and of a mind alienated from Adam, as He who previously with each...

### BOOK ONE

# THE FIRST BOOK

Whereas God, the Creator of all things, used to speak with living creatures and beasts, He now deemed it beneath Him to speak face to face with man the sinner. Nevertheless, so that the most merciful Father would not leave him utterly deprived of all consolation, He immediately sent an angel, from whom he might learn more fully of the future restoration of such a great ruin. For so the **Kabbalists** <term>Kabbalists: Practitioners of Jewish mysticism who believe in a secret, oral tradition passed down from antiquity.</term> write in their commentaries on the **Book of Yetzirah** <term>Book of Yetzirah: The *Sefer Yetzirah* or "Book of Formation," one of the earliest and most influential books of Jewish mysticism.</term>: "The teachers of the patriarchs were known angels; specifically, the teacher of Adam himself was **Raziel**." <note>original Hebrew: "שהאבות רבותיהם חיו מלאכים ידועים רבו של אדם רזיאל"</note> <note>Raziel is often depicted in mystical lore as the angel who gave Adam a book of celestial secrets to help him after his expulsion from Eden.</note> This angel, by the will of the supreme God, showed him the way of expiation and explained, in the Kabbalistic manner, that the divine word must be received through **allegory**; for in that word, not only is no single phrasing, but not even a letter—however tiny or thin—nor even a single stroke, placed in vain.

Now I call upon you, **Philolaus**, and you, **Marranus** <note>These are fictionalized characters in the author’s dialogue, representing different philosophical schools (Pythagorean and Christian/Hebrew scholar).</note>—the most learned of all learned men—grant me this indulgence: perhaps religion would have forbidden me from betraying such hidden and secret things to those outside our sect and uninitiated into the Jewish rite. The knowledge of these things (as God loves me!) is often and greatly denied even to our own disciples, so that it is barely possible to find these things even in rare books, unless they are wrapped in coverings and riddles. For thus it is read in the **Talmud**: "The secrets of the Law are not handed over except to a counselor, a wise master of the craftsmen, and one who understands a secret." <note>original Hebrew: "אין מוסרים סתרי תורה אלא ליועץ וחכם חרשים ונבון לחש"</note>

Therefore, shall I say more or remain silent? Both the prohibitions of the masters and the immense ardor of both of you (inflamed, as I believe, by a divine fire) to scrutinize the most profound things make me hesitate quite a bit. But I will boldly be more indulgent with myself and temper the harshness of those precepts; for I see that the light of the sun is dispersed over everyone without discrimination, provided the barrier is removed. I will speak, although quite inelegantly according to the custom of our people, yet as best I can, of those things which I have received as having been spoken by the most learned and wise men and left behind in divinely inspired writings. 

And nonetheless, I will explain a truly most hidden speech held by the Creator of the world with the blessed angels in the innermost chambers of His divinity. For God said: "Behold, **Adam** is like one of us." <note>Genesis 3:22</note> He did not say "of you," but "one of us." For in you angels, there is number and otherness. In "us"—that is, in God—there is an infinite, eternal, most simple, and most absolute unity. Nor can that "one" within the angels, if it exists at all, be like the "One" in God. Therefore, God did not count the angels alongside Himself when speaking of unity, because it is impossible for something to be "one" in nature with both God and angels, so great is the distance between the Creator and the creature.

[...that] the earthly Adam was rejected by God, whom He had formed from clay with His own hands and driven out of the garden. And when He had indicated the person of the future redeemer to the angels, lest they should perhaps think that he would quickly and perfunctorily turn away the hatred of such a wicked crime through some sudden intercession, He immediately removed any doubt and postponed the matter to a later time, adding: "And now, at this present time, lest this my unique one in eternity, who subsists from me, should put forth his hand and take also from the tree of life," implying, of course, that what He prohibited from happening now, He would one day grant. By this they wisely understood that, although not now, yet later, in the course of time, through this Heavenly Adam—who is co-eternal with God—this ruin caused by the fruit of the tree would be repaired.

Therefore, as the Lord of the universe sat upon His throne, all the hosts of heaven standing by Him—as **Micah** says, on the right and on the left <note>A reference to 1 Kings 22:19, where the prophet Micah describes a vision of God’s celestial court.</note>—gave thanks for such great mercy toward the weakness of mortals.

[Kab]balah, the herald of primordial salvation. O pleasing thing, O desirable cause! What could be more beneficial? What more acceptable? What could be brought from the heavens more opportunely for the lost condition of mortals? What help could be <margin>T</margin> provided more suitably than that they should announce the common salvation to the captives? This is 그 holy and supreme revelation into which all divine revelations are reduced; this is the most desired tradition, this is the most healthy reception, in which all Kabbalistic "receptions" are recapitulated—all traditions of the divine, all instructions of the celestial, and the visions of the prophets and the meditations of the blessed are united and communicated.

For this reason, when Adam had openly announced each of these things to his wife, he began, in her presence, to sacrifice to God at an altar erected for the commemoration of posterity and for the giving of thanks. ...[it] should <note>Completing the word "deberet" from the previous page.</note> "Then it was begun to call upon the name of the Lord" <note>original Hebrew: *az huchal likro beshem Adonai* (Genesis 4:26)</note>. These events were either past—as Cain was so called because "I have possessed" <note>The name Cain is linked to the Hebrew word *qanah*, meaning to get or possess</note>; or present—as Enos was called "Man"; or future—as Abel was called because he would bring grief to his parents. Therefore, according to the Kabbalah, he placed his hope in "wood," for as Job says: "For there is hope for a tree" <note>original Hebrew: *ki yesh la-etz tikvah* (Job 14:7)</note>. He was made more certain of this destiny: that life had been promised to man through wood, though confusion followed after his drunkenness. From this also comes the name Babel, which is now Babylon—from *Balbel*, which in the Chaldean language <note>Aramaic</note> means "confusion." This arose among the family and children of Noah. Abel, however, being unarmed, did not resist the armed man, but willingly and gladly offered himself up to death. He was prepared not only to give satisfaction to God the creditor on our behalf, but even to pay the original debt entirely if possible, and to be presented as an acceptable, devoted, and appointed sacrifice in payment. After he had died without children, Adam waited for a long time, hoping perhaps that what he had not found in his sons might happen in his grandsons. But what could he now hope for in the rejected generation of Cain? He saw that this entire line had vanished from all trust; he saw them all devoted to sedentary arts and crafts <note>Reuchlin refers to the "sellulariis artibus," or the trades of Cain's descendants (like Tubal-Cain), which he views as spiritually inferior to the contemplative life</note>, performing their work with a servile zeal, pursuing meager comforts and duties necessary only for the body, thinking nothing of the divine, nothing of the noble, and nothing worthy of a heroic man. For this reason, he sought and obtained another offspring and another seed from God, by which that most pious father was cheered beyond what can be expressed, saying: "God has appointed for me another seed in place of Abel, <margin>X</margin> whom Cain killed." Therefore he called his name Seth, whom he fathered in his own image and likeness—not because his other children did not have a human form and image, for they were also men. But because the generation of the rest until now, except for Abel, was to be called a generation of demons rather than of men, on account of their cursed malice and detestable vices. It is not, therefore, that he had fathered literal demons and devils—as certain impious and profane people lie—but that they were evil by their own will. For nothing is evil except vice and the demonic. I shall proceed, therefore, if you wish, so that I may travel further through the door I have entered. And they replied: "Go on diligently, we beseech you." For this reason, he was called Enos, that is, "Man." At that time it was thought—and indeed greatly hoped—that he would be named according to the angelic Kabbalah through the four-letter name I.H.V.H. <note>The Tetragrammaton, the four-letter name of God</note>, or at least more Kabbalistically in "mercies" through the letter *Shin* placed in the middle of the four letters I.H.V.H. <note>Reuchlin is hinting at the name *Yeheshuah* (Jesus), which Christian Kabbalists formed by placing the letter *Shin* (ש) into the middle of the name of God (יהוה), signifying the Word becoming flesh</note>. ...[would] have <note>This is a fragment of the word "haberet" from the previous page.</note> then it was hoped <note>Hebrew original: *az huchal likro beshem IHVH* (Genesis 4:26)</note> that he would be called by the letter *Shin* from the middle of the name <term>I.H.V.H.</term> <note>The Tetragrammaton, the four-letter sacred name of God. In Christian Kabbalah, inserting the letter 'S' (Shin) into this name was thought to produce the name of Jesus.</note> as if, by an angel's announcement, Enos would take from the tree of life and redeem the world. He was himself named a hero, *I.H.*, in the mercies of *V.H.*—mark the secret and pay attention to the mystery! When, however, he was no longer designated by any angel in this way, they left that hope behind and placed it in another. 

<margin>z</margin>For by the warning of angels—that is, the messengers of God—names were given to the patriarchs based on various events. These were either past, as when Cain was named because of "I have possessed" <note>Derived from the Hebrew *qanah*, referencing Eve's statement: "I have gotten a man from the Lord."</note>; or present, as when Enos was named because of "man" <note>The name *Enosh* in Hebrew implies a mortal, frail human being.</note>; or future, as when Abel was named because he was destined to bring grief to his parents. 

This expectation was drawn out into the fourth generation from Enos, and from Jared was born Enoch, who walked with God but then disappeared because God took him away. Three generations later came Noah, for the public consolation of everyone who had heard and hoped for salvation with right faith; out of the entire population, only eight were found who were pleasing to God. For Noah was a righteous man and perfect in his generations, and he walked with God. He received the command to make an ark of wood in which he might save the world. 

According to the <term>Kabbalah</term> <note>The Jewish mystical tradition of interpreting scripture.</note>, he therefore placed his hope in "the wood" <note>The wood of the Ark is often seen as a symbolic precursor to the wood of the Cross.</note>, for so Job says: "For there is hope for a tree" <note>Hebrew original: *ki yesh la-etz tikvah* (Job 14:7)</note>. He was made certain of this destiny: that the promise to mankind would be found in the "tree of life." But after his drunkenness, confusion followed. From this, the place is also named Babel (which is now Babylon), from *Balbel*, which in the <term>Chaldean</term> <note>An ancient language related to Hebrew; here referring to Aramaic/Babylonian.</note> language means "confusion." This arose under the family and children of Noah. 

His sons were Shem, Ham, and Japheth. Thus, regarding the future servant of God, Shem—in whom Noah hoped for salvation above the others—he blessed him thus: "Blessed be the Lord God of Shem" <note>Hebrew original: *Barukh IHVH Elohei Shem* (Genesis 9:26)</note>. In the Kabbalistic sense, this is translated as: "Blessed by the four letters of God be Shem." By this, the Kabbalists say: "He made it known that Shem would be a servant of God" <note>Hebrew original: *hodia ki IHVH Shem oved ha-Elohim*</note>, as <term>Rabbi Moses of Gerona</term> <note>Also known as Nahmanides or Ramban, a prominent 13th-century scholar and mystic.</note> writes. 

By this we understand that it was the pious father's desire that Shem be blessed with the name of the four letters, *I.H.V.H.*, so that he might become the redeemer of original sin. But even then, the time appointed by God for the repair of such a great fall had not yet come, as the angel Jophiel announced to Shem himself. For so the Kabbalists write: "The teacher of Shem was Jophiel" <note>Hebrew original: *rabo shel Shem Yophiel*</note>. Therefore, those ages suspended their thoughts on such matters until the years of Abraham, son of Terah, who was first named Abram. To this man, there was a certain familiar angel, Zadkiel. For so the Kabbalists write: "The teacher of Abraham was Zadkiel" <note>Hebrew original: *rabo shel Avraham Tzadkiel*</note>, who handed down to him the same Kabbalah that Raziel gave to Adam, the first-formed. Finally, as I judge, the remaining facts are not unknown: how long he had been called Abram, and his wife...

# 118 ON THE KABBALISTIC ART

Sarai and her husband had for a long time never fathered an heir for themselves. But after the husband’s name was changed to Abraham, and the wife’s name to Sarah, they soon received a son, Isaac. Concerning him, when God had commanded that Abraham take his only-begotten son whom he loved, Isaac, and sacrifice him upon the wood on a certain high mountain of Moriah, it seems incredible with what joy and how much gladness he exulted. He was mindful of the divine promise, in which God promised him with these words: "I will establish," He said, "my covenant between me and you, and between your seed after you in their generations for an everlasting covenant, that I may be your God and the God of your seed after you, and in you shall all the families of the earth be blessed." <note>original Latin: "Statuam... pactum meum... fœdere sempiterno..." citing Genesis 17 and 22.</note>

->Therefore, he was confident that he would bring the salvation of the human race, which we have mentioned, in the person of his son.<-
Upon hearing the voice of God, he immediately took him up, and with his own hands he cut all the wood for the offering. Truly, an oracle had taught that the original fall <note>The "original fall" refers to the sin of Adam and Eve in Eden.</note> could be repaired through wood. Hence the Scripture says that Abraham took the wood of the offering, and laid it upon Isaac his son, and placed him on the altar upon the pile of wood, and stretched out his hand and took the sword to sacrifice his son. For if Isaac had not received from his father the <term>Cabala</term> <note>The "Kabbalah" or oral tradition/received secret knowledge.</note> of human salvation passed down through the "wood of life" and the future offering of a certain just man, then—since dying is naturally horrible to all living things—he certainly would not have embraced his seen death so willingly, with such great benevolence and such a cheerful face and joyful spirit. Instead, as is the condition of mortals, he would have either dodged the drawn blade or at least mitigated his father’s severity with some gentle words, or perhaps fled. But suspecting that he himself might be the one through whom the restoration of the primordial ruin <note>The "primordial ruin" refers to the spiritual destruction caused by the Fall of Man.</note> would happen, he considered nothing more pleasant than that sacrifice, and nothing sweeter than that death, for the sake of which he believed the entire human race would be redeemed.

->He surely held this very hope all the more firmly<-
because God had destined that same place for sacrifices since the founding of the world. For the land of Moriah was pointed out to Abraham by the finger of God; it was there that <margin>B</margin> the first Adam built an altar and offered gifts to God, and where Cain and Abel, and where Noah and his sons sacrificed. This is as our Masters dispute in the *Chapters of Rabbi Eliezer*, <note>original: "capitulis Rabi Eliæzer," referring to the *Pirkei De-Rabbi Eliezer*, a midrashic work.</note> supported by <term>Ramban</term> <note>Rabbi Moses ben Nachman, also known as Nachmanides, a major medieval Jewish scholar.</note> and Rabbi Joseph the son of Gikatilla <note>original: "Rabi Ioseph filio Carnitolis," referring to Joseph Gikatilla, author of *Sha'are Orah*.</note> in the book *The Gates of Justice*, and the holy city of Jerusalem was constructed in that same place, as Solomon the Gaul <note>original: "Salomone Gallo," likely referring to Rashi (Rabbi Shlomo Itzhaki), who lived in what is now France (Gaul).</note> testifies. But the matter being left unfinished, when the father and son departed from Moriah, the voice of <term>Zadkiel</term> <note>The Archangel Zadkiel, often associated with mercy and the angel who stayed Abraham's hand.</note> was heard, spoken to Abraham: "In your seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed." By this, it was recognized that universal salvation was prolonged <margin>A</margin> into a future generation. And the voice of God itself, through the angel <term>Raphael</term>, <note>The Archangel Raphael, whose name means "God heals."</note> fell from heaven upon Isaac also: "In your seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed," lest perhaps he should believe himself to be that savior. For this also belongs to the Kabbalists, who write thus:

# XIII
## BOOK ONE

**The teacher of Isaac was Raphael** <note>original Hebrew: רבו של יצחק רפאל</note>, that is, the teacher of Isaac himself was Raphael. There was no hope for another of his sons, who had already lost his father's blessing through his habit of hunting; his name was Esau. Regarding the other son, the father promised great things for himself and foretold the future with these words, which offered a prophecy of things to come:
<margin>C</margin>
**Peoples shall serve you, and nations shall adore you.** Therefore, it was not without reason that such a great expectation of universal salvation was placed upon Jacob (for so that son was called) by our ancestors. It was because he was the first of all mortals to see the gate of heaven opened, and a ladder stretching from earth to heaven, and upon it standing the four letters **i . h . u . h .** <note>These letters—Yod, He, Vav, He—form the Tetragrammaton, the sacred and unpronounceable name of God.</note> which he carried in his prayers to grasp. To this work he added the consonant **Sin** [ש], designating **Oil** <note>original Hebrew: שמן (Shemen)</note> through the method of <term>Notariacon</term> <note>A Kabbalistic system of shorthand or acrostics where single letters represent whole words.</note>, with which he anointed the stone he built into a certain temple named Bethel. Suspicion grew because the angel Peliel was an intimate of Jacob, who forewarned him of many things through constant
<margin>H</margin>
opinion and speech; both because God chose Jacob for Himself, and because "blessed is he whose help is the God of Jacob." The <term>Kabbalists</term> <note>Scholars of Jewish mysticism.</note> write it thus: **The teacher of Jacob was Peliel** <note>original Hebrew: רבו של יעקב פליאל</note>, that is, the Teacher of Jacob was Peliel. But having been well-instructed by his angel, Jacob realized that he himself would not be that Savior whom the heavenly Kabbalah had hitherto put forward. He deferred the matter to another age through divine revelation, saying: "Gather yourselves together, and I will tell you
<margin>D</margin>
what shall happen in the last days. The scepter shall not be taken from Judah, nor a lawgiver from between his feet, until **Shiloh** comes, and unto him shall the gathering of the nations be." By this prophecy, it became known that someone would eventually be the savior of the human race, who would be born both from the line of Judah and in the final days; he would be "Shiloh," he would carry the scepter of the kingdom, and the nations would flock to him.

Therefore, after these patriarchs, the great Moses did not offer himself to death of his own accord, as Abel once did, or as Isaac did long ago. Instead, he refused, and wished to withdraw himself from the care of the people, even though he spoke with God as a friend speaks with a friend, face to face, and he used a staff as a scepter, and the entire nation of the Jews flocked to him. However, he knew that he was not from the family of Judah, but was born from the house of Levi; nor was he born in the final days, nor was he **Shiloh**, which—according to the Syriac translation of Onkelos the Chaldean <note>Onkelos was a famous translator of the Torah into Aramaic (Chaldean) in the 2nd century AD.</note>—signifies the **Anointed One**, whom we call the **Messiah**. Nevertheless, concerning every reason and
<margin>E</margin>
method for restoring the state of the original fall, he was more than sufficiently instructed by his angel **Metatron**. For the Kabbalists write thus: **The teacher of Moses was Metatron** <note>original Hebrew: רבו של משה מטטרון</note>, who is the messenger of **Shaddai** <note>Sadai/Shaddai is a name for God, often translated as "The Almighty." Metatron is a high-ranking angel in mystical tradition.</note>.

And so, the community of prophets accepted this revelation of the most holy Jacob: that in the final days, one shall be born
<margin>F</margin>
from the seed of Judah who is to abolish original sin—the Messiah, the King of Peace—at the time when the scepter and the leadership of Judah cease, and the nations are called together from everywhere. Thus far reaches the "reception" <note>The word "Kabbalah" literally means "reception" or "tradition."</note> from the fathers to the college of prophets.

# XIX
## ON THE KABBALISTIC ART

...[the knowledge] of the prophets passed through a succession, as they all, one by one, conferred among themselves in daily discussion regarding the golden age of the Messiah. In 
<margin>G</margin>
that blessed school of the Holy Spirit, they exulted with the highest joy, bringing forth their gladness from the depths of their hearts. They were joined by a single bond of fellowship in that same Messiah and Savior, for though they spoke at different times about that same coming King in many and various ways, yet each one arrived at an equal and clearly similar conclusion. This one indeed spoke in these words:
> *I beseech you, Lord: send him whom you are going to send,* <note>original Latin: "Obſecro Domine: mitte quem miſſurus es." A quote from Exodus 4:13.</note>
another, speaking in the person of the Messiah, says:
> *Send me,*
this is *shlach* <note>original Hebrew: שלח (Sh-L-H), meaning "send."</note> which in <term>arithmetical progression</term> <note>Referring to Gematria, the Kabbalistic practice of calculating the numerical value of Hebrew letters to find hidden meanings.</note>—through the ingenious method of the <term>Kabbalah</term>—signifies both the four-letter dignity of excellence <note>The Tetragrammaton, the four-letter name of God, Y-H-V-H.</note> and also, according to the tradition of Raziel <note>The *Sefer Raziel HaMalakh*, a famous grimoire of Kabbalistic secrets attributed to the angel Raziel.</note> mentioned above, the proper name of that Messiah itself. This is revealed through the numerical equality of **three hundred and ninety-eight.** 
<margin>H</margin>
And again:
> *O that you would rend the heavens and come down!*
Another said:
> *Stir up your power and come to save us; turn us back, O God, and show your face, and we shall be saved.*
Another:
> *I will wait for God my savior.*
Another:
> *Behold, the Lord will come out of his place and descend.*
Another:
> *He will subdue our iniquities and cast all our sins into the depths of the sea.*
Another:
> *He who is coming will come and will not delay; you went forth for the salvation of your people, for salvation with your Messiah.*
Another, who consoled our nation, said:
> *The Lord has taken away your judgment. The King of Israel—signified by the four letters—will be in your midst; you shall see evil no more. The Lord your God in your midst will be strong; he himself will save.*
Another, who promised in the person of the Messiah:
> *And it shall be that as you were a curse among the nations, O house of Judah and house of Israel, so I will save you and you shall be a blessing... and they shall be as they were when I had not cast them off.*
And another thus:
> *Unto you who fear my name shall the sun of righteousness arise.*
Why do I linger over many examples? All rejoice with one heart, all speak all good things with one mouth, and all praise that day of this Savior. They long for that time about which David cried out before God:
> *Send out your light and your truth; they shall lead me and bring me to your holy mountain and into your dwellings.*
Concerning that word "light," **Rabbi Solomon of France** <note>original: "Rabi Salomon Gallus." Better known as Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval commentator on the Torah and Talmud.</note> said: "Your light" refers to the King Messiah, 
<margin>I</margin>
according to what is written:
> *I have prepared a lamp for my Messiah.*
From this we are made certain that David was led by no personal pride to believe that he himself was that same King Messiah who would reconcile the human race to God, even though the divine oracle had declared:
> *I have found David my servant, with my holy oil I have anointed him,*
because the "Anointed One" is called the Messiah. [God said:] *And I will make him my firstborn, higher than the kings of the earth. I will keep my mercy for him forever, and my covenant shall stand faithful with him; and I will establish [his offspring] forever.*

...his seed forever, and his throne as the days of heaven. <note>original Latin: "seculi semen eius, & sedem eius sicut dies cœlorum." <margin>L</margin>
*In his days, there shall be an abundance of peace, until the moon is taken away.* <note>Psalm 72:7.</note> Therefore, it had to be understood as referring to another of his descendants rather than the son of Bathsheba; for that Solomon loved many women, through whom his heart was led astray so that he followed strange gods, and his heart was not perfect with the Lord his God like the heart of David his father. > At the beginning of the creation of the world, the **Divine Presence** <note>Hebrew: *Shekhinah* (שכינה), the indwelling presence of God on earth.</note> lived among those below. While the Divine Presence was below, heaven and earth were found to be united, and the springs and channels functioned in perfection, flowing from above to below. Thus the Name (blessed be He) was found filling both above and below. Then the first man, **Adam**, came and sinned; the orderly rows were corrupted, the channels were broken, the pool ceased, the Divine Presence withdrew, and the bond was severed. Afterward, Solomon came and built the House <note>The Temple.</note>, and then the rows and the channels returned...

<margin>N</margin>
...that is, "In the beginning of the creation of the world, the divine habitation was descending into the lower things, and when the divine habitation was below, the heavens and earth were found united, and the springs and channels were active in perfection, and were drawn from the higher to the lower, and God was found filling things above and below. 

<margin>O</margin>
The first Adam came and sinned, and the descents were torn down, the channels were shattered, the aqueduct failed, the divine habitation ceased, and the fellowship was divided. Afterwards Solomon came and built the house, and then the channels returned, along with the derivations, or conduits, and the rest." Where the Kabbalists, speaking of Solomon, seem to allude to the reality rather than the name, since they understand it as referring to a certain coming **King of Peace**, according to the words of **Isaiah**, whom the worker of miracles himself shall name: *Counselor, Mighty God, Father of the future age,* **Prince of Peace** <note>original Hebrew: שר שלום (*Sar Shalom*).
