# XIII
## BOOK ONE

...moving daily wars and battles within the souls of men, because our parents sinned, as Jeremiah wrote in the Book of Lamentations: *Our fathers sinned and are no more, and we have borne their iniquities.* <note>Lamentations 5:7</note>. So indeed it could have seemed to Jonathan the Chaldean <note>The author of the Aramaic paraphrase (Targum) of the Prophets.</note>, who, in the place mentioned above, translated **Prince of Peace** <note>original Hebrew: *Sar Shalom*</note> as the *Messiah of Peace.* <note>original Aramaic: *Messiha de-Shalma*</note>.

<margin>L</margin>
Regarding him, Isaiah says again: *The punishment of our peace was upon him, and by his bruises and wounds we are healed.* <note>Isaiah 53:5</note>. This will be that true **Solomon** who will erect a much more sublime temple, one that is clearly everlasting and indestructible. For so the **Kabbalists** write: *Because the house of the sanctuary which is below is arranged over against the house of the sanctuary which is above.* <note>original Hebrew: *Ki beit ha-mikdash shel mata mechuvan kineged beit ha-mikdash shel ma'ala*</note>. This means the earthly sanctuary is built to correspond to a heavenly, spiritual reality.

From Solomon, the founder of that earthly temple, down to King Jehoiachin (who is the same as Jeconiah—for both names contain the same letters, though rearranged), 

<margin>M</margin>
the expectation of universal salvation was placed in the coming **Messiah** among the whole assembly of prophets, from Isaiah down to Malachi, who said: *The Ruler whom you seek shall suddenly come to his temple.* <note>Malachi 3:1</note>. Regarding this, **Rabbi David Kimhi** <note>A famous medieval Hebrew grammarian and biblical commentator (1160–1235).</note> writes that this "Ruler" is the Messiah, who will himself be the messenger of the covenant, and whom Jonathan the Chaldean interprets as *Rabona* <note>An Aramaic title meaning "Our Master."</note>.

After the Prophets, the expectation of the Messiah’s life-giving arrival and the whole **Kabbalistic** practice—which they rightly gather, entwine, and lead back toward the eternal liberation brought by that same Messiah—descended entirely to the Scribes of the Law and the Elders. These they called the "Heads of the Fathers," who are too numerous to count. 

<margin>N</margin>
The tradition then passed to the men of the **Great Assembly** <note>The *Anshei Knesset HaGedolah*, a council of 120 elders including the last prophets and early scholars who led the Jewish people after the Babylonian exile.</note>, received successively in the manner of the schools, starting from **Ezra** <note>The priest and scribe who led the return to Jerusalem.</note>, who handed down the **Kabbalah** to **Simeon the Just**, the high priest and head of the synagogue. 

<margin>O</margin>
In turn, it was received from him by his student **Antigonus** and his associates, among whom were **Zadok** and **Boethus**, the root of the heretics, from whom the **Sadducees** and **Boethusians** were named, as **Judah the Levite** <note>Judah Halevi (c. 1075–1141), a famous Jewish philosopher and poet.</note> writes in the third discourse of his book *The Kuzari* <note>original: *Alcosder*</note>. Then it passed to **Joseph son of Joezer** and **Joseph son of Johanan** of Jerusalem; from them to **Joshua son of Perahiah**, who had a certain disciple named **Jesus the Nazarene** in the time of the Maccabees (not the one belonging to the Christians). And also to **Nittai of Arbela**, from whom it went to **Judah son of Tabbai** and **Simeon son of Shetah**, and from them to **Shemaiah** and **Abtalion**. From these it reached **Hillel** and **Shammai**, who had many thousands of disciples. From them it came to **Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai**, who nurtured five specific disciples: **Eliezer** (whom they write as Eliezer son of Hyrcanus), **Joshua son of Hananiah**, **Yose the Priest**, **Simeon son of Nathanael**, and **Eleazar son of Arach**. From Rabban Yohanan, who lived one hundred and twenty years, was obtained...

## XV

Rabban Gamaliel received his **Kabbalah** <note>The Hebrew word for "tradition" or "that which is received."</note>, from whom came his son Simeon, and from his children came Judah Nagid <note>Judah the Prince, the compiler of the Mishnah.</note>, who is called "Our Holy Teacher." His son Gamaliel followed him by receiving the same tradition. Thus far, these were the "Kabbalists" <note>original: *Cabalæi*</note> whose sayings and other allegorical expositions of Holy Scripture were followed by the assembly of Kabbalists: Hanania son of Asasia, Abba Saul, Rabbi Tarphon, Akavia son of Mahalalel, Hanania the prince of priests, Hanina son of Teradion, Hanania son of Hachinai, Nehunia son of Hakanah, Halafta, Duscha son of Jannai, Hanina son of Dosa, Dosa son of Archinas, Rabbi Akiba, Eleazar son of Azariah, and Eleazar Hasma. Then Rab Levita, Rabbi Johanan son of Baroka, and after him Simeon from among the children. Then Tzadok, then Jose; he was followed by Ishmael, and from another lineage Rabbi Meir, from whom received Eleazar son of Jacob, Johanan the Sandal-maker, and Eleazar son of Shammua.

<margin>P</margin>
Then came Nehorai, after whom were Jannai, Mattathiah, and Samuel the Lesser, Elissah son of Abuiah, Eleazar of Kaphar, Judah son of Tema, and Joshua son of Levi. Besides these, there were many others who are sometimes called **Tannaim** <note>original: *Thanaim*, from the Hebrew word for "repeaters" or "teachers."</note> or "dictators" because of their Talmudic disputations. Because of their meditations on the highest things—drawn from individual lower things toward the more sublime, received from their elders, and passed to posterity—those who lean upon these studies with all their zeal are called **Mekablim** in Hebrew <note>The Receivers</note>. In our own age, following the lead of Giovanni Pico, Count of Mirandola <note>A famous Italian Renaissance philosopher (1463–1494) who was the first to synthesize Jewish Kabbalah with Christian theology.</note>, before whom their name was unknown to the Roman language, they are called **Cabalistae** or **Cabalici** in Latin.

<margin>Q</margin>
Then **MARRANUS** <note>A character in this dialogue, representing a converted Jew or someone familiar with Jewish tradition.</note> spoke: "Are you not familiar, most learned Simon, with that man who first brought the word 'Kabbalah' to the Latins?"

And **SIMON** <note>The character representing the Jewish perspective in Reuchlin's dialogue.</note> replied: "Indeed I know him, I believe. I heard he was once an exile from his home among the Gauls and Savoyards, driven from his fatherland and pursued most bitterly by envious men in a certain detestable persecution because of his exceptional studies in philosophy and his noble genius. There is indeed a race of men, as Terence says, who wish themselves to be the first in all things, yet they are not. They are perhaps born from the crow—a bird which, as the fables say, was clothed in white feathers until the years of Coroneus, but later in black. It offers them a garment of both white and black, which is why they are called the 'Brothers Clad in Black' <note>original: *fratres Atrati*. This is likely a satirical reference to certain monastic orders who opposed Pico's work.</note>. That bird is always hateful to Apollo <note>original: *Phœbo*</note> because of its impious betrayal. But this poetry is known to both of you. These men were the gadflies, the whips, the dogs who were so 'noble' and 'learned' as Christians, yet in our century, it was Pico who most learnedly shared many of the secret dogmas of the Hebrews with Roman ears."

At this, **PHILOLAUS** <note>The character representing the Pythagorean or Greek philosophical tradition.</note> said: "Leaving aside these past deeds, I suggest we should return to the **Kabbalistic art**, if you trust me; for it will grow dark shortly, and it can hardly be said how much our desires tend elsewhere."

"I have indeed run through the individual points," said Simon, "and you shall expect nothing false from me further."

<margin>R 4</margin>

Although not all are complete in every part—for of some only fragments have floated to the surface—the rest, alas, are so extinguished that they are scarcely known by the record of their names in the monuments of the most learned men."

<margin>8</margin>

This happened either by antiquity, which consumes all things, or by the malice of wars, or by flood and devastation, or by the unforeseen accident of fire, or sometimes by shameful and detestable hatred and envy, which has incited the lazy and the foolish to be book-burners even in our own age."

...the library of Darius <note>Darius I, the Persian King</note>, as recorded in the Book of Ezra, which was a precious collection located in Ecbatana. By a similar example, countless authors have perished in our own century, although we do not doubt that many works survive which we ourselves have not yet seen. Nor can I boast of the same glory as **Pico della Mirandola** <note>original: *Mirandulo*; the famous Italian Renaissance philosopher who integrated Kabbalah into Christian thought</note>, who claimed that he had acquired at great expense those seventy volumes of Kabbalistic secrets which Ezra once commanded to be written down. I do not possess nearly enough gold or silver to even bid for such books if they were still in existence and offered for sale.

We use, therefore, a collection that is not quite so voluminous, but nevertheless, according to our ability, we study the book of our father Abraham, which is titled **יצירה** <note>original Hebrew: *Yetzirah*, meaning "Formation" or "Creation"</note> concerning creation. This work is assigned by certain learned men to **Master Akiba**, and it is certainly adorned with noble commentaries, as it would otherwise remain hidden and obscure. We also use the book **זהר** <note>original Hebrew: *Zohar*, meaning "Splendor"</note> concerning splendor, which was composed by **Simeon son of Yochai** while he lay hidden for twenty-four years in a vast and dark cave. And we use the book **בהיר** <note>original Hebrew: *Bahir*, meaning "Brightness" or "Brilliance"</note> concerning brilliance, which is called *Lucidarius* <note>A common title for medieval handbooks of enlightenment</note> by your people. 

There are also the works published on Kabbalah by the famous **Abraham Abulafia** <note>original: *Abrahā Alaphia*</note>, and the distinguished commentaries of **Ramban**—for this is the collective name for **Rabbi Moses son of Nahman** <note>also known as Nahmanides</note>—concerning the secrets of the Law, whom you call "the Gerundian" <note>He was from Gerona, Spain</note>. There are also the commentaries of that most learned of all recipients, **Rabbi Menahem Recanati**, on the secrets of Ramban. And there is the *Book of the Perplexed* by **Rambam** (ending with "M"), that is, **Rabbi Moses son of Maimon**, whom they call the "Egyptian Moses" <note>Maimonides lived and worked in Cairo, Egypt</note>.

And the book **האמונה** <note>original Hebrew: *Ha-Emunah*</note>, that is, *On Beliefs*, whose author in Asia was **Rabbi Saadia** <note>Saadia Gaon</note>. # IV ON THE KABBALISTIC ART
### iii

**"For there is no good Kabbalah except with a good heart"** <note>original Hebrew: *Ki ein Kabbalah tovah ela im ha-lev ha-tov*</note>, that is, that there is no good Kabbalah except with a good heart. In this saying, it seems to me he has very wisely repelled malicious Sophists from such holy contemplation; those who, like **dying flies**, destroy the sweetness of any ointment, no matter how precious <note>A reference to Ecclesiastes 10:1: "Dead flies cause the ointment of the apothecary to send forth a stinking savor."</note>. Finally, we use commentaries on the book **Yetzirah** <note>original Hebrew: *Yetzirah*, the "Book of Formation," one of the earliest Jewish mystical texts</note> by **Master Jacob Cohen** and, on the same book, the composition of **Rabbi Isaac**, which he titled *The Explanation of the Holy Name*. There is also a book published by **Rabbi Todros Levi** <note>original: *Tedacus Leui*; likely Todros ben Joseph Abulafia, a 13th-century Kabbalist</note> concerning the **ten Kabbalistic numerations** <term>Sefirot: the ten channels of divine energy through which God interacts with the universe</term>. I do not wish to add the book attributed to Solomon under the name of **Raziel** <note>The *Sefer Raziel HaMalakh*, a grimoire of practical Kabbalah and angelology</note>, for it is a magical fiction.

Up to this point, I have clearly revealed to you, as strangers, the "paper-thin poverty" of my personal library <note>Simon uses a self-deprecating metaphor to describe his small collection of books compared to the great libraries of antiquity</note>, which I certainly did not used to show to others. But in my opinion, no one has ever written about this art more skillfully, more distinctly, or more clearly until recently than **Rabbi Joseph son of Abraham of Castile**, a citizen of Cuenca <note>original: *Ioseph Bar Abrahã Castiliensis ciuis Salemitamus*; this refers to Joseph Gikatilla (1248–c. 1305), a major figure in Spanish Kabbalah</note>. He laboriously produced three volumes of this discipline, by which he made all Kabbalistic instruction clearer: the first on words, the second on letters, and the third volume on vowel points. The title of his book stands as **The Garden of the Nut** <note>original Hebrew: *Ginnat Egoz*</note>, following the Song of Solomon: *I went down into the garden of nuts to see the pleasant shrubs.*

<margin>V</margin> It appears that this "nut" is like a **golden apple enclosed in a silver network**, as it is read in the Proverbs: *A word spoken according to its ways is like golden apples in silver settings.* <note>Proverbs 25:11. This metaphor was famously used by Maimonides to explain the relationship between the literal "silver" meaning of scripture and its hidden "golden" spiritual truth.</note> So is Kabbalah: that golden and divine apple bound around with silver threads—namely, ingenious instructions and human arts—just as is customarily done by the goldsmith's craft. Through subtle engravings, they do not entirely cover or hide the sweet-smelling golden apple with silver so that nothing of it can be seen, but rather, through certain hollowed-out openings and silver lattices, they allow the color of the apple to stand out and the scent of amber to waft forth. To those looking from afar, the whole of what is networked seems to be solid silver; however, to those looking closer, if they search diligently, they will at the same time find the gold as well.

<margin>X</margin> And the more gold differs from silver, by so much more is **Kabbalah** proved to differ from the **Kabbalistic art**, <margin>Y</margin> although one genus of spiritual instinct encompasses both species. But one precedes the other as the divine oracle precedes the priests, and as gold of a single genus: one indeed is "good," but the other is "best." This is the manner in which it is told in the Pentateuch <note>The first five books of the Bible</note> concerning **Havilah** <note>original: *Heuila*</note>, that *the gold of that land is good* <margin>Z</margin>—for it is not written "best" there, as some read it, but "good." And in Isaiah regarding **Ophir**: *I will make a man more precious than fine gold, even than the gold of Ophir.* Thus, whatever lovers of the best arts learn from Holy Scripture through natural science is equal to "good gold," and it is called the **Work of Bereshit** <note>original: *Bresith*; referring to *Ma'aseh Bereshit*, the "Work of Creation" or the study of physics and the natural world in a mystical context</note>. But what...

# BOOK ONE
### Page XVII

...[wis]dom <note>The word fragment "entia" likely completes "sapientia" (wisdom) from the previous page</note> we receive spiritually; it is called the **Work of the Chariot** <term>Ma’aseh Merkavah: the study of the highest divine mysteries and the throne of God</term>, and it is likened to the finest and purest gold. For the Kabbalists write thus:

<margin>A</margin> **The Work of Creation is the wisdom of nature, and the Work of the Chariot is the wisdom of divinity** <note>original Hebrew: *She-Ma'aseh Bereshit chokmat ha-teva u-Ma'aseh Merkavah hu chokmat ha-elohut*</note>. And since both forms of wisdom are concerned in some way with the world and those things that exist within the world, there is a unanimous judgment among both the Talmudists and the Kabbalists in this matter: that there are two worlds. The first is the intellectual world, which is called **the World to Come** <note>original Hebrew: *Olam HaBa*</note>, that is, that world which is "coming" in relation to us. 

<margin>B</margin> And the second is the sensible <note>Meaning the physical world perceivable by the senses</note> world, which is called **this present world** <note>original Hebrew: *Olam HaZeh*</note>. This we have received from the words of our sages concerning the devoted student of the divine name of forty-two letters, of whom they say: **"Beloved above and cherished below, and inheriting two worlds, the present world and the future world"** <note>original Hebrew: *Ahuv le-ma'alah ve-nechmad le-mata ve-nochel shenei olamot*</note>.

<margin>C</margin> Therefore, the Talmudists and the Kabbalists are divided into two branches of study, even though both similarly arise and flow from received traditions. For both place their faith in the traditions of their ancestors, even when no logical reason is provided. But they are distinguished by this specific arrangement: the happy and blessed Kabbalist ultimately transfers and translates every study, every effort, every counsel, labor, and diligence—indeed, the entire intention of his mind—

<margin>D</margin> from the sensible world to the intellectual world. The Talmudist, however, remains in the sensible world and does not transcend the soul of this universal world. Even if he occasionally and lawfully proceeds toward God and the blessed spirits, he does not approach God Himself as immanent and absolute, but rather as the Craftsman and cause of things, occupied with His creations. He assigns the angels to daily ministries and the execution of the effects of the divine will, always relating the contemplation of the highest things back to this lower world. 

<margin>E</margin> Nevertheless, one of these disciplines often borrows the insights of the other and draws them toward its own purpose. Indeed, sometimes the Talmudists and Kabbalists communicate their studies back and forth between themselves, much like the active and contemplative lives. Often, they take one and the same passage of Holy Scripture, yet one may be drawn to it by a servant's fear while the other is invited by a son's love, each through their own graceful persuasion. It will appear through sharp study that the Talmudist resides over the precepts and commandments of the Law, explaining them, directing them, venerating and kissing them. Thus, we may correctly define the Talmud as nothing other than the explanation of the Law according to the intention of its Author. Hence the Talmudists are called **Explainers** <note>original Hebrew: *Meforshim*</note> and **Pharisees** <note>original Hebrew: *Perushim*, meaning "expositors" or "those who are set apart"</note>, who always persist in their work from the pulpit and the chair of Moses, preaching and exhorting the people, saying with the royal Prophet: "Serve [the Lord...]" <note>Likely referring to Psalm 2:11 or 100:2</note>

<meta>catchword: ui (vi)</meta>

<summary>This page defines the distinction between the Work of Creation (natural science) and the Work of the Chariot (divine science), while contrasting the Kabbalist's focus on the intellectual/spiritual world with the Talmudist's focus on the sensible/physical world and legal exposition.</summary>

# ON THE ART OF THE KABBALAH

**The Righteous** <note>original Hebrew: *Tzadikim*</note>—that is, the just—are said to be living even in their death, and the wicked are said to be dead even in their life. To those skilled in the Kabbalah, God’s sentence will not be obscure: *In the day that you eat of it, you shall die the death* <note>Genesis 2:17</note>—namely, not a corporal death but a spiritual one. For Adam lived more than nine hundred years after the forbidden eating; yet in that very moment, as soon as he had transgressed the law, he "died the death." He died, I say, in his sin, which was a source far too poisonous and contagious for the whole human race and the propagation of future offspring, who were thereby 

<margin>O</margin> destined for the eternal dwellings of the lower regions <note>The author refers to the "infernum," the state of separation from God after death before the coming of the Messiah</note>. This remained so until, by God’s pleasure, that Messiah the Redeemer should come, who would lead man back into paradise—not a terrestrial one but a celestial one—and restore to the children the life which the parent had lost: a life that is eternal, not temporal; of the soul, not of the body; that very intimacy with God and the most pleasant sight of divinity, filled with every delight. In him, all true Kabbalists—not the sophistical ones—fix and place their whole trust; upon him they turn all the saving prophecies of the Holy Scriptures. They understand the promises of the **Land of Promise**, the city of **Jerusalem** (the sharing of which is in itself), the **Mountain of God** and His **holy place**, the **holy way**, the **sanctuary**, the **courts of the Lord**, the **temple of the Lord**, the **house of the Lord**, the **gate of the Lord**, and many other similar things, which **Rabbi Moses the Egyptian** <note>Maimonides (1138–1204), the preeminent Jewish philosopher</note> in his **Mishneh** <term>Mishneh Torah: Maimonides’ code of Jewish law; the author equates "Mishneh" with "Deuteronomy" or the "repetition of the law"</term>, also wished to be understood as referring to celestial blessedness. 

For this reason, we often and greatly contend with the **Talmudists**, and for the most part, we both go in two different directions of opinion. 

<margin>P</margin> They attempt to refer every liberation by King Messiah from our corporal captivity—or more truly, our dispersion—to tumult, the noise of arms, military expeditions, the conquest of regions and devastation of lands, and the victory of the Israelite army. They see it as we read happened to our ancestors of old under **Moses** the Savior against the Canaanites and Philistines; or at least they look for a refined genius of escape, which many have used craftily (though I think piously) in other liberations, when for so many centuries they have wandered in exile under so many kingdoms: such as seventy years under the **Babylonian**, fifty-four under the **Persian**, one hundred and thirty under the **Greek**, and now one thousand four hundred under the **Roman**—and the end is not yet. 

We, on the contrary—and in my judgment, more correctly—as Kabbalists, believe the **Messiah** is to come to free the wretched mortals of the human race from the chains of **original injustice** <term>Original Sin: the innate fallen state of humanity inherited from Adam</term>, to remit sins, and to save the souls of those piously serving God, who were 

<margin>Q</margin> excluded from eternal life in Adam our father, until the satisfaction of the Messiah. In order that the justice of the merciful and clement God may be fulfilled, the Messiah might "put forth his hand and take from the **Tree of Life** and eat of it," so that through him we may live forever. That satisfaction <note>Atonement or payment of a debt</note> ought not to have been made in royal pride, nor in the boasting of honor and glory, because the original sin to be expiated by the Messiah sprouted from pride and elation.

<summary>This page contrasts the Talmudic expectation of a political, military Messiah with the Kabbalistic view of a spiritual Redeemer who heals the soul from the "spiritual death" caused by Adam's pride.</summary>

But rather in humility and endurance, not in chariots and in horses, but in the name of the Lord our God; and not in victory, nor in human triumph, but in labor, fasting, vigils, strength of mind, contempt for vainglory, compassionate mercy, the primary love of God, the right love of men, and finally in that very heroic, generous, and voluntary death. For since vice is fought by virtue alone, no wise man has ever highly valued the empires, princedoms, genealogies, and crowns of this world. Indeed, 

<margin>R</margin> this is what it means to be wise: to despise the glory of this world, because when the glorious rich man dies, he shall not take all things with him, as the <note>original: "Psaltes"</note> Psalmist says, nor shall his glory descend with him. Therefore, whatever is written concerning trophies and the subjection of peoples in the sacred writings, all of it—once the history of the events narrated has been believed—is nevertheless understood by the Kabbalists to refer to the intellectual world and the heavenly powers. Thus, the future King Messiah, by the highest right, will not only neglect but even despise these light and abject delusions of this world—magistracies, honors, and kingdoms—as vain and foolish things; he comes instead to abolish the guilt of the human race and to open the way to virtue. Whence the true Messiah himself, if we are led by right reason, will be more clearly recognized from that single noble chapter of Isaiah, which begins thus: <term>Behold, my servant shall understand</term> <note>original Hebrew: "הנה ישכיל עבדי" (Hinneh yaskil avdi), Isaiah 52:13</note>. That is, "Behold, my servant shall have understanding," 

<margin>S</margin> and it concludes thus: <term>and he shall pray for the transgressors</term> <note>original Hebrew: "ול פשעים יפגיע" (ve-la-pish'im yapgi'a), Isaiah 53:12</note>. Concerning this, I marvel more than can be said—and not without a unique sense of shame before other foreign nations, though I speak confidently to you alone—that Rabbi Solomon <note>Rabbi Solomon ben Isaac, known as Rashi (1040–1105), a preeminent medieval commentator</note> and David Kimhi <note>David Kimhi, known as Radak (1160–1235), a famous grammarian and exegete</note>, and other men of our sect who are not a little learned, through some sort of faint-heartedness, or perhaps through shame in the presence of the Gentiles, interpret that whole context of Isaiah as referring only to the people of Israel now scattered everywhere. Yet it is most plainly prophesied concerning that very Messiah, which the Chaldean translation of Jonathan <note>The Targum Jonathan, an ancient Aramaic translation and interpretation of the Prophets</note> expresses by name, saying: <term>Behold, my servant the Messiah shall prosper</term> <note>original Aramaic: "הא יצלח עבדי משיחא" (Ha yatzlach avdi meshicha)</note>. That is, "Behold, my servant the Messiah shall be successful." This is the one truly seen by Isaiah in the prophetic spirit in that place: a man of sorrows and experienced in weakness, with a hidden face, a man of no honorable reputation, touched by a divine stroke, despised and avoided, shorn like a lamb, slain like a sheep, cut off from the land of the living, and accounted among the wicked, and inglorious among the sons of men. But truly, what is he among the sons of God? Clearly, he is greatly exalted and elevated and exceedingly sublime. For who shall tell of his generation? And the will of the Lord God is directed by his hand, and the Lord abolished in him the iniquity of us all, because he struck him for the crime of the people. For he himself was wounded for our crimes, and bruised for our iniquities; he who certainly never committed iniquity, nor was there deceit in his mouth, but the Lord willed his crushing.

<margin>X</margin>
**And by the spirit of his lips he shall slay the wicked.** These are the words of the aforementioned Kabbalistic volume, by which we are reminded that the King Messiah overcomes the adversaries of God's people not by hand, but by his mouth; not with arms, but by the spirit. He grants the sevenfold grace of God to the pious and slays the impious, and all this by the "spirit of his mouth"—that is, by his spiritual doctrine, which he will scatter and sow among all nations through righteous men and chosen disciples of the Just One. Regarding this time of the Messiah, Jonathan son of Uzziel <note>An important 1st-century translator of the Hebrew Bible into Aramaic</note> interpreted the oracle of Isaiah, *You shall draw waters from the fountains of the Savior*, into the Chaldean language <note>Aramaic</note> with these words: **"And you shall receive a new doctrine with joy from the chosen of the righteous."**

<margin>Y</margin>
That indeed is the new doctrine, which shines as the true light; and he who hates it is in darkness, but he who loves it lives in the light. The end of the commandments, therefore, is this: that we should love one another in the doctrine of the Messiah, **who will teach the nations to walk**

**in the ways of the Lord** <note>original Hebrew: *Ihuh* / YHWH</note>, as Rabbi David Kimhi <note>A famous medieval Jewish commentator (1160–1235), also known as Radak</note> writes concerning that same prophet in the fifty-first chapter, on the verse: *because a law shall go out from me*. This is the law which, if a person follows it, will save them; if they despise it, they shall perish. For the old things belong to fear, but the new things belong to charity.

# BOOK ONE.

**"Upright love from a whole heart"** <note>original Hebrew: *ahavah yesharah mi-lev shalem*</note>, which is the path of righteous love from a sincere heart according to Our Masters. Therefore, the Messiah shall be the example of life for all who are to be set free, upon whom the universal salvation of the world depends—which is called "eternal salvation"—and is explained by our people throughout all the ages of the world, where it is read: *Israel is saved in the Lord with an eternal salvation.* Regarding this, a significant passage is written in the book of the **Kabbalah Hacadma** <term>Kabbalah Hacadma<note>Literally "The Ancient Kabbalah," referring to early mystical traditions or a specific foundational text</note></term>: **"And this is the secret of the King Messiah, who will come quickly in our days, whose entire operation begins with the letters V and H and also Y and H, and this is the secret of the seventh day, and this name—that is, his complete name—is perfect, and all the work shall be completed by his hands."** <note>original Hebrew: *ve-hu sod Melekh ha-Mashiach...*</note>

And this is the mystery of the King Messiah, who will come quickly in our days, whose every work will begin in *y. h.* and also *v. h.* <note>The components of the Tetragrammaton, the four-letter name of God</note>, which is the mystery of the seventh day; and this name is his complete name, and every work shall be perfected in his hand. Behold, it has been defined by the wise **Kabbalists** <term>Kabbalists<note>Students of Jewish mysticism who seek the hidden meanings of the Torah</note></term> that all things are to be perfected through the Messiah, and his entire operation is carried out through the most sacred four letters *i, h, u, h*, in the mystery of the seventh day—not, to be sure, named for the number of days, but for the transition from the active life to the contemplative life, that is, in the very quietude of the soul and peaceful tranquility, withdrawing from the excessive anxieties of this world and from the physical labors performed by builders.

<margin>B</margin>
For it is written: *And he rested on the seventh day from all the work that he had performed.* Although the **Talmudists** <term>Talmudists<note>Scholars of the Talmud, the central text of Jewish civil and ceremonial law</note></term> attribute many names to this king—as may be understood from the citations of many doctors in the book **Sanhedrin** <term>Sanhedrin<note>A tractate of the Talmud dealing with law and the Messianic age</note></term>, in the volume titled *Helek*, cited from the beginning where it is written: *And Rabbi Jochanan said, "What is the name of the Messiah?"* up to the place where it says: *And Rabbi Eliezer took up the word, saying: "The days of the Messiah."* And later, in many of their writings, such as the commentaries on the song of the synagogue, **"Head and First"** <note>original Hebrew: *Rosh ve-Rishon*</note>, the names of the Messiah are explained as *Shiloh*, *Yinon*, *David*, *Hanina*, "the branch," "the righteous," and "the comforter." However, these individual names are thought to be honorary titles or symbolic names, like the seven examples listed there: the ark, the mercy seat, the tablets, the rod of Aaron, the jar of manna, and the spirit of God.

But according to the Kabbalists, you have heard how this one ineffable name **the Lord** <note>original Hebrew: *YHWH*</note> is proper to the Messiah, which will complete and perfect his substantive name. For they teach that it is necessary to believe this is his integral name, which is piously and holily made whole in mercies. No Talmudist can secretly deny this, since that great Master said in the passage of the Talmud mentioned above that the name of the Messiah will come to be called similarly *Hanina*—that is, "mercy"—citing a verse from Jeremiah 16. However, the Romans <note>referring to the Latin Vulgate translation</note> read this verse loosely and improperly as "who will not give you rest." But that is not an etymological interpretation. For in my judgment, it is more correctly read as: "for I will not give you mercy." **Jonathan the Chaldean** <term>Jonathan the Chaldean<note>The traditional author of the Aramaic Targum (translation/paraphrase) of the Prophets</note></term> translated this as **"mercies"** <note>original Aramaic: *rachamin*</note>, as one who, according to the Talmudists, wished to say that...

# ON THE ART OF THE KABBALAH

<margin>C</margin> "To you who walk in the wickedness of your heart, so that you do not hear God, there will be no Messiah who is named 'Mercies.'" <note>original Latin: *miserationes*</note> From this it clearly becomes known that **Mercies** <note>original Hebrew: *Rachamim* (**רחמים**)</note>—that is, within the mercies of the middle of Y.H.V.H.—shall be the proper name of the Savior Messiah. Although his dignity and office consist of rigor and severity, according to the prophecy of King David expressed without any controversy regarding the Messiah himself: *He shall judge your people,* he says, *in justice, and your poor in judgment.* Yet, because judgment—that is, <margin>D</margin> **Judgment** <note>original Hebrew: *Mishpat* (**משפט**)</note>—according to all Kabbalists, also admits clemency alongside justice. For so it is read in the fourth chapter of the *Gates of Light* <note>original Latin: *Portae lucis*; Hebrew: *Sha'are Orah*, a foundational Kabbalistic text by Joseph Gikatilla</note>: **"Because judgment is half rigor and half mercy."** <note>original Hebrew: *ki ha-mishpat chetsyo din ve-chetsyo chesed*</note> That is, Judgment is partly rigor and partly mildness. By these modes, the reconciliation of the first fall [of man] shall occur through a repeated union and a certain new betrothal of the people with God, as Hosea foretold: *I will betroth you to me in justice and judgment, in mercy and in mercies,* where the word **Mercies** <note>original Hebrew: *Rachamim* (**רחמים**)</note> is placed. Therefore, lest anyone think that the very coming of the Messiah is destined out of some legal necessity and not rather from pure grace <margin>E</margin> and the most liberal gift of God, the renowned name of "Clemency" is rightly bestowed upon this Savior. This name shall be composed of letters—both vowels and a consonant—that signify nothing other than mercy alone. 

And we conjecture that this shall be through the four holy letters by which the Ineffable Name is depicted as if by signs and symbols, and through the consonant *Shin* (**ש**) by which the Ineffable Name is "named" [pronounced]. For it is a common saying in the Kabbalah that this mark, *Shin* <note>original Hebrew: *Shin* (**שין**)</note>, is explained through **Notaricon** <term>Notaricon<note>A Kabbalistic shorthand where each letter of a word stands for another word</note></term> as **"The name of the Lord is called"** <note>original Hebrew: *Shem Y.H.V.H. Nikra* (**שם יהוה נקרא**)</note>. This means the name is "brought forth" or "uttered." Moreover, there are no other letters by which pure mercy is designated except these five: Y. H. V. H. and the consonant *Shin* (that is, *S*). Regarding the four vowels, it is read thus in the book of the *Gates of Justice* <note>original Latin: *Portarũ iusticię*; Hebrew: *Sha'are Tzedek*</note>: **"And this is the secret of what our Rabbis of blessed memory said: 'Behold, the Lord comes out of His place'; He comes out from the attribute of mercy."** <note>original Hebrew: *ve-zehu sod she-amru... ki hinneh Y.H.V.H. yotze mi-mekomo...*</note> That is: and this is the mystery that our Teachers (may their memory be in peace) spoke of, that "Behold the four-letter name," as Micah says, "Y.H.V.H. shall go out from his place," meaning He shall go out through the property of mercies. 

Furthermore, concerning the consonant *Shin*, all Kabbalists who are not ignorant in Kabbalistic **Gematria** <term>Gematria<note>The practice of assigning numerical values to letters to find mystical connections between words</note></term> will not deny that the letter *Shin* contains within itself the arithmetic proportion of the entire four-letter name, and that it likewise possesses the same property of clemency and mercy. <margin>F</margin> Therefore, the salvation of all men must be expected from the mercy of God alone, which Habakkuk expressed openly when addressing God thus: *When you are angry, you will remember mercy.* Where David Kamhi <note>David Kimhi (c. 1160–1235), a famous medieval Jewish grammarian and biblical commentator</note>—whom our people call Kimhi, just as others pronounce it *Rabi*, and Germany says *Ribi* by an easy conversion of the vowel 'a' into 'i'—as there exists a similar judgment among the Greeks and Latins; for they say *grammatikoi* and *logikoi*, while we say *grammatica* and *logica*; they say *mitir*, we say *mater*. So Solomon...

### BOOK ONE.

...Simson, and Kamhi [David] Kimhi, and many others. That David, a Spanish Jew <note>The famous medieval scholar David Kimhi (c. 1160–1235), also known as the Radak</note>, teaches that through the name *Racham* <note>original Hebrew: **רחם**, meaning 'womb' or 'mercy'</note>—that is, "Mercies," placed there according to the arithmetic proportion of the Kabbalah <note>The practice of Gematria, where letters have numerical values</note>, which is to say, understood symbolically—it refers to Abraham. It is as if Habakkuk were saying: "O God, when you are moved by the anger of our sin, remember the seed of Abraham, to whom you promised that in him all the families of the earth would be blessed." <margin>J</margin> And again: "O God, you spoke to him: in your seed all the nations of the earth shall be blessed." But so that Habakkuk himself might indicate what that seed would be, he added: "You went forth for the salvation of your people, for salvation with your Messiah." <margin>M</margin> Where the same David Kimhi writes: *hu Mashiach ben David* <note>original Hebrew: **הוא משיח בן דוד**</note>, that is, "this is the Messiah, the son of David." I say, therefore, with the wise Kabbalists, that the true salvation of us all depends upon the Messiah, as many of us as reach out to him.

<margin>G</margin> From this it follows that, detaching ourselves as much as possible from all created things, we should strive to ascend through all the stages and migrate into him, so that even if we do not fully attain him, we may at least approach him to the best of each man's ability. For he is our very own, to whose coming the whole Law is referred by us, even intellectually; and not only the scripture of Moses, but also that of the Prophets and whatever is contained in the Hagiographa <term>the 'Holy Writings' or *Ketuvim*, the third section of the Hebrew Bible</term>. <margin>H</margin> For the whole context of what we call the *Essrim Varba* <note>original Hebrew: *Esrim ve-Arba*, meaning 'Twenty-Four'</note>—that is, the twenty-four books—and what you call the Bible, we call the whole thing by the name *Torah* <note>original Hebrew: **תורה**</note>, that is, the Law. As in Daniel chapter 9: "Walking in the law of the Lord our God, which he set before us by the hand of his servants the prophets." We have determined this scripture alone to be so stable and so firm that we can safely ground all our thoughts upon it, and place the sublime contemplations of speculative men without confusion. This is both because it was promulgated by the supreme voice of God, and because it is accustomed to work with such powers of energy in the minds of the most contemplative men. Through it, we are able to ascend from any composite things to the simple, from the simple to the most simple, from effects to causes, and finally from the lower world to the higher, and from the higher to the Messiah, who is the supreme object of our mind and conceivable in the final degree as the King of the Ages. <margin>I</margin> Through him, we may clearly and finally pass over into the incomprehensible God. It is also because through these Sacred Letters—as if by Jacob's Ladder, touching the heavens with its top, upon which God himself leans—our angels ascend and descend: carriers of prayers from here and gifts from there, who carry petitions back and forth and bring help in return, as one of your own authors says. <margin>K</margin> And indeed, I feel nothing else could be imagined that would weave our soul more closely to God, like a thread woven into a fabric, than that same Sacred Scripture of which mention is made, which leads us first into the wonder of divine things, then into the knowledge <note>original: *agnitionem*</note> of them according to human capacity, and finally into that most ardent [knowledge of the divinity]...

->**ON THE ART OF THE KABBALAH**<-

...love, carrying with it the most certain effect of hope. By means of this [Kabbalah], as if with Ezekiel’s living creatures and wheels <note>A reference to the "Merkavah" or Chariot vision in Ezekiel 1:15–21, where the prophet sees divine beings and wheels moving in perfect unison</note>, we raise ourselves from the earth, so that we go when they go, and we stand when they stand. This is the only field of true contemplation, in which every single word is a sacred mystery, and every single discourse, syllable, stroke, and point is full of secret meanings—a fact attested to not only by our own authors, but even by Christians. <margin>L</margin> This is the Kabbalah, which does not permit us to dwell upon the ground, but lifts our mind to the highest goal of comprehension. Yet, this comprehension cannot reasonably transcend the soul of the Messiah, except by a certain incomprehensible intuition, by way of a momentary rapture <note>The state of mystical ecstasy or "devekut," where the soul clings to the Divine</note>. By this rapture, we believe it is not impossible for us Kabbalists to be snatched up in spirit near to the "third world," where the Messiah dwells, flowing into all lower things.

For in the most general sense, there are three worlds. <margin>M</margin> The first is the material, the second is the formal, and the third is the formless. Or, if you prefer it this way: the first is the lowest, which is the "sensible" <note>The world perceived by the senses</note>; the second is the supreme and mental, which is the "intelligible" <note>The world of pure intellect and ideas</note>; and the third is the most supreme <note>original Greek: **ὑπερωτάτος** (hyperotatos)</note>, or if one may say so, the "supremest," incomparable and divine. I intended for this corporeal world, which supports the others, to be considered the "first" world in relation to us—though perhaps in a reversed order, since by the just logic of causes it ought to have been the last, acting as the receptacle for all higher things. 

This world is constituted, first, of the heavens and celestial beings; second, of the elements and things made of elements; and third, of human nature and individual men. <margin>H</margin> Man is called in Hebrew the "Small World" <note>original Hebrew: **עולם הקטן**, *Olam Ha-Katan*</note>, in Greek the *microcosmos* <note>original Greek: **μικρόκοσμος**</note>, and in Latin the *parvus mundus*. This entire universe, as your Aristotle suggests in his book *On the Universe* <note>The treatise *De Mundo*, historically attributed to Aristotle</note>, is a globe composed of heaven and earth and the natures contained within them. Indeed, it contains seven heavenly dwellings and seven earthly dwellings, which Rabbi Menachem Recanati <note>An influential 14th-century Italian Kabbalist</note> enumerates in his commentary on chapter 25 of Leviticus. Those pertaining to the heavens are: *Shamayim* (Heavens), *Raquia* (Firmament), *Shechakim* (Clouds), *Zevul* (Abode), *Ma’on* (Dwelling), *Machon* (Place), and *Aravot* (Clouds/Highest Heaven). <note>original Hebrew: **שמים, רקיע, שחקים, זבול, מעון, מכון, ערבות**</note>. Secondly, those pertaining to the earth are: *Eretz* (Earth), *Arka* (Land), *Geya* (Valley), *Yevashah* (Dry Land), *Charevah* (Parched Land), *Tevel* (World), and *Cheled* (Duration). <note>original Hebrew: **ארץ, ארקא, גיא, יבשה, חרבה, תבל, חלד**</note>. Furthermore, Joseph of Salamanca <note>referring to Joseph Gikatilla (1248–c. 1305), author of *Ginnat Egoz* or "The Garden of Nuts"</note> in his *Garden of Nuts* listed by name the seven dwellings of the lower world, as you heard a little earlier. 

Regarding the Microcosm <note>Man as a miniature reflection of the universe</note>, it is no secret to any of us that seven things pertain to the condition of man, in whichever direction you look. These are the body, the soul, and the composite of the two which we call the "living person" <note>original Hebrew: **נפש**, *Nephesh*</note>. This is illustrated by the King of Sodom's words: "Give me the person" <note>Genesis 14:21; original Hebrew: **תן לי הנפש**, *Ten li ha-nephesh*</note>, meaning "Give me the man." This man is composed of the four powers of the soul and the four qualities of the greater world; and since this world is indeed animated, it is illuminated by its own mind, which is called Metattron <note>A supreme archangel in Kabbalistic lore, often associated with the "Prince of the Countenance" or the celestial scribe</note>. 

The second world is the supreme world of the "separate intelligences" <note>term: <term>separate intelligences</term>, spiritual beings or angels that exist apart from physical matter</note>. These are called by the Kabbalists the "Separate Intellects" <note>original Hebrew: **שכלים נפרדים**, *Sekhalim Nifradim*</note>, and by the Hebrew philosophers they are called "Knowledges" <note>original Hebrew: **דעות**, *De'ot*</note>.

<margin>N</margin>
<term>Separate entities</term> <note>original: נפרדות (*nifradot*), referring to spiritual beings like angels or souls that exist apart from physical matter</note>. That world, which is filled with species, forms, detached minds, and angels, is embraced, surrounded, and governed by the **Soul of the Messiah** itself. Among the Kabbalists <note>Jewish mystics who study the "received" tradition of the inner workings of God</note>, this soul is the "Idea of all Ideas" regarding all life; it is the source to which every individual, specific, and general vitality is referred. From there, as if from a nursery or a living pond, all life is drawn forth, and it is called by the Kabbalists the **Land of the Living**. <margin>Therefore they commented on the verse: "Let the earth bring forth the living soul according to its kind" <note>Genesis 1:24</note>, this is the **Soul of the Messiah**.</margin> <note>original Hebrew: לפיכך דרשו בפסוק תוצא הארץ נפש חיה למינה זו נפש של משיח</note> These words are read in the second chapter of the *Gates of Light* <note>original: *Portae Lucis*; the *Sha'are Orah*, a fundamental Kabbalistic text by Joseph Gikatilla</note>. And just as in the human world—which is called the <term>Microcosm</term> <note>the "little world," meaning man is a miniature reflection of the universe</note>—the mind rules the soul of man, so **Metattron** <note>the supreme archangel and heavenly scribe</note> rules the celestial world, and the **Soul of the Messiah** rules the angelic world, and **Adonai** <note>the Lord</note> rules the incomparable world. Furthermore, just as the light of the mind is the "active intellect," so the light of Metattron is **Shaddai** <note>Almighty</note>, and the light of the Soul of the Messiah is **Elhai** (that is, the **Living God**), and the light of Adonai is the **Ein Sof** <note>original: *Ensoph*, meaning the "Infinite" or "Without End," God in His absolute, unknowable essence</note>.

<margin>O</margin>
Since it seems evident to the most learned observers of natural things that the lowest part of a higher nature communicates with the highest part of a lower nature—to such an extent that one often doubts whether closely connected things are merely touching or are actually continuous—it is difficult to say what the nature of that bond is which joins them. It is much like the place where a horse’s leg meets its hoof; one might ask if that connection is made of horn or of flesh, because of their immediate and overlapping existence. For this reason, I believe it can be said without error that man, the Microcosm, and that great sensible world <note>the world we perceive through our senses</note> communicate through the **Mind**. Likewise, the corporeal world and the intellectual world communicate through **Metattron**, who is the "active intellect" of the first moved sphere, being one with the celestial nature as his lower part and with the angelic nature as his higher part. Moreover, the supreme world communicates with the third, incomparable, and most-supreme world through the **Soul of the Messiah**. This soul is a kind of essence that is continuous with both the angelic and the divine worlds, for the Soul of the Messiah and **Elhai** <note>the Living God</note> are not separated by any gap. Rather, Elhai is the fountain of living waters, and the Soul of the Messiah is the stream of life. The third world is that of the **Deity**, which is constituted by that which the <term>Seraphim</term> <note>the highest order of angels</note> called: "**Holy, Holy, Holy**," the <term>Tetragrammaton</term> <note>the sacred four-letter name of God, YHWH</note>. In Deuteronomy, He is called **Great, Mighty, and Awesome** <note>Deut. 10:17</note>. He was Great before creation, Mighty during creation, and Awesome after creation.

<margin>P</margin>
And this is **One** <note>original Hebrew: אחד (*Echad*)</note>; or rather, more properly, He is the **Principle of Unity**. This is because the letter *Aleph* <note>the first letter of the Hebrew alphabet, numerical value 1</note> designates the "Beginning," and *had* means "one"—as if He were the beginning of the one, folding all things into the simplicity of His unity. According to the Kabbalists, His emanation is **Spirit, Word, Voice** <note>original Hebrew: רוח דבר קול (*Ruach, Davar, Kol*)</note>. For thus did **Rabbi Azariel** <note>Azriel of Gerona, a 13th-century Kabbalist</note> write in his *Commentary on Holiness*, following the very points I have just recounted, in these words:

->### ON THE ART OF THE KABBALAH<-

<margin>M</margin> ...from the spirit comes forth the word and the voice without the opening of the lips and without the speech of the tongue, and not by the breath <note>original: *anhelitu*, referring to physical human breathing</note> of man. <note>original Hebrew: מרות יוצא הדבר והקול בלא פתיחת שפתים ובלא דבור לשון ולא נשמת אדם</note> And these three are one spirit, because God is one, as we read in the *Book of Formation* <note>original: *Ietzira* (*Sefer Yetzirah*), an ancient foundational text of Jewish mysticism</note> concerning creation in these words: **One is the Spirit of the living God, blessed be He, and blessed be His name, who lives forever—Voice, Spirit, and Word; and this is the Holy Spirit. Two is the Spirit from Spirit.** <note>original Hebrew: אחת רוח אלהים חיים ברוך הוא ומבורך שמו של חי העולמים קול ורוח ודבר וזו היא רוח הקדש שתים רוח מרוח</note> These are the words of Abraham our father. And this is in accordance with what Rabbi Hammai <note>a legendary figure in early Kabbalah</note> wrote in his *Book of Speculation* <note>original: *Sefer Ha-Iyun*</note>: These three, who are one, hold a proportion between themselves, such as **One, Unifying, and Unified**. <note>original Hebrew/Latin: אחד מיוחד יחיד (*Echad, Meyuchad, Yachid*); these represent the Knower, the Knowledge, and the Known as a single unity in God</note> Furthermore, a little earlier the same author says: **They are the beginning, the middle, and the end** <note>original Hebrew: סוף ראש ואמצע וסוף</note>, and these are one point, and He is the **Lord of the Universe** <note>original Hebrew: אדון הכל (*Adon Ha-Kol*)</note>. So it is written in the cited volume.

Therefore, that third world—incomparably the highest—is constituted from these three which are one, as if from the supreme essence, power, and operation. It extends into eternity and beyond; it is neither concave, nor convex, nor keeled <note>original: *carinatus*, shaped like a ship's hull</note>, nor does it have a surface. For as Azriel <note>Azriel of Gerona, a 13th-century Kabbalist who synthesized early traditions</note> writes in the previously mentioned *Book of Holiness*: **He is first without beginning, and He is last without end** <note>original Hebrew: הוא ראשון בלי תחלה והוא אחרון בלי תכלה</note>, truly reaching where even our thoughts cannot penetrate. And He is named **Ein Sof** <note>original: *Ensoph*, Hebrew for "The Infinite" or "Without End"</note>, which is a certain supreme reality, incomprehensible and ineffable in itself. In the most remote withdrawal of His divinity and in the inaccessible abyss of the fountain-light, He withdraws and conceals Himself, so that nothing can be understood to proceed from Him. He remains as the most absolute Deity, at rest within the total enclosure of Himself within Himself, naked without clothing, and without any garment of circumstances. He is neither poured out of Himself nor expanded by His splendor. In Him, <term>Being</term> <note>original Latin: *ens*; Hebrew: *Yesh*</note> and <term>Non-being</term> <note>original Latin: *non ens*; Hebrew: *Ayin*</note> are indistinguishable, as are all things which to our reason seem contrary and contradictory to one another. He is a segregated and free unity, enfolding all things in the simplest way. For thus we read in the *Book of Faith and Trust*: <margin>q Q</margin> **I have already told you that He who brings forth Being from Non-being lacks nothing; and that Being is in Non-being in the manner of Non-being, and Non-being is in Being in the manner of Being. This is so you may learn that Non-being is Being and Being is Non-being.** <note>original Hebrew: כבר אמרתי לך כי המוציא יש מאין אינו חסר ובי היש הוא באין בענין אין והאין הוא ביש בענין יש ללמוד שחאין הוא היש והיש הוא האין</note> Thus it is written there. This, however, transcends all our understanding, which cannot combine contradictions in their first principle by the path of reason; for we walk by those things which are made manifest to us by nature itself, which, falling far from this infinite power, is itself contradictory...

<summary>This page explores the Kabbalistic concept of the highest world and the nature of God as the Infinite (Ein Sof). It emphasizes the unity of the divine spirit (Voice, Spirit, Word) and the mystical paradox where Being and Non-being are unified within the absolute Deity.</summary>

<page-num>XXIII</page-num>
<header>BOOK ONE</header>

...contraries <note>completing "contraria" from the previous page</note> separated by an infinite distance, as a certain most philosophical German, a high priest of the sun <note>original: *archiflamen dialis*, a classical title Reuchlin uses here to refer to the great philosopher-theologian Cardinal Nicholas of Cusa</note>, left for posterity some fifty-two years ago. Therefore, with the weight of temporal cares set aside, and the sophisms of old wives' disputes despised, the happy Kabbalist, through Kabbalah—that is, the path of the received and the believed—breaks through the darkness and leaps forward into splendor. By this splendor he reaches the light, and thus from light he migrates into the Brightness; and through that Brightness, as much as human nature can grasp, he apprehends that true Luminary under the mode of Being, but not as non-being, unless this is done through the abstraction of all things that are not the absolutely first Principle. And since frequently by this way, through ineffable joy and alacrity of spirit, the mind of the Kabbalist itself—leaving behind humble and earthly things within the secret of a profound silence—is transferred to super-celestial and invisible things that transcend all human sense, then, even if still dwelling in mortal skin, he nonetheless becomes a companion of angels. He becomes, as it were, a resident of the super-celestial home, whose conversation is known to be so frequent in the heavens. And then, at times, he walks to higher places with them as companions of his journeys and visits the Soul of the Messiah; at other times, however, he descends to the lower powers of nature, both celestial and otherwise, under angelic guidance (yet not without his own reason), and he strives to understand their dignities and operations, and to venerate them with singular honor.

<margin>S</margin>
From this arises the Kabbalist's intimate friendship with the angels, through which, sometimes by rightly knowing the divine names, he performs wonderful things which the common people call miracles. For instance, Rabbi Meir, through a divine name—even one uttered by a Gentile—preserved his wife's sister from the corruption of a brothel; though she was forced into prostitution, none of the revelers, however robust, were able to violate or defile her once the word was spoken. These things are recounted at the beginning of the *Gates of Light* <note>original: *Portae lucis*, referring to the *Sha'are Orah* by Joseph Gikatilla</note>, along with many other such stories and their authors. In the memory of the fathers, the performance of such miracles was so easy for Kabbalists that they were often ignominiously called "cunning magicians" by the envious and profane, as if Michael <note>the archangel</note> had not performed those works, but rather, and most especially, Samael <note>a figure in Jewish lore often associated with the accuser or the angel of death</note>—namely through Egyptian incantations and certain secrets. Nevertheless, the staff of the Kabbalists always devours the staffs of the sorcerers <note>an allusion to Aaron's rod devouring the rods of Pharaoh's magicians in Exodus</note>, and a healthy divine power performs whatever it does better than any demonic power. For the art of Kabbalah always tends toward the salvation of men, whereas the poisonous craft of magical vanity always turns toward destruction; the latter acts through the names of darkness and evil spirits, the former through the names of light and blessed angels. Concerning these things—unless the Sabbath day of rest were already approaching this very hour in the evening, as is our custom—since it pertains to this matter as the fruit of this art which you so greatly desire, I would certainly then...

<meta>catchword: indeed.</meta>

whatever I might feel, I would treat more amply. But it is nearly night, most excellent men, and we must withdraw, not only so that I do not get beaten <note>Simon uses a humorous, perhaps metaphorical, reference to being "beaten" like a schoolboy for neglecting his religious duties</note> for being negligent of my instructions, but also so that I do not fail my Kabbalistic profession. Therefore, after that Sabbath of yours, Simon, since you bear with us with such singular kindness, we shall return." And he said, "Return boldly, and meanwhile, stay in good health."

## BOOK TWO.
### XXV.

->E<-

...they were torn away from their most pleasant conversation and postponed until the day after tomorrow, not without a troublesome waste of time, since they did not know what they were to do on the following day. Then, walking along, they ruminated on the essence of the doctrine they had received, recounting to each other short summaries of what had been said. While they were burning with the fervor of learning, there came to mind and suddenly returned to memory the speech of that admirable Jewish man—the sharpness of his debating, and his grave and learned instruction which delights without causing satiety; it was not disguised or colored, but where it most lacked the "flowers" of rhetoric, there it brought forth the most fruit. And when they had hurried from their journey into the inn, soon in that very gathering, before they had even caught their breath, **MARRANUS** began: "Of all the wise men whom I have heard since my tender years, I do not know if any has ever seemed to me more clever in speaking or more sublime in thinking than this one man Simon. Even now I hold him in my memory; though his speech was plain, simple, unaffected, not sought from afar, and not at all smelling of Demosthenes’ lamp <note>original: *Demosthenis oleum olente*; a classical idiom referring to the lamp oil used by the Greek orator Demosthenes during his long nights of study, implying a speech that is overly rehearsed or artificial</note>, but rather extemporaneous and everyday, he excited my soul to contemplate difficult things so much that I have grasped nothing more pleasing. Good gods! A Jewish man born, nourished, educated, and taught among Jews—a nation held everywhere among peoples to be barbarian, superstitious, vile, abject, and alienated from the splendor of all the good arts—believe me, I would have spent this whole night with a leaning desire to see this man’s face and hear the words of his speech, if this wretched Sabbath <note>Marranus likely calls it "wretched" only because it forces a pause in their exciting lessons</note> had not intervened this evening." Then **Philolaus** said: "Not even all the Greeks, to whom the discipline of many arts, the sharpness of minds, and the abundance of speech are granted by everyone’s consent, could have ascended so high into the lofty summits of secret things, unless perhaps that one man Pythagoras of mine, the father of philosophy—who, however, did not receive that excellence of doctrine from the Greeks, but rather from those very Jews.

<margin>A</margin>

Therefore, he himself was also to be called a 'Cabalist' <note>The author is arguing that the Greek philosopher Pythagoras was actually a student of Jewish mystical tradition</note> by the best right. Like someone who, after a long pilgrimage, brings back from afar something worthy of admiration to his fatherland so that the common people might more easily believe it, he was the first to change that name of 'Kabbalah,' which was unknown to his people, into the Greek name of 'Philosophy.' We correctly infer this by the argument that he left his disciples no faculty for inquiring by some reason; rather, he wanted the first principle of his

<margin>B</margin>

dogma to be that, to those asking for a cause, they should respond: 'He himself said' <note>original Greek: *αὐτὸς ἔφα* (*autos epha*). This phrase became famous as the "Ipse dixit" of the Pythagoreans, where the master's word was final</note>. This is exactly the manner of the Cabalists, who cite the reasons for knowing things in almost no other way than when they say: 'The sages said' <note>original Hebrew: *Amru Hachamim* (אמרו חכמים)</note>. Thus our famous 'He himself said.' Moreover, this is the same Pythagoras who is said to have given the name to 'Philosophy' in this way: because the highest authors of the Hebrews were called 'Hachamim' <note>Hebrew for 'Wise Men'</note> and the Greeks before him were once called 'Sophi' <note>Greek for 'Wise Men'</note>, he attempted to clothe the ancient discipline with the ornament of a new name."

# ON THE CABALISTIC ART

<margin>C</margin> Nor, indeed, should those things that Simon the Jew brought forth seem to you worthy of less praise because they were taken from an ignoble teacher of the Hebrew race—as if from barbarian <note>In the Renaissance context, "barbarian" simply referred to any people or language that was not Greek or Roman, rather than implying they were uncivilized.</note> authors—and delivered by a barbarian man. For our own Pythagoras, the greatest of all, began his first studies of the sciences together with a certain barbarian named Zoro <note>referring to Zoroaster, the legendary Persian prophet and sage</note>. He did this far outside of Greece, during the time he practiced philosophy among the Egyptians (who were then called prophets), the Chaldeans of the Assyrians, the Druids of the Gauls, the Samanaeans <note>Buddhist or Jain monks/ascetics</note> from the Bactrians, many of the Celts, the Magi among the Persians, the Gymnosophists <note>literally "naked wise men," referring to Indian ascetics</note> among the Indians, that famous Anacharsis among the Scythians, and Zamolxis in Thrace (who was previously Pythagoras’s own slave). All of this was left in writing by that famous Alexander, surnamed the Polyhistor <note>a Greek scholar from the 1st century BCE known for his vast compilations of history and geography</note>, in his book *On Pythagorean Symbols* <note>original: *περὶ πυθαγορικῶν συμβόλων* / *de Pythagoricis notis*</note>. Finally, among the Indians, there were the Jews whom they called Brahmans, as Aristobulus the Peripatetic <note>a Jewish philosopher who lived in Alexandria during the 2nd century BCE</note> records. Truly, if we may speak the truth, it has certainly never been found that Pythagoras learned anything of either divine or human matters from the Greeks or the Romans. Rather, as Antiphon published in his book *On the Life of Those Who Excelled in Virtue* <note>original: *περὶ τοῦ βίου τῶν ἐν ἀρετῆ πρωτευσάντων* / *de uita eorū qui uirtute pręstiterūt*</note>, Pythagoras went to the Egyptians, the Arabs, and the Chaldeans for the sake of learning, after he had obtained Pherecydes as his master and teacher from Syria—which is also called Judea. Because of this, he himself was then commonly called a Syrian, though others called him a Tyrian, and others a Tyrrhenian. They agree that he, the first of the philosophers, was "as a barbarian and not a Greek" <note>original: *ὥσπερ βάρβαρον ἀλλ' οὐχ' Ἕλλωνα γεγονέναι συνομολογοῦσιν ὃν πρῶτον φιλοσόφων*</note>.

I know for certain, my most learned guest Marranus, that you have read these things written in the works of Eusebius Pamphili <note>Eusebius of Caesarea, a 4th-century Christian historian</note>—in the eleventh volume, if I remember correctly, of the *Preparation for the Gospel*. He also published this: "Save only that they have nothing regarding the wise Greeks, dwelling in a poverty of wisdom and lack of experience" <note>original: *μόνον ὅτι περὶ τῶν σιφῶν ἑλλήνων ἔχοιεν οὐδὲν, πινία σοφίας καὶ ἀπειρία συνοικούντων*</note>. Regarding these matters, as it is written in Plato's *Timaeus*, a certain barbarian Egyptian—and a very old one at that—seemed to have said quite truly to Solon: "O Solon, Solon, you Greeks are always children; you have no ancient opinion, nor any discipline grey with age." 

Nor should we fail to highly praise Pythagoras, a man of outstanding wisdom and nobility, for this: that in a foreign and distant soil, he gathered through immense labor, cold, and sweat—with much commentary and meditation over not a few years—those things which he brought back on his own shoulders, so to speak, into his fatherland (specifically to Italy, which was then called Magna Graecia <note>"Great Greece," the coastal areas of Southern Italy colonized by Greek settlers</note>). I will not say these things were bettered by him, but they were certainly made more splendid. This he did to the incredible admiration of all toward himself and his followers, so much so that anyone who excelled in wisdom and learning was believed to have been a student of Pythagoras. From this, the "Italic Philosophy" primarily took its name from him. Numenius the Pythagorean <note>a 2nd-century philosopher who sought to link Plato and Pythagoras to ancient Near Eastern wisdom</note> supports this praise...

<summary>This page argues that ancient Greek philosophy, specifically that of Pythagoras, originated from "barbarian" sources including Jews, Egyptians, and Persians. It challenges the idea of Greek intellectual supremacy by citing historical authorities like Eusebius and Plato to suggest that true wisdom is much older than Greek civilization.</summary>

<page-num>XXVI</page-num>
->### BOOK TWO<-

The Pythagorean <note>likely referring to Numenius of Apamea, a 2nd-century philosopher who famously asked, "What is Plato but Moses speaking Attic Greek?"</note> says in his first volume *On the Good* that whatever the Brahmans, Magi, Egyptians, and Jews discovered, Plato and Pythagoras themselves set forth in the Greek language. On this account, we suspect most strongly that what the most learned men and those skilled in various languages assert is true: that the Jewish findings, whether accepted by tradition or newly discovered, are set forth through the thefts of others—Greeks on one side, Latins on the other—and that nothing in our philosophy is ours which was not previously the property of the Jews. This is true however much in this present age their deserved glory is stripped from them, and now all their works are despised, because the current generation desires a more illustrious and polished explanation of all fields of study.

"Then you report the truth most excellently, Philolaus," said Marranus, "which makes me agree all the more with the saying <note>original: λόγος γὰρ ἐκτ’ ἀδοξούντων ἰὼν κ᾿ ἀκ τῶν δοκούντων αὑτὸς οὐ ταυτὸν σθένει</note> from Euripides' *Hecuba*: *For the same speech, when it proceeds from those of no repute and from those of high standing, does not have the same power.* For if some Aristotle or any Theophrastus <note>Theophrastus was Aristotle’s successor as the head of the Peripatetic school of philosophy.</note> had brought forth those things which Simon taught us today, nothing in the opinion of everyone would be more worthy of hearing, nothing more weighty, and nothing more memorable. He would have added only a more even style of speaking and some veneer of eloquence. 

Now, because it is a Jew who, in his own way, has handled the whole matter a little more roughly and concisely, there is no doubt but that these things will seem filthy in the ears of those 'sophists' <note>In the Renaissance, "sophist" was often a derogatory term used by Humanists to describe the overly technical or logic-chopping medieval scholars.</note> of ours—as they see themselves, clearly very subtle—if any of them should listen or be about to listen. Or rather, to all those who now philosophize either perversely or foolishly, these things may appear entangled, clamorous, gaping, meager, and harsh, sounding of rustic bitterness and foreign strangeness. This is despite the fact that, as is their habit, they have not yet examined the matter as much as is necessary; it is as if gold were not gold simply because we find it in the mud. 

But since we have now returned by a straight path from this man to our inn without anyone needing to show us the way, and since by chance our intended dinner is not yet ready, I suggest that we each recite among ourselves what we have heard—especially the more worthy parts—and fix them in our memory so they do not slip away while everything is still fresh in our minds."

And Philolaus said, "How prudently you have pre-planned those things, Marranus! For in this way we shall approach the man better prepared to listen the day after tomorrow, after this portent of the Sabbath and the rites observed by the Jew—as Ovid says, <note>original: septima sacra uiro</note> *the seventh day sacred to the man.* <note>A quote from Ovid's *Art of Love*, referring to the Jewish Sabbath as a day when business and travel might be paused.</note> Meanwhile, you take this chair, I’ll take the other, and sitting confidently, let us speak quickly of everything until those things suitable for dinner appear. However, lest room be given to useless argument while we are alone—for that would be nothing other than a waste of time—you speak first, whatever comes to mind, whether for the sake of recording the past or commenting on the present, in whatever manner it happens."

Thus Marranus began to weave his discourse. "And although the whole business," he said, "around which we have spent our time this afternoon, seems to me, as I weigh each point precisely, to be deeper than we, lying here on the ground, can look up to, nevertheless quite often..."

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Marranus and Philolaus. # ON THE CABALISTIC ART
### BOOK TWO

First, he affirms that the knowledge of immediate principles is indemonstrable. A little later he says, "And we say that there is not only knowledge, but also a certain principle of knowledge, by which we recognize the terms." <note>Aristotle, *Posterior Analytics* 1.3 and 2.19. "Terms" refers to the basic concepts in a logical proposition.</note> Themistius <note>A 4th-century Greek rhetorician and philosopher who wrote influential paraphrases of Aristotle.</note> calls our **Mind** the principle of knowledge in that passage, and the "terms"—from which the highest axioms are composed—he calls the **subject** and the **predicate**. But Philoponus (commonly called John the Grammarian) <note>John Philoponus (c. 490–570), a Christian philosopher and commentator whose work bridged Neoplatonism and Aristotelianism.</note> explained these things in a much more sublime and truer way, writing as follows: 

The philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> handed down the explanation of the proposed saying in this way: taking the "principle of knowledge" to be the **Mind**—not our own mind, but the **Divine Mind** which is above us; and the "terms" to be the **intelligible and divine forms** themselves. Indeed, he says they are called "terms" because they are the ends <note>Greek: *perata* (limits or boundaries)</note> of all things. <note>original: ὁ μὲν φιλόσοφος τὴν ἐξήγησιν τοῦ προκειμένου ῥητοῦ οὕτως ἀπέδωκεν· ἀρχὴν μὲν ἐπιστήμης τὸν νοῦν εἴληφώς οὐ τὸν ἡμέτερον ἀλλὰ τὸν θεῖον καὶ ὑπὲρ ἡμᾶς· ὅρους δὲ τὰ νοητὰ καὶ θεῖα εἴδη . ὅρους δὲ αὐτὰ καλεῖσθαι διὰ τὸ πέρατα εἶναι πάντων.</note>

Therefore, the cognition of supernatural matters of faith depends on the **Mind**, not on **Reason**, which can err through the process of reasoning. For Aristotle writes the same thing: "It admits of falsehood, just as opinion does, and also *logismus*." <note>original: ἐπιδέχεται τὸ ψεῦδος οἷον δόξα, καὶ λογισμός</note> That is, it admits the false, just as opinion does, so too does *logismus*, which is **reasoning** (from which the word "syllogism" is derived). Finally, he concludes the *Posterior Analytics* thus: "All science," he says, "is with *logos*, that is, with **reason**. Of the principles, there will certainly not be 'science' [in the technical sense]. But since nothing happens to be more true than science except the **Mind**, it is the Mind that pertains to the principles." 

Principles are called the "first things." Hesiod and all the ancient theologians made the Gods to be the "principles"; therefore, this cognition is properly named **Divine**. And as that same Stagirite <note>Aristotle, so called because he was born in Stagira.</note> wrote in the first book of the *Metaphysics*, <note>referred to here as *postnaturalium*, a literal translation of "after the physics."</note> the possession of this is "justly not human," <note>original: δικαίως ἂν οὐκ ἀνθρωπίνη</note> because either God alone or God most of all possesses it, and it would be unworthy for a man to seek any science concerning Him. For "God alone has this honor," according to Simonides. <note>A famous Greek lyric poet.</note>

But since nothing contributes more to our happiness than the cognition of the highest and divine things, I ask you, Philolaus, by what other path must a man proceed toward them, if not by science? By what modes is such great loftiness to be grasped?

Then **PHILOLAUS** replied: "By Castor, you yourself have shown a plain and open path! For since there are five workers of cognition—according to the testimony of Ammonius, <note>Ammonius Hermiae, a 5th-century philosopher.</note> following Aristotle, who mentions only four of them in the first book *On the Soul*—these are: **Mind, Discourse, Opinion, Imagination, and Sensation**. <note>original: νοῦς. διάνοια. δόξα. φαντασία. αἴσθησις.</note> The Mind and the Senses do not use syllogisms; the one is far above reason, the other far below it. But neither does Imagination, even though it is the station of the senses and the reservoir of appearances migrating from there. Since the senses do not reason in any way...
