PAGE XXVIII

# BOOK TWO

...it should not even be thought that the appearances of the senses are capable of reasoning. Therefore, **opinion** and **discourse** will remain. But opinion is the conclusion of discourse itself; for that reason, opinion does not itself form <term>syllogisms</term> <note>A syllogism is a formal logical argument consisting of a major premise, a minor premise, and a conclusion.</note>. Thus, the faculty of forming syllogisms is left to discourse alone, which is named <term>dianoea</term> <note>Greek: *dianoia*. In Greek philosophy, this refers to the type of discursive, step-by-step reasoning used in mathematics or logic.</note>. This is the opinion of Ammonius <note>Ammonius Hermiae (c. 440–517 AD), an influential philosopher who taught in Alexandria and wrote commentaries on Aristotle’s logic.</note> in the commentaries he published on Aristotle’s *Prior Analytics*. 

And since I have briefly touched upon the list of things perceived and the ways they are perceived, so that my speech does not wander too far, I am of the opinion that **divine matters are above the syllogism**. They cannot be understood by human reason, for they do not derive their origin of knowing from the senses. Instead, they depend on pure faith, received only through love for the one revealing them, and believed for the sake of human blessedness. There are, however, many things indeed which are often mixed into divine speculation in such a way—just as freedmen and tenants of a single family are sometimes accustomed to use a common name for themselves—and those things frequently (for I confess it so) allow themselves to be handled by the faculty of theology. This is because they have obtained some order toward God, either through themselves or through a process of reduction, or perhaps by some other reason such as creation, conservation, perfection, justification, bliss, salvation, and the like. 

Indeed, I am not thinking of those things at present, because I know that those things are made known to us naturally; their demonstration is either offered in "post-natural" studies <note>The "post-natural" refers to Metaphysics, the study of things beyond the physical world.</note> as to *that* they are, or in theological studies as to *why* they are. I certainly grant reason to those things—since they once arose from the senses and are devoted to human discourse—but as for those things whose truth depends solely on the authority of the revealer, I do not think there is a "science" of them, nor would I wish the syllogism to dominate them. Instead, let there be only that which is more excellent than all: **Faith**. Whoever possesses this is called by Aristotle in his *Prior Analytics* "in a better state than one who possesses scientific knowledge" <note>original: βέλτιον διακείμενος ἢ ἐκ ἐπιστήμην εἰδὼς</note>. Philoponus explained this to mean "to know better than through demonstration."

At this, Marranus said: I agree with you, Philolaus. I also forbid those very things, which are matters of pure faith and pure belief, from being subjected to "logical snares." These are clearly more of a detriment than a gain to those who contemplate. Our own teachers, both Greek and Latin, assert the same. The great Jerome of Dalmatia <note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), the scholar and translator of the Bible into Latin.</note>, writing on the 104th Psalm, compares the art of the syllogism applied to theology to the **plagues of Egypt**, saying: "The sting of the dialectic art is understood as the *Cyniphes* <note>The "Cyniphes" (gnats or stinging flies) were the third plague of Egypt in Exodus. Jerome uses them as a metaphor for the annoying, biting nature of logical nitpicking.</note>. Although it may seem to have a small sting of seduction in reality, it nevertheless wounds human minds most grievously."

For this reason, that most learned man [Jerome]—who labels this technique as both a "vanity of the senses" and an "obscurity of the mind"—removed it entirely from Hebrew studies and rejected it. He did this often elsewhere, but most clearly to Damasus regarding the questions proposed to him, when he uses these words in the second part: "When disputing about Hebrew matters, it is not fitting to search for the arguments of Aristotle." And in the 143rd Psalm, he writes thus concerning the <term>theosophists</term> <note>In this context, theosophists refers to those who claim to have a "divine wisdom" but use it merely for empty, argumentative wordplay.</note>: "When they begin to dispute with you, their words [are thus]..."

### ON THE ART OF THE KABBALAH

First, he affirms that the science of things known immediately is indemonstrable <note>In Aristotelian logic, "immediate" truths are those so fundamental they cannot be proven by something else; they are self-evident.</note>. Shortly after, he says: "And we say that there is not only science, but also a certain principle of science, by which we recognize terms." Themistius <note>Themistius (c. 317–387 AD) was a prominent statesman and philosopher who wrote paraphrases of Aristotle.</note> calls our own mind the "principle of science" in that context, and the "terms" refer to the subject and predicate from which the greatest propositions are composed. 

But Philoponus, who is commonly called John the Grammarian <note>John Philoponus (c. 490–570 AD) was an Alexandrian Christian philosopher and scientist known for his critical commentaries on Aristotle.</note>, explained these things in a far more sublime and truer way, writing as follows: "The Philosopher [Aristotle] indeed provided the explanation of the proposed saying in this way: taking the principle of science to be the Mind—not our own, but the divine one or that which is above us—and the 'terms' to be the intellectual and divine forms; he says they are called terms because they are the boundaries of all things." <note>original Greek: "ὁ μὲν Φιλόσοφος τὴν ἐξήγησιν τοῦ προκειμένου ῥητοῦ οὕτως ἀπέδωκεν. ἀρχὴν μὲν ἐπιστήμης τὸν νοῦν ἔιληφὼς οὐ τὸν ἡμέτερον ἀλλὰ τὸν θεῖον ἢ ὑπὲρ ἡμᾶς. ὅρους δὲ τὰ νοητὰ καὶ θεῖα εἴδη, ὅρους δὲ αὐτὰ καλεῖσθαι ὡς ἂν πέρατα εἶναι πάντων."</note> 

Therefore, the knowledge of supernatural beliefs depends on the mind, not on reason, which can err through the process of ratiocination <note>Ratiocination is the process of logical, step-by-step reasoning.</note>. For Aristotle himself writes: "Falsehood is possible in things like opinion and reasoning." <note>original Greek: "ἐπιδέχεται δὲ ψεῦδος οἷον δόξα, καὶ λογισμός."</note> That is to say, it admits what is false, just as opinion does, so too does *logismos*, which is reasoning—from which the <term>syllogism</term> <note>A formal logical argument where a conclusion is drawn from two premises.</note> gets its name. Finally, he concludes the *Posterior Analytics* thus: "All science," he says, "is with *logos*, that is, with reason. Of the principles, there will certainly not be science. But since nothing happens to be truer than science except the mind, the mind will surely be the principle of the principles." 

Furthermore, "principles" are called the "first things," and Hesiod <note>An ancient Greek poet, often cited alongside Homer as a foundational "theologian" of Greek myth.</note> and all the ancient theologians made the gods to be the principles; therefore, this knowledge is properly named "divine." And as that same Stagirite <note>A common nickname for Aristotle, referring to his birthplace, Stagira.</note> wrote in the first book of the *Metaphysics*, the possession of it is "justly not human." <note>original Greek: "δικαίως ἂν οὐκ᾿ ἀνθρωπίνη"</note> That is, it is rightly not human, because either God alone or God most of all possesses it, and man is unworthy to seek any science concerning Him. For "God alone holds this honor," according to Simonides <note>Simonides of Ceos (c. 556–468 BC), a Greek lyric poet.</note>. 

But since nothing contributes more to our happiness than the knowledge of the highest and divine things, by what path, I ask you, Philolaus, must a man proceed toward them if not by science? In what ways is such great height to be grasped?

Then **PHILOLAUS** said: By Hercules! You yourself have shown a plain and open path. For since there are five "workers" of knowledge, according to the testimony of Ammonius following Aristotle (who mentions only four of them in the first book *On the Soul*). They are: <term>Mind</term>, <term>Discourse</term>, <term>Opinion</term>, <term>Imagination</term>, and <term>Sense</term>. <note>original Greek/Latin: "νοῦς (Mind), διάνοια (Discourse), δόξα (Opinion), φαντασία (Imagination), αἴσθησις (Sense)."</note> 

Mind and sense do not form syllogisms; one is far above reason, the other much below it. Nor does imagination, although it is a station for the senses and a storehouse for the images migrating from them. Since the senses are by no means capable of reasoning...

## BOOK TWO

...it must not even be thought that the appearances of the senses are able to reason. Therefore, opinion and discourse will remain; but opinion is the conclusion of discourse itself, wherefore it does not itself syllogize <note>To syllogize is to use a formal logical argument consisting of a major and minor premise and a conclusion.</note>. Thus, the faculty of syllogizing is left to discourse alone, which is called *dianoia* <term>dianoia: the Greek term for discursive or rational thought, often contrasted with direct intellectual intuition</term>. This is the opinion of Ammonius <note>Ammonius Hermiae (c. 440–517 AD) was a philosopher and commentator on the works of Aristotle.</note> in the commentaries he published on Aristotle's *Prior Analytics* <note>The source refers to these as the "first resolutions."</note>. 

And since I have briefly touched upon the enumeration of ways of comprehending and things comprehended—lest my speech wander further—I believe that divine things are above the syllogism and cannot be understood by human reason. These things do not draw the origin of their knowledge from the senses, but depend on pure faith, received only through love for the one revealing them and believed for human blessedness. Yet there are certainly many things that often intermix with divine speculation, just as the freedmen and lodgers of a single family are sometimes accustomed to use a common name for themselves; and these things—I admit—frequently allow themselves to be treated by the theological faculty because they have obtained some order in relation to God, either through themselves or through reduction, or perhaps by some other reason such as creation, conservation, perfection, justification, blessedness, salvation, and the like. 

Indeed, I do not think of those at present, because I know those things become known to us naturally, for which a demonstration is offered in "post-natural" matters <note>Metaphysics</note> as to *that they are*, or in theological matters as to *why they are*. I certainly allow reason to those things, since they once arose from the senses and were given over to human discourse; but of those things whose truth depends solely on the authority of the one revealing, I do not think there is "science" <term>scientia: in this context, certain knowledge derived from logical proof</term>, nor would I want the syllogism to dominate them. 

But only that which will be superior to all: faith. He who possesses it is called by Aristotle in the *Prior Analytics* "better disposed than if he were knowing by chance" <note>original Greek: βέλτιον διακείμενος ἢ ἐπιτύγχανον εἰδώς. This refers to a state of certain conviction that surpasses technical knowledge.</note>, which Philoponus <note>John Philoponus, the Alexandrian commentator mentioned on the previous page.</note> explained as knowing better than through demonstration. 

To this Marranus said: "I agree with you, Philolaus, and with you I also forbid those things which are of pure faith and pure belief to be subjected to logical snares, which are clearly more of a detriment than a gain to those contemplating; and our people, both Greeks and Latins, assert the same. Jerome, that Dalmatian <note>St. Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), the scholar most famous for translating the Bible into Latin (the Vulgate).</note>, writing on the 104th Psalm, compares the art of syllogizing applied to theology to the plagues of Egypt, and says: 

> The gnats <note>Latin: *Cyniphes*; referring to the third plague of Egypt in Exodus.</note> are understood as the sting of the dialectical art, which, although it seems to have a small needle of seduction in the thing itself, nevertheless wounds human minds most severely. 

For this reason, that most learned man completely removed and rejected from Hebrew studies this craft, which he nicknames both the "vanity of the senses" and the "obscurity of the mind." He did this both on many other occasions and most clearly to Damasus regarding the questions proposed to him, when in the second part he uses these words: 

> It is not fitting for one disputing about Hebrew matters to seek out the arguments of Aristotle. 

And in the 143rd Psalm, he writes thus concerning the theosophists <note>theosophists: those who seek knowledge of God through spiritual ecstasy or direct intuition rather than logic.</note>: 

> When they begin to dispute with you, thus the words...

<meta>This page continues Philolaus’s argument that divine truths exist beyond the reach of human logic. He transitions from discussing the mechanics of the "dianoia" (discursive reason) to warning against the trap of overly complex logical arguments (syllogisms) when dealing with faith.</meta>

### ON THE ART OF THE KABBALAH

...their arguments are brief, yet so enclosed in artful speech that it is difficult for you to escape them. For when they have bound you with their syllogisms and shut you in—having woven and built a syllogism for you like a stone wall—it cannot fall, and you cannot pass through. You are held trapped; there is no ruin in the wall, nor any way across. And when they have held you there, as if enclosed in a circle, then you will not be on the narrow path that leads to life, but on the broad one that leads to death. <note>original Greek: ὥστε καὶ ἡ τῆς ἁπλότητος πίστις, βελτίων ἐστὶ τῆς ἐκ πολυεργασίας πιθανολογίας</note> That is: "Thus the faith of simplicity is better than the persuasive reasoning of elaborate labor," as Athanasius <note>St. Athanasius (c. 296–373 AD) was a Greek Church Father and the main defender of Trinitarianism against Arianism.</note> said in his third book *Against the Arians*. He confirms this same point in his work *Against the Greeks*, which begins: <note>original Greek: ἡ μὲν περὶ τῆς θεοσεβείας καὶ τῆς τῶν ὅλων ἀληθείας γνῶσις, οὐ τοσοῦτον τῆς παρὰ τῶν ἀνθρώπων διδασκαλίας δεῖται, ὅσον ἀφ' ἑαυτῆς ἔχει τὸ γνώριμον</note> That is: "The knowledge of divine worship and the truth of all things does not so much require instruction from men as it possesses its own clarity within itself." So says Athanasius.

Let everyone establish for themselves that nothing is truer than this. For what eagerness for speaking or what effort at persuasion will be needed for that which I am prepared to believe of my own accord? I have already received it gladly, purely through my love and singular reverence for the one revealing it, not forced or led by even the slightest power of reason—certainly not the kind of reason that the dullness of a mind submerged and bound in this body could devise.

Justin, that Christian philosopher, treats these things much more fully in his book *On the Right Confession*, citing that ancient iambic verse: <note>original Greek: οὐδὲ γὰρ ἀνθρώποισι τῶν θείων σαφές</note> That is: "Nothing of divine things is manifest to men." This phrase also flowed from the mouth of Socrates. There is a letter of Xenophon the Socratic to Aeschines, where he says it is clear to everyone that divine things cannot be grasped by human knowledge; therefore, it is enough to worship the gods themselves piously and from the heart. What they are like is neither possible for us to find, nor is it right for us to seek. For it is not useful for servants, nor would I call it praiseworthy, if they wish to scrutinize the plans of their masters beyond what pertains to their own service.

And as the same author wrote in his *Memorabilia* concerning Socrates and the followers of other philosophers: <note>original Greek: ἐθαύμαζε δ' εἰ μὴ φανερὸν αὐτοῖς ἐστὶν, ὅτι ταῦτα οὐ δυνατὸν ἐστὶν ἀνθρώποις εὑρεῖν</note> That is: "Socrates wondered if it was not obvious to them that it is impossible for men to find these things out." This has always been the opinion of all ages and nearly all religions: that those things which were not previously in human sense-perception cannot be grasped by the human intellect. And what the intellect does not grasp, reason does not discuss. Furthermore, what reason does not discuss, that discourse of reasoning which they call <term>dianoia: the Greek term for discursive or step-by-step rational thought</term> will not judge. This is especially true of divinely revealed truth, even if we form imaginary concepts of some of those truths in our minds, so that whatever we have received religiously and piously, it [escapes] the force of argument...

XXIX

->**BOOK TWO**<-

...nor should we subject ourselves to the violence of logical investigation, or to any mental image proposed to us. Therefore, that famous Gregory of Nazianzus <note>Gregory of Nazianzus (c. 329–390 AD) was a 4th-century Archbishop of Constantinople and a "Cappadocian Father" celebrated for his eloquence and defense of the Trinity.</note>, who stands out among all our people in every kind of theological faculty, with all beauty of words and thoughts, as well as gravity, supports this teaching in a similar way. In his second book of theology, he asserts that <note>original Greek: οὐ μὴ ληπτὸν εἶναι ἀνθρωπίνῃ διανοίᾳ τὸ θεῖον, μηδὲ ὅλον ὅσον ἐστὶ φαντάζεσθαι</note> the Divine cannot be grasped by human discursive reason, nor can it be imagined in its entirety, however much one might try to visualize it.

"Lest you, Marranus, suspect me of being utterly ignorant or negligent regarding Christian matters," Philolaus replied, "I remember that Athenagoras <note>Athenagoras of Athens (c. 133–190 AD) was a philosopher and Christian apologist who wrote to the Roman Emperors to defend the faith against charges of atheism.</note>, the Athenian philosopher, said this to the emperors Marcus Aurelius Antoninus and Lucius Aurelius Commodus as an envoy on behalf of the Christians: <note>original Greek: ἐπεὶ καὶ περὶ αὐτῶν τῶν δογμάτων, οἷς προσέχομεν, οὐκ᾽ ἀνθρωπικοῖς οὖσιν, ἀλλὰ θεσφάτοις καὶ θεοδιδάκτοις πεῖσαι ὑμᾶς μὴ ὡς περὶ ἀθέων ἔχειν δυνάμεθα</note> 'Indeed, regarding the very doctrines we hold—which are certainly not human, but sent from heaven and taught by God—we can persuade you not to regard us as godless men.' Here he suggests that one is persuaded in one way concerning profane matters, and in another way concerning divine ones. 

Although I know many among you who confound everything with <term>logical inventions</term> <note>Referring to the scholastic method of using Aristotelian logic to parse theological truths.</note>, and who—treating things upside down—establish and confirm natural things by mathematical principles, and again, theological things by natural ones. But divine causes are by no means equal to natural ones; nor are natural things capable of directing the divine. Much less can those things which stand by faith alone be demonstrated by any humanly knowable reason. Just as things that are purely believed do not necessarily result in things naturally known. 

For your most excellent Dionysius the Areopagite <note>Pseudo-Dionysius was a Christian mystic whose writings blended Neoplatonism with theology; Reuchlin here links him to the "Pythagorean" tradition of hidden wisdom.</note>—whom I would not foolishly consider to be either a remnant or an embodiment of the Pythagoreans—speaks thus concerning these theological cognitions in his book *On the Divine Names*: <note>original Greek: οὐδὲν ἀκριβὴς ἐμφέρεια τοῖς αἰτιατοῖς καὶ τοῖς αἰτίοις; ἀλλ᾽ ἔχει μὲν τὰ αἰτιατὰ τὰς τῶν αἰτιῶν δεχομένας εἰκόνας, αὐτὰ δὲ αἴτια τῶν αἰτιατῶν ἐξήρηται. Ὡς περιῄρηται κατὰ τὸν τῆς οἰκείας ἀρχῆς λόγον</note> 'There is no exact resemblance between effects and their causes; but effects do indeed possess those received images of their causes, while the causes themselves are set apart from the effects, and reside above them according to the principle of their own governance.'

<margin>F</margin>

Because of this, the snare and deceptive dogma of some among you is all the more insidious: they claim that in matters consisting of things revealed by faith alone, one must not only use the specific tools of <term>syllogisms</term> <note>A syllogism is a form of reasoning where a conclusion is drawn from two given or assumed premises (e.g., All men are mortal; Socrates is a man; therefore Socrates is mortal).</note>, but also believe with equal dignity whatever follows from the sacred oracles through the artifice of logic, inferred by a necessary formal and logical consequence. For nothing is so far apart as that which is divinely revealed and that which is humanly discovered. Therefore, in the realm of pure faith and things that are purely to be believed, believing and knowing are most disparate; there, the conclusion of a syllogism can never be...

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Philolaus and Marranus. Philolaus is expanding on his argument that divine truth (faith) and human logic (reason) belong to different spheres and should not be confused or treated as having equal authority.</meta>

XIX

# ON THE CABALISTIC ART

...is more evident from the premises; for even if certain evidence is mixed into the premises, the conclusion always follows the weaker part. Therefore, we rightly affirm this: that in the same subject and regarding the same truth, the habit of acquired faith and the habit of science <term>scientia; here meaning certain knowledge gained through logical demonstration</term> generated through demonstration cannot exist together. Therefore, he who contradicts the sacred oracles contradicts faith in a disgraceful manner. 

But truly, if someone contradicts a conclusion—one collected and inferred from the revelations of the sacred oracles by human ingenuity, subtle little inventions, **Aristotelian** tricks, and the **Eleatic** discipline (of which **Zeno** was the <note>original Greek: ἐλετικῆς φιλοσοφίας ἀρχηγὸς</note> "leader of the dialectical philosophy," as Galen says), or by the snares of **Chrysippus**, or the syllogisms of the **Sophists**—that person does not contradict faith, but rather fights against human science. He is not rejecting divine illumination, but mortal industry—not in a disgraceful way, but perhaps erringly, or sometimes even perceptively, but certainly not shamefully. 

How, then, would anyone dare to affirm that what is divinely revealed and what is humanly invented should be believed with equal dignity? Only someone who is fed entirely on the **syllogism** <term>a form of logical argument where a conclusion is drawn from two premises</term>, just as an ox is fed on hay. Indeed, I ask you, what parity of dignity exists between the former and the latter? The former is a matter of faith, while the latter is a matter of knowledge. The seat of the former is the **Mind**, and of the latter, **Reason**. The former flows down from the supernal light; the latter derives its origin from the senses. 

In the region of the Mind, some things are necessary which are impossible in Reason. In the Mind, it is granted that contraries and contradictories may coincide, while in Reason they are separated by the greatest distance. It is, therefore, not entirely true that if the premises belong to faith, the conclusion will therefore belong to faith. For this proposition is disgraceful: "No creator is to be adored." Even more disgraceful is this one: "Every carved image is to be adored." In both of these, faith is blasphemed. And yet, the following conclusion is neither sacred nor a matter of faith: "No carved image is a creator," because we can demonstrate it by natural reason. Therefore, its truth does not depend on the authority of the one revealing it. Its evidence is far less than that of faith, which is believed. 

By a similar persuasion, we are deceived into thinking that because a conclusion belongs to faith, one of the premises must necessarily belong to faith. For who is ignorant of the fact that it is believed with the highest faith by the **Hebrews**, **Christians**, and **Agarenes** <note>a historical term for Muslims, referring to descendants of Hagar</note> that a carved image is not to be adored? Yet, to bring forth the assertion of this truth, I shall use natural premises: "No stone is to be adored," and "We see that a carved image is a stone." 

Then **Marranus** said: "Philolaus, you bring back to my memory the sophistical refutations of some of our people, when they say, 'The conclusion is heretical, therefore one of the premises must be.' In this matter, I wonder more than can be said that these people ever find any men who believe such things from them. But why do I try to <note>Proverbial: "to wash an Ethiopian" means to labor in vain or try to change the unchangeable.</note> wash an Ethiopian white, who can never be made bright by any effort? Furthermore, there are things which, although they are revealed, also follow from revealed things, which..."

<summary>Philolaus argues that divine revelation (faith) is superior to and distinct from human logic (reason). He demonstrates that logical conclusions about religious truths do not carry the same weight as faith itself, as reason relies on the senses while faith comes from divine light.</summary>

->### BOOK TWO<-

XXX

...if they are accepted by the believer, they will be matters of faith rather than things revealed, and knowledge rather than things inferred. Just as those things which my church commands to be believed—even if composed by whatever ingenuity—are presumed to be revealed by the Holy Spirit rather than discovered by human reason, no matter how much they are introduced with a certain syllogistic <term>syllogism: a logical argument where a conclusion is drawn from two premises</term> subtlety. So it was that the Emperor **Constantine** wrote to the church of **Alexandria** regarding the **Council of Nicaea**, saying: "For what pleased the three hundred bishops together is nothing other than the mind of God, especially since the Holy Spirit, dwelling in the minds of such and so many men, has brought the divine will to light." <note>original Greek: ὁ γὰρ τοῖς τριακοσίοις ὁμοῦ ἤρεσεν ἐπισκόποις, οὐδὲν ἐστὶν ἕτερον ἢ τοῦ θεοῦ γνώμη, μάλιστα ὅπου τὸ ἅγιον πνεῦμα τοιούτων καὶ τηλικούτων ἀνθρώπων ταῖς διανοίαις ἐγκείμενον, τὴν θείαν βούλησιν ἐξεφώτισε</note> He speaks here of bishops representing the universal church stirred by the divine spirit, not of the irregular, brainless heads of any "Polyphemuses" <note>original: polyphemorum; a reference to the one-eyed giants of myth, here implying people with a single, limited perspective</note> whatsoever. <margin>H</margin> Let them keep to their own workshop, therefore, their mixtures of syllogisms about being, about the necessary, and about the contingent, or any other possibilities or impossibilities of logical curiosity. For there is no equal comparison between a speech faithfully believed and a necessary proposition, since a "necessary" thing can be doubtful, whereas nothing is more evident than what is revealed. Therefore, let not mixtures of this kind occupy the inner shrines of the sacred, nor let them trouble the priests <term>hierophantas; initiates or priests of sacred mysteries</term>; rather, if they wish to achieve anything, let them retire to the manual trades <term>artes sellularias; literally "sedentary arts," referring to low-status manual labor</term>, or to the work of masons, or to mathematical calculations. Let them not cross the boundaries, nor touch "the unspoken and hidden tradition of the symbolic mysteries." <note>original Greek: τὴν ἀπόῤῥητον καὶ κρυφίαν μυστηρίων συμβόλων παράδοσιν</note>

"You walk straight, my friend," says **Philolaus**, "toward the obscure hiding places of **Pythagoras**—a man certainly imbued with a more divine teaching—places not to be searched out by any clever tricks of human ingenuity, which strike us with a fear of doubting rather than generating the firmness of adherence. For such great splendor of divine things cannot be seen so narrowly by our nocturnal eyes through such thin and old-womanish cracks of sophisms. Instead, there will be a need for the greatest powers of thinking and believing, <margin>G</margin> and especially, as **Terence** says, 'faith and silence.' Moved by this, **Pythagoras**—having drunk from all the disciplines in the whole world and being the first 'creditor' of philosophy—taught his disciples nothing before he taught them to be silent, as **Apuleius** wrote. For this was the first lesson of contemplative wisdom: to learn to meditate, and to unlearn how to chatter. It was as if the Pythagorean sublimity of such august majesty were much more worthy than what could be grasped by talking and babbling with childishly boasted trifles. 

Indeed, it is clear enough to us from what we received from **Simon** that **Pythagoras**, just like the rest of the **Kabbalists**, also brought this kind of teaching into **Greece**—namely, that a disciple who is about to ask about the highest question should remain silent. When questioned, however, he should only respond: "He himself said it." <note>original Greek: αὐτὸς ἔφα, Latin: Ipse dixit</note>

<summary>Philolaus argues that divine revelation and church decrees carry a divine authority that human logic cannot match. He cites Pythagoras and the Kabbalistic tradition to emphasize that the highest truths require silent contemplation and faith rather than argumentative "babbling."</summary>

Thus the Cabalists respond <term>the Sages have said <note>original Hebrew: amru hakhamim</note></term>, that is, "The Sages have said." And Christians also say to their own <term>believe <note>original Greek: pisteuson</note></term>, that is, "Believe." Then Marranus <note>A character in the dialogue representing a Jewish convert to Christianity</note> said: Perhaps you are criticizing us, Philolaus, with the same things for which the Emperor **Julian** <note>Julian the Apostate, a Roman Emperor who rejected Christianity</note> reproached us, saying, <term>Your irrationality and boorishness—which is nothing beyond that [command] "believe"—is your wisdom <note>original Greek: hymōn hē alogia kai hē agroikia, hē ouden hyper to, pisteuson, tēs hymeteras sophias</note></term>, that is: "The irrationality and rusticity of you Christians, and nothing beyond that very word 'believe,' constitutes your wisdom." **Gregory Nazianzen** <note>A 4th-century influential theologian and Church Father</note> prudently countered this insult in his first invective, noting that this is likewise the first and greatest foundation of discipline for the **Pythagoreans**: to keep silent, and then to provide no reason for what is said except <term>he himself said it <note>original Greek: autos epha; a famous reference to the absolute authority of Pythagoras over his students</note></term>. Therefore, Julian wrongly rebukes us, since <term>the Pythagorean "he himself said it" amounts to the same thing as our "believe," though in different syllables and words <note>original Greek: eis tauto hēkontos tou, autos epha, tō, par’ hēmin pisteuson, en allais syllabais te kai rhēmasi</note></term>, that is: "That phrase 'he himself said' and our 'believe' come to the same thing, though they use different syllables and words." So says Nazianzen.

We now have in our memory the unanimous way of learning used by those who have handled sacred matters more diligently than all others: namely, the <term>Cabala <note>original Hebrew: qabbalah; meaning "that which is received"</note></term> of the Cabalists, the <term>he said it <note>original Greek: epha</note></term> of the Pythagoreans, and the <term>believe <note>original Greek: pisteuson</note></term> of the <margin>H</margin> Christians. Otherwise, whatever belongs to others is not divine. Indeed, for a long time I [Philolaus] only thought that all those things flowed from the Cabala of the Hebrews; now I know it more certain than certainty, for I see clearly that whatever **Simon** <note>The Cabalist character in the dialogue</note> showed us of the **Italian philosophy** <note>Pythagoreanism is called "Italian" because Pythagoras established his school in southern Italy</note> corresponds exactly, so that I would not be wrong to judge that all things among the Cabalists and the Pythagoreans are of the same kind. For both of our studies lead back to the salvation of the human race, and they refer all beings that exist or subsist continually to the **Ideas** which truly are, and to the Idea of Ideas.

Whence both schools have asserted that there are three worlds, and a fourth infinite one, or rather a non-finite one. All things consist of three, <term>for just as the Pythagoreans say, the whole and all things are determined by threes <note>original Greek: kathaper gar phasin hoi pythagoreioi to pan kai ta panta tois trisin hōristai</note></term>, that is: "For just as the Pythagoreans say, the whole and all things are bounded by three," as **Aristotle** wrote in his books *On the Heavens*. For some things, he says, are bodies and magnitudes; others truly inhabit and observe bodies and magnitudes; and finally, others are the sovereignties and origins of those inhabitants and guardians. <margin>D</margin> I understand it thus: Since the lower world encompasses bodies and magnitudes, each with its own powers and intelligences appropriated to the movements of the spheres, and with the curators and guardians of things that are born and perish. These are said to observe bodies providently, as a province is assigned to each. Antiquity sometimes called them "powers," sometimes "angels," sometimes "gods," and also "daemons" <note>In the Renaissance context, these are guiding spirits or planetary intelligences, not necessarily "demons" in the modern evil sense</note>; or, due to their concern for the anxious matters to which they are bound, it frequently called them "demons" as well. About whom **Homer** sings: <term>the gods inhabiting Olympian homes <note>original Greek: theoi olympia dōmat’ echontes</note></term>, that is: "The gods inhabiting the Olympian dwellings," namely, those who, being set over natural things, are often disturbed by complaining affection, and being relegated from the highest to the lowest, [contemplate] the causes of their labors...

->IX<-

<margin>1</margin> ...namely, that we are endowed with an immortal and divine <term>aeon <note>From the Latin 'aevum' and Greek 'aion,' referring to an eternal or divine age/duration, often personified as a celestial being.</note></term>. From this same age, it has also been dispensed and granted to others to exist and to live—to some more clearly, to others more obscurely, as Aristotle also said. But as for what that thing is through which existence is dispensed and granted to other things (that is, inferior things) from this divine and immortal age, it is not something accidental that slipped in by chance or superficially. Rather, it is the substantive nature of every species. Certainly, the first of all the Pythagoreans, Socrates and Plato, following their teacher [Pythagoras], taught the disciples of that school this very thing. Having heard Pythagoras (who always spoke obscurely about divine matters) habitually say that the <term>Tetractys <note>The 'four-fold' number ten (1+2+3+4), which the Pythagoreans viewed as the source of all nature and the divine signature in the universe.</note></term> delivers the source of perennial nature to our souls, they then clearly understood that the Tetractys is the **Idea** in the divine mind that delivers, the source is the **exemplary Idea** delivered, and the perennial nature is the **essential Idea** of things received.

Therefore, as Alcinous <note>A Middle Platonist philosopher whose 'Handbook of Platonism' was a key source for Renaissance scholars.</note> testifies, they spoke in this manner: <note>original Greek: ἔστι δὲ ἡ ἰδέα ὡς μὲν πρὸς θεὸν, νόησις αὐτοῦ, ὡς δὲ πρὸς τὸν αἰσθητὸν κόσμον, παράδειγμα ὡς δὲ πρὸς αὐτὴν ἐξεταζομένη, οὐσία</note> "The Idea is, in relation to God, His thought; in relation to the sensible world, a pattern; and examined in relation to itself, an essence." This is just like the voice of one speaking, as it is found in the [Pseudo-Dionysius] the **Areopagite**; although it is one and the same, it is perceived as one by many ears. For the voice is first in the speaker, second in the vocality [the sound in the air], and third in any listener. 

Just as in the sensible world the prior sphere always influences all those following it, so in the intellectual world we believe not only that the higher choirs influence all the lower choirs, but also that the entire higher world influences the entire lower world. In this way, all things—according to their capacity and as much as is possible—may be led back from the momentary to the eternal, and from the lowest to the highest. 

Yet nothing of mere creatures can be led back to the third world; for nothing is capable of such sublimity by its own nature except God. But I say that this third world, the super-supreme, containing all other worlds, belongs to the Deity alone and consists of a single divine essence. It seems to me quite rightly named the <note>original Greek: παντοκρατορικὴ ἕδρα</note> **seat of the Almighty**, located—or rather, existing—above every age and every century. For it is the century of centuries, <note>original Greek: ὑπάρξεως. ὑποστάσεως. οὐσίας. φύσεως, ὀντότητος καὶ ἑνότητος προοῦσα</note> pre-existing existence, substance, essence, nature, entity, and unity. This is what our **Pythagoras** called it, and **Parmenides** the Pythagorean as well, both with a similar reasoning: <note>original Greek: ὅτι τὸ ὑπερούσιον, ἕν. καὶ τὸ ὄν, ἕν</note> "that the super-essential is one, and Being is one." 

But let no one be so hateful of antiquity or such a despiser of our ancestors that they would think the great and wise Pythagoras was seized by such old-womanly madness as to think that the numbers on an abacus, or the dice of children with which they cast the "four vultures," or the counters of merchants and other things of that kind were...

...one <note>The text here continues from the previous page, likely referring to the "One" as the first principle.</note> principles of all things, which not only do not preside over things, but even happen according to things. Rather, he wanted it to be understood as the essentially and simply **One**, from which, and out of which, and through which, and in which, and toward which all things are, and are ordered, and remain, and are contained, and are filled, and are turned back. This same thing is the first **One** and the first **Being**, which Aristotle testifies in the second book of his <term>Metaphysics <note>Original: "postnaturalia." This refers to Aristotle's "Metaphysics," literally the books "after the physics."</note></term> in these words: <note>original Greek: "πάντων μὲν γὰρ καὶ πυθαγόρειοι οὐκ' ἑτερόν τὶ τὸ ὅν, οὐδὲ τὸ ἓν: ἀλλὰ αὐτῶν τὴν φύσιν εἶναι, ὡς οὔσης τῆς οὐσίας ταὐτὸ, καὶ τῶ ἓν εἶναι καὶ τῶ ὅν."</note> *That is, for Plato and the Pythagoreans, Being itself and the One itself are not something else, but this is their very nature, as if the essence were the same as being one and being.* Indeed, that famous Xenophanes, the teacher of Parmenides and a contemporary of Pythagoras—although it was the custom of those men to hide everything—still seemed to explain most clearly to us what they understood that **One** to be, of which they spoke in the principles of things.

He said, moreover, that this **One** is **God**, by which the secrets of Pythagoras are more clearly revealed to us when he established that the infinite, the one, and number are the first principles of things. By "the infinite," he signified nothing other than **Power** itself <note>original Latin: "ipsum posse." In Renaissance philosophy, this refers to the absolute potentiality or "ability-to-be" that resides in God.</note>; for no one has ever even thought of anything prior to **Power** itself, which is most infinite in God—indeed, God himself is the infinite, in whom "to be" and "to be able" are not separated. This Power contains the essences, virtues, and operations of all and each producible thing, with all the connected differences and unions of properties and accidents. Furthermore, Anaxagoras also agrees with Pythagoras in this matter; <term>Eusebius Pamphili <note>An early Christian historian (c. 260–339 AD) whose "Preparation for the Gospel" sought to show that Greek philosophy prepared the way for Christianity.</note></term> is the authority that before these men, none of the Greeks had any knowledge of God.

For Anaxagoras said, "Since all things were together." And Democritus said, "All things were together in potentiality," <note>original Greek: "δυνάμει"</note> that is, in **Power** itself. This is also that "mixture" or commingling of things spoken of by Empedocles and Anaxagoras; yet it was by no means confused in some <term>Chaos <note>The formless state preceding the creation of the universe in Greek mythology.</note></term>, Night, or Erebus of Hesiod or Aristophanes. Rather, it was distinct in the full light of the deity, and ordered in the innermost sanctuary of that infinite light. However, if Hesiod is understood fairly, he certainly established that Chaos, Night, and Darkness are not the principles of things, but arose from principles. For he brought this forth in his *Theogony*: <note>original Greek: "ἠ ἀρχῆς καὶ ὅπερ ὅτι πρῶτον γενετ' αὐτῶν. ἤτοι μὲν πρώτιστα χάος γένετο."</note> Then it follows: <note>original Greek: "ἐκ χάεος δ' ἔρεβόσ τε μέλαινά τε νὺξ ἐγένοντο"</note> *That is, from the beginning, if ever any of them was first made, certainly first Chaos was made. From Chaos, however, Erebus and black Night were born.*

Aristophanes, however, wrote differently in *The Birds*: <note>original Greek: "χάος ἦν καὶ νὺξ ἔρεβόσ τε μέλαν πρῶτον"</note> *That is, Chaos existed, and Night and black Erebus first.* But he fashions this poetically in the manner of the Muses, alluding to his birds, so that Love could hatch from an egg; and at the same time he plays the parasite to Orpheus in the *Argonautica*, who felt similarly. Therefore, by repeating this same thing again and again, I should remember,

->### ON THE ART OF THE KABBALAH<-

...namely, us, foreordained for an immortal and divine age <note>The author uses "aeon" (age) here to refer to eternity or the divine realm.</note>. From that same age, being and life have also been distributed and granted to others—to some more clearly, to others more obscurely, as Aristotle likewise said. But as for what that thing is through which existence is distributed and granted—by this divine and immortal being to other things, that is, to lower things—and that it is not something fallen in by chance, in passing, or superficially, <margin>i</margin> but is a substantive likeness of each species: certainly the first of all, the Pythagoreans, and then Socrates and Plato following their teacher, taught the disciples of that school. Having heard that Pythagoras always spoke obscurely about divine matters, saying he was accustomed to state that the **Tetractys** <term>Tetractys <note>A mystical symbol of ten points arranged in a triangle, which the Pythagoreans used to represent the organization of the universe and the four elements.</note></term> handed down to our soul the fountain of perennial nature, they then clearly understood that the **Tetractys** is the **Idea** in the divine mind which hands it down; that the fountain is the **exemplary Idea** handed down; and that the perennial nature is the **essential Idea** of things received.

Therefore, as Alcinous <note>A Middle Platonist philosopher who summarized Platonic teachings.</note> testifies, they spoke in this manner: *The Idea is, in relation to God, His cognition; in relation to the sensible world, a model; but considered in relation to itself, essence.* <note>original Greek: "ἔστιν ἡ ἰδέα ὡς μὲν πρὸς θεὸν, νόησις αὐτοῦ, ὡς δὲ πρὸς τὸν αἰσθητὸν κόσμον, παράδειγμα ὡς δὲ πρὸς αὑτὸν ἐξεταζομένη, οὐσία"</note> This is like the voice of one speaking, as it appears in the works of the <term>Areopagite <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, an early Christian theologian whose works blended Neoplatonism with Christianity.</note></term>; though it is one and the same, it is perceived as one by many ears. For the voice is first in the speaker, second in the vocalization, and third in each listener. Just as in the sensible world a higher sphere always flows into all those following it, so in the intellectual world we believe not only that individual higher choirs <note>Orders or groupings of intellectual or angelic beings.</note> flow into all lower choirs, but indeed that the entire higher world flows into the entire lower world, so that all things—to the extent of their capacity—may be led back from the momentary to the eternal, and from the lowest to the highest. 

Yet nothing merely of the creatures can be led back to the third world, for nothing is capable of such sublimity by its own nature except God. And yet that third world, I say—that most supreme world containing all other worlds—belongs to the Deity alone and consists of a single divine essence. It seems to me quite rightly named the **all-ruling seat** <note>original Greek: "παντοκρατορικὴ ἕδρα"</note>, or rather, the almighty seat situated—no, existing—above every age and above every era. For it is the era of eras, **pre-existing existence, substance, essence, nature, being, and unity.** <note>original Greek: "ὑπάρξεως. ὑποστάσεως, οὐσίας. φύσεως, ὀντότητος καὶ ἑνότητος προοῦσα"</note> This is what our Pythagoras called the **One**, as did Parmenides the Pythagorean; both for a not dissimilar reason held **that the super-essential is one, and being is one.** <note>original Greek: "ὅτι τὸ πρῶτον, ἕν. καὶ τ’ ὄν, ἕν"</note> 

But let no one be so hateful toward antiquity or such a despiser of his ancestors as to wish to think that the great and wise Pythagoras was seized by such grandmotherly madness as to think that the numbers of an abacus, or children’s dice with which they might throw "four vultures" <note>A "vulture" (vultorius) was a specific high-scoring throw in ancient Roman and Greek dice games.</note>, or the counting-stones of merchants and other things of that sort...

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the "One" as the ultimate principle of reality. It moves from the definition of the Idea to the historical consensus among ancient philosophers—including Plato, Pythagoras, and the Pre-Socratics—that the "One" and "Being" are identical and reside in God.</meta>

-># SECOND BOOK <-

...as the principles of all essences, which not only precede things, but also occur according to the nature of those things. Rather, he intended it to be understood as the essentially and simply **One**, from which, out of which, through which, in which, and toward which all things exist, are ordered, remain, are contained, are fulfilled, and are returned. This "One" is the same as the "First Being," which Aristotle testifies to in his *Metaphysics* <note>original: "postnaturalia," a literal translation of the Greek "Metaphysics," referring to the books following the "Physics."</note> with these words: <note>original Greek: "πλάτων μὲν γὰρ καὶ πυθαγόρειοι οὐχ᾿ ἕτερον τὸ ὄν, οὐδὲ τὸ ἕν, ἀλλὰ τὴν αὐτῶν τὴν φύσιν εἶναι, ὡς οὔσης τῆς οὐσίας ταὐτὸ, τὸ ἕν εἶναι."</note> *For Plato and the Pythagoreans, "being" and "the one" are not something different from one another; rather, this is their very nature, as if essence and being one were the same thing.* That is to say, Plato and the Pythagoreans did not consider "being itself" and "the one itself" to be anything other than their own nature, just as the "one" and "a certain being" are the same for an existing essence. 

Certainly, the famous Xenophanes <note>A pre-Socratic philosopher known for his early monotheism.</note>, the teacher of Parmenides and a contemporary of Pythagoras, although it was the custom of those men to hide everything in mystery, nevertheless seemed to explain to us very clearly what they understood "the one itself" to be when they spoke of the principles of things. For he said that "the one" is God. Through this, the secrets of Pythagoras are more clearly revealed to us when he established that the **infinite**, the **one**, and **number** are the first principles of things. 

By "the infinite," he signified nothing other than **Power** <term>Power <note>original: "posse." In this philosophical context, "posse" (to be able) refers to the divine potentiality or the absolute capacity of God to bring things into existence.</note></term> itself. For no one could ever even think of anything prior to "being able" (*posse*) itself, which is most truly infinite in God; indeed, God is the infinite itself. In Him, "to be" (*esse*) and "to be able" (*posse*) are not separated, for He contains the essences, virtues, and operations of all producible things and every individual thing, along with all the connecting differences and unions of properties and accidents. 

Furthermore, Anaxagoras agrees with Pythagoras on this matter; Eusebius Pamphili <note>A 4th-century Christian historian and bishop.</note> is the authority for the claim that before these men, no Greeks possessed any knowledge of God. For Anaxagoras said, "Since all things were together." And Democritus said, "All things were together in potentiality," clearly meaning <note>original Greek: "δυνάμει"</note> **in potentiality**, that is, in "power" (*posse*) itself. This is also that "mixture" or mingling of things spoken of by Empedocles and Anaximander. However, it was by no means confused in some "Chaos," "Night," or "Erebus" <note>Erebus: A primordial deity representing deep darkness or the underworld.</note> as in Hesiod or Aristophanes, but was distinct in the full light of the deity, and ordered in the inmost sanctuary of infinite light. 

Yet, if Hesiod is understood fairly, he certainly established that Chaos, Night, and darkness are not the *principles* of things, but rather arose *from* the principles. For he declared this in his *Theogony*: <note>original Greek: "ἐξ ἀρχῆς καὶ πρῶτ᾿ ὅτι πρῶτον γένετ’ αὐτῶν. ἤτοι μὲν πρώτιστα χάος γένετο."</note> *From the beginning, and whatever was the first of them to be born: surely first of all Chaos came to be.* Then follows: <note>original Greek: "ἐκ χάεος δ’ ἔρεβός τε μέλαινά τε νὺξ ἐγένοντο."</note> *And from Chaos, Erebus and black Night were born.* That is: *From the principle, and if ever any of them was first made, surely Chaos was made first. But from Chaos, Erebus and black Night were born.* 

Aristophanes, however, wrote differently in *The Birds*: <note>original Greek: "χάος ἦν καὶ νὺξ ἔρεβός τε μέλαν πρῶτον."</note> *Chaos was, and Night, and black Erebus first.* But he fashions this poetically in the manner of the Muses, alluding to his "birds" so that Love might hatch from an egg; at the same time, he plays the flatterer to Orpheus in the *Argonautica*, who felt similarly. For this reason, let me remember this same point by repeating it again and again...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "One" (God) and how all things exist within the divine mind as "Ideas." <page-num>IX</page-num>
# ON THE CABALISTIC ART

...all and each individual thing are possible in that very power, not in confusion, not in chaos, not in the darkness of the underworld, nor in the gloom of night, but distinctly and orderly in full light. That is to say, they exist in that very luminous and most brilliant clarity of all the most radiant rays, and in the intuitive knowledge and cognition of the illustrious and illuminating divine essence. This is called **Idea** by the most ancient philosophers with the best justification, from the Greek <term>to see and to know</term> <note>original: "ἐκ τ' ίδω, & γινώσκω"</note>. This "possibility of being," since it encompasses all things—mental, rational, intelligible, sensible, vital, substantial, those capable of adhering, and those that are inherent—not only of those things that are, but also of those which are not, could then truly be called the *Infinite* by <term>Pythagoras</term>. This was also called by the wisest men <term>to have infinite power</term> <note>original: "ἀπειροδύνασθαι"</note>, because it is itself infinite and encompasses infinite things within one and the same infinite and essential **Idea**. For nothing either was, is, or will be in the supercelestial, celestial, earthly, corporeal, or incorporeal realms—among angels, men, beasts, plants, or in the entire nature of the universe—that is not "possible," or, to speak grammatically, "able." From this, all things proceed, and this is the <term>infinitely powerful and almighty power-producing power</term> <note>original: "ἀπειροδύναμος καὶ πανροδύναμος δυναμοποιὸς δύναμις"</note>, which is nothing other than the divine essence, within which, before all things, the **One** produces the **Two**.

Here you have, <term>Marranus</term> <note>One of the characters in this dialogue, representing a Muslim perspective.</note>, the whole of my <term>Pythagoras</term>. Two is the first number, but One is the principle of number. If you believe <term>Xenophanes</term> <note>A pre-Socratic philosopher who argued for the unity of God.</note>, as you heard before, that "One" is God; and since the production of the Two remains within the divine essence—for number constitutes itself, according to the Peripatetic author <term>Boethius</term> <note>A 6th-century philosopher; "Peripatetic" refers to the school of Aristotle.</note>—and since only the "Two" <note>the binary</note> naturally follows the "One," then those Two must also necessarily be God, since within God, there is nothing but God. Therefore, since these three things are the principle and the first, and do not depart from the one essence of God, they are clearly **one God**. For the essence is not split by the fact that Two produced from One are counted, just as it often happens in corporeal things that a unity moved into a duality—if the comparison may be pardoned—progresses all the way to a trinity while the substance of the things remains the same: as with a tree trunk and its shoots, or more aptly, as with a human body, an arm, and a finger. 

Thus, from the One producing in divine matters and the Two produced, a **trinity** arises. If the essence, which is formally distinct from them, is added to these things, there will be a **formal quaternary** <note>a set of four</note>, which is the infinite, the one, and the number of two. This is the substance, perfection, and end of all number. For one, two, three, and four, in a collective progression, make **ten**, and beyond ten there is nothing. <note>1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10. In Pythagorean thought, 10 represents the completion of the number system.</note> For this reason, <term>Pythagoras</term> understood that there is a certain principle of all things, which he named the <term>Tetractys</term>. For *tetras* in Greek is a quaternary (fourness), and *actys* is the form of the sun, or a ray. From such formality—though it is now beyond-substantial—my own mind constitutes one illustrious name of the quaternary, as if consisting of four things formally distinct among themselves.

### BOOK TWO

And so that he might separate the sacred from the profane, he wrote the holy name with an *ypsilon* <note>original: "y"</note> for the best of reasons, whereas the word for "ray" <note>original: "ἀκτὶς"</note> is commonly written with an *iota* <note>original: "i"</note>. Furthermore, he himself also presented the **Tetractys** <term>the Pythagorean name for the number four, viewed as a divine source of nature</term> as a certain god in this passage, specifically using the masculine gender. This follows the custom of the ancient Latins who pronounced *Cupid* or *Venus* as masculine, even though in other contexts they speak of the instrumental number of the "four-fold" itself as *Tetractys* in the feminine gender. He wished to show that this was the god by whom he swore the oath: "No, by the Tetractys!" <note>original: "μὰ τὸν τερακτὺν"</note>, than which nothing should be considered more worthy of veneration. For as **Aristotle** says, "An oath is a most honorable thing" <note>original: "ὅρκος δ' τιμιώτατόν ἐστιν"</note>. I certainly will not agree with **Hierocles** <note>a 5th-century Neoplatonist commentator</note> on this point, as I believe **Pythagoras** himself wrote the *Golden Verses*. Yet I would equally wish, out of reverence for its wondrous holiness, that the *Tetractys* were named in the Roman tongue not as a "four-fold" or "four-ness," but with a changed voice as a "quaternio" or "quaternitudo." You see this same practice observed among us Christians, separating the sacred from the usage of the profane commoners. For while "threeness" or "triad" <note>original: "ternus & ternitas"</note> might be read popularly, you call the most holy hypostasis by the name **Trinity** <note>original: "trinitatem"</note>, as if it were a "unity of three," borrowing a letter from the word "one" <note>original: "uno"</note> because of the united nature of the individual persons. But to call a retreat: I say that the **Tetractys**, the **Pythagorean** principle, is a certain single supreme reality of all things.

Then **Marranus** said: I recall from this example of **Philolaus** <note>a student of Pythagoras</note> that most beautiful four-letter "character" <note>original: "charagma"</note>, in which the entire salvation of the human race is present. **Simon** confirmed this to us with such an abundance of scriptural evidence, where it seemed to me that **Pythagoras** did not do badly to change the Jewish **Tetragrammaton** <term>the four-letter name of God, YHWH</term>—or rather the four letters from which the name of the **Savior** is composed—into the Greek symbol of the **Tetractys**.

Immediately then, **Philolaus** spoke: I have certainly not yet departed satisfied by that Tetragrammaton and that "salvation" to which **Simon** has reduced almost the entire human race. Therefore, when I return to him, I will seek more extensive answers about these matters if he is willing—especially concerning that man who is to bring salvation to each of us, as if he were the anointed king of all things, and is therefore called the **Messiah**. But I would like you to see whether it might be **Esculapius** <note>Asclepius, the god of medicine</note> coming into this world again, perhaps through <term>transanimation</term> <note>the migration of a soul from one body to another; reincarnation</note> as they say. Concerning him, the Emperor **Julian** <note>Julian the Apostate, who opposed Christianity</note> writes as follows in his second book *Against the Galilaeans*:

He appeared in human form around Epidaurus <note>a Greek city famous for its sanctuary of Asclepius, the god of healing</note>; his success grew there and eventually spread across the entire world, extending his healing right hand to restore souls that were poorly disposed and bodies that were weak. If he had possessed a name composed of those four letters <note>referring to the Tetragrammaton, the four-letter name of God</note>, with any other reading character added, he would truly have been considered the Savior himself. Or certainly, how great was that **Hercules**, the son of Alcmene born of the divine seed of Jupiter, whom the people of Thasos <note>an island in the northern Aegean Sea</note> named "Savior" and inscribed on their public coins as: **Hercules, Savior of the Thasians** <note>original Greek: "ἡρακλους σωτῆρος θασίων"</note>. I recently turned over and back with these fingers of mine an ancient silver coin of this kind, struck in the old style, with that incredible pleasure I usually feel toward ancient things. From this, I reasonably conjectured that by the voice and consent of all, Hercules was placed among the gods and proclaimed a savior. 

Aside from these, there is no doubt that there were many others who brought aid to mortals as saviors, among whose number we recall King **Ptolemy** of Egypt, who bore the name **Soter** <term>the Greek word for "Savior"</term>. For the Romans, **Curtius** himself restored the land to safety by his own death <note>referring to Marcus Curtius, who leaped into a chasm to save Rome</note>, and the two **Decii** <note>a father and son who both sacrificed themselves in battle for Rome</note> bravely sacrificed their own lives to preserve the fatherland—wondrous authors of the common salvation.

Then **Marranus** <note>one of the characters in this dialogue</note> said: "I would gladly interrupt to advise you to observe more clearly and understand more fairly what was passed down to us by **Simon** <note>Simon ben Jochai, the fictionalized Jewish sage in this text</note>. He used to say it was what is called the 'universal restoration' of the human race after the primordial fall, which is named **salvation**. This salvation would be given by a just and peaceful man, a heroic man, whose name would contain four letters <note>likely referring to the four-letter name of God incorporated into the name of the Messiah</note> in its mercies. We ourselves, freeing ourselves from all secular business, ought to freely strive to ascend through all suitable steps and migrate into him, each according to his own strength. All our acts are to be formed toward this, all contemplation directed here; here all the sacred scripture of the Jews should tend. For us, scripture can be like **Jacob’s ladder** <note>the ladder seen in a vision by the patriarch Jacob (Genesis 28:12)</note>, set upon the earth and with its top touching the heavens. Through it, we transcend this bodily world and reach into the other, angelic world, even to the very soul of that **Messiah** the Savior. This soul is the rest and satisfaction of all souls to be saved, and the final end beyond which we cannot progress, since it terminates at the highest dwelling of the supreme world and communicates with the 'super-supreme' world—or, if the grammarians permit the word, the *most supreme* <note>original: "supremissimo"</note>—rather...

...incomparable, in short, that this is the eternal salvation of all mankind, made complete by the gathering together of every good thing. For you should consider what many others have felt about your **Asclepius** <note>The Greek god of healing</note>. They assert that he was born from a shameful, incestuous union with **Coronis**, a charming young woman of whom it is sung: *In all of Thessaly, there was no one more beautiful than Coronis of Larissa.* They say the priests in the temple of Apollo often subdued and overpowered her, and then they fabricated the story that the Asclepius born from their adulterous embraces was the son of the God worshiped in that place. 

Furthermore, **Apis the Egyptian**—who first brought the art of medicine to Greece and was such a distinguished temple-dweller of that age that he was worshiped as a god in temples even after death—was led by a singular favor toward the priests of Apollo. He took the infant Asclepius to be nourished and instructed. He later entrusted him to his former disciple, **Chiron the Centaur**, a most skilled physician, so that he might pour the art of healing and protecting the body into Asclepius. 

Having done this, Asclepius grew into a man of great fame and wealth. However, he was then driven by greed and a desire for honor; he traveled through different regions of the world to scrape together money through his medical art. Now abounding in great riches and possessed of immense fame, he foolishly called himself a God, promising not only health to the sick, but even life once again to the dead. For this pride, he paid the penalty to **Jupiter** <note>The king of the gods</note>, for he perished after being struck by a lightning bolt. 

Indeed, that Pythagorean, **Pindar**, sang of Asclepius in his third Pythian ode: <term>Jupiter, casting with both hands, suddenly snatched the breath from his heart, and the blazing thunderbolt inflicted death</term> <note>original Greek: "χερσὶ δ' ἄρα κρονίων ῥίψας δι’ ἀμφοῖν, ἀμπνοὰν στέρνων καθεῖλεν ὠκέως, αἴθων δὲ κεραυνὸς ἐνέσκιψε μόρον"</note>. In this same vein, the poet **Euripides** portrays a complaining Apollo mourning the death of his son Asclepius: <term>For Zeus was the cause, killing my son Asclepius by casting a flame into his chest</term> <note>original Greek: "ζεὺς γὰρ κατακτὰς παῖδα τὸν ἐμὸν αἴτιος ἀσκληπιὸν στέρνοισιν ἐμβάλλων φλόγα"</note>.

-># ON THE ART OF THE KABBALAH<-

...not to admit to the virtues of others, but even to curse them. It was not enough for you, as I see it, and for those like you, to argue that the best men—who were famous for virtue in their own age and whom antiquity raised to the status of gods for their outstanding deeds—are not gods, unless you also turn them into hellish devils. In this, you have imitated your **Lactantius** <note>Lactantius (c. 250 – c. 325) was an early Christian advisor to Constantine who wrote the *Divine Institutes* to criticize pagan philosophy and religion.</note>, who wrote as follows in the tenth chapter of his first book to the Emperor Constantine:

> **Asclepius** himself, born not without the crime of Apollo, did nothing else worthy of divine honors except for healing **Hippolytus** <note>Hippolytus was brought back to life by Asclepius; this act of defying death angered Zeus, who then struck Asclepius down with a thunderbolt.</note>. He certainly had a more famous death, in that he deserved to be struck by lightning by God.

So he wrote. But every tongue that is infected with gall lacks a true sense of taste. Yet he admits that it is a thing worthy of divine honor to bestow health, a fact which every sick person acknowledges. But if Lactantius did not know what else Asclepius had done, let him ask **Socrates**, the wisest of men. Socrates knew that a cock should be offered to Asclepius, as is recorded in Plato’s *Phaedo*. He did this not so that his body might be healed—for he had already been sentenced to death and had drunk the poison—but so that he might return his soul, as he was peacefully dying, with joy, jubilation, and a song of praise to his father Apollo. By Apollo, he meant the primary and incorporeal **Sun**, the dispenser of eternal life. 

For the cock is sacred to Apollo-Phoebus, who is called the Sun, as the joyful herald of the hours and the day. Indeed, Asclepius was called by the ancients the "jubilation of Apollo," his victory and triumph, which is termed a **Paean** <note>original: "pæan". A *paean* was a song of triumph or thanksgiving, specifically associated with Apollo as a healer.</note>, because they named it for the pause, cessation, and rest that comes after liberation. In that age, it was the custom to enter into battle first for **Mars**, and after the fight, the victors would return a *paean* to Apollo. 

Therefore, let the right judgments of the most learned men see how aptly Socrates, on the verge of death, worshipped the Sun as the giver of life through Asclepius (who is the *paean*). He surely judged it worthy and a duty for every good man to offer to Asclepius—that is, to celebrate a *paean*—when the great serpent of this world, **Python** <note>The monstrous serpent slain by Apollo; symbolically, the struggle of life or the corruption of the material world.</note>, has been conquered and trampled underfoot, and a journey is quickly taken through death toward the true life. Thus **Orpheus**, the most ancient of poets and a contemporary of those gods (for he is said to have sailed with the sons of Tyndareus and **Hercules**), sang in his hymns:

> Healer of all, Lord Asclepius, the Paean, come, blessed savior, granting a good end to life.
<note>original Greek: "ἰητὴρ πάντων ἀσκληπιὲ δέσποτα παιάν, ἔλ- θὲ μάκαρ σωτὴρ βιοτῆς τέλος ἐσθλὸν ὀπάζων"</note>

The Emperor **Julian** <note>Julian "the Apostate" (r. 361–363), the last pagan Roman Emperor.</note> asserted that he knew many people who had been helped by Asclepius in the greatest dangers, and he himself confessed that while suffering severely, he had often escaped to safety through Asclepius's healing, citing **Jupiter** as a witness to this. 

"But what does this have to do with the whole world?" **Marranus** replied, "the one whose Messiah is proclaimed as the Savior, not just of bodies, but of souls?" 

To this **Philolaus** said: "Indeed, Marranus, what about Hercules? Was he not a molder of character and a teacher of every noble discipline in all places of the world? From this comes that most ancient and indeed lifelike image of Hercules among the **Celts** <note>Referring to the "Gallic Hercules" or Ogmios, who was depicted leading men by chains of gold and amber attached from his tongue to their ears, symbolizing the power of eloquence and education.</note>, where he...

LXXXI

# ON THE CABALISTIC ART

the fourth of the *Verrines* <note>referring to Cicero’s famous legal orations against the corrupt governor Verres</note>. But this has nothing to do with this place, where we are treating the true salvation of men, which those figures did not provide. For true salvation is eternal permanence, which exists in God and is granted by God. As **Aristotle** wrote to **Alexander** in the book *On the Universe* <note>original: *De Mundo*; a treatise historically attributed to Aristotle, though now often considered pseudo-Aristotelian</note>: "From God," he says, "and through God all things consist for us, and no nature is self-sufficient if it lacks that salvation which comes from Him." Then he adds: **in essence, for he is indeed truly the savior of all things** <note>original Greek: τῆ γε οὐσία, σωτὴρ μὲν γὰρ ὄντως ἁπάντων ἐστὶν</note>; that is, God is the savior of all things by his very essence, or essentially. Wherefore, in the fourteenth book of the *Metaphysics* <note>original: *postnaturalia*, literally "the things after the natural," a common Renaissance term for Aristotle's *Metaphysics*</note>, Aristotle says again: **It is a wonder if in the first and eternal and most self-sufficient being, this very thing does not exist as a primary good, namely self-sufficiency and salvation** <note>original Greek: θαυμαστὸν δ’ εὶ τῷ πρώτῳ ἀἰΐδιῳ καὶ αὐταρκεστάτῳ τοῦτ’ αὐτὸ δ’ πρώτῳ οὐχ’ ὡς ἀγαθὸν ὑπάρχει δ’ αὐταρκὲς καὶ ἡ σωτηρία</note>. By this we are advised that our true salvation consists in the first, eternal, and most sufficient Good, which is God the Best and Greatest, and it is not to be sought elsewhere.

For only that supreme Architect and ruler of the world, out of the most merciful will of his super-eminent liberality, can give incorruption to corruptible things, eternity to those subject to time, and indissoluble permanence to transitory things—even though it is the proper nature of such things to die after being born and to grow old after increasing. For thus speaks God in the *Timaeus* of **Plato**: "The things made by me are indissoluble if I so will; otherwise, everything that is bound together is indeed dissolvable." Behold, we receive testimony not only from the Peripatetics <note>followers of Aristotle</note>, but even from Plato himself and the Platonists, that permanence is granted to any things according to their capacity solely by the will of God, and this is true salvation. 

For we are said "to be saved" when we are preserved from harm so that things may remain in tranquility. The magnificent and most distinguished legates of the Greeks once explained this with unanimous consent in the year of the birth of JESUS, 1438, at the universal **Council of Basel** <note>a major ecclesiastical council where attempts were made to reunify the Roman Catholic and Eastern Orthodox churches</note>, in a certain illustrious and most eloquent speech, saying in these words: **For to be saved and to be preserved and salvation itself, simply mean nothing else among the Greeks and in our language than to remain and to be** <note>original Greek: τὸ γὰρ σωθῆναι καὶ σώζεσθαι καὶ ἡ σωτηρία ἁπλῶς οὐδὲν ἄλλο παρὰ τοῖς ἕλλησι & τῇ ἡμετέρα βούλεται γλώττῃ, ἢ τὸ διαμένειν εἶναι</note>. 

Therefore, men who are by their nature subject to death—so that they would cease to be—are rightly said to have achieved salvation when they conform themselves to the will of God so that they will be immortal and enjoy a blessed age. And He who grants them that blessedness of immortality is rightly called a **Savior** (*Salvator*). This is a term that the descendants of **Cicero** <note>referring to later Latin writers and Christian theologians who expanded the classical Latin vocabulary</note> adopted for use, though it was previously unheard of, so that now "Savior" can be said in Latin. Truly, every other kind of "salvation" is named improperly and imaginatively. For what of it? If a doctor confers health upon a brute animal today, and the day after tomorrow it relapses into plague and dies, never to return, shall that be called "salvation"? What of that, which

XXXVI

# BOOK TWO

M

If a gardener helps a wilting flower that is destined to fall tomorrow and be ground into dust, should this three-day preservation of a fleeting thing be called "salvation"? In this way, **Hercules** once helped the people of **Thasos**, whereby he is said to have given them salvation—yet they died frequently afterward, and today nothing remains of them but their name. Thus **Ptolemy** saved Egypt, which was later devastated by so many wars and enemy incursions. Thus the **Decii** <note>A famous Roman family known for sacrificing their lives in battle to save the Republic</note> liberated Rome, yet it was nonetheless demolished in a subsequent overthrow and fire.

Believe me, all salvation that is broken by time is imperfect; perfect is that which makes the fragile eternal. As **Apollo** taught concerning **Helen**, who was snatched away from death in **Euripides'** *Orestes*, when he says: **"It is she whom you see in the folds of the air, saved and not dead by your hand. I saved her."** <note>original Greek: ἥδ' ἐστὶν, ἣν ὁρᾶτ' ἐν αἰθέρος πτυχαῖς σεσωσμένη τε, κ' οὐ θανου̃σα πρὸς σέθεν. ἐγώνιν ἐξέσωσα</note>. And so that we are not ignorant that this salvation proceeded not from Apollo, nor from other gods—except perhaps as mediators—but more truly from the Supreme God, to whom she dedicated herself with singular virtue, he then adds: **"For being of Zeus, it was fitting for her to live incorruptible."** <note>original Greek: Ζηνὸς γὰρ οὐ̃σαν, ζῆν νιν ἄφθιτον χρεών</note>.

"By Castor, the brother of Helen!" said **Philolaus**, "**Marranus**, you speak the truth, and you seem to have spoken wisely about true salvation. I agree that the **Savior**—of whom the sacred oracles prophesy so magnificently and so perpetually—must be he who is the preserver and restorer not so much of this 'great world' <term>macrocosm; the universe</term>, nor of regions and cities, nor of the lowest elements and stars, nor of wood and stone, nor of plants and trees, nor of fish, birds, or cattle. All these follow the guide of nature and the instinct of their condition unerringly and properly, and they remain what they are toward their appointed end.

Instead, he must be the savior of that 'minor world' <term>microcosm; the human being</term>, that is, of man. For man, often falling away from the norm of equity handed down to him and from the judgment of right reason, voluntarily casts his own nobility into deep pools of evil and the abyss of eternal corruption through a heap of vices. From there, he cannot retrace his steps by his own strength or help. Here, Marranus, here I say, we have need of salvation; here we have need of a Savior. **Pythagoras** calls this class of creatures **"men having self-chosen woes"** <note>original Greek: ἀνθρώπους αὐθαιρέτα πήματ' ἔχοντας</note>. Regarding them, he wrote thus in the ***Golden Verses***: **"Wretched men, they neither see nor hear the good near them; and few understand the release from evils: such a fate of mortals harms their minds, and like rollers they are carried now here, now there, possessing infinite woes."** <note>original Greek: τλήμονες οἵτ' ἀγαθῶν πέλας ὄντων οὐκ' ἐσορῶσιν, οὔτε κλύουσι: λύσιν δὲ κακῶν παυ̃ροι συνίασιν: τοίη μοῖρα βροτῶν βλάπτει φρένας, οἳ δὲ κυλίνδροις ἄλλοτ' ἐπ' ἄλλα φέρονται ἀπείρονα πήματ' ἔχοντες</note>. Indeed, our very own of philosophers...

<summary>Marranus and Philolaus argue that true salvation is not a temporary earthly rescue but an eternal preservation of the human soul. They contrast the natural world, which follows its divine instinct perfectly, with humanity (the microcosm), which requires a Savior to escape the "self-chosen woes" of vice and corruption.</summary>
