LXXXX

->### ON THE CABALISTIC ART<-

<meta>catchword: opinion</meta>

This chief principle was undoubtedly taken from the Hebrew Cabalists, as we can accept from Simon <note>Simon is one of the three interlocutors in Reuchlin's dialogue, representing the Jewish Cabalistic tradition</note>. He perceived that the rational man is more noble than other things—even more divine—and is not content with just one operation or a uniform effect, like other things which are led by nature alone in a single manner. Instead, man is endowed with various gifts like a **Pandora**, which he may use spontaneously in every event according to his free will. On account of this liberty, he [Pythagoras] says: **"The race of mortals is divine, to whom sacred nature, bringing forth, reveals each thing."** <note>original Greek: Θεῖον γένος ἐστὶ βροτοῖσιν οἷς ἱερὰ προφέρουσα φύσις δείκνυσιν ἕκαστα</note>. That is, there is a divine race in men, to whom nature, promoting sacred things, shows individual truths. Indeed, that "sacred nature" is the **intellectual soul**. Therefore, according to the intellect, man approaches God, as the pure to the pure; but according to the lower senses, he recedes from God like the impure from the pure. 

From this it happens that **reason**, which shows us each thing (as he says), makes us blessed when it turns itself toward the enjoyment of the mind. Conversely, when it runs down into the lust of the senses, it makes us wretched. Thus, man seems to be placed in the middle between virtue and vice, like a substitute apex in the **letter of Pythagoras** <note>The Greek letter 'Y' (Upsilon), which Pythagoras used to symbolize the diverging paths of life: the narrow path of virtue and the broad path of vice</note> divided by its two-horned distinction, where that **Hercules** of Prodicus sat down, pensive in his tender age.

Just as **Solon** (according to Herodotus) affirmed to **Croesus**, no one should be called blessed before their death and final funeral; so too, surely no one should be considered truly wretched while they live this life. But the final day must always be awaited for a man, who, if he remains burdened with vices after casting off the body, begins to be truly wretched. Pythagoras divided that misery into two types, as you heard in the previous discourse. For after death, the wretched either have good things nearby—which are the gifts of blessedness—even though they neither see nor hear them because they do not yet enjoy the vision of God. These are among the number of those to be saved, not weighed down by extreme misery, so that they may finally escape the established punishments. Or, finally, good things are at a very great distance from them, so that their evils shall never have any end. These are called those possessing **infinite losses**. 

<margin>121</margin>Therefore, two dwellings of the lower world are described here: the **Elysian Field**, which is transitory, for those who have good things nearby so that they may see the convex heavens again; and **Tartarus**, named from its horrible sound (*tartar*), as if it were a **torturer** (*tortor*), or foul (*teter*), or **terror** <note>Reuchlin is using Latin wordplay here to explain the etymology of Tartarus through similar-sounding words for suffering</note>. This is for those whose losses are infinite. <margin>M</margin> They hang bound to the cylinders and spokes of wheels, where the unhappy **Theseus** sits and shall sit eternally, along with those like him, **"from where they never emerge,"** <note>original Greek: ὅθεν οὔ ποτε ἐκβαίνουσι</note> as written by **Plato** imitating Pythagoras.

Here let the scolders approach me, those who do not cease to babble against this same Pythagoras—so great and distinguished a man, whose dictates were believed like an oracle of the gods. For this reason, he was named in that age the "Dictator of Truth," like a second **Apollo**, which the very name "Pythagoras" signifies <note>Reuchlin suggests an etymological link between the name Pythagoras and the Pythian Apollo, the god of truth and prophecy</note>. However, they spread a rumor about him everywhere that this was his opinion...

It describes the two states of the afterlife: a transitory state for those awaiting salvation (Elysian Fields) and eternal damnation for the irredeemable (Tartarus).</summary>

<meta>This page continues the defense of Pythagoras, addressing the controversial doctrine of metempsychosis (the transmigration of souls). The text argues that the idea of human souls entering animal bodies is a misunderstanding or a malicious slander by his rivals, rather than his true teaching.</meta>

XXXVII

->BOOK TWO<-

G

<meta>catchword: opinion</meta>

...opinion that the human soul, after the death of certain individuals, takes the form of the bodies of beasts. This ought to seem incredible to men who use their reason, considering it concerns such an excellent author of philosophy and such an abundant fountain of the sciences, from whom the knowledge of things divine and human has flowed down to us. Rather, that suspicion of "trans-animation" <note>original: transanimatio; the movement of a soul from one body to another</note> arose from men who were partly ignorant of the Pythagorean mysteries and partly hateful of them out of envy. Indeed, the outstanding virtue of that man, his most innocent life, his eminent teaching, and his celebrated fame did not lack the malice of rivals. As often happens, envious critics left nothing unpolluted—men such as Timon, Xenophanes, Cratinus, Aristophon, Hermippus, and others, of whom there is no small multitude. These men wrote many lies about Pythagoras in their books and handed down things that were never said or written by him. Or, if he had said anything of that sort, they nevertheless twisted it into a worse sense, so that it might easily be believed that such a great man had wandered into thoughtless teaching concerning the principles of things, numbers, the forbidden eating of beans, abstaining from the flesh of living creatures, the underworld, and **metempsychosis** <term>the Greek term for the "displacement of the soul" or reincarnation</term> or the passage of souls, which we are now discussing. 

For how could he—who distinguished the patterns and species of things so clearly that they cannot be mutually transmuted or confused—communicate the human essence (which is its own form) to a beast? For, as he himself taught, not even a substantive unit of a certain number is, according to nature, the unit of another number. Therefore he says: **"The units in the dyad itself are incomparable to those in the triad itself."** <note>original Greek: αἱ δὲ μονάδες ἐν τῇ δυάδι αὐτῇ πρὸς τὰς ἐν τῇ τριάδι αὐτῇ ἀσύμβλητοι. This refers to the Pythagorean idea that the "1" that makes up a "2" is conceptually distinct from the "1" that makes up a "3".</note> This remains constant in the study of nature, though it is treated quite differently in Mathematics, which is not our business at present. 

The "One" of each thing is its participated essence, which will not occupy the essence of another thing. As it is said: **"For each substance participates in one species."** <note>original Greek: ἑκάστη γὰρ οὐσία ἑνὸς εἴδους μετέχει</note>. Therefore, it cannot pass into the life of a different living creature, nor into any beast whatsoever. Rather, it remains within the law of its own nature, holding its own duty, **"So that every species yields and does not merge."** <note>original Greek: ὡς πᾶν εἶδος εἴκει οὐ συνέρχεται</note>. For even if one seal, pressed into many pieces of wax, shapes them into many forms, the same piece of wax cannot bear the diverse forms of several different seals. Therefore, the seal of the human form—which is the image of God—is not permitted to "seal" or stamp a lower nature. Just as Pythagoras proposed all his teachings enigmatically, he also designated the certain meaning of this opinion with his own special mark. Among other symbols, he celebrated this one as his favorite: **"In a ring, do not carry about the image of God."** <note>original Greek: ἐν δακτυλίῳ Θεοῦ εἰκόνα μὴ περιφέρειν</note>. In my judgment, this is rightly understood in roughly this way: the image of God, which is the soul of man, cannot seal or form other natures round about it. Thus...

<summary>This page argues that Pythagoras did not actually believe human souls transmigrate into animal bodies, attributing that "absurd" idea to the slanders of his enemies or a misinterpretation of his mathematical and symbolic philosophy.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the defense of Pythagoras's philosophy, specifically addressing the nature of the soul. Reuchlin is arguing that the "descent" of the soul mentioned by ancient philosophers is not a physical movement or a literal reincarnation into animals, but a metaphysical description of the soul's relationship to the body and its divine origin.</meta>

LXXX

### ON THE ART OF THE KABBALAH

For indeed Hermes Trismegistus <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure presented as a teacher of secret wisdom, often associated with the Egyptian god Thoth</note>, the teacher of the Egyptians, says in his book addressed to Asclepius: "One part of man is simple, which we call the form of divine likeness." And a little later: "There are two images of God: namely, the world and man." Therefore, those who are either envious or ignorant have unfairly explained his views regarding the passage of souls after death, as well as their descent before the generation of a human being. Surely there is no one now, provided they are endowed with any mind at all, who does not agree with me on this. For when many thought the human soul was drawn out from the power of matter, our teacher himself <note>Pythagoras</note> determined that it is more believable that the soul is infused into the body by God himself. On that account, he asserted that the soul exists before the body—which is not to be understood in terms of time, but in terms of purity and the dignity of its nature. 

Therefore, he called this infusion the "descent of the soul," which his followers later treated in various ways with many twists and turns, each in his own way—and not always according to the author's intent. For Pythagoras commanded that the descent of the human soul into the body should not be understood according to physical location, nor according to a movement from the intellectual world through individual spheres to the elemental world (as Proclus <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher</note> and other supporters claim), but rather according to the series of natural forms, in which the rational soul is the ultimate perfection of the human body. This soul completes the whole in such a way that man may most rightfully be called a "divine animal."

<margin>How Pythagoras feels about the soul</margin>
Pythagoras therefore intended that only those living beings whose sacred nature—that is, reason—demonstrates their individuality, are of a divine race, namely propagated by God. As he declared in his *Golden Verses*, their species is neither changed nor converted; thus, the forms of individual kinds are permanent, even if they differ within that same form. After the death of a man, however, if he has died a just man, his soul transcends the pure ether and spends its age with the blessed, as a god among gods. For he says:

*Having established the best judgment as the charioteer from above, if you, having left the body, come into the free ether, you shall be an immortal god, incorruptible, and no longer mortal.* <note>original Greek: ἡνίοχον γνώμην στήσας καθ' ὑπερθενα βίστην, ἢν δ' ἀπολείψας σῶμα, ἐς αἰθέρ' ἐλεύθερον ἔλθῃς, ἔσεαι ἀθάνατος θεὸς ἄμβροτος οὐκ' ἔτι θνητὸς</note>

That is: setting up the best judgment as a charioteer from above, when you come into the free ether leaving the body, you will be an immortal God, incorruptible, and no longer subject to death. 

But if a man dies as an unjust and wicked person in incurable and mortal sins, then Pythagoras taught that his soul must wash away all its guilt through various punishments. He taught that those punishments would be more or less harsh and durable according to the magnitude and multitude of the crimes. To these souls are assigned these lower places of nature and bodies—sometimes imaginary or figurative, and sometimes true—not so that the soul might give them form as an essential part, but so that it might inhabit them like a tenant <note>original: inquilini more</note> for the sake of enduring punishments, or so that it might stay near them through local proximity (like an internal mover to the thing being moved), or around which it might be tormented by tortures. This is like Tityus <note>A giant in mythology whose liver was eaten by vultures</note> among the vultures, and Ixion <note>King punished by being bound to a forever-turning wheel of fire/serpents</note> at the wheels of serpents, and Tantalus in the river, and Sisyphus at the rock, and Prometheus with the eagles. Since a demon of Tartarus <note>The deep abyss/hell of Greek mythology</note> can at times seize and beset a body, why should a foul soul not...

...condemned to the punishments of the underworld, or whether a body of any species might truly enter by God’s dispensation, or whether, having clothed itself in air, it might display some form to our sight. This is as Dido, about to die, addresses Aeneas:
> I shall follow you, burning 
> with dark fires. <note>original: "Sequar atris ignibus ardens" — from Virgil’s Aeneid. Dido threatens to haunt Aeneas as a ghost after her suicide.</note>
And Pliny the Younger writes of a story believed to be true, concerning the house that the philosopher Athenodorus of Tarsus had bought; he writes that it was infamous for a troublesome noise because the phantom of a horrific old man was seen there. Even in our own age, similar terrifying sights occur daily, appearing sometimes in thinner, sometimes in thicker "spoils" <note>term: exuuiis (spoils/skins) — here used to mean the external "shell" or form a spirit assumes to become visible</note>. Then, the appearances and faces of wild beasts trick us in various ways: for it will suddenly become a bristling boar, a black tiger, a scaly dragon, and a lioness with a golden neck; or it will give off the sharp sound of flame. It transforms itself into all the wonders of nature: fire, a horrible beast, and a flowing river. These we surely call "phantastic" bodies—that is, "apparitional"—which the souls of released humans as well as demons can take on. We know this from the story of the Lamia <note>A mythological creature, often a female demon or succubus that seduces young men</note>, the lover of Menippus the Lycian philosopher, who was changed into a beautiful woman at Corinth. Apollonius of Tyana publicly exposed her as being a *lemure* <note>In Roman belief, lemures were the wandering, restless ghosts of the dead</note>. Finally, there is that ragged old man and beggar who was once the cause of a plague for the Ephesians; he is noted for this type of metamorphosis, for they say that after he was crushed under stones, he was seen as a dog, specifically a Molossian hound. Philostratus the Second wrote about both of these in the fourth book of his *Life of Apollonius*.

As for what Pythagoras is said to have claimed—that he was once Euphorbus <note>A Trojan hero in the Iliad; Pythagoras famously claimed he could remember his past life as this warrior</note>—there is another explanation. For he was not the first to establish such a way of speaking; rather, it had been used long before in popular custom among the most ancient people: that whoever was endowed with a particular virtue or vice would be likened to another who had previously existed in that same condition to an eminent degree. For example, they called any man they wished to describe as being of outstanding strength "Hercules." Thus Marcus Varro Rusticellus says that a man called Hercules lifted his own mule. And Numenius the Pythagorean <note>A 2nd-century philosopher who sought the Eastern origins of Greek philosophy</note> writes openly that Plato is nothing other than "Moses speaking in the Attic language" <note>Attic was the dialect of Athens; Numenius meant that Plato's philosophy was a Greek version of the wisdom found in the Hebrew Torah</note>. 

Often, too, Cicero was said to be the "Latin Demosthenes." All these comparisons arise from an equality of virtues and works and a similarity of character, not because of a shared single substance. Thus Libanus, a slave in the play by Plautus, said that Argyrippus was "Solon" <note>A famous Athenian lawmaker and sage</note> because he was likewise writing laws; in the *Asinaria*, he says of him:
> For now he is busy during the day; clearly
> he is a Solon, so that he may write laws.
These words of Plautus indicate an ingrained custom of speaking among the ancients, where they would say this man is that certain person because he was similar in nature, character, habits, love, affection, and work. Hence the Romans used to add the word "another" to this proverb, as in: "You are another me" (*alter ego*), and "I am another you," even though they knew and saw that in reality I am not you, nor are you me. But in both of us, we perceive that there is the same character, equal zeal, the same will, the same effort, [spi...] <note>The text cuts off mid-word, likely "spiritus" or "spirando," continuing the theme of shared spirit or breath.</note>

<summary>Reuchlin explains that "metempsychosis" or reincarnation in Pythagorean thought is often a figure of speech for shared character traits rather than literal soul-migration. He also distinguishes between human souls and "phantastic" apparitions or demons that assume various physical forms.</summary>

### ON THE ART OF THE KABBALAH

LXVIII

...ritual, a soul **not changed in their essence** <note>original Greek: οὐ τῇ οὐσίᾳ αὐτῶν μεταβαλλομένοις</note>. For the ancients said that "souls" were the movements and wills of men; for this reason, people of a single custom, care, and diligence, having a similar purpose, equal motivation, and equal movement and feeling, are usually called **unanimous** <note>literally "of one soul"</note>. It is by no means foreign to the ancient philosophers to say that the soul is the moving and sensing principle in man; for Aristotle says, **"The animate seems to differ from the inanimate"** <note>original Greek: τὸ ἔμψυχον γὰρ τοῦ ἀψύχου</note> **"chiefly in two ways: by motion and by the act of sensing."** Therefore, whoever is affected and moved toward the same thing, and who seems to think and feel the same way, is commonly said to be of **one soul** <note>original Greek: ψυχῆς</note>. 

Whence that famous <term>metempsychosis</term>—that is, *transanimation*—is in truth nothing other to rightly learned men than an equal care, a similar movement, and an equal zeal of some deceased man found, after some time, in another or the same living man. By such an emulation of common and ordinary speech, Pythagoras, once returning from the **Magi** <note>wise men or sorcerers</note> of the Persians (for so those wise men name their own), perhaps for the sake of cheering a banquet among friends, was able to use the custom of the Magi and say that he contained within himself the soul of Euphorbus (the former Trojan soldier and son of Panthous), of Hermotimus, of Pyrrhus, of Pyrandrus, of Calidon, of Alces, and finally his own soul as Pythagoras. He said this because he bore an affection, zeal, and will inclined toward certain noble qualities situated especially in each of those men—qualities toward which those very men were more prone to be moved in their own lives. 

But most of all, since warlike virtue had shone in Euphorbus the Trojan, Pythagoras was said to have obtained the soul of Euphorbus as if he now possessed the heart of Euphorbus. Concerning this, he was certainly able to boast when the practitioners of military training praised him, seeing the strength of his sides, arms, and his whole body, and weighing his incredible love toward the strongest **Athletes**. He showed this love to them then both by his precious equipment and magnificent expense; for previously, athletes were nourished on dried figs, soft cheese, and wheat, but our Pythagoras himself was then the first found to have nourished them with meat. Therefore, when they wondered how such a great love of fighting could exist in a philosopher dedicated to the study of letters, what wonder if he responded that the soul of Euphorbus flourished in him? This is to say that the genius, zeal, movement, and will of Euphorbus resided within him—who, although he was a teacher of peace and an author of quiet contemplation, nevertheless felt within himself a desire for war, as if he were a Trojan. 

When this was heard,

<margin>Envy always gnaws at the best things</margin>

a rumor soon arose among those who believe rashly, and the story spread—either through ignorance of the Pythagorean mysteries or through the malice of the envious, who always pervert the best things and repeat what they have heard far differently than it was said—that the soul of Euphorbus, who was killed in the Trojan War, had migrated into Pythagoras. This opinion was later assisted by writers and poets. From this, Ovid says in the fifteenth book of his *Metamorphoses* <note>original: Transfigurationis libro; Reuchlin uses a Latinized title for Ovid's famous work on transformations.</note>...

# BOOK TWO

XXXIX

Ovid, borrowing these things among other trifles from the Greeks—who are, after their fashion, accustomed to "playing the Cretan" <note>original Latin: *Cretizin*; an ancient idiom for lying, as Cretans were proverbially called liars.</note>—sang thus of Pythagoras: **"Souls are free from death, and having always left their prior seat, they live and are received into new homes. I myself (for I remember it) was Euphorbus, son of Panthous, in the time of the Trojan war; in my chest once stuck the heavy spear of the younger son of Atreus. I recognized the shield, the burden of my left hand, recently in the temple of Juno at Argos of the Abantians."** <note>This famous passage is from Ovid's *Metamorphoses*, Book XV, where he uses Pythagoras as a mouthpiece for the theme of change.</note>

But do not be amazed, excellent Marranus; you will find nothing of these things written in the books of Pythagoras himself. For he only published three volumes: the first **Educational** <note>original Greek: παιδευτικόν (*paideutikon*)</note>, the second **Political** <note>original Greek: πολιτικόν (*politikon*)</note>, and the third **Natural** <note>original Greek: φυσικόν (*physikon*)</note>, which some attribute to Lysis; therefore let the **Golden Verses** be our third book. 

Run through every single point, and you will nowhere find anything in that man concerning **transanimation** <note>The literal movement of a soul from one body to another.</note>. By this, you may more easily believe that whatever is fabled about that <term>metempsychosis</term> <note>original Greek: μετεμψυχώσει; the transmigration of souls.</note> was sown as a false rumor by the envious. The sheer variety of the story clearly indicates this: some assert this shield was brought to the temple of Juno at Argos, others that it was dedicated to Pallas at Athens. They even claim this was the inscription on the shield: **"To Pallas Athena, Menelaus took this from Euphorbus"** <note>original Greek: παλλὰδι ἀθηνᾷ, μενέλεως ἀπὸ εὐφόρβου</note>; Maximus of Tyre is the authority for this in his sixteenth dissertation. Legal experts may judge how much credit such testimony deserves. 

Truly, I cannot be brought to believe that Ovid’s fable about the passage of souls was actually taught by a man so excellent in all knowledge and so grave. I think it even less believable because more excellent authors have handed down a different tradition. For what many assert—that Pythagoras was the first among the Greeks to discover that souls are immortal—is a manifest falsehood. 

Homer, by far the most ancient of the Greeks, set forth this dogma long before him; in Homer's work, the souls of the deceased discuss many things in the underworld and prophesy many things. I ask you, what else does that admirable song of his concerning **the spirits of the dead** <note>original Greek: Λί’ ὅλους τ’ νέκυας; likely a corrupted OCR of a Homeric phrase referring to the "shades" or spirits of the deceased.</note> suggest, if not that our souls remain after death? Furthermore, in the case of Ulysses' companions, he openly showed that the souls of unwise men, when separated from the body, do not truly take on the *natures* of beasts, but only put on the **habits of brutes** <note>Meaning their outward behaviors, appearances, or appetites rather than a change in their human essence.</note>, and suffer the punishments Circe commanded with such horror. However, those who hold the root and flower of **Moly** <note>A magical herb given to Odysseus by Hermes (Mercury) to protect him from Circe's transformative magic.</note> will have secure souls, according to Mercury, as found in the tenth book of the *Odyssey*. 

But let us return to that irony concerning Euphorbus. Whenever suitable authors write of him, they confess that all the divine dogmas of Pythagoras were **spoken in riddles** <note>original Greek: αἰνίττεσθαι (*ainittesthai*)</note>, that is, delivered through obscure allegory. Apollonius of Tyana, that famous Pythagorean, confirms this in a discourse with Thespesion, the chief philosopher of the **Gymnosophists** <note>A sect of ancient Indian philosophers whom the Greeks believed practiced a form of ascetic wisdom.</note>, in the sixth volume of Philostratus, speaking thus: **"If I touch upon riddles, the wisdom of Pythagoras allows these things, for he gave them over as if to be spoken in riddles..."** <note>original Greek: εἰ δ’ αἰνιγμάτων ἅπτομαι, σοφία πυθαγόρου ξυγχωρεῖ ταῦτα...</note>

For he also handed down teachings through riddles. However, when he was disputing with the Brahmans <note>Ancient Indian philosophers and priests.</note> of India in his third book, asking how they felt about the soul, Iarchas said: "Just as Pythagoras handed it down to you, we handed it down to the Egyptians." Apollonius replied: "Will you then say that you were one of the Trojans? Just as Pythagoras said he was Euphorbus?" Listen now, Marranus, to how cleverly Thespesion responded, first asking whom among the Greek leaders at Troy he considered more worthy of admiration. To which Apollonius replied that Achilles had obtained the first rank in Homer's poetry. Then Iarchas, looking at him, said: "And consider him my ancestor, or rather, the **ancestral body**; for this is what Pythagoras also considered Euphorbus." <note>Original Greek: πρὸς αὐτὸν ἔφη ἀποβλέπων καὶ τὸν πρόγονον θεωρεῖ τὸν ἐμὸν, μᾶλλον δὲ, τὸ πρόγονον σῶμα . τουτὶ γὰρ κὶ πυθαγόρας εὔφορβον ἡγεῖτο. The phrase "progenitor body" suggests a material lineage rather than a spiritual one.</note> 

Then he recounts how Gangen, once king of the Indians and son of the river Ganges, surpassed Achilles in many virtues, and that he himself was that progenitor body which he now was. These words do not indicate the transmigration of souls, but the **transformation of bodies**, just like any matter that is suited to receive this or that form. It is just as if a Comedy should say, "I was previously a Tragedy," because from the same letters and elements both tragedy and comedy are born, as Aristotle says in his first book *On Generation*. Or if a certain dog said, "I was formerly a horse," because of the body of a certain horse which the dog devoured; since the nourishment was converted into the substance of the thing nourished, that horse might be called, in common speech, the dog's **ancestral body** <term>progonon sōma <note>original Greek: πρόγονον σῶμα; a technical term meaning the material precursor or "parental body" from which new life is physically sustained or generated.</note></term>, namely, that from which he was produced. 

However, no one will think from this speech that the horse's soul passed into the dog. For what reason then should I believe Pythagoras taught that souls pass into other bodies, solely because he said he had previously been Euphorbus? Especially since it is clearly consistent and agreed upon that it was not the soul, but the body itself that was judged to be Euphorbus. Furthermore, this saying of his was not plain but a pure riddle, by which he wished to hint at a certain secret unknown to that age: namely, that **prime matter** <term>materia prima <note>In the philosophy of the time, this is the "first matter"—a formless substance that underlies all physical change in the universe.</note></term> is not only capable of receiving all forms, but is even greedy for them and, always moved by desire, is never satisfied by any single form. 

This was equally seen by the most philosophical Emperor Marcus Antoninus, when he wrote in the third book of his *Meditations*: **"That the nature of the whole loves nothing so much as to change all things and make new things like them. For every existing thing is, in a way, the seed of that which will be from it."** <note>original Greek: ὅτι οὐδὲν οὕτως φιλεῖ ἡ τῶν ὅλων φύσις ὡς τὸ τὰ πάντα μεταβάλλειν κὶ ποιεῖν νέα ὅμοια . σπέρμα γὰρ τρόπον τινὰ πᾶν τὸ ὂν τοῦ ἐξ αὐτοῦ ἐσομένου</note> And the same in the seventh book: **"The nature of the whole, out of the universal essence as if from wax, at one time molded a little horse, then melting it down into the nature of a tree, then blending fire with it, then into a little man, then into something else..."** <note>original Greek: ἡ τῶν ὅλων Φύσις, ἐκ τῆς ὅλης οὐσίας ὡς κηροῦ νῦν μὲν ἵππάριον ἔπλασε, συγχέασα δὲ αὐτὸ εἰς δένδρου φύσιν, συνπεριχέασα τὸ πῦρ κὶ αὐτὸ, εἶτα εἰς ἀνθρωπάριον εἶτα εἰς ἀλλό τι</note> That is, the nature of the universe out of the universal essence—

He supports this using Aristotelian logic and quotes from Marcus Aurelius regarding the constant transformation of the natural world.</summary>

## SECOND BOOK

...the essence having been changed like wax; now indeed it fashioned a little horse. But blending that into the nature of a tree, it used its material at the same time. Then it turned into a little man, then into something else. This is why it is named by Orpheus with these titles: the **much-contriving mother** <note>Original Greek: πολυμήχανος μήτηρ (polymēchanos mētēr)</note> and the **ordainer of foreign figures** <note>Original Greek: ἀλλομορφοπλάστης (allomorphoplastēs)</note>. Whatever the case may have been, I for my part would far rather believe that if Pythagoras said he had been Euphorbus <note>A Trojan hero whose soul Pythagoras claimed to inhabit.</note> or someone else, he introduced that riddle for the sake of an example. <margin>o</margin> But if he is believed to have woven a historical account, surely he must be thought to have done so for no other reason than to show that the soul, once separated from the body, can return again—by God's authority—into that very same body which it had entirely left and deserted, and not into any other. For we were able to learn long ago from Iarchas, the wisest of the Indians, that it was one and the same body, by however many different names it was called, in which Pythagoras lived again so many times. This was not a matter of size and quantity, but of substance and being. It is just as the sea, although it is uniform and one, yet we say this part is the Aegean, that the Ionian, this the Myrtoan, and another the Crisaean. 

In the same way, they named one man, born again several times, first Aethalides, then Euphorbus, later Hermotimus, then Pyrrhus, and finally our famous Pythagoras. As a philosopher of the most deep-thinking and divine sort, he did not attribute these many <term>Regenerations</term> <note>The original term is *Palingenesia*, referring to the process of being born again or restored.</note> to the powers of nature, but to God alone. According to Heraclides Ponticus, in this context of Rebirth, Pythagoras called God "Mercury" <note>Hermes, the messenger god and guide of souls.</note> to show that no one returns to life except by divine power. For as Justin—the philosopher and Christian martyr—recites in his *Exhortation to the Greeks*, God was especially honored by Pythagoras with this title: he is called the **Animation of the Universe** <note>Original Greek: ψύχωσις τῶν ὅλων (psychōsis tōn holōn)</note>, because he pours the soul into all humans, takes away what was poured in, and restores what was taken away as often and whenever he wishes. 

Such a thing has often been seen in other men and confirmed by certain experience, as recorded by the most noble writers. <margin><unclear>ink marks</unclear></margin> For Aristeas of Proconnesus once died in a fuller's shop. Then, seven years later, he appeared alive to the citizens of that city, and he then composed poems about the "one-eyed" Arimaspians who live beyond the north wind, which Herodotus mentions excellently in the fourth book of his *Histories*. Furthermore, there lived in Armenia a man named Er, a Pamphylian by race. When he had fallen in battle and the other corpses were picked up on the tenth day already decayed, he was found whole in an uncorrupted body. He was carried home for his funeral, but on the twelfth day after death, while he was placed upon the pyre, he rose again and reported what he had seen in the afterlife. Plato wrote about this in the tenth volume of his *Republic*. To this also occurs what we read: that a girl who had died in Rome, while being carried to her tomb, was restored to life by Apollonius of Tyana, as recorded in the fourth book [of his life].

# ON THE CABALISTIC ART
### 9
<meta>catchword: wisdom of</meta>

...profess, for that distinguished writer Aristoxenus says that Pythagoras did not abstain from living things, but ate meat, which Porphyry proves in the first book of *On Abstinence from Animal Food* <note>Original Greek: περὶ ἀποχῆς ἐμψύχων (*peri apoches empsychon*). Porphyry was a 3rd-century Neoplatonist who wrote extensively on vegetarianism.</note>. He argues that while some athletes were nourished by others on cheese and previously on figs, Pythagoras was the first of all to feed them on a diet of meat. He is said to have <margin>q</margin> remarked that meat possessed an incredible power for acquiring strength; so says Porphyry. And Apollodorus the mathematician <note>Possibly Apollodorus of Cyzicus</note> testifies that he sacrificed a hundred oxen when he discovered **that in a right-angled triangle, the side subtending the right angle is equal in power to the sides containing it** <note>Original Greek: ὅτι ἡ τρίγωνος ὀρθογωνίου ἡ τὴν ὀρθὴν γωνίαν ὑποτείνουσα δύναται ταῖς περιεχούσαις (*hoti hē trigōnos orthogōniou hē tēn orthēn gōnian hypoteinousa dynatai tais periechousais*). This is the famous Pythagorean Theorem.</note>, that is, that the side lying opposite the right angle of a right-angled triangle was worth as much as those which enclosed it. He was, however, of a most modest life, of moderate nourishment, and drank very little, as Lycon of Iasos writes concerning Pythagoras. Hence, perhaps, his use of meat was rare, for he often fed only on a little honey; all these things are found in the tenth book of Athenaeus’s *The Banquet of the Learned* <note>Original title: *Deipnosophistae*.</note>. And for this reason, if he had diligently warned students of literature to avoid those things which would be heavy food, lest the brain be harmed by an incautious burden on the stomach—whereby they might be able to apply themselves more vehemently to contemplation—who would not give praise for this to so faithful a teacher? Just as he might have learned among the Hebrews that heavy foods were prohibited in their law, or as he might have known among the Indians that certain things should be avoided, such as sea fish, which are neither useful to the stomach nor accepted in the offerings of the gods (for no one has ever heard of a fish being sacrificed). Finally, what he had received from the Egyptians regarding the bean <note>The "Pythagorean bean" taboo is a famous historical enigma.</note>—that it is not a clean legume, as Herodotus noted in his *Euterpe*—they clearly should not take as food, seeking tranquility of mind through the perpetual study of letters. Nevertheless, he did not wish such pious warnings to be observed so exactly and "to the nail" <note>A Latin idiom, *ad unguem*, meaning with perfect precision.</note> as if they were the Law of the Twelve Tables. For he himself is reported by Xenophilus, Aristoxenus, and certain others of the older generation, nearly his contemporaries, to have lived on young piglets and tender kids <note>Young goats.</note>. In the fourth book of Aulus Gellius's *Attic Nights*, you will find that he used no legume more often than the bean, so that it might gently ease the bowels. But concerning beans, an explanation will be given later among the other symbols. Now, let those earlier things I said about numbers come to your mind, as well as the later things I am about to say, so that you may recognize how impiously certain base buffoons <note><term>Sanniones</term>: Clowns or mimes who make mocking gestures.</note> of philosophy deride Pythagoras, the prince of philosophers, with a poetic sneer because he taught that **number is the principle of all things**. They argue that since number is more truly a discrete quantity, it follows after things rather than preceding them—as if he himself understood numbers to be like counting-pebbles <margin>D</margin> from which all things originated. I marvel at these people, not without a laugh, because although they have heard frequently from the testimony of the wisest men that almost all Pythagorean philosophy—and especially that which exists concerning divine matters—is mystical and proposed through enigmas, they nevertheless treat this wisdom of...

# BOOK TWO
### XLII
<meta>catchword: the meaning</meta>

[of wisdom], <note>The text begins mid-word: "sapientiae" (of wisdom).</note> the most divine part concerning numbers, by imitating the folly of the Etruscans <note>Original: "Tyrrhenorum." The author refers to the Etruscans, whom the Romans often associated with ancient, sometimes "foolish" or superstitious rituals.</note>, they command it to be taken plainly and without any metaphor. However, it was the custom of the ancients and the wise men of the earliest age to hand down the deep investigation of wisdom through the allegories of secret letters and the mysteries of the senses. Thus, the works of the most ancient philosophers and poets are entirely full of enigmas—both because of the obscurity of the subjects and out of a slight contempt for the common crowd. As Maximus Tyrius says in his tenth dissertation: "For since things are not clearly seen because of human weakness, a myth is a more graceful interpreter." <note>Original Greek: πραγματων γαρ υπ᾿ ανθρωπινης ασθενειας ου καθορωμενων σαφως, ευσχημονεστερος ερμηνευς ο μυθος (*pragmatōn gar hyp’ anthrōpinēs astheneias ou kathorōmenōn saphōs, euschēmonesteros hermēneus ho mythos*).</note> That is to say, for things not clearly perceived due to human frailty, a fable is a more suitable interpreter. Indeed, as Macrobius <note>A 5th-century Latin writer whose "Commentary on the Dream of Scipio" was a primary source for Neoplatonism in the Middle Ages.</note> attests, it is right and proper for philosophers to use a pious veil of fictions to announce noble things, clothed in honorable subjects and names.

I believe this most carefully excites and introduces the minds of students to the understanding of wonderful things; for that which is ready at the door is sought with less diligence than that which is hidden far away in the depths of an abyss. Thus, believe one who has experienced it: ease of apprehension produces negligence in the studies of disciples, and that which is obtained most easily is sought only coldly. It also happens sometimes that we cannot express hidden things with any proper set of words, and we would be forced to express them with long digressions and variously composed speech, had it not been conveniently found how to use a brief enigma.

Furthermore, this is useful in practical matters; for commanders in opposing camps are accustomed to issue certain signs, which they call tokens <term>tessaras: military watchwords or passwords used for identification</term>, so that each leader can recognize his own soldiers, and they can recognize each other. Just as in Caesar’s war the watchword was "Mother Venus," for Sulla it was "Delphic Apollo," for Marius "the god Lar," and for Jephthah "Shibboleth." <note>A reference to Judges 12:6, where a password was used to identify members of a specific tribe based on their pronunciation.</note> Thus, it was not at all unseemly to hand down the peculiar and secret symbols of doctrine to one’s associates, so that whichever of the disciples used them more frequently would become dear to the master and love one another more than the rest.

From this, the Pythagoreans fashioned for themselves a certain chain of indissoluble love and friendship through certain secret symbols. For Pythagoras was, above all, most studious in reconciling friendship; if he learned that someone had shared in his symbols, he immediately accepted him as a companion and friend, as Laertius <note>Diogenes Laertius, biographer of the Greek philosophers.</note> confirms. Because of this, everyone desired more ardently to use the Pythagorean symbols—that is, the signs of the mysteries—both because they would be more pleasing to the teacher and so they might appear to all as noble Pythagoreans. 

Moved by this, as Plutarch writes in the eighth book of his *Table Talk*, Philinus—alone among all the guests of Sulla of Carthage—abstained from animal products during the feast so that he might be recognized as a Pythagorean. For this, he was rebuked by Leucius, a native of Etruria and a disciple of the Pythagorean Moderatus, for following the written letter of that dogma more than its **meaning**.

It compares these philosophical "symbols" to military passwords and concludes with an anecdote about a man following the Pythagorean diet too literally.</summary>

...which was also worthy of blame in other Pythagoreans who, immoderately affected by strange and singular habits, either did not break bread at the dinners of their companions and friends like others, or did not eat brains, or rolled up their blankets when rising from sleep, or sacrificed with bare feet, or turned away from the sun when about to speak, or, leaving the common road, traveled by side-paths, or never or rarely laughed with those who were laughing, or abstained entirely from eating beans, and managed their households with great care, led more by superstition than by right reason. These people only imitated the symbols on the surface <note>Original: "ad corticem" — literally "to the bark," a common metaphor for the literal or superficial meaning of a text as opposed to its "pith" or inner truth.</note>, neglecting the underlying intention, so that they might be recognized by such marks and appear to the common people as Pythagoreans of that same order.

Therefore, symbols of this kind are the signs of a single school. But let us also add that enigmatic symbols provide a great deal of assistance to the memory when we are measuring the vast spaces of divine and human affairs and handling countless matters. These are marks fixed in the mind so that, whenever we wish to remember, they are quickly presented to our sight. Thus, the most convenient symbol for the principles of things will be **One** and **Two**. For what occurs more quickly to those looking at individual things than "one" and "two," when we wish to examine the causes <margin>S</margin> and the origin of the universe? For at first glance, the eyes perceive that which is the *same itself* and is not *another*. From this, we first conceive in the mind that "the same" and "the other" are One and Two.

Now, Alcmaeon of Croton <note>A 5th-century BC natural philosopher and medical theorist often associated with the early Pythagoreans.</note>, who lived in the time of Pythagoras, called "two" the "many," which he said were "contrarieties," like the "Strife" perhaps of Empedocles <note>Empedocles (c. 490–430 BC) taught that the universe was governed by two opposing forces: Love (attraction) and Strife (repulsion).</note>. Yet he set those down as wandering and infinitely diverse—such as white and black, sweet and bitter, good and evil, small and large—as Aristotle testifies in the first book of the *Metaphysics* <note>Original: "postnaturalia" — literally "the things after the physical," the Latin term for Aristotle's *Metaphysics*.</note>. But the Pythagoreans, for the sake of their love for the mathematical art, compressed those diverse things which were mutually contrary—which the followers of Alcmaeon called "contrarieties"—into the number **ten** <term>denarium</term> <note>The Decad (10), which the Pythagoreans considered the "perfect number" because it contains the sum of the first four numbers (1+2+3+4=10).</note>, that celebrated number that contains all things: such as finite and infinite, odd and even, one and many, right and left, masculine and feminine, resting and moving, straight and curved, light and darkness, good and evil, square and oblong.

But these things are such that whichever side they fall on, because they are two, they are diverse for the very reason that they are two. For if they were one, they would not be <margin>T</margin> contraries. Indeed, they reduced all things to ten because this number is the most perfect of all, by which all nations and all peoples (except the Thracians), both Greek and Barbarian, count individual things, not stopping before it nor proceeding beyond it, as if using the natural counters of the ten fingers. Truly, this most adorned world we see shows its perfection, for according to the Pythagoreans, it is moved by only ten spheres; it is also more perfect than the rest by as much as it contains more types of counting,

# BOOK II
## ON THE CABALISTIC ART

...it contains the even, the odd, the square, the cube, the oblong, the plane, the <term>prime uncompounded number</term><note>Referring to prime numbers, which cannot be divided by any number other than one and themselves.</note>, and the first composite number. Nothing is more absolute than this, because within the ten proportions, four cubic numbers are completed, by which the Pythagoreans say all things in the universe consist. Archytas also, that noble Pythagorean of Tarentum, encompasses everything that exists within the number ten. Aristotle the Stagirite, imitating him as the leader of the Peripatetic school, names the ten genera of being the <term>ten categories</term><note>Aristotle's fundamental list of ten ways in which something can be said to exist (e.g., substance, quantity, quality).</note>. He chose to title his volume with this name, showing philosophically—as Eustathius maintained—that they are ten *matters* <note>Original Greek: πράγματα (*pragmata*)</note>, that is, real entities; or as Alexander of Aphrodisias held, ten *voices* <note>Original Greek: φωνάς (*phōnas*)</note>, that is, words; or as Porphyry held, ten *thoughts* <note>Original Greek: νοήματα (*noēmata*)</note>, that is, understandings or concepts.

Or, as Iamblichus perhaps more correctly said, they are ten simple words—not merely as words, but as signs for the simple things themselves, mediated by ten simple concepts. Alexander of Aegae, Ammonius the son of Hermias, and Simplicius—those distinguished lovers of wisdom—assent to this. They even diligently judged that within these ten most general beings, two principal ones can be found into which the rest may be divided (even though they arise from a single essence): such as substance and accident, or the corporeal and the incorporeal, or the material and the immaterial, or the simple and the composite. For the number ten so loves the number two that, having progressed from the one, it is born through the two, and through the two it returns to the one.

For the first uncompounded number is the <term>triad</term><note>The number three.</note>. It does not indeed consist of one and two as a "composition," but as a "consistency," because "one" does not have position according to Iamblichus. Therefore, it does not create a composition, if we wish to follow the proper use of words. <note>Original Greek: οὔτε γὰρ ἡ μονὰς μείνουσα ἔτι μονὰς θέσιν προσλαμβάνει οὔτε ἡ στιγμὴ μείνουσα στιγμὴ τὴν θέσιν ἀποβάλλει.</note> "For neither does the unit, while remaining a unit, take on position; nor does the point, while remaining a point, lose its position," as Simplicius says in his commentaries on the category of quantity. From this we can recognize the difference by which the <term>unit</term> <note>The Monad, or the concept of 'one' in arithmetic.</note> is distinguished from the <term>point</term> <note>The geometric equivalent of the unit.</note>.

And since nothing exists before the one, we rightly say that the one is first. The <term>dyad</term><note>The number two.</note>, however, is not "composed" of numbers, because it is formed from only one unit and another; thus it is the first number because it is the first multitude. It can be measured by no number except by the unit alone, which is the common measure of all numbers; for "once two" is nothing other than two. Wherefore that multitude which is called the triad is most truly named by the mathematicians as the "first uncompounded number"; for the dyad preceding it is not an "uncompounded" number, but more properly "not composed." Therefore, the triad—desiring not to be idle, but rather that its goodness be multiplied among all creatures without envy—progresses from power into action. That fruitful element within it, which is highly productive of multitude (like number from number), and that essential element which is the one within it...

...it contains even, odd, square, cube, long, plane, the first **incomposite** <note>Meaning a prime number, which cannot be divided by any number other than itself and one.</note>, and the first **composite**. Nothing is more absolute than this, because within the ten proportions the four cubic numbers are exhausted, from which the Pythagoreans say all things consist. Archytas also, that noble Pythagorean of Tarentum, encompasses all that exists within the number ten; Aristotle the Stagirite, imitating him as the leader of the Peripatetic school, names ten genera of being as the **ten categories**. Under this name, he chose to title his volume, showing philosophically (as Eustathius maintained) ten *pragmata* <note>original: πράγματα</note>, that is, real entities; or as Alexander of Aphrodisias held, ten *phōnas* <note>original: φωνάς</note>, that is, voices; or as Porphyry held, ten *noēmata* <note>original: νοήματα</note>, that is, intellects or concepts. Or, as Iamblichus perhaps more correctly held, ten simple voices—not merely as sounds, but as things signifying simple realities through the medium of ten simple concepts.

Alexander of Aegeus, Ammonius (the son of Hermias), and Simplicius—those distinguished lovers of wisdom—agree with this. They diligently judged that within these ten most general beings, two principal types can be found into which they may be divided, even if they arise from a single essence: such as **substance and accident**, or **corporeal and incorporeal**, or **material and immaterial**, or **simple and composite**. For the Decad <note>The number ten</note> loves the number two in such a way that, having progressed from the One, it is born through two, and through two it returns to the One. 

For the first incomposite <note>prime</note> number is the **ternary** <note>The number three</note>; it does not indeed consist of one and two as a "composition," but as a standing-together, because "one" does not have "position" according to Iamblichus; therefore, it does not create a composition, if we wish to follow the proper meaning of words. 

*For neither does the unit, while remaining a unit, take on position; nor does the point, while remaining a point, lose its position* <note>original: οὔτε γὰρ ἡ μονὰς μένουσα ἔτι μονὰς θέσιν προσλαμβάνει, οὔτε ἡ στιγμὴ μένουσα στιγμὴ τὴν θέσιν ἀποβάλλει</note>, as Simplicius says in his commentaries on the category of Quantity. From this, we can recognize the difference by which a unit [one] differs from a geometric point. Since nothing exists before the **One**, we rightly say that One is the first. 

The **binary** [two], however, is not "composed" of numbers, because it is coordinated from only one unit and another unit; it is the "first number" only because it is the first "multitude." It can be measured by no number except by the unit alone, which is the common measure of all numbers; for "once two" is nothing other than two. For this reason, that multitude which is called the **ternary** [three] is most truly called the "first incomposite number" by arithmeticians. The binary [two] preceding it is not an "incomposite number," but is more properly "not composite." 

The ternary, therefore, desiring not to be idle, but rather that its goodness be multiplied among all creatures without envy, proceeds from potentiality into operation. That which is fruitful within it is highly productive of multitude (just as a number is produced from a number), and that which is essential within it is one...

# ON THE CABALISTIC ART

LIX

The source and origin of every production, as well as the beginning of every procession and the eternal permanence of every immutable substance, is contemplated and observed by the eternal mind. It thus turns back into itself, multiplying itself through the mode of unity and duality and saying: "once two times two are four." Behold that **Tetractys** <note>A triangular figure of ten points arranged in four rows (1+2+3+4=10), which the Pythagoreans considered a sacred symbol of the organization of the universe.</note> or fourfold nature of which I spoke with you before; this is the **Idea** of all created things, since, as the mathematicians say, every progression is completed by the number four. From this arises that **Decad** <note>The number ten, representing the totality of the universe.</note> which we call the ten most general categories of all things. For one, two, three, and four, emerging from omnipotent power into the act of energy <note>original: *energiæ*</note>, produce ten, the half of which is five.

Therefore, place five in the middle like a standard-bearer in the middle of an army. On its right side, place the next higher number, which is six, and on the left side, the next lower number, which is four; these two joined also constitute ten. Again, place on the right side the next higher number, which is seven, and on the left side the next lower number, which is three; these two joined similarly constitute ten. Again, place on the right side the next higher number, which is eight, and on the left side the next lower number, which is two; these two joined also constitute ten. Finally, place on the right side the remaining nine and on the left side one. Now reduce those nine to one and ten arises again, which when related to twenty begin once more to be a unity, and so on through all the cardinal numbers up to a hundred. For just as twice one makes two, and three times one three, and four times one four, and so on beyond, so twice ten makes twenty, and three times ten thirty, and four times ten forty, and so on beyond—likewise with a hundred, and no differently with a thousand and beyond.

This indeed is the reason why we write ten as an *iota* <note>The Greek letter 'I' which represents the number ten.</note>, which is an upright stroke in Greek, or we denote it by a single point in Hebrew <note>The letter *Yod*, the smallest letter of the Hebrew alphabet, which has the numerical value of ten and looks like a small point or stroke.</note>. Yet these signs, to foreigners as well as Latins, otherwise represent a simple unity, for from it the number ten arises and into it it ends. There exists the Pythagorean symbol, namely "one [and] two," which **Zaratas** <note>A name for Zoroaster, whom Renaissance scholars often identified as a teacher of Pythagoras.</note>, the teacher of Pythagoras, was accustomed to pronounce through names of propagation, calling one "Father" and two "Mother," as testified by **Plutarch of Chaeronea** in the *Psychogony of the Timaeus*. For as you heard before, one and two, together with the divine essence, produce that fourfold nature, the **Tetractys**, which is the **Idea** of all things brought to completion in the number ten. Pythagoras affirms that it is the **fountain of eternal nature** <note>original: "παγὰν ἀεννάου φύσεως"</note>, which is nothing other than the knowledge of things in the divine mind acting rationally. Indeed, Pythagoras called the very Mind of God "number" allegorically, since he said that number is the principle of all things. So Plutarch writes in his fourth book *On the Opinions of the Philosophers* that Pythagoras [regarded] number...

XLIII

# BOOK TWO

H ii

Pythagoras takes number for the mind <note>original: "πυθαγόρας αὐτὸ τ̃ο̃ νοῦ προσλαμβάνεῖ"</note>. This is a perfectly reasonable sign, because among incorporeal things, nothing is more divine than the mind, and among separate things, nothing is simpler than number. Nor can anything else be imagined that is more similar to the mind. From this fountain of eternal nature, the Pythagorean number—one and two—flows down through streams and channels. That which was, will be, and indeed always is, gushing abundantly in the eternal fountain of the immense Ocean itself, is what the men of the ancient age named **Zena** <note>A Greek form of the name Zeus, associated here with the number One.</note>. This is that very "One," just as Aristotle intended when citing this line of Homer: "Let there be one prince" <note>original: "εἰς κοίρανος ἔσω"</note>. They called him *Zena* instead of *Zeua*, clearly from the word for "living" <note>An ancient etymological connection between Zeus (Zena) and the Greek verb *zen* (to live).</note>, whom the Romans called Jove <note>Jupiter</note>, as if from *Zeua*. Furthermore, Cornutus, in his book on Greek theology, asserts that he is the soul of the entire world.

The "Two," however, was named **Hera** <note>Juno</note>, who is both the sister and the spouse of that *Zenos* (that is, Jove). Regarding her, Homer says in the fourteenth book of the *Iliad*: "Hera of the golden throne saw with her eyes her own brother and brother-in-law, Zena, sitting on the highest peak of many-fountained Ida" <note>original: "ἥρη δ᾽ εἰσεῖδε χρυσόθρονος..."</note>. We can more easily understand the meanings of the wisest poets regarding the origin of things by noting that Jove and Juno reside on "many-fountained Ida." This mountain is named for "sight" <note>original: "ἀπὸ τ̃ο̃ ἰδεῖν"</note> or from "pre-knowledge" <note>original: "ἐκ τ̃ο̃ ἴδεω τὸ γινώσκω"</note>. They sit there as if they were the "One" and the "Two" within that flowing **Idea** of the fourfold nature <note>The Tetractys</note>.

From this source flow the principles of all things, which philosophers of a later age named **Form** and **Matter**. For us, Form and the first Matter are the same as what the most ancient philosophers called "One" and "Two," and what the suitable and illustrious poets called "Jove" and "Juno." They join together on Mount Gargarus in Ida and meet in the "Idea" of the divine mind. Both are drawn by two chariots and both by four horses <note>A metaphor for the mathematical progression of the Tetractys</note>; but in descending, Jove remains on Olympus, while Juno tends toward the lower regions. Homer testifies to this, saying: "For I am going to see the ends of the fertile earth... but now I come here for your sake on Olympus" <note>original: "εἶμι γὰρ ὀψομένη..."</note>. Yet, neither ever entirely deserts the other.

In this way, therefore, the beginning of the universe emerges from the divine mind. For when the **Tetractys** <note>The sacred Pythagorean number four/ten</note> looks back toward its own essence, which is the "First Unity"—the producer of all things—and simultaneously remembers its own origin from the first product (since it is the binary/two), it speaks thus: "once one, twice two." Presently the "fourfold" stands firm, having the supreme Unity at the peak of its summit. Suddenly it becomes a **Pyramid**, the base of which is the "plane four," which among mathematicians signifies a surface. Over this base, the already mentioned radiating light of the divine Unity creates the form and appearance of **incorporeal fire**. Because of the departure of Juno (that is, Matter) toward the lower regions, the nature of essential light immediately arises—not a burning light, but an illuminating one. And this is the creation of the **Middle World**, which Simon the Jew <note>A figure likely representing a specific Cabalistic tradition known to the author.</note> called "the Supreme," because of its comparison to the world of the Deity.

This is seen more clearly when number, by emanating from its own divinity, has declined a little and turned toward the shape of created things. For then, let us set down a square for the <term>Tetractys</term> <note>A triangular figure consisting of ten points arranged in four rows (1, 2, 3, and 4), which was a sacred symbol for Pythagoreans representing the organization of the universe.</note>, and in each of its angles a point representing units; and for the unit of the peak, which now begins to have a fixed position, let us raise the highest apex as much as possible. Once that is done, the four sides raised on high will be four triangles constructed over their four-sided base and drawn together into a single point at the top. Behold the **pyramid** itself, which is the form of fire, according to the testimony of **Timaeus of Locri** the Pythagorean in his book *On the Soul of the World*, writing in the Doric dialect thus: "From which the pyramid, having four bases and equal angles, is composed—the most mobile and thin-parted form of fire." <note>original: "ἐξ ὧν ἁ πυραμὶς τέσσαρας βάσιας καὶ τὰς ἴσας γωνίας ἔχοισα συντίθεται, εἶδος πυρὸς ὠκινάτότατον καὶ λεπτομερέστατον"</note>

This form is indeed without matter; it is essential light, separated [from the body], nearest to God, and eternal life. This is read in the twelfth book of the *Metaphysics* <note>original: "postnaturalia," a literal translation of the Greek 'meta-physics'.</note> and in the second book of *On the Heavens*: "The handiwork of the Mind is life; but the operation of God is immortality, and that is eternal life." **Aristotle** borrowed these ideas from the Pythagoreans. 

Yet God Himself is not a created light, but the "light-giving" author of all light. Therefore, God the Best and Greatest, in the divine trinity within Himself, contains the most absolute and "tetracty-like" pyramid of the incomparable world, rising from a triangular base into the heights, which similarly signifies fiery vigor. For this reason, both the **Chaldeans** and the **Hebrews** claim that God is fire. 

The pyramid produced by the <term>quaternio</term> <note>The number four</note> is the fiery light of the incorporeal and immaterial world of separate intelligences, outside the visible heaven. This is called **Aion** <note>original: "αἰών"</note> by the Greeks, and by us "the age," "eternity," and "the ether." From this, "aethra" is said to be the flash of eternity, where there is no body, no place, no vacuum, no time, no old age, and no change. Instead, there are unalterable and impassive beings, possessing the best life, which they enjoy for the whole *aon*—that is, for eternity or the age. These are almost the very words of the **Stagirite** <note>Aristotle, who was born in the city of Stagira.</note>, which both he and the followers of Plato and Socrates derived from Pythagoras, who wrote thus in the *Golden Verses*: "If, having left the body, you reach the free ether, you will be an immortal god." Having overcome [earthly things] in this life, you will know...

The **condition** of that world is that whatever it is, it is entirely of the purest form; they assert its nature is "Jovial" <note>Relating to the god Jove or Jupiter, signifying a life-giving, kingly nature</note>, which gives form to both immortal and mortal things, and by a specific nourishment preserves all things of both worlds in their own being. Concerning this, the famous line of **Maro** <note>The Roman poet Virgil</note> stands: *O father, O eternal power of men and gods* <note>original: *O pater, o hominum, diuumq; ætherna potestas* from the Aeneid, Book 10</note>. Therefore, on account of this nourishing heat, the spiritual sun was called **Jupiter** by the ancients. Whence the **Salii** <note>The "leaping priests" of Mars in ancient Rome</note>, the priests of Mars Gradivus, called him **Lucecium** <note>Meaning "Bringer of Light"</note>, and the Cretans called him **Phosphorus** <note>The "Light-bearer" or Morning Star</note>. From this, **Olympus** was named, because it is entirely bright, over which the whole of Jove presides and rules—indeed, he is everything that it is. Hence that passage also in the ninth book of the *Aeneid*: *He nodded and made all Olympus tremble with his nod.* Its **condition**, I say, is to receive simple, immaterial forms, separate and existing through themselves, both universal and individual. For it contains all the "Idealized Ideas" <note>The perfect blueprints of all things as they exist in the mind of the Creator</note> of genera and species, just as the examples themselves are imitated by more limited copies; the original seal of these examples resides in the Divine Mind. For thus we wish to name that which is the absolute model of the deity in the world: in the **intelligible world** it is the abstract example; in the **sensible world** <note>The physical world we perceive with our senses</note> it is not the example itself, but that model contracted, much like a seal, the figure on the seal, and the wax that has been stamped.

To this is added, second, the **chorus**, another property named "from rejoicing" <note>original: *ἀπὸ τοῦ χαίρειν*</note>, that is, from the infinite joy of the blessed spirits and the immutable pleasure of the gods, who, as the inhabitants and citizens of that spring-like dwelling, exulting with the **Olympionic** myrtle crown, perpetually enjoy the ambrosia and nectar of the divine banquet, laughing an inextinguishable laughter. Concerning this, **Homer**, the wisest of poets, wrote: *And truly, inextinguishable laughter was raised among the blessed gods* <note>original: *ἄσβεστος δ' ἄρ' ἐνῶρτο γέλως μακάρεσσι θεοῖσιν* from the Iliad, Book 1</note>; this signifies their eternal happiness, which the famous **Melesigenes** <note>An ancient surname for Homer</note> there elegantly expressed in the first book of the *Iliad* as a continuous harmony of lyres and other instruments of the Muses, with dancing, choruses, banquets, restful beds, and sometimes sweet sleep.

### ON THE ART OF THE KABBALAH

...signifies to look upon and to see; they are also sometimes called angels when they announce what they have seen to others, just as **Orpheus** <note>The legendary Greek poet and musician</note>, invoking **Mercury**, says: *Hear me, Hermes, messenger of Zeus, son of Maia, interpreter of all things* <note>original Greek: κλῦθι μου ἑρμεία Διὸς ἄγγελε μαιάδος υἱέ. ἑρμηνεῦ πάντων</note>. For we use the word "to announce" <note>original: *ἀγγέλλειν* (angellein)</note> to mean both to report and to explain. However, we frequently use one term for the other without considering their specific offices, so that in common speech we use "gods" and "angels" interchangeably. For when **Porphyry** <note>A Neoplatonic philosopher and student of Plotinus</note> wrote in his *Isagoge* that "both we and the angels are rational," **Boethius** <note>The 6th-century Roman philosopher</note>, translating it into Latin, said, "both we and the gods are rational"; this usage is found in the books of many others as well. 

Therefore, let no one think that when we name "gods," they are being made equal to the highest and ineffable God who has no name. For we call that supreme majesty "God" because He infinitely penetrates all beings and runs through each individual thing, derived from *theein* <note>original: *ἀπὸ τοῦ θέειν*</note>, that is, "to run." Indeed, God is much more internal and more intimate to every single thing than that thing is to itself, so that He who is nowhere is yet everywhere. But we do not call those "Gods" in the same way who only carry out a limited province assigned to them and are sent to a destined task. 

**Demons**, however—no matter how good they may be—are not admitted into this middle chorus of the world by **Pythagoras** and his followers. For so says **Plotinus** <note>The founder of Neoplatonism</note>—who, according to Porphyry and Longinus, was seen to follow the mysteries of the Pythagoreans most perfectly—in his book *On Love*: "We say and believe that the race of **Gods** is free from passion. But we attach passions to **demons**, even though we say they are eternal, occupying the rank immediately following the Gods." It is certainly better to call no one in the **intelligible world** <term>intelligible world: the realm of pure thought and divine forms, beyond the physical senses</term> a "demon"; indeed, even if a demon is placed there, one should consider it to be a God. Thus far Plotinus; he is certainly brief in all his teaching, yet he must be weighed with an attentive mind, especially in this difficult passage where the secrets of the ancient poets speaking about the gods can be read without trouble and without provoking the bitterness of many.

The third property of the **intelligible world** was demonstrated by the same Pythagoras when he said: *If you live by right reason, grieving for evil deeds and rejoicing in good ones, and pray to the Gods to bring your work to perfection, then, having stripped off the body and set out into the ether, you shall be an immortal God.* We must consider the **order** Pythagoras observes here in the pursuit of human blessedness. For that incorporeal heaven of the middle world and that invisible Olympus of the blessed admits nothing impure; therefore, vices must be fled and virtues embraced. Furthermore, the salvation of men is the mercy of God; wherefore the divinity is to be worshipped, and the higher powers are to be entreated to perfect our work. Finally, nothing of matter, nothing of the body, nothing of the mixed is received there; therefore, one must first die and holily strip off the body before being numbered among the Gods. This is the order of the "age of ages," so that for pure and chosen men who have finished their lives, the supracelestial hall of the indigenous Gods may be granted, and that it may be equally common to

# BOOK III ON THE CABALISTIC ART

whom we set as architect over the sensible world. For among the principles of things, there is no memory held of the "seven" <note>the number seven, or the heptad</note>, because as a virgin she brings forth nothing; for this reason, she is called Pallas <note>Pallas Athena, the Greek goddess of wisdom, who was said to be a "virgin" because the number seven does not produce any other number within the first ten by multiplication, nor is it produced by any except the number one.</note>. We turn, therefore, to the first cube, a truly fertile number and the leader of multitude and variety, as one constituted by "two" and "four." Wherefore, just as Pythagoras’s teacher Zaratas <note>likely referring to Zoroaster</note> named the "two" as mother, so we call the cube proceeding from it the "matter" of all natural things—the ground, the foundation, and the seat of substantial forms. Regarding this, Timaeus of Locri, that famous Pythagorean, writes in his book *On the Soul of the World*: From the square is born the cube, the most stable and firm body in every way: having six sides and eight angles <note>original Greek: ἐκ δὲ τῷ τετρα- γώνῳ γεννᾶται ὃν κύβον ἑδραιότατον καὶ σαλαῖον πάντη σῶμα: ἕξ μὲν πλευρὰς, ὀκτὼ δὲ γωνίας ἔχον</note>. If any form, having been immersed, should lean upon this ground—if it should be placed into this solid receptacle and deposited into this material seat—it is not received in a wandering or common way. Instead, it becomes individual and incommunicable in a stable and singular fashion, as if bound to the soil <note>original Latin: ascriptitia glebæ, a legal term for a serf tied to a piece of land</note>, subject to time and place, and as if outlawed from freedom into the slavery of matter.

Therefore, we see two principles of temporal things flow from a single source: the Pyramid and the Cube—that is, "form" and "matter." We find that both have come forth from the same square <term>tetragonus: a four-sided plane</term>, whose Idea <note>in the Platonic sense of a divine pattern</note>, as we have shown before, is the Tetractys <term>Tetractys: a sacred Pythagorean symbol of four rows of dots adding up to ten, representing the organization of the universe</term>, the divine model of Pythagoras. I have explained these primordial symbols as briefly as I could; in truth, they designate nothing other than matter and form.

And since it is necessary to propose a third thing by which they may be united—for they do not flow together of their own accord, nor does a chance meeting of any forms into matter happen by accident, nor does the matter of one thing receive the form of another by chance (for brass or iron is not generated from a human body as soon as the soul departs, nor is wool made from stone)—since, I say, it is necessary to propose a third thing by which they are united, it will be necessary, in my opinion, to bring in a principle other than the Aristotelian "privation" <note>Aristotle’s "privation" refers to the absence of a form that a subject is naturally suited to have</note>. By this principle, matter is moved toward a desire for form, so that as this or that form ceases, another is introduced in its turn. For "privation" and "potential" act upon nothing substantively, since they possess no real activity and are of the least possible entity; how much less could they join or unite a specific form to any matter? For this reason, some were found who said that, in place of "privation," "motion" was the third principle. But since motion is an "accident" <note>a non-essential property</note>, how can it be a principle of "substance"? Or who shall be the mover of that motion? Wherefore, those two more wise Athenians, Socrates (son of Sophroniscus) and Plato (son of Ariston), placed God—the most agile of all active things—in the place of motion or privation. They said that there are three principles of things: God, the Idea, and Matter.

# BOOK TWO

<sig>M</sig>
<meta>catchword: ans</meta>

...history, which Pythagoras previously symbolized in secret with these arcane marks, by asserting that the principles of all things are the Infinite, the One, and the Two. He designated the God of Infinity, the Form of Unity, and the Matter of Alterity as the authors. He placed the Infinite in the super-supreme and incomparable world, the One (or Identity) in the intellectual world, and the Two (or Alterity) in the sensible world; for matter is indeed the mother of alteration. However, God joins matter and form through a law imposed upon nature itself. For this reason, even before the time of Pythagoras, that most ancient Orpheus, in his book of hymns, placed after Jupiter—that is, Form, whom he calls the <term>principle of all</term> <note>original Greek: ἀρχὴ πάντων</note>—and after Juno—that is, Matter, whom they call <term>Jupiter’s all-producing consort</term> <note>original Greek: Διὸς σύλλεκτρον παγγενέθλου</note>, for he addresses matter by the name of Juno in these words:

> <term>For without you, nothing at all has known the nature of life; for you share in all things, mixed with the holy air.</term> <note>original Greek: χωρὶς γὰρ σέθεν οὐδὲν ὅλως ζωῆς φύσιν ἔγνω. κοινωνεῖς γὰρ ἅπασιν κεκραμένη ἠέρι σεμνῷ</note>

That is to say: Without you, nothing has known the nature of life, since you communicate with all things, being mixed in a manner more than modest. Therefore, after Jupiter (Form) and Juno (Matter), the same Orpheus added "Law"—that is, distribution—so that there would be a third principle of nature, and he named it the <term>just seal of nature</term> <note>original Greek: φύσεως σφραγίδα δικαίαν</note>, which is to say, that which confirms nature. For "Law" is called *nomos* in Greek, which our scholars derive from *nemo* [<term>I distribute</term> <note>original Greek: νεμείζω</note>], because it distributes to everyone what is their own or what belongs to them. He says this is the <term>heavenly law, a just seal</term> <note>original Greek: οὐράνιον νόμου σφραγίδα δικαίαν</note>. Thus he sang in his hymns: "the heavenly law is a just seal." For the law of nature seals many pieces of matter with a single form, just as a notary seals many waxes with the single image of a ring. Indeed, any forms sealed into matter are no longer called "Ideas" (that is, species), but <term>the Ides</term> <note>original Greek: τὰ εἴδη</note>, namely "forms in matter," <term>just as those impressions in wax are inseparable from the material</term> <note>original Greek: ὡς τὰ ἐν τοῖς κηροῖς ἐκτυπώματα ἀχώριστα τῇ ὕλης</note>, as Ammonius <note>Ammonius Hermiae, a Greek philosopher and commentator</note> wrote.

Consequently, the origin of this sensible world now stands open before us, which the marriage of the pyramid and the cube, celebrated by the law of nature, has brought forth. The square bases of these figures, being joined together, produce the Pythagorean <term>dodecahedron</term> <note>a twelve-sided geometric solid</note>—a symbol used to designate the universe itself, composed of matter and form. Alcinous <note>a Middle Platonist philosopher</note> rightly mentions this concerning the dogma of Plato, saying: <term>God used the dodecahedron for the whole universe</term> <note>original Greek: τῶ δὲ δωδεκαέδρῳ εἰς τὸ πᾶν ὁ θεὸς κατεχρήσατο</note>. That is to say, He used it when He was fabricating this world. For if you place a pyramid, raised from four equilateral triangles, atop an eight-angled cube, you will have skillfully constructed the building of a dodecahedron; here the cube (or the die) submits as the mother, and the pyramid rests upon it as the father. For thus said Timaeus of Locri, that noble Pythagorean, in his book *On the Soul of the World*:
