### ON THE CABALISTIC ART

...through the Athenian guest <note>A reference to the character in Plato’s "Laws" who represents Plato's own advanced views</note> in the *Laws*, and the *Epinomis*, and other places in his books. Porphyry in *On Abstinence from Animal Food*. Iamblichus in *On the Mysteries*. Proclus in his commentary *On the Alcibiades*. Plotinus in his book *On Love*, and in his book *On One's Own Guardian Spirit*. Maximus Tyrius in two discussions *On the Spirit of Socrates*, and many other Greeks, whom among the Latins Cicero followed in his volumes *On the Nature of the Gods*, *On Divination*, and in the sixth book of *The Republic*; and also that man of Madaura, Apuleius, in his book *On the God of Socrates*, and the rest who followed and imitated them. Nor are there lacking among the <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>The followers of Aristotle, known for walking while teaching</note> those who have treated the movers of the orbits of the planets and stars, and the governors of the elements—whether they assist those bodies from without, or exist within each of them as their soul—I will pass over these for now. Now we shall briefly enumerate only those things that remain concerning the sensible world. 

Pythagoras therefore said that this world, which is an imitator of eternity, is the containment of all wholes according to the order established within it; and although it is corporeal, it possesses incorporeal first principles. The Stoics did not agree with him on this, for they thought those principles were corporeal because they were spiritual. He asserted that this same world was both generated and corruptible, but through the providence and indulgence of God, it would never actually be destroyed. He also said that the corporeal elements are round, except for fire, which takes the shape of a cone. He defined Color as the appearance of a body. Time he called a circle, the outermost edge of the world; Motion he called a certain difference or "otherness" in matter; and he said that matter is subject to generation and corruption. 

He claimed that Necessity broods over the world, and that some things happen by necessity, some by fate, some by choice, some by fortune, and some by chance; the cause of these is hidden from human reason, a view supported also by Anaxagoras. Our author <note>Pythagoras</note> also thinks the world began from fire. Its right side is in the east, and its left is in the west. Then, following Thales, he divided the heavens into five zones, then into the two equinoxes and two solstices, and the <term>Bear</term> <note>The constellation Ursa Major, used as a primary point for celestial navigation</note>. He divided the earth in the same way. Furthermore, he was the first of all to discover the slant of the zodiac along the sun's path. He used to say the moon looked like a solitary piece of ignited earth, containing within itself fields, mountains, and valleys. 

<margin>Thus many things concerning the <unclear>Immortality</unclear> of the soul regarding its <unclear>substance</unclear>.</margin> 

Concerning the soul, he pronounced in this manner: that it is a self-moving number. He distributed it through the faculties as follows: the vital part around the heart, and the rational and mental part around the head. He held that the soul as a whole cannot perish, for the rational part is the work of the eternal God, while the irrational part is corruptible. To the same author should be attributed a truer form of divination related to sacrifices. He maintained that human seed is the foam of the most useful blood of the corporeal matter, but endowed with an incorporeal power. Furthermore, he held that the female likewise emits seed. Finally, he believed that not only humans but other living creatures also possess reason, though without "mind" <note>Latin: *mens*, referring to the higher, intuitive intellect distinguished from basic reasoning</note>. However, the fact that a great part of these animals do not seem to act rationally...

### BOOK TWO

...certainly, a <term>dyscrasia</term> <note>original: "dyscrasia"; a medical and philosophical term referring to an imbalance of the bodily humors or elements</note> of bodies is blamed, because they are not endowed with the necessary instruments; for this reason, they do not have words, whether they be tame or wild animals, but they hold certain symbols and signs in place of words, by which signs they express their thoughts among themselves. Thus, therefore, beasts "talk" but do not "speak," as the Greeks say more significantly: <note>original: "λαλοῦσι μὲν, οὐ φράζουσι δὲ" (lalousi men, ou phrazousi de)</note> "they chatter, but do not articulate." The many volumes of Plutarch on the *Opinions of the Philosophers* are very good witnesses to all these things. Concerning the remaining things of this world, whether they be substances or accidents, there exist almost innumerable writers in every sect of philosophers. Some of these have spoken generally about the nature of the universe, such as Aristotle, Theophrastus, and your Arabs and almost all the Moors; others have written particularly about each individual thing, such as Julius Pollux, Dioscorides, Pliny, and those similar to them. 

However, every later scholar has seized upon the headings of all disciplines from Pythagoras—the treasury of philosophy—as if they were his heirs. They have cultivated that inheritance through literary study, and according to the unique quality of their own genius, each has adorned and extended it to the best of their ability. But what does it help to either know or form opinions on everything if, in this life, they do not take away all our sorrow and torment, and in the next life, after the removal of evils, they do not add the most abundant collection of all the good things we have so studiously learned? What does it profit us, finally, that by knowing well we do evil, and by doing evil we cannot be entirely free from fear, and thus can have no tranquil state of mind? Or again, what does it profit us that, obediently following warnings like beasts of burden, we always carry out orders, but in all other matters are foolish, dull, fatuous, "mushrooms," slow-witted, and idiots, in no way differing from a brute animal? 

For this reason, it seemed opportune to Pythagoras to direct all philosophy toward the summit of desired happiness and the ready security of eternal joy, which he placed in the contemplation of the highest and divine things. He believed that such fruit, as if from a "happy tree," would undoubtedly follow our tireless studies of philosophy if we—having first purified our souls—vehemently turn away from vices and diligently cultivate virtues. Then, conscious of no evil within ourselves, we may apply ourselves with a joyful mind and cheerful study to mathematical speculations. 

<margin>A</margin>

These mathematical studies stand for us in the middle ground between natural and divine things. For they are partly inseparable from matter (like natural things) and partly separated from it (like divine things). For a circle or a harmony, although it does not exist without matter, is nevertheless understood to be without matter; indeed, no concern for matter is involved when we treat any mathematical subject. Since, therefore, it was difficult—if not impossible—for our intellect to jump suddenly from natural things to supernatural things, and from the entirely material to the inwardly immaterial, Pythagoras wished to place certain middle things before his disciples, which they could comprehend both by sense and by intellect. For this reason, he called the demonstrations of these things <term>mathemata</term> or <term>matheseis</term> <note>From the Greek "mathema," meaning "that which is learned" or "lesson"</note>, that is...

->## BOOK TWO<-

...certainly a bodily *dyscrasia* <term>dyscrasia: a medical term for an imbalance of the bodily humors or a "bad mixture" of physical elements</term> is blamed, because they are not endowed with the proper instruments; for this reason they lack words, whether they be tame or wild, but they hold certain symbols and signs in place of words, and by these signs they express their thoughts among themselves. Thus, beasts speak, but they do not *articulate*; as the Greeks say even more significantly: "They chatter, but they do not speak" <note>original Greek: λαλοῦσι μὲν, οὐ φράζουσι δὲ</note>. All those volumes by Plutarch on the *Opinions of the Philosophers* <note>original: "de placitis philosophorum"</note> are very good witnesses to this. Concerning the rest of this world—whether substances or accidents—there exist almost innumerable writers in every sect of philosophers. Some have spoken generally about the nature of the universe, such as Aristotle, Theophrastus, and your Arabs and nearly all the Moors; others have written particularly about individual things, such as Julius Pollux, Dioscorides, Pliny, and those like them. Yet every one of the later writers took up the main points of all these disciplines from Pythagoras, the treasury of philosophy, as if they were his heirs; they cultivated that inheritance through literary study, and each, according to the particular quality of his own genius, adorned and extended it to the best of his ability. 

But what does it profit us to know or to form opinions on all things, if in this life they do not take away all our sorrow and torment, and in the next life—after we are free from evils—they do not add the most abundant gathering of all the goods we have so studiously learned? What does it profit us, finally, that we do evil while knowing what is good, and in doing evil we can never be free from fear and thus can enjoy no tranquil state of mind? Furthermore, what does it profit us if, while being obedient to warnings, we always execute orders like beasts of burden, yet in all other matters we remain foolish, dull, fatuous, "mushrooms," slow-witted, and simpletons, no different from a brute animal? 

For this reason, it seemed appropriate to Pythagoras to direct all philosophy toward the height of longed-for blessedness and the ready security of eternal joy, which he placed in the contemplation of the highest and most divine things. He believed that such fruit would undoubtedly follow our tireless studies of philosophy (like the fruit of a happy tree) if we first, having purified the soul, turned away sharply from vices and diligently cultivated the virtues. Then, conscious of no evil within ourselves, we might apply ourselves with a joyful mind and cheerful study to mathematical speculations. 

<margin>A</margin> These speculations stand in the middle between natural and divine things; for they are partly inseparable from matter (like natural things) and partly separate from it (like divine things). For a circle or a harmony, although it does not exist without matter, is nevertheless understood without matter; indeed, no concern for matter is involved when we treat any mathematical subject. 

Therefore, since it would have been difficult—if not impossible—for our intellect to leap suddenly from natural things to supernatural things, and from the entirely material to the utterly immaterial, Pythagoras wanted to place certain things in the middle for his disciples, which they could comprehend both by the senses (in some way) and by the intellect. For this reason, he called the demonstrations of these things *mathemata* or *mathesis*—that is,

# THE SECOND BOOK

...from points come lines, from lines plane figures, from planes solid figures, and from these, solid bodies and that sensible globe of the world with its orbits are made and arise, along with the elements of mixed things: fire, air, water, and earth. Nearly every one of these things, as is his [Pythagoras’s] custom, is wrapped in allegory. Then, finally, having likewise left behind the mathematical matters which he showed through his **Paedeutic** <note>original: *Paedeuticum*, a term for a work on "the instruction of children or youths"</note>—that is, his work on education—I think I should briefly review what he taught concerning morals. He wrote about these at greater length in his *Politics*, and more concisely in the *Golden Verses*, which serve as a summary. Since these are read publicly in our age, I shall now follow only those symbols of his that were handed down without being written. He did this so that his disciples, relying on the powers of their memory, would become accustomed to living by these spoken signs with good morals, and would daily affirm their professed order of philosophy among themselves with these secret passwords. A great many of these symbols were clearly expressed by the illustrious **Erasmus of Rotterdam** <note>Desiderius Erasmus (c. 1466–1536), the famous Renaissance humanist and theologian</note>, a theologian by profession and easily the prince of the most eloquent men of our century—a sweet Siren who, by his own right, deserves the highest praise from all students of refined literature—in his books of *Adages*, which are to be admired by all posterity. In pursuing virtues, Pythagoras certainly attributed much to habit; indeed, it matters a great deal to become accustomed to things in one's tender years. This is why **morals** <note>original: *mores*</note> are called *ethe* as if they were *ethe* <note>original Greek: ἤθη and ἔθη; the author is playing on the Greek words for "character" and "habit," which are nearly identical</note>, that is, "habits." This is something that **the Stagirite** <note>A common nickname for the philosopher Aristotle, who was born in the city of Stagira</note> often approves in his *Ethics*. Our master himself commanded us to choose the best way of life, for habit, he said, will render it pleasant. He therefore organized the whole of moral philosophy into three goals: First, into the worship of God and divine things. 

<margin>C</margin> 

Second, into the respect that each individual has for himself. Finally, into one's duty toward others. Regarding what pertains more excellently to the divine, he taught first of all that nothing is pleasing to the powers above which is not free from filth and clearly purified. For this reason, he handed down a certain adage that should be frequently on one's lips: **do not pour libations to the gods from unpruned vines** <note>original Greek: μὴ σπένδειν θεοῖς ἐξ ἀμπέλων ἀτμήτων; this symbol suggests that one should not offer God the fruits of a neglected or wild life</note>. He also established that sacrifices should be made from the purest grain. From this comes his saying: **Do not sacrifice without flour.** This Pythagorean sacrifice is most ancient, being performed with wine and bread. Furthermore, those things which are dedicated to God must not be transferred to human uses; he therefore frequently warned, saying: **Abstain from the white rooster** <note>Since white roosters were often sacred to deities like the Sun or Moon, they were not to be eaten as common food</note>. He also commanded true worshippers to persevere in humility with this symbol: **sit while worshipping** <note>original Greek: καθῆσθαι προσκυνοῦντας</note>. As for the fact that one ought to look all around during worship, from which that saying arose—**Worship having turned around**—this indicates prudence concerning divine prayers, lest it could be justly thrown back at us: "You do not know what you are asking for." Moreover, the norm of right living for ourselves consists in human decorum, which is the **mean between extremes** <note>The "Golden Mean"—the virtuous middle ground between having too much and having too little</note>, between abundance and deficiency; for in either...

This was so that it might explain not only those things which concern the multitude, but also the individual concerns of each person, which belong to morals and virtue. For he who is placed in charge of a city is clearly chosen under a bad omen unless he is also worthy to rule his own house and even himself.

<margin>A</margin> **"It seems, therefore, that the treatment of character is a part and a beginning of politics,"** <note>original: *μέρος ἐστὶν ἄρα ὡς ἔοικεν ἀρχὴ ἡ περὶ τὰ ἤθη πραγματεία τῆς πολιτικῆς*</note>—that is, the study of morals is a portion and a principle of politics itself, as Aristotle says in the book of the *Great Ethics*. Indeed, a city consists of the whole number of virtues, whose parts are men endowed with virtue admitted into one community. For a gathering of the wicked is no longer to be considered a city, but a den where vices reside, just as virtue resides among good men. As the famous **Theognis of Megara** <note>A Greek gnomic poet of the 6th century BCE</note> says in his book to Cyrnus: *You will learn rightly from the right, but if you associate with the wicked, you will ruin both yourself and your soul.* Having thus set aside contemplative wisdom, which Pythagoras referred to nature and enclosed in his book on *Physics* concerning principles and the modes of causes—how from the **Monad** <note>The number one, representing unity or the Divine</note> comes the **Indefinite Duality** <note>The "Indefinite Dyad," representing the principle of plurality or matter</note>, from these come numbers, and from numbers points...

<meta>catchword: ...from points</meta>

<summary>Philolaus describes how Pythagoras derived the liberal arts from a single source and argues that true "Politics" begins with the moral self-governance of the individual. He transitions from natural philosophy (Physics) back to the Pythagorean metaphysical derivation of the physical world from the Monad and Dyad.</summary>

## BOOK TWO
### I iii

...from points come lines; from lines, plane figures; from planes, solid figures. From these, solid bodies and that perceptible globe of the world—with its spheres and the elements of mixed things: fire, air, water, and earth—are created and arise. Nearly every one of these details was, as is his custom, wrapped in allegory. Finally, setting aside the mathematical studies which he showed to his followers through the **Paedeutic** <note>original: *liber Pædeuticum*, the instructional book mentioned on the previous page</note> (that is, the book on education), I think I should briefly review what he taught regarding morals. He wrote about these at greater length in his work on politics, and more concisely in the *Golden Verses*, which serve as a summary. Since these are read publicly in our own time, I will now pursue only those symbols of this kind that were handed down without being written. He did this so that his disciples, relying on the power of their memory, might become accustomed to living according to these spoken signs with good character, and daily affirm their professing of the philosophical order among themselves through secret passwords. 

Among their number, quite a few were clearly expressed in the books of his *Adages* <note>The *Adagia*, a famous collection of Greek and Latin proverbs</note>—which are to be admired by posterity—by the illustrious **ERASMUS** of **ROTTERDAM**, a theologian by profession, easily the prince of the most eloquent men of our century, and a "sweet Siren" who, by his own great merit, deserves the highest praise from all students of refined literature. Indeed, in the pursuit of virtues, Pythagoras attributed no small amount to habit, for it matters a great deal to become accustomed to things in one’s tender years. This is why morals are called *ēthē* <note>original: *ἤθη*</note> as if from *ethē* <note>original: *ἔθη*</note>, which means "habits" or "customs." The **Stagirite** <note>Aristotle, who was born in the city of Stagira</note> often approves of this in his *Ethics*, and our master himself commanded us to choose the best way of life, for habit, he said, would render it pleasant. He therefore organized all of moral philosophy into three goals. First, the worship of God and divine things. 

<margin>C</margin> 

Second, the respect of each individual toward themselves. Finally, duty toward others. Regarding what pertains more excellently to the divine, he taught first that nothing is pleasing to the powers above that is not free from filth and clearly purified. For this reason, he handed down this adage to be held frequently on the lips: *Do not make libations to the gods from unpruned vines* <note>original: *μὴ σπένδειν θεοῖς ἐξ ἀμπέλων ἀτμήτων*</note>. He also established that sacrifices should be made from the purest grain. From this comes his saying: *Do not sacrifice without meal* <note>A reference to the use of flour or bread in rituals</note>. This Pythagorean sacrifice is extremely ancient, being performed with wine and bread. Furthermore, things that have been dedicated to God should not thereafter be transferred to human uses; he therefore often warned, saying: *Abstain from the white cock.* <note>The white cock was often considered sacred to the gods of light or the sun</note> That true worshippers must persevere in humility was commanded by this symbol: *Those about to worship should sit* <note>original: *καθίσας προσκυνήσοντας*</note>. As for the requirement to look around in every direction during adoration—from which arose the saying, *Worship by turning around*—this indicates <term>prudence</term> <note>practical wisdom or foresight</note> regarding divine prayers, lest it could rightly be thrown back at us: "You do not know what you ask for." Otherwise, as far as we ourselves are concerned, the norm for living rightly consists in human decorum, which is the middle path between extremes, between abundance and deficiency; for in either...

## ON THE CABALISTIC ART

<margin>
Salt is a symbol and a mark of modesty.
</margin>

...is faulty, crippled, and "hundred-handed" <note>original: *centimanus*, a reference to the mythical giants, used here to describe someone who is grasping or overly busy</note>. Hence this symbol, **Do not overstep the balance**, commands that moderation be applied to all studies and actions. More clearly, however, what he himself said—**Set salt on the table**—pertains directly to our affections, which are called the passions. For salt is a mark of modesty, since in human food it is admitted neither in excess nor in too little; indeed, both are rejected: that which is tasteless and that which is oversalted. Therefore, **Do not overstep the salt** was also a proverb. Furthermore, the affections and all the passions within us are moved by some appearance of good or evil: we rejoice in present goods and are saddened by evils; likewise, we desire future goods and fear future evils. Therefore, joy and sorrow are the elements of the passions from which all the movements of our souls arise; their uprightness is called virtue, and their distortion is called vice. However, things that are evil often appear to us as good, and conversely, things that are good seem not to be good; for, as **Seneca** <note>Lucius Annaeus Seneca, the Roman Stoic philosopher</note> says, there is a great difference between the truth and that which is merely "truth-like" (the probable). For this reason, error easily befalls the unskilled common crowd, which exists in great abundance. Behold, Pythagoras sought to turn his disciples away from this, symbolically warning: **Do not walk on the public road**—that is, do not follow the errors of the common people. Yet, because he also wished this to be practiced: **Do not go outside the public way**, he had already insinuated that one should speak like the many—or rather, that you should not fight against what is established among all people. Hence comes that saying: **Do not speak against the sun**, meaning that you should not fall into dangers; and that which rightly warns: **Avoid the sharp sword**. This is achieved if you use honest shame in public, the mark of which is: **Do not urinate against the sun**. Now, therefore, with the error concerning good and evil removed, he determined that one must temper pleasure and sorrow, desire and fear. For this reason he said: **Hands should not be given over to laughter and sorrow alike**. For he commanded that we enjoy joys and pleasure according to "harmony"—that is, with a certain honest temperance, which he called the **lyre**. Hence this symbol: <note>original Greek: ᾠδαῖς χρῆσθαι πρὸς λύραν</note> **to use songs to the accompaniment of the lyre** was not a totally empty mystery. They always used this before the beginning of sleep, so that they might not be troubled by disturbed dreams; when these dreams had rushed in, he commanded those rising to shake out and roll up the bed-covers—that is, to bundle the dreams together and cast them away, so that they would not weigh upon the mind when remembered. Concerning sorrow, he spoke thus: **Do not wear a tight ring**, by which he excluded all pain of the soul, except for that regarding a committed sin; for which reason he sang thus in his poems: **If you have done evil things, grieve**. In other matters, Pythagoras commanded that **The heart must not be eaten**—that is, you should not torment yourself. Furthermore, when you boil over in anger, **Disturb the mark of the pot in the ashes**, which signifies that one must cool down from anger and that the memory of past evils must be wiped away. Regarding desire, he spoke in this way: **Do not nurture things with hooked talons**, and this is established against grasping hands; indeed, you should not even be [anxious] about daily food...

# BOOK TWO

I iiii
<meta>Ink stamp with characters "A B O" over the header. Catchword at bottom left is partially obscured.</meta>

...abundantly anxious, which is why he said: **Do not sit on a daily ration** <note>original: *Choenicine insideas*. A *choenix* was a Greek measure of grain roughly equal to a day's sustenance for one man.</note>; for a *choenix* is a day’s worth of food, which some call a stipend and others call small gifts. Likewise, so that you might show no evidence of greed hidden in your soul, he gave this warning: **Do not pick up what has fallen**, by which he forbade anyone from being too ardent a lover of even their own possessions. Concerning fear, he said: **Do not turn back when you reach the boundaries**, by which symbol he not only prohibits trembling at death, but also at whatever fate has in store, however much it may terrify. For these are the defined and determined boundaries that you will not be able to cross. Therefore, you fear in vain that which you can neither turn back from nor avoid; indeed, to never shrink from such an event is a mark of praised courage and extraordinary greatness of soul. We have briefly enumerated the Pythagorean signs—first those pertaining to the divine, then those pertaining to individual men. Now listen to a few words on how one should behave toward another. Since nothing is more desirable than friendship, the greatest care after the gods must be applied to gaining friends through virtue—as is said in the *Golden Verses* <note>A collection of moral exhortations attributed to Pythagoras</note>—yet not just any passing person. For this reason, he himself said: **Do not extend your right hand to everyone**. And when you have found a friend worthy of your inner chambers, make him a partner in all your affairs. For that reason, Pythagoras himself was the first to use this adage before all others: **Friends hold all things in common**, as **Timaeus** and **Cicero** <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero, the Roman orator and philosopher</note> attest. For a friend is another self, which is why friendship is **equality** <note>original: *isotes*</note>, that is, one and the same soul. However, men who are otherwise "white" <note>pure-looking</note> on the inside but wear a **black tail** on the outside are by no means to be admitted into friendship—believe one who has experience—for the earth bears nothing more pestilential than these: like the beggar-magpies <note>the *Cyanoleuca* or blue-and-white bird</note> with a black tail between their shoulder blades, they are hypocrites, feigning and dissembling everything. Pythagoras therefore said: **Do not taste those with black tails** <note>original: *mē geuesthai tōn melanourōn*</note>, that is, do not taste of those who have a black tail; these are the false brothers, whom they call the "black-clad ones," for **the false thing turns black at its extremities** <note>original Greek: *hō to pleiston en tois echatois meresi melainetai*</note>, as Tryphon the grammarian wrote. As for others of lighter friendship who are of little use, whether they be relatives or friends, you should neither despise them nor accept them beyond measure. This is what this allegory establishes: **Do not collect or step on the clippings of nails or hair**. Nor is it out of place that we are commanded to carefully avoid every ungrateful companion and every whisperer and talkative person; hence that saying: **Do not have swallows living with us** <note>Swallows were often symbols of idle chatter or fair-weather friends who leave when winter comes</note>. Furthermore, a friend is to be received with deliberation, but once received, he is not easily cast aside. Indeed, to break a friendship is inhumane, which is why he said: **Do not break bread**. You, however, should wish to be a friend in such a way that you care for all the friend's affairs just as your own, one whom you do not please with flattering words and the "dye" of speeches, but with the zeal for truth. <margin>The seat of friendship is truth.</margin> For the seat of friendship is truth, not flattery; because of this, he himself said: **Do not wipe the seat with oil** <note>A metaphor for avoiding "oily" or slippery flattery in favor of solid truth</note>.

# ON THE ART OF THE KABBALAH

<meta>The header "DE ARTE CABALISTICA" is the title of the work. The signature "iiii 1" at the bottom indicates the first leaf of the fourth gathering of the book.</meta>

And just as the love of the good must be won over, so the anger of the wicked must not be stirred up; this very thing he warns: **Do not stir the fire with a sword** <note>original: *Ignem gladio ne fodito*. This proverb suggests that one should not provoke or "poke" someone who is already burning with anger.</note>. Furthermore, it is the duty of a good man to be useful to everyone and to harm no one. For if you approach someone either as the author of their distress or as a companion in imposing a burden, you cannot be said to have been helpful; rather, you are said to have weighed them down further, so that you seem to have given way to vice. You will instead earn favor for your virtue when you assist someone who is setting down a burden, so that they may be relieved of the weight more quickly. This is what he meant by: **Help take off a load, do not help put it on** <note>original: *Φορτιον συμϰαθερλειν μη συνεπίτιθεναι* (Phortion synkathairein mē synepitithenai). This emphasizes the duty of alleviating the struggles of others rather than adding to them.</note>; it is just as if he were to say: help so that men may be relieved of their trouble, not weighed down. Truly, a man of unworthy and perverse character, just as he should not be killed suddenly, should also not be nourished by you. For this reason, he forbade: **Do not put food into a chamber pot** <note>original: *Cibū in matellam ne immittas*. This suggests that good advice or wisdom—the "food"—should not be wasted on a corrupt or "foul" mind.</note>. Finally, it is necessary that we set aside such ferocity so that absolutely no one acts cruelly toward any innocent person. Pythagoras also commanded this: **A mild tree is not to be harmed or injured.** From this comes that saying in the symbols: **Do not taste fish.** Indeed, a fish is the kind of animal that by its very nature does not harm humans in any way.

Now, as far as the Commonwealth is concerned, there remains to be cited what he himself said: **Do not pluck the crown**, meaning the law must not be violated. And also this: **Do not cut wood on the road**, by which we are warned that public matters and those belonging to the community are not to be disturbed. Truly, how much pride, the inflation of majesty, or the swelling of public honor is unbecoming to a wise man, this secret symbol exhorts us: **Abstain from beans.** For magistrates were elected with beans according to the custom of the ancients <note>In ancient Athens and other Greek cities, beans were often used as lots or ballots for selecting public officials.</note>. Anyone who is anxiously occupied in seizing the Republic desires an innumerable evil. Therefore, lest he cause offense by openly discouraging the people, he preferred, as a faithful teacher, to turn his disciples away from all ambition through a hidden mystery, so that they would always keep in memory: namely, **that one ought not to engage in politics** <note>original: *ότι ου δεί πολιτεύεσθαι* (hoti ou dei politeuesthai)</note>. There is no doubt that Hipparchus and Lysis, listeners of Pythagoras who held the doctor's precepts in their memory—which they, along with other fellow students, preserved in their own minds instead of in books—brought these forth in the auditorium of Thebes. However, I have not seen all of them, and hurrying toward the end, I did not wish to touch upon everything. I wanted this one thing: that you should not be ignorant of, nor should you commit to oblivion, the fact that almost all Pythagorean philosophy is full of word-signs and coverings for things. It is believed that he was the first to translate that manner of teaching—as I said before—from the Hebrews and Egyptians to the Greeks.

## BOOK TWO.

to all, but understood only by the initiates and those practicing the mysteries through hieroglyphics, just as Chaeremon and Orus <note>Horus Apollo, the supposed author of a treatise on Egyptian hieroglyphs.</note>, and many of the Egyptians have written. Thus my Pythagoras did not think it the part of a wise man to "display a lyre to a donkey" <note>original: *asino lyram exponere*. A proverb for offering something beautiful to someone unable to appreciate it.</note>, or to offer mysteries that would be received as a pig treats a trumpet, a jackdaw a lute, or a beetle perfume. For this reason, he commanded silence from his disciples, so that they would not disclose the secrets of divine matters to the common crowd—matters which are apprehended more easily through meditation than through speech.

Then **Marranus** said: I pray, my Philolaus, do not possess Pythagoras for yourself alone, but allow him to be ours, not yours only. Indeed, I seem to myself to have emerged as a "Pythagorean" who is neither entirely deaf to your discourse nor forgetful. In order to commit to memory all the mysteries, metaphors, enigmas, maxims, apophthegms, allegories, symbols, marks, signs, and sacraments of such a great man (the first of all philosophers), which you have reviewed in passing and superficially in the form of a catalog, I have made use of the "Tullian places" <note>original: *locis Tullianis*. A reference to the "Method of Loci" or memory palace technique described by Marcus Tullius Cicero.</note> and the art of the rhetoricians while listening to you. Why, do you wish me to put it to the test?

For you asserted, if I remember correctly, that Pythagoras encompassed all branches of philosophy in three volumes: the physical, the educational, and the political—that is, the natural, the disciplinary, and the moral. It is said that when he was dying, he entrusted these to his daughter by his will, so that she should not publish them even outside the family, or rather, not publish them at all. Yet while he lived, he demonstrated all that was contained there clearly through the "living voice," using no veil, but only to those who were worthy and few in number—and especially in the case of mathematics <note>original: *mathematica*. In the Pythagorean tradition, this refers to the "mathemata" or the core objects of study: number, geometry, music, and astronomy.</note>. To the rest, he spoke other things in parables.

Therefore, speaking one way while thinking another—and yet always remaining the same wise man—he imparted his doctrine to his followers through certain symbols as if they were memory-aids, so that in imitation of the ancients, one thing was said but another understanding was conveyed. From him, to begin from the very first principles:

*   **The Infinite and the One** are put for **God**.
*   **Numbers** for **incorporeal things**.
*   **Figures** for **corporeal things**.
*   **Harmony** for **mixed things**.
*   **Unpruned vines** for **filth and sins**.
*   **Flour** for that which is **purest in life**.
*   **A white rooster** is the mark of one **dedicated to God**.
*   **Sitting** designates **humility**.
*   **Turning around** signifies **prudence**.

And these pertain to divine matters. The following regard private affairs and the virtues:

*   **The Balance (scales)** is the symbol of **justice**.
*   **Salt** notes **moderation**.
*   **The public road** signifies the **errors of the common people**.
*   **The Sun** is placed in the stead of the **manifest and open**.
*   **A sharp sword** signifies **dangers**.
*   **Urine** signifies **shamelessness**.
*   **Song** signifies **pleasure**.
*   **The lyre** signifies **harmony**.
*   **Bed covers** signify **insomnia**.
*   **A tight ring** signifies **pain**.
*   **Eating the heart** signifies **torment**.
*   **A boiling pot** signifies the **ebullition of anger**.
*   **Hooked claws** signify **plunder**.
*   **The Phoenix** <note>original: *Phoenix*. This likely refers to the bird as a symbol of self-sufficiency or renewal, though its placement here next to "nourishment" (*alimentum*) is specific to this Pythagorean catalog.</note> signifies **nourishment**.
*   **Falling things** signify **fortune**.
*   **Boundaries** signify **fate**.

These are the symbols for a man regarding himself; that which follows deals with his conduct toward others:

*   **The right hand** notes **friendship**.
*   **A black tail** signifies **false brothers**.
*   **Nails and hair** are symbols of **relatives**.
*   **Swallows** represent **talkative people**.
*   **Those who depart** are the **ungrateful**.

# LIIII 3
# ON THE ART OF THE KABBALAH

...the [essence] of things, which you have seen through abstraction from physical objects. You should experience this within yourself, so that through reason you may return to the mind and disentangle yourself from all external things, just as the Emperor Marcus Antoninus commands: "Simplify yourself." <note>original: *haplōson seauton*. This is a famous exhortation from Marcus Aurelius's *Meditations* (4.26), calling for spiritual focus and the removal of worldly vanities.</note> For one departing from this life into the other must have stripped off every garment and set forth naked—not only from all matter and bodily attachments, but also as an exile and free man from the entire mass of disturbances, affections, and passions. Lucian of Samosata taught this quite skillfully in his dialogue of Charon and Mercury—a most philosophical work—which, if you have not read it, you should read and imitate. <note>In Lucian's *Dialogues of the Dead*, the god Hermes (Mercury) forces souls to strip off their wealth, beauty, and pride before they can board Charon's boat to the underworld.</note>

What else, I ask, is it that Pythagoras divided into three parts, which place us in the footsteps of divine virtue, if not **purgation**, **illumination**, and **perfectio**? <term>purgation, illumination, and perfection</term> <note>These are the three stages of the mystical path: cleansing the soul of sin, receiving divine light, and achieving union with God.</note> For he says: "Labor at these things, meditate on these things, these you must love; these will set you in the tracks of divine virtue." <note>original: *tauta ponei taut' ekmeleta toutōn chrē eran se, tauta se tēs theias aretēs eis ichnia thēsei*. These are lines 47-48 from the *Golden Verses*, a collection of moral exhortations attributed to Pythagoras.</note> Hierocles <note>Hierocles of Alexandria, a 5th-century commentator on Pythagoras.</note> wished this to be understood as applying to the powers of our rational soul when they are dedicated to the love of divine things; "and these," he says, "will make us like God."

Let us consider the words of Pythagoras. For he proposed three things which, when joined <term>anagogically</term> <note>Anagoge is a method of spiritual interpretation that "leads upward" from the literal or material sense to the divine.</note>, allow us to reach the highest happiness: the **Labor** of virtue, which consists in action; **Meditation**, which is nourished by many studies of the disciplines; and **Love**, which connects us to God like a necessary bond. Moral philosophy provides the first; natural philosophy combined with mathematics provides the second; and theology provides the third in abundance to those who are diligent. Nor is one sufficient by itself, but these three must come together.

Porphyry, the greatest explorer of the Pythagoreans, treats this matter learnedly (as he does all things) in the first book of *On Abstinence from Animal Food* in these words, which I have chosen to cite because of the weighty authority of the testimony: "Blessed contemplation for us," he says, "is not an accumulation of words or a multitude of disciplines, as someone might perhaps think, nor is it established according to this, nor does it increase according to the quantity of arguments and speeches. For if it were so, nothing would prevent those who gather every discipline from being blessed." <note>original Greek: *ouk esti hē eudaimonikē hēmin theōria...* from Porphyry's *De Abstinentia* 1.29.</note>

And a little later, omitting the rest for the sake of brevity, he says: "And we must, if indeed we wish to return from here to what is truly our own, cast off everything we have taken on from our mortal nature, along with the very affection for those things through which our descent occurred; we must remember the blessed and eternal essence, and hasten to return to the incorporeal and immaterial, making two efforts: one by which we cast off all that is material and mortal, and another by which we return and come together, ascending to those things in the opposite way from which we descended here." <note>original Greek: *kai hēmas dei enteuthen...* from *De Abstinentia* 1.30, describing the Neoplatonic "ascent" of the soul back to the Divine.</note>

<meta>catchword: bus</meta>

# LV
## BOOK TWO
### K

...of essence, and striving to ascend to the incorporeal and impassible, performing two meditations: one by which we set aside everything material and mortal, and the other by which we might return and go back, ascending to those heights in a different way than we descended to this place. And again, after a short discourse, Porphyry <note>Porphyry (c. 234–305 AD) was a Neoplatonic philosopher and student of Plotinus who wrote extensively on the soul's journey back to the divine.</note> commands us there to separate the mind entirely from sense, from imagination, and from every irrational condition and passion of that sort that follows from them, as far as the necessity of nature permits. He bids us to rightly arrange and articulately compose those things which pertain to the mind, preparing tranquility and peace from the war we have waged against irrationality. In this way, we might not only hear about the intellect and the intelligible world, but also, as much as we are able, enjoy its contemplation—first being translated into the incorporeal nature, and then living with the truth through the mind, no longer living falsely with the kinships of bodies. Therefore, we must loosen many garments: both this visible fleshy garment and those with which we are inwardly clothed, which are closest to the skins. <note>original: *pelliceis proxima*. This is a reference to the "garments of skin" from Genesis 3:21, interpreted by mystics as the physical body or the heavy, material state of the soul after the Fall.</note> Thus far speaks Porphyry, who follows these matters with much more discussion, all tending toward the goal that through sensible things we might come to the enjoyment of the intelligible and mental good—by living honorably, contemplating purely, and loving divinely. All these things he drew from our Pythagoras, as if from a great river of all disciplines.

Then Marranus said: Truly, from these things you have recounted to me in order, I am plainly moved to the opinion that Pythagoras limited that river of his from the infinite sea of the Kabbalists—the happy navigation of which Simon promises us—into the fields of the Greeks, from whence we might finally irrigate our own studies. Thus, the discourses and sentiments of Simon regarding the Kabbalists and yours regarding the Pythagoreans seem to me to be equal to one another. For what else does either a Kabbalist or a Pythagoras intend, except to return the souls of men to the Gods—that is, to promote them to perfect happiness? 

<margin>
On behalf of the Kabbalists and Pythagoreans
The soul toward immortality
They teach this through numbers
Vows
</margin>

And what other way is there than the similar method of teaching for both, and an equal exercise for both through symbols and notes, adages and proverbs, through numbers and figures, and through letters, syllables, and words? Thus the *upsilon* <note>The "Pythagorean Y" was a famous symbol where the stem represents childhood and the two branches represent the choice between the difficult path of virtue and the easy path of vice.</note> of Pythagoras stands as a symbol of youth. Thus the first syllable of the *Iliad* is a sign and note of all the books of Homer, how many they are in number in both works. <note>original: *prima syllaba Iliados*. The first syllable of the *Iliad* is *mē* (from *mēnin*), and in the Greek system of using letters as numbers, the 24 books of the *Iliad* and *Odyssey* are labeled with the 24 letters of the alphabet.</note> Thus the word "white" signifies good, and "black" signifies evil. In no different a way does our Simon transfer the first letter of the Pentateuch <note>The Pentateuch refers to the first five books of the Bible (the Torah).</note> and the middle of the pentagrammaton <note>original: *pentagrammati mediam*. In Reuchlin’s Christian Kabbalah, the "Pentagrammaton" is the five-letter name YHShVH (Jesus), formed by adding the letter *Shin* to the middle of the four-letter Divine Name YHVH.</note> to other things; and he borrowed *Raham*, on the authority of David Kimhi, <note>David Kimhi (c. 1160–1235) was a famous medieval Jewish biblical commentator and grammarian. *Raham* (mercy) is often linked etymologically or allegorically to the name Abraham.</note> as an allegory for Abraham, and other things which we remember well enough from the discourse held with us.

But listen! With what a great shout the innkeeper himself calls us to the dining room: "Hey! To the feast!" And Philolaus said: "Indeed, I shall eat greedily; let us go." 

The End.

-># ON THE ART OF THE KABBALAH, BOOK FOUR<-

->### K<-

...then we serve God. This is where our Kabbalists lean when they say <note>original: "שבת היא סוד אל חי" (*Shabbat hi sod El Chai*)</note> *the Sabbath is the mystery of the living God*, as found in the *Gates of Light* <note>The *Porta Lucis* or *Sha'are Orah* is a foundational 13th-century Kabbalistic text by Joseph Gikatilla that explains the ten Sefirot (divine attributes).</note> chapter 2. For it stands as a symbol of the upper world—that is, the eternal <term>Jubilee</term><note>In Kabbalah, the "Upper Jubilee" refers to the Sefirah of *Binah* (Understanding), a source of liberation and the "World to Come" where the soul finds rest.</note>—where all labor ceases. For this reason, in the laws of the fifth book, Deuteronomy, it is commanded with a double usage: *Observe the Sabbath day*, which is intended to be understood regarding external actions according to the lower world. From Exodus 20: *Remember the Sabbath day to sanctify it*, namely, by joining the powers of the soul to the mind for the advancement of contemplation according to the upper world. 

Do you recognize it now? That the Sabbath is a sign of divine service, by which the senses and reason are released from material occupations (as far as human weakness permits), and the energy of the mind is bound to formal occupations to consider those things that are above. The Law wished to suggest this through these two words: <note>original: "שמור וזכור" (*Shamor v’Zakhor*)</note> *observe and remember*. Regarding these, some of our masters understand the precept of the Sabbath to be both affirmative and negative. They say *observe* means *beware* (which for them always signifies avoidance), insofar as it restrains us from everything contrary to holiness. 

<margin>A</margin> Others explain *observe* as *guard*, attributing "guarding" to the night and "remembrance" to the day. This fits quite directly with the foundation of the Kabbalists, who think that this world is "night," and the world to come—that is, the upper and intellectual world—is "day." In the former, servants dwell; in the latter, the free live. To the former one must say *beware, guard, observe*; to the latter, *reminisce, record, remember*. For this word <note>original: "זכור" (*Zakhor*)</note> *remember*, containing an affirmative commandment, proceeds from love; 

<margin>B</margin> but the word *beware*, a negative commandment, is fulfilled out of fear. Love belongs to the free, while fear belongs to servants. Thus, we consider one of these commandments to be more noble than the other. Moses Gerundensis <note>Moses ben Nachman, also known as Nachmanides (1194–1270), a leading medieval Jewish scholar and mystic.</note> wrote on Exodus in a long treatise almost to this effect, in which we accept that there are two Sabbaths, led by the testimony of scripture in Ezekiel 20: *I gave them my Sabbaths*. Indeed, the plural phrasing is satisfied by the number two, not only so that God might generally reproach us under one name for each kind of feast day enumerated in the law—as David Kimhi <note>A famous medieval biblical commentator and grammarian (c. 1160–1235).</note> and the Talmudists <note>Scholars of the Talmud, the central text of Jewish civil and ceremonial law.</note> think—but also so that we might always embrace with a mindful spirit this "best and perfect gift" granted to us by God, which we call the Upper Jubilee. 

<margin>D</margin> Concerning which the *Gates of Light* says: <note>original: "זו היא שביעית שנקראת יובל" (*Zu hi shevi'it she-nikret yovel*)</note> *this is the celestial seventh, which is called Jubilee*. From here all release, propitiation, and infusion of grace descends, which no one is able to speak of sufficiently, since "no eye has ever seen it, O God, except yours." For it is the <note>original: "שבת שבתון" (*Shabbat Shabbaton*)</note> *Sabbath of rest* and the *Sabbath of Sabbaths*, by which all human souls...

...all who are pure, having finally cast off the stain of sin, will return freely to the inheritance of their fathers, and they shall be sent into that possession which is truly and properly ours. The Latin text interprets "Jubilee" here as a spiritual state of liberation.</note>. That most excellent Kabbalist, Rabbi Amma <note>original: "Sopher Ama"</note>, interprets this in the *Book of Secrets* <note>original: "חרזים" (*Sefer Ha-Razim*)</note>, on the verse of the nineteenth Psalm: *Day unto day*. 

<note>original: "ודל איש אל משפחתו ואל נחלת אבותיו ישוב. כלומר שיתעלו בכחות אל מקום אצילותו שהוא פלג אלהים מלא מים"</note> 
That is to say: *Each man shall return to his family and to the inheritance of his fathers.* This means that they shall ascend through the angelic powers to the place of their destination, which is the "river of God full of water." These are the words of Rabbi Amma, and they refer to the waters that are above the heavens in the intelligible world, <note>original: "שהוא מרוח הקדוש" (*she-hu me-ruach ha-kodesh*)</note> which is from the Holy Spirit. There, those who observe the Sabbath enjoy and are nourished by the inheritance of Jacob their father, as Isaiah said. 

Truly, this is the very Sabbath of the Kabbalists, which is to be sanctified at all times. In this state, we follow the will of the soul rather than the flesh, and we meditate upon divine things, intending nothing against God. This stands as a law for all nations, since it springs from nature itself. For you, to whom the Law of Moses was not given, are not bound by the ceremonies of the Jews to serve a specific number of rites—a point which Iarchas <note>Iarchas was a legendary Indian sage mentioned in the biography of Apollonius of Tyana.</note> once rightly denied to Apollonius. Nor will I extort a "number" of rituals from you; instead, I ask for a quiet and tranquil mind, devoted to God and divine things alone. This consists chiefly in <term>anagogical speculation</term> <note>A method of mystical interpretation that seeks to find the "uplifting" or spiritual meaning of a text, pointing toward heaven or the future life.</note>, just as in this discussion of ours which you have so greatly desired.

Then Marranus said: "This must certainly be completed. For you have begun to treat the Kabbalah in a most charming manner, and you have already shown us more than clearly that we not only can, but indeed ought to, discourse on these most sublime matters today. Do you not demand the same, Philolaus?"

<margin>B</margin>
And he replied: "Certainly. Indeed, we have now boarded the ship of this discipline, and already at the very prow we feel that the Kabbalah is nothing other than—to speak in the Pythagorean manner—a **symbolic theology**. In this, not only are letters and names signs of things, but things themselves are signs of other things. By this we perceive that almost the whole philosophy of Pythagoras originated from the Kabbalists; he likewise transferred this symbolic method of teaching to the Greeks. Therefore, I also, along with my companion here, earnestly pray that you proceed in speaking—or rather, in teaching."

<margin>H</margin>
Then Simon said: "I would not claim so much arrogance as to dare to 'teach' you. Nor would it be quite safe in a matter so complex and not yet known to outsiders, especially those educated in the Roman fashion—except for the very few things which, in previous years, Giovanni Pico, Count of Mirandola <note>A famous Italian Renaissance philosopher who was the first to attempt a synthesis of Kabbalah and Christian theology in the 15th century.</note>, [wrote]..."

# ON THE ART OF THE KABBALAH
## BOOK THREE
### Sig. iii X

...which Paulus Ricius <note>A prominent 16th-century humanist and Jewish convert to Christianity who translated Kabbalistic texts into Latin and served as physician to Emperor Maximilian I.</note>, formerly one of our own, have published; yet even to this day, they are not sufficiently understood by the Latin-speaking world. For I fear that if I were to teach such foreign dogmas, I might—just as has happened to many good men before me—be shouted down by a crowd of envious people. These are the sorts who condemn everything they do not know, and in their eagerness for malice, they easily twist words into a sense unintended by the speaker. Cicero calls such people "calumniators"; if I may be allowed to speak grammatically, I would call them "calumnious-ites," since you yourselves are equally accustomed to calling my theologians "Pharisees" <note>A reference to the legalistic Jewish sect, here used as a derogatory term for narrow-minded or hypocritical scholastics.</note>. 

But I openly testify to both of you that I do not wish to *teach* anything, but rather to *discuss* and *review* what I have read among the Kabbalists that I think might not displease you. Therefore, I will pursue first what they intend as the ultimate goal: for they take care to devote all their study and effort to this one purpose—to attain happiness in this life and, according to each person's capacity, eternal bliss in the age to come. They are confident this can be done by this means: if they finally grasp, with diligence and industry, that which they perceive to be the best for the state of both worlds. The possession of this brings a pleasant and perfect rest to those who attain it. For even brute animals seem to exult in their own happiness when they enjoy what they consider best and reach those things that satisfy their desires. 

You see an ox grazing in some flowery green meadow—not eating everything, but by deliberate choice seeking now this herb, now that. Suddenly it leaves one herb behind and bypasses another entirely, until it arrives at the food that is suitable and nourishing for it, where it then settles and rests. In this same way, after traversing the vast fields of the sciences and the meadows of contemplation adorned with every beauty, the Kabbalists taste many various herbs of different scents. Finally, having surveyed the entire pasture, they find that divine Moly <note>original: *Moly*. A mythical herb from Homer's *Odyssey* given to Odysseus by Hermes to protect him from Circe's magic. In Renaissance philosophy, it often symbolized secret spiritual knowledge or the power of reason over animal passion.</note>. Although its root is black, its flower—in Homer’s opinion—shines white <margin>G</margin> as milk. Once found, all miseries seem driven away, and they have achieved the happy end of their desire in this world. 

The virtue of the Moly is this: the root represents difficult works, and the flower represents the tranquility of souls. One could hardly believe this to be anything other than the true happiness of the present age. However, the bliss of the future is the apprehension of the highest good <note>original: *summi boni*</note>, above which there is no good, and from which all goodness comes—a thing that cannot be fully grasped by any mere creature. But it is said to be "apprehended" when, according to each person’s <margin>H</margin> capacity, one draws as close as possible—just as if someone were to grasp the hem of a garment, they would be said to have grasped the man wearing it. But that good which is called God cannot be reached by us clearly, due to the fragility of our condition, except by ascending through steps and ladders, which indeed, as you say...

# BOOK THREE LVIII

...you are accustomed to the likeness of the Homeric chain <note>A reference to the *Aurea Catena Homeri* from the Iliad, which medieval and Renaissance philosophers used to describe the "Great Chain of Being" connecting all levels of existence from God down to inanimate matter.</note>; but as we Jews say according to the divine utterances, surely in the likeness of the ladder of our father Jacob, they reach down from the heavenly heights to the earth. They are like a certain rope or golden cord directed toward us from the sky, just like a line of visual sight <note>original: "linea uisualis"</note> penetrating various natures. For you behold the sun, whose ray travels to our sight through the sphere of Venus, through the sphere of Mercury, through the sphere of the Moon, through the sphere of fire, and through the sphere of air. It touches the opaque body of a concave mirror and reflects from there to tinder or dry wool, which it ignites violently with its brilliance until it turns to ash. The image <note>original: "species"; in medieval optics, this refers to the formal likeness of an object traveling through a medium.</note> of that same flame reaches our eyes and is received by our inner sensation; once received, it is judged by the faculty of estimation, and finally it is traversed by reason. Reason travels back along the path by which this entire present operation proceeded. 

Then this wisely shows us in what way inner forms are carried through the animal spirits <note>In traditional physiology, these were refined substances—not "ghosts"—that acted as the medium for sensation and thought within the body.</note> to the imagination and the judgment of estimation; also, in what way external things are received by internal ones; and likewise, how the image from the flame is directed through the transparent medium <note>original: "perspicuo"</note> all the way to the pupil. It shows by what path the flame arose from the burning caused by the concave mirror, how the ray was able to ignite it, and finally, how brilliance is maintained through many media that are not of its own nature. It shows, in turn, by what proportion air is to be compared to fire, fire to the sphere of the moon, and the remaining spheres to one another. Our reason debates each of these through the path of "composition and resolution" <note>The logical method of building up a concept (composition) and breaking it down into its parts (resolution).</note>, stepping back and forth, thinking now of this and now of that. It does not cease its reasoning until—by way of the phantom-image, the likeness, the mental representations <note>original: "intentions"</note>, the brilliance, the luminescence, and the light—it returns to the luminary itself: that is, to the very sun of which we speak. 

First, reason recognizes the bright image; then it judges it to be the specific flame of the tinder that the eyes had seen a moment ago. Next, it recognizes that its mental representation, produced outwardly from the thing seen through the transparent medium <note>original: "diaphanon"</note> to the eye, was also received within. It recognizes that the tinder is of the earth, the brilliance is of the air, the flame is of fire, and the brightness is an "accident" <note>A philosophical term for a property (like color) that exists in a subject but is not part of its essential nature.</note> inherent in the transparent medium. It recognizes that this brightness passes through what is clear and transparent, whether that be air, or fire, or something celestial, according to the energy and peculiar operation of the substantial form <note>The essential nature that makes a thing what it is.</note>. 

Then, always adapting its meditations to whatever is more noble, reason leaves matter behind and begins to debate with itself concerning "form." It does not deal here with artificial form—the scrutiny of which does not belong here, and which is more correctly called "figure" than "form"—but only with natural or higher form. Thus reason proceeds and finds that some forms are particular (existing "now and here"), while others are universal (existing "always and everywhere"). It finds some forms existing within bodies, to which they grant the power *to be*; other forms it finds "co-assisting," to which they grant the power *to be in such a way*; and still others it finds entirely separate from corporeal things in their essence, power, and operation—though these nonetheless sometimes [retain the] name...

### III ON THE KABBALISTIC ART

...they lose their forms <note>In this context, "forms" refers to the specific physical characteristics that define a material object.</note> and are called either gods, or angels, or intelligences, or blessed souls, or minds, or by any other name one pleases. Moreover, whatever things are universal are no longer called forms, but **Ideas** or **species** <note>original: "Ideæ siue species"; Reuchlin is drawing a parallel between Plato’s Theory of Forms and Kabbalistic concepts.</note> by many who have learned to speak with great propriety. Thus, indeed, reason will ascend for as long as it can; however, when it has been so exhausted by its discourse that it cannot comprehend forms which are neither in nor attached to bodies (as they are not subject to nature), it soon summons the *subsidiary intellect* as an aid.

This intellect—just as it clearly abstracts this matter from this form (like that of a certain donkey buried in a field, which nature clothes with the form of grass blooming from that corpse <note>A vivid Renaissance metaphor: the "donkey-form" is gone, and the matter has been taken up into a new "grass-form."</note>), so again it attempts to abstract form itself simply from matter. It finds this to be arduous and full of labor; for it is easy to abstract matter from form, but difficult to abstract form from matter. Therefore, that intellect raises itself to a purer state, so that it may offer an opportunity for the **Mind** to flow into it. Relying on the clarity of this Mind, the intellect recognizes that some forms are entirely freed from corporeal things in their essence, power, and operation. For that reason, they are enclosed by neither place nor time; wherefore it is truly necessary to judge them to be "above the heavens," where motion and time cease.

From here, the intellect instructs our will to believe that there are certain beings outside the heavens leading the best life, which they enjoy for all eternity. It teaches that there a "second world" begins—most full of living lights and the purest minds—which the human soul can enter by gazing intently through contemplation. This is certainly much more possible than it is for the bodily eye to transcend the sun's orb by looking sharply. And just as we do not look at the sun unless the sun looks at us, so we cannot see the higher world unless it also sees us; for that world is itself an entire eye, even brighter than the sun.

Moreover, we comprehend the sun through solar light; likewise, we comprehend divine things through **divine light**. And since by bodily sight we can grasp not only the sun's orb but even the higher stars and the highest point of heaven, why should our mind—which in a certain way infinitely excels corporeal power—not be able to look up higher and see the contents of the **archetypal world** <note>The "archetypal world" (mundus archetypus) is the world of divine ideas or the Sephirot in Kabbalah, which serves as the blueprint for the physical universe.</note>? This is possible because the concave and convex surfaces of the supreme heaven are joined with such proximity that the horizon of eternity seems to be not at all distant from that outer edge.

Believe me, therefore, we gaze upon the divine things of the other world mutually, and they in turn gaze upon us, just like two directly opposed eyes moved reciprocally through a single visual line.

Then **Philolaus** <note>A character in the dialogue representing the Pythagorean tradition.</note> said: "Everything you teach, Simon, is Pythagorean and proper to the **Italian philosophy** <note>Pythagoras founded his school in Crotone, Southern Italy, hence his teachings were often called "the Italian philosophy" in the Renaissance.</note>, which Marranus and I discussed briefly between us yesterday."

To this he replied: "What you choose to call Pythagorean, I do not know; but this I know: these things I have proposed so far are **Kabbalistic**, handed down by the ancient Kabbalists and all contained within the divine law of the Hebrews. From here..."

<summary>Simon explains how the human intellect abstracts forms from matter to reach the "archetypal world" of divine ideas, asserting that this process is rooted in ancient Hebrew Kabbalah despite its similarities to Pythagorean philosophy.</summary>
<keywords>abstraction, form and matter, archetypal world, divine light, Pythagoras, Italian philosophy, Kabbalah, Philolaus, Simon, contemplation</keywords>

### BOOK THREE

IVXXIII

...from this is born that enumeration of the **Fifty Gates of Understanding**, about which the studies of the **Kabbalists** <term>Kabbalists: Practitioners of Jewish mysticism who seek to understand the relationship between the eternal, mysterious Infinite and the finite universe.</term> labor so greatly. These gates were divinely received by Moses, the servant of God, who also passed on the knowledge of them to us, his descendants, explaining the condition of the universe. For our Masters have already said: **Fifty gates of understanding were created in the world, and all of them were delivered to Moses except for one, as it is said: You have made him a little lower than the angels.** <note>Original Hebrew: "וכבר אמרו רבותינו חמשים שערי בינה נבראו בעולם וכלן נמסרו למשה חוץ מאחד שנא' ותחסרהו מעט מאלהים". The Latin text translates "Elohim" as "gods/angels" following the Vulgate; the verse is Psalm 8:5.</note> Regarding this discourse of the Kabbalists, **Ramban** <note>Rabbi Moses ben Nahman, or Nachmanides (1194–1270), a famous Sephardic scholar and mystic.</note> said in the beginning of Genesis that everything of this kind delivered to Moses through the gates of understanding is contained in the divine Law of the Jews, either in the literal or allegorical sense, through words, or arithmetic calculations <note>Refers to Gematria, where letters have numerical values.</note>, or the geometric shapes of letters (whether written or transposed), or the harmonies resulting from the forms of the characters, their junctions, separations, twists, straightness, defects, abundances, smallness, greatness, crowning, closure, opening, and order.

And through that same Law, the most wise King Solomon also attained by the divine spirit everything he knew. It is written of him in the Book of Kings that God gave him wisdom and very great prudence, "like the sand on the seashore," and the wisdom of Solomon grew beyond the wisdom of all the Easterners and Egyptians. He was wiser than all men, and he spoke of trees, from the cedar of Lebanon to the hyssop that grows out of the wall; he also discussed beasts, birds, reptiles, and fish. Beyond this, **the one from Gerona** <note>Gerundensis: Another name for Nachmanides, after his birthplace, Girona.</note> confirms our view and concludes thus: **He knew it all through the Torah, and he found everything in it through its interpretations, its grammatical subtleties, its letters, and its flourishes.** <note>Original Hebrew: "והכל מצא בה בפירושיה בדקדוקיה באותיותיה ובקוציה". The "flourishes" or "thorns" (kotzim) refer to the *tagin*, the decorative crowns on Hebrew letters used in sacred scrolls.</note> This happened to him after he had fully attained the rationale of the **forty-eight gates of understanding**, which open up the knowledge of all created things.

For all things are generally distributed into **five conditions**. For they are either elements, or composed of elements, or souls, or celestial bodies, or super-celestial incorporeal beings. Each of these perhaps receives ten considerations, the headings of which follow: most general genera, special genera, general species, most special species, individual things (which further consist of matter and form, or certain things proportional to both), and are uniquely limited by differences, properties, and accidents. These ten [categories] of both essences and intelligences...

# ON THE ART OF KABBALAH

## PAGE 12

...these modes, multiplied by five, open the **fifty gates**, through which we enter those secret inner chambers of created things, marked by prominent signs in the works of the six days [of creation], and diligently discovered and received by the **Kabbalists**. Now, by this device, the enigmatic difficulty proposed by the **Count of Mirandola** <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494), a famous Renaissance philosopher who sought to harmonize Kabbalah with Christianity.</note> among his nine hundred conclusions will be easily explained. For he said: "He who knows what the **ten** <note>Original Latin: *denarius*. In Pythagorean and Kabbalistic thought, ten represents the completion of a cycle and the totality of the Sephirot.</note> is in formal arithmetic, and has known the nature of the **first spherical number**, will know the secret of the fifty gates of understanding, and of the **Great Jubilee**, and of the thousandth generation, and the kingdom of all ages." These are the words of Mirandola. 

Therefore, I would like a flat sphere or circle of ten numerical figures to be drawn around a center which is five—for five is the middle of ten—and on its circumference, let the individual numbers of the decimal calculation be described specifically. Let a diameter pass from the minimum to the maximum, that is, from one to nine, the division of which will create two semicircles. On the right side of the sphere, after one and before nine, let the two, three, four, and five mentioned above be placed; on the left side, after one and before nine, let five, six, seven, and eight be placed; and let lines be drawn through the center from two to eight, from three to seven, from four to six, and from five to five. 

Then, if you subtract from each maximum as much as it exceeds five (which is the center of the decimal sphere), and add the same amount to its minimum (which falls short of five), the results from both opposite numbers will always rise to an equalized five and five. Therefore, by comparing the points of the lines with each other, any numerical description of the line results in five and five. 

The number **five** <note>Original Latin: *quinarius*.</note> is therefore called **spherical** in the circle of the decimal revolution because, as you have seen, all the numbers of the sphere are reduced to five. This is achieved through five lines drawn in the sphere, each of which contains ten. Thus, that spherical number multiplied by ten produces the **fifty**—whether they be the gates of understanding or the years of the **Jubilee** <term>Jubilee: In the Hebrew Bible, a year of release for slaves and return of lands, occurring every fiftieth year.</term>. Its double proportion—which is formal arithmetic—multiplied by itself, will procreate the thousandth generation. If you do this perpetually, infinity will appear, which is the **Kingdom of All Ages**, called ***Ensoph*** <note>Original: *Ensoph*, referring to *Ein Sof* (Hebrew for "Without End"), the Infinite or Divine Essence before manifestation.</note> by the Kabbalists; it is the Deity itself without a garment. 

For God produced the remaining things "clothed in light as with a garment," so that it might be light from light. And then, with the light of His garment, He created the intelligible world of separate and invisible spirits, which the Kabbalists call "Heaven," as you have often heard from me. In this manner, I understand the words of the most wise and great **Rabbi Eliezer** <note>Likely referring to Rabbi Eliezer ben Hurcanus, to whom the *Pirkei De-Rabbi Eliezer* is attributed.</note>, who, when he proposed this question—"From what was heaven created?"—answered: **He took from the light of His garment.** <note>Original Hebrew: מאור לבושו לקח (*Me-or levusho lakach*). This is a classic Kabbalistic reference to the process of *Tzimtzum* or divine contraction/manifestation.</note> **Moses Maimonides** <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), the preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher.</note>, the "Discloser of Perplexities" <note>Referring to Maimonides' major work, *Moreh Nevukhim* or *The Guide for the Perplexed*.</note>, recounts these things...

...[they received], as the **Kabbalists** <term>Kabbalists: Practitioners of Kabbalah, the Jewish mystical tradition that seeks to understand the divine nature through scripture and symbolism.</term> do, since it is written of **Moses** in the thirty-fourth chapter of **Deuteronomy**: *No prophet has arisen again in **Israel** like **Moses***. We say these words were passed down and received through the path of the **Kabbalah**, insofar as he would not dare to write anything else except what he had received; and that was two degrees lower than the reception of **Moses**.

After God, the second gate is the archetypal world <note>The world of "Ideas" or the blueprints of creation.</note>, and it is called "Heaven," created by the God of the **Tetragrammaton** <term>Tetragrammaton: The sacred four-letter Name of God (YHWH).</term> in wisdom, according to the **Jerusalem Targum** <note>An Aramaic translation and expansion of the Hebrew Bible.</note> which, in place of *Bereshit* <note>Hebrew: "In the beginning," the first word of Genesis.</note> (that is, "In the beginning"), placed *be-chokhma* <note>Hebrew: "In wisdom."</note> (that is, "In wisdom"). But this visible world is understood as "Earth," which we assert to be the third among the gates. Through "the void" <note>original: *inane*</note>, we shall think matter is symbolically noted: the fourth gate of understanding. Through "emptiness" <note>original: *uacuum*</note>, that is, privation <note>The philosophical state of "lacking" a form.</note>, the fifth. For now, the imprints of the four elements indicate four gates; for the pure element of fire, according to **Moses the Egyptian** <note>Maimonides (1138–1204), the great Jewish philosopher.</note> in the twenty-sixth chapter of the second book of *The Guide for the Perplexed* <note>original: *libri perplexorum*</note>, is called "Darkness." "**Night**" refers to occult properties <note>Hidden or magical qualities of a substance.</note>, "**Evening**" to the path of corruption <note>The process of decay and passing away.</note>, and "**Morning**" to generation <note>The process of being born or created.</note>. On the second day, the "waters above the firmament" are the universal species of things. The "firmament" is the horizon of eternity and time. The "waters below the firmament" are the natural influences of the celestial bodies. On the third day follows another visible and material heaven, namely the nineteenth gate; then the earth we tread, then the seas we navigate, then herbs, seeds, wood, and fruits. Furthermore, the remaining stars designate the thirty-ninth gate; then on the fifth day, living souls come forth...
