Sixth, the walking animal on the earth, and the terrestrial reptile, and beasts of burden, and wild animals. Finally, the fiftieth gate, which is man. These are the forty-nine modes of knowing created things—the **Gates of Understanding** <note>original Hebrew: *Sha'arei Binah*</note>—and the supreme gate is the one Creator of all, clearly known by no man except the **Messiah**, since He Himself is the light of God and the light of the nations; therefore, He both knows God, and God is known through Him. For the royal prophet **David** cries out to God in this way: *Send out your light*, which **Rabbi Solomon the Frenchman** <note>original: *Rabbi Salomon Gallus*, better known as **Rashi** (1040–1105), the most influential medieval Jewish commentator.</note> interprets as the **Messiah** <note>original Hebrew: *ha-Mashiach*. The quote refers to the lamp of the Messiah compared to light, based on Psalm 132:17: "I have prepared a lamp for my anointed."</note>. *That is, the Messiah, who is compared to light, because it is written: "I have prepared a lamp for my Christ [Anointed]." And Isaiah says: "I have given you as a covenant of the people, as a light to the nations." And again: "The nations shall walk in your light."*

Moreover, **Aristotle** wrote what I judge to be true: that vision cannot happen except with light, as we read in the book *On the Soul*: *Nothing is visible without light* <note>original Greek: *ouch horaton aneu photos*</note>. Therefore, as we walk toward the inspection of all things, it is very helpful to bring a light for the journey, so that with mature foresight we may choose a path by which we can proceed without injury to our feet. To this end, the **Kabbalists** <term>Kabbalists: Scholars of Kabbalah, the Jewish mystical tradition that explores the divine mysteries through the Hebrew alphabet and sacred numbers.</term> received certain luminous tracks and illustrious experiences, which they called the **Thirty-Two Paths of Wisdom** <note>original Hebrew: *Lamed-Bet Netivot ha-Chokhmah*</note>, of which **Abraham** makes mention in the *Book of Creation* <term>Book of Creation: The *Sefer Yetzirah*, one of the oldest and most cryptic texts of the Kabbalah, describing how God created the world through the 22 letters of the Hebrew alphabet and the 10 numbers (Sefirot).</term>, which he begins in this way: *With thirty-two wondrous paths of wisdom, Yah, the **Tetragrammaton** <term>Tetragrammaton: The sacred four-letter Name of God, YHWH.</term> of Hosts, engraved or carved out His name.*

Concerning this, **Rabbi Jacob Cohen** <note>A 13th-century Spanish Kabbalist known for his work on the emanations of the left side (evil).</note> wrote that where it says "wondrous," he means that these paths are arcane, hidden, and secret, confirming his interpretation through the **Targum** <note>An ancient Aramaic translation/paraphrase of the Bible.</note>; and the commentator **Rabbi Isaac** <note>Likely Isaac the Blind (c. 1160–1235), credited with being the first to describe the Sefirot as we know them today.</note> testifies in the same *Book of Creation* <note>original: *Yetzirah*</note> that the ancient wise men—prudent, mild, and upright—highly practiced in the **Kabbalah** through the foundations of the Law, taught us that our ancestors and fathers walked through many ways, so that they might finally stand in those paths which are called the wonders of wisdom, handed down by the angel **Zadkiel** to our father **Abraham** in the tradition of the covenant. Thus he says.

I will therefore review them for you, excellent listeners, if only you judge it to be something worthy of your estimation. And **Philolaus** says: *Proceed, I beg you*. And **Marranus** says: *Indeed, I implore you, weave together what you have begun immediately*.

Then he said: These thirty-two paths stretch from the highest peak to the lowest base, and are to be noted in this manner. The first of these is the **Miraculous Intelligence** <note>original Hebrew: *Sekhel Mufla*</note>, as it is called by some, but it is much more correctly named the **Concealed Intelligence**. For **Rabbi Solomon the Frenchman** in the book of **Deuteronomy**, chapter thirty, proves this word...

DE ARTE CABALISTICA

**Wondrous** <note>original Hebrew: *Pele* (פליאה)</note> means **hidden** <note>original Hebrew: *mekhusah* (מכוסה)</note> in the verse: "since this commandment which I command you today is not above you" <note>Deuteronomy 30:11</note>. Here it teaches it should be read as "not hidden from you," and thus it is understood through the Chaldean <note>Aramaic</note> translations cited there. It is, moreover, a light giving understanding to the preceding things without beginning, and it is called the **first glory**, since no creature is able to approach its mere essence and truth.

The second is the **Sanctifying Intelligence** <note>original Hebrew: *Sekhel Mekuddash* (שכל מקודש)</note>; it is the foundation of eternal wisdom, which is called faith, and it is named the parent of faith, because faith is infused from its power.

The third is the **Absolute Intelligence** <note>original Hebrew: *Sekhel Shalem* (שכל שלם)</note>; it is the intention of the principles which has not taken root so as to bring back any things to itself into the inner chambers of its majesty which are infused from what is before it.

The fourth is the **Pure Intelligence** <note>original Hebrew: *Sekhel Tahor* (שכל טהור)</note>; it purifies the Kabbalistic numerations <note>the *Sefirot*, or divine emanations</note> and refines their configuration, and it arranges their boundaries and extremities so that they are without cutting or dispersion.

The fifth is the **Radiant Intelligence** <note>original Hebrew: *Sekhel Mizzohar* (שכל מזוהר)</note>; it is called by the Kabbalists the "second glory."

The sixth is the **Resplendent Intelligence** <note>original Hebrew: *Sekhel Mitnotzetz* (שכל מתנוצץ)</note>; it sits upon the throne of splendor, and it illuminates with the flash of the luminaries, and it pours its influence upon the prince of the surface and of high places.

The seventh is the **Guiding Intelligence** <note>original Hebrew: *Sekhel Manhig* (שכל מנהיג)</note>; it is the throne of glory itself, and it perfects the truth of spiritual communications.

The eighth is the **Rooted Intelligence** <note>original Hebrew: *Sekhel Nishrash* (שכל נשרש)</note>, which is called the "fitting union," and it is the proper seat of that prudence which is infused by the higher wisdom.

The ninth is the **Triumphant or Eternal Intelligence** <note>original Hebrew: *Sekhel Nitzchi* (שכל נצחי)</note>; it is called the "paradise of pleasure" prepared for the saints.

The tenth is the **Disposing Intelligence** <note>original Hebrew: *Sekhel ha-Mitnaheg* (שכל המתנהג)</note>; it prepares for the saints in faith the equipment so they may be clothed in the Holy Spirit, and it is that which is called **Tiferet** <note>original Hebrew: *Thiphereth* (תפארת), meaning Beauty or Glory</note> in the state of the heavenly beings.

The eleventh is the **Intelligence of Clarity** <note>original Hebrew: *Sekhel Tzakh* (שכל צח)</note>; it is the very appearance of magnificence, called *Chazkhit* <note>original Hebrew: חזחית, a term related to vision or mirrors</note> because from it arises the vision for the prophets who see visions.

The twelfth is the **Fixed Intelligence** <note>original Hebrew: *Sekhel Kavu’a* (שכל קבוע)</note>, distinguished by its ecstasy, from which spiritual virtues flow down like an infusion of one from another according to the energy of the first influencer.

The thirteenth is the **Hidden Intelligence** <note>original Hebrew: *Sekhel Nistar* (שכל נסתר)</note>; it illuminates only the powers of those intellects who see through the thought of the faith they have believed.

The fourteenth is the **Illuminating Intelligence** <note>original Hebrew: *Sekhel Me’ir* (שכל מאיר)</note>, which is the **Chashmal** <note>original Latin: *Hasmal*; a reference to the "shining metal" or "amber" seen in Ezekiel's vision</note> angel of Ezekiel, appearing like electrum, the instructor of the secrets of the holy living creatures and their purpose.

The fifteenth is the **Refined Intelligence** <note>original Hebrew: *Sekhel Metzuchtzach* (שכל מצוחצח)</note>; it arranges the order by which access is granted through the steps of ascent.

The sixteenth is the **Faithful Intelligence** <note>original Hebrew: *Sekhel Ne’eman* (שכל נאמן)</note>, by which the graced virtues are increased according to the lives of those in whom they dwell.

The twentieth is the **Constituting Intelligence** <note>original Hebrew: *Sekhel Ma’amid* (שכל מעמיד)</note>; it makes creation itself stand in **pure darkness**. And the masters of Kabbalah say that it is darkness according to the verse: "darkness was round about Him" <note>Psalm 18:11</note>. The twenty-first is the **Innovating Intelligence** <note>original Hebrew: *Sekhel Mekhadesh* (שכל מחדש)</note>, through which all created things in this world are repaired and renewed. The twenty-second is the **Intelligence of the House of Abundance** <note>original Hebrew: *Sekhel Beit ha-Shefa* (שכל בית השפע)</note>; from the midst of its infusion are drawn the secret and the hidden thing, which dwell in its shadow and adhere to the study of bringing forth and the diligence of promoting toward the heights. The twenty-third is the **Intelligence of Activities** <note>original Hebrew: *Sekhel ha-Pe’ulot* (שכל הפעולות)</note>; it is the collection and universality of spiritual operations, so called because of the influx that is gathered in it from the source of the higher sea and the exalted glory. The thirty-first is the **Imaginary Intelligence** <note>original Hebrew: *Sekhel Dimyoni* (שכל דמיוני)</note>, by which all created figures and images are varied and altered according to the surfaces of things and their natures. <meta>This page continues the discussion of the Thirty-Two Paths of Wisdom from the Sefer Yetzirah, moving from the specific list of Intelligences to the mathematical and mystical structure of the Kabbalistic system. It introduces the relationship between the twenty-two letters of the Hebrew alphabet and the Fifty Gates of Understanding, leading to the derivation of the seventy-two angels of the Divine Name.</meta>

### ON THE KABBALISTIC ART

...and they treat the thirty-two paths of wisdom in many books with a more difficult level of study. It is certainly a subject worthy of a better teacher, requiring much sweat, which carries the greatest power to urge us to dwell almost always with the angels in the contemplation of the highest and divine matters. If we begin to be familiar with these things, nothing will be difficult for us to either say or do. The letters, which are their gift, provide that familiarity. If we apply these letters to the ten Kabbalistic <term>numerations or *Sefirot*</term>, the number thirty-two immediately arises. This is read in the **Book of Formation** <note>original: *Lib. Ietzira* (Sefer Yetzirah)</note> as: **"Ten numerations of nothingness and twenty-two letters"** <note>original Hebrew: *Eser Sefirot Belima ve-Esrim u-Shetayim Otiyot*. The word *Belima* (בלימה) is often interpreted as "without anything" or "restraint," implying the abstract nature of these divine emanations.</note>. For this reason, many writers combine these ten properties worthy of silence with the twenty-two letters to form this sum of paths, which I have arranged in that order according to my own custom, though others do not observe it in quite the same way.

<margin>N</margin> But truly, if we diligently apply that assembly of letters to the **fifty gates** <note>The Fifty Gates of Understanding (*Binah*) are a traditional Kabbalistic concept representing levels of insight into the divine creation.</note>, we will find from there the blessed series of **seventy-two angels**. It is said that the **Shem HaMephorash** <note>original: *Semhamaphores*, a Latinization of the Hebrew for "The Explicit Name" or "The Name of Extension."</note>—that is, that great explanatory name of the most high God—consists of these. For seventy-two is produced by adding twenty-two to fifty. These are the powerful angels of the whole earth, through whom that Moses, the performer of miracles, is thought to have divided the sea with his hand until it was dry, because they themselves are the "angels of division." And **God divided the earth according to the number of His angels**. For so we read among other things in the book **The Gates of Justice** <note>original: *Portarum Iustitiae*, the Latin title for *Sha’are Orah*, written by Rabbi Joseph ben Gikatilla</note>, which Rabbi Joseph ben Carnitol <note>Joseph ben Abraham Gikatilla (1248–c. 1305), a Spanish Kabbalist</note>, a famous master in the Kabbalah, wrote: **"And all the nations were left handed over into the power of the seventy prefects"** <note>original Hebrew: *ve-nish’aru kol umot mesurot be-yad shiv’im*</note>, that is, the princely angels. To these, Recanati <note>Menahem ben Benjamin Recanati (1250–1310), an influential Italian Kabbalist</note>, a most skilled Kabbalist, assigns those **seventy palm trees** near the **twelve springs** (which you know) in his commentary on **Genesis 48** <note>The biblical reference for the 70 palms and 12 springs is actually Exodus 15:27, but the author follows Recanati’s specific structural commentary here.</note>. Furthermore, it is certain that there were two columns there, of cloud and of fire, over which two angels were placed. Therefore, we will not think in vain that in such a cutting of the sea and the liberation of the children of Israel, the seventy angels of the world and those two pillar-angels came to the aid of Moses for the service of salvation. This salvation clearly comes to us from the **Ineffable Tetragrammaton** <note>The four-letter name of God, YHVH</note> through the seventy-two names, which are gathered from the explanation of Holy Scripture in **Exodus 14**, starting from the verse: **"And the angel... taking himself up"** <note>Exodus 14:19</note> until the end, where it is read: **"and the water was divided."** <note>The 72 names of God are traditionally derived from three consecutive verses in Exodus 14:19-21, each containing exactly 72 Hebrew letters.</note> These are surely our sacred seals in this present age, stored in a mindful soul—symbols by which angels were called to help men, to the praise and glory of the ineffable God. Concerning this, Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi (Solomon ben Isaac), the famous medieval commentator</note> wrote in his exposition of the **Talmud**, as evidenced by the Gerundian <note>Nahmanides (Moses ben Nahman of Gerona)</note> at the beginning of Genesis.

"Indeed, we are most ready," they both say, "for we have faced the many dangers of travel for this very reason, spending so much and so great a sum. But go on," they say, "so that we may learn something of these angels, whose names have never been heard by me, Marrano, nor, I believe, by you either, Philolaus." "Certainly," says Philolaus, "just as these angels have never been seen by me, so their names are unknown to me. But we will love you, most excellent man, if you continue without ceasing."

Then Simon said: "That there were many angels who gathered for that great and wonderful work of Moses, when he divided the waters of the sea so that the Israelites might cross with dry feet, we can discover from Holy Scripture itself, lest anyone think me a deceiver. For the divine words in that passage are these: <insert>And the messenger of the gods moved</insert> <note>original Hebrew: *Va-yissa Malakh ha-Elohim* (Exodus 14:19)</note>, that is, 'and the angel of the angels moved.' But it is not written even here simply as 'an angel of Elohim,' as it frequently is elsewhere. He asks: 'I pray, why is it written everywhere "the angel of Adonai," but here it says "the angel of **the** Elohim"?' To which he responds: <insert>The word 'Elohim' in every place refers only to a judge or a prefect.</insert> Therefore, that angel is understood to have been present together with the seventy presiding governors of the provinces; for this reason, he is called *Mallach ha-Elohim*, the angel of those governors or prefects. And another angel of fire was also a companion of those same governors, so that by best right seventy-two are numbered, whose signs you have already seen described by me. If you wish—or rather, because you wish, for I know that you do—I give them to you."

<meta>This page continues Simon’s explanation of the seventy-two divine names. Having previously listed the names themselves, Simon now demonstrates the technical method (the "Kabbalistic way") of extracting these three-letter names from the three specific verses of Exodus 14:19–21.</meta>

# ON THE KABBALISTIC ART

### BOOK THREE

...[I will show] by what path they are drawn forth from the sacred scriptures. Now, take these same three verses—<note>Exodus 14:19, 20, and 21</note> <insert>Vav-He-Vav, Yod-Lamed-Yod, Samekh-Yod-Tet</insert> <note>original Hebrew: והו ילי סיט</note>—and, in the manner of an upright column, write them down individually according to the Kabbalistic custom from right to left. Arrange them so that the letters of each verse follow one another continuously from top to bottom. Then, place the first character of the first verse, which is named *Vav*. Next, take the last character of the second verse by moving in a backward direction, which is *He*. Then, finally, return to the beginning of the third verse, which you will find is once again *Vav*. When you have joined these three characters in that order, the memorial name of the first angel will be born: *Vav-He-Vav*. And the second: *Yod-Lamed-Yod*. And the third: *Samekh-Yod-Tet*. So it goes for all the rest, always in groups of three. In this way, with the three columns rightly erected as they should be, an expository seal of the <term>Tetragrammaton</term> <note>The four-letter name of God, YHWH, here expanded into seventy-two names</note> will be forged from each.

Oh, see, consider, and contemplate well: is this not the very height of joy, surpassing every gladness of this world? To remember the holy signals of God and the divine countenances which the Hebrews call <term>Malakhim</term> <note>original: *Mallachim*; Hebrew for messengers or angels</note>, the Greeks call *Angels*, and the Latins call *Gods*. To handle in mind and hands such pure, pious, and consecrated things! To converse studiously with those most bright forms, whose splendor shines only for the keen eyes of noble minds. To be present at the banquets and conversations of the blessed spirits, who love us more brotherly than is the custom of all mortals—and they do not just love us, they cherish us. The very walls seem to me to leap for joy and to congratulate us humans that, by God's goodness, it has come to pass that through certain seals and artistic <term>marks</term> <note>original: *charagmata*; a Greek term for engraved or mystic characters</note> of human weakness, we are admitted into the cheerful gatherings of the angels, according to the capacity of our strength. With them, we may rejoice and be glad with a tranquil heart; we may cherish and venerate them, paying them the honor due to such a sublime nature, and in turn be loved, instructed, and guarded by them.

Then Marranus said, "I see the characters, certainly, but I do not hear the sounds of the names; therefore, I do not know with what pronunciation the angels should be invoked." To this Simon replied, "As they are seen by the eyes, so they are heard by the ears; and as they see us, so they hear those who call upon them. How this can be done, I will say in two words: <note>original: *In spiritu & ueritate*</note> **In spirit and in truth**, so that our minds have such tongues as the angels have ears. And just as the divine spirits speak with the tongues of angels, so may human spirits listen with the ears of their minds. Therefore, they do not impose names upon themselves by necessity because they wish to be named and called out loud, but they hand down memorial seals because they desire to be remembered by us—lest you think all divine power lies hidden in the voice. These symbols, therefore, demand frequent memory of the angels; diligent remembrance of them leads us mutually into the love of God, and in turn, love leads us into dwelling with Him."

<page-num>LXIIII</page-num>
->**BOOK THREE**<-

For we remember frequently those whom we love strongly; as the proverb says, *Lovers remember everything.* <note>original: "Meminerunt omnia amantes."</note> For this reason, God granted us the **Tetragrammaton** <note>The four-letter name of God, YHWH</note>, not so that we might call upon Him by it—for it is ineffable, and rightly called by you **Anekphoniton** <note>original: "Anekphoniton"; Greek for "unpronounceable"</note>, that is, "not to be spoken"—but for another purpose. For what did the Creator answer Moses when he asked, "What is your name?" He surely said this: *I. H. V. H.* <note>The letters Yod, He, Vav, He</note> "This is my name forever, and this is my memorial from generation to generation." Therefore, the Tetragrammaton is a name for eternity, but for the present generation it is only a memorial, because no human voice can compose a name that could equal the nature of divinity.

We know the angels by their works; therefore, we pronounce names for them according to those same works of power. For instance, **Raphael** is named from medicine <note>The name means "God heals"</note>, **Gabriel** from virility or strength <note>The name means "God is my strength"</note>, and **Michael** from wonder and admiration, which we interpret as "Who is so strong?" <note>Usually interpreted as "Who is like God?"</note> As for their own true names, since we are ignorant of their essence, the weakness of our mortal nature is not able to find them, nor to assign them once found, except for what has been granted to us by divine revelation.

Therefore, from the numbers and figures handed down by God, the most contemplative men are taught to form names for themselves according to the wills of the angels, just as children are taught to compose words from letters—whether Hebrew, Greek, Roman, Arabic, or Egyptian. This is not because the voice to be spoken needs letters of this kind, but for the sake of the memory of our own weakness. These names act as "notations" <note>original: "notamina"</note> which might stir our senses by either their shape or their sound; in turn, the sense moves the imagination, the imagination moves the memory, the memory moves the reason, the reason moves the intellect, the intellect moves the mind, and the mind moves the angel.

A certain philosopher of yours, of distinguished name, Maximus of Tyre, wrote something of this kind quite elegantly in the book <term>of the dissertations in Rome of the first visit</term> <note>original Greek: "τῶν ἐν ρώμῃ διαλέξεων τῆς πρώτης ἐπιδημίας"</note> in the eighth discussion. From this, it becomes known to you by conjecture that it is enough if you read the three verses—previously resolved by me in reverence and veneration of the seventy-two angels—in the order which the Holy Spirit dictated. Through their love, you shall dwell in the most burning love and ecstatic adoration of the name of the most high God, considering carefully that just as the number of seventy-two proceeds from the number of the **Tetragrammaton** by arithmetic proportion, so the seventy-two angels are produced from the seal of the Creator by a certain divine outflow.

Since each Hebrew letter designates a specific number, the seventy-two arise from **Yod, He, Vav, He** in this way: **Yod** denotes ten, **He** five, **Vav** six, and **He** again five. The whole of this is gathered from the art of arithmetic thus: **Yod** is ten; **Yod He** is fifteen; **Yod He Vav** is twenty-one; **Yod He Vav He** is twenty-six. Now, grasp these individual sums: ten, fifteen, twenty-one, and twenty-six... <note>The text breaks off as it begins to sum these four results: 10+15+21+26 = 72</note>

twenty-six, and seventy-two arise. Considering these things with yourselves, you will clearly 
understand that to invoke spirits, a spiritual voice is needed, and not
shouting, as was the case with the priests of Baal, to whom it is said by the prophet Elijah in the 
third book of **Kings, chapter 18**: <note>In the Latin Vulgate, 1 Kings is titled 3 Kings. This refers to 1 Kings 18:27.</note> "Cry out with a louder voice; perhaps your God is in a lodging, 
or on a journey, or surely he sleeps and must be awakened." But if we use any prayer in our 
supplications, it is not done so that we may move God or the angels with syllables or 
words as if we were dealing with mortals, but so that we may incite our own powers into 
their ardor, and fix our confidence in them like an anchor. It is just as when 
sailors, in bringing a ship into port, are accustomed to cast out a rope or extend a cable 
to pull themselves toward the land—even though the land is immobile—by which effort they 
draw themselves to the shore. By a similar reasoning, through sensible signs 
composed by whatever method, we seem to "draw" the invisible divinity to us, when in 
truth we, who are movable, draw ourselves to the immobile divinity. On this 
secret foundation, all the sacraments and the rites of ceremonies persist. 
For this reason we use signs, characters, and the voice; for this reason hymns and songs, 
the drum and the choir, strings, cymbals, and the organ, and other 
musical instruments of that kind. This is not to soften God as if he were a woman, nor so that 
the angels might be captured by our charms and flatteries. Rather, it is so that by 
exalting God and divine things, we may acknowledge the smallness of our condition, 
profess our subjection and obedience most humbly, and direct all human 
pleasure toward divine matters. Ultimately, by this means, we may 
conceive an intense and burning love toward the divinity—which one thing, 
above all others, makes us most capable of receiving all graces. For this reason 
we stretch out our palms, expand our arms, bend our knees, and pray while 
standing; we are also commanded to divide down the middle a three-year-old heifer, a three-year-old goat, a turtle-dove, and a 
pigeon; <note>A reference to the "Covenant between the Pieces" in Genesis 15:9.</note> we slay with a sword the ram caught by its horns in the thicket and 
burn it with fire; <note>The sacrifice of Isaac in Genesis 22.</note> we mark the **Tau** <note>The Hebrew letter Tav, often interpreted by Christians as a cross, used here in the context of the Passover blood on the doorposts.</note> upon the doorposts of our houses with 
blood; we look upon the Bronze Serpent; we fashion the Cherubim and other images. 
We speak composed words and make vows; we build a Sanctuary; we 
look with astonishment upon the High Priest clothed in such varied and wonderful vestments. 
All these and similar things are done for our own sake: so that 
they may move us, incite us, turn us away, and convert us—namely, from 
visible things to the invisible; that they may increase faith, confirm hope, and 
transfer true charity among us (which is most pleasing to God) into a love for divine things 
by a diligent **recapitulation**. <note>original: "Anacephalæosi"; a Greek rhetorical term for a summary or summing up.</note> All these are the teachings of the 
Cabalists, who, as the third book of the *Guide for the Perplexed* by Moses the Egyptian <note>Moses the Egyptian is Maimonides (1138–1204). This quote is from Part 3, Chapter 44 of his *Guide for the Perplexed*.</note> 
attests, say this: **The purpose of those acts of worship is the remembrance of the Name that guides, and the fear of Him, and the love of Him, and the keeping of all the commandments, and that one should believe in the Name (Blessed be He) what is necessary for everyone.** <note>original Hebrew: שכונת העבודות ההם זכרון השם המורה ויראתו ואהבתו ושמירת המצות כולן ושיאמין בשם ית׳ מה שהוא הכרחי לכל</note> That is, the intention of such ceremonies is the frequent memory of God...

<meta>This page continues the argument from the previous page regarding the use of "sensible signs"—such as music, symbols, and spoken words—as tools to elevate the human soul toward the divine, despite God's own immaterial nature.</meta>

<page-num>LXV</page-num>
<header>BOOK THREE</header>

...is frequent, as is the fear of Him, the love of Him, and the observance of all His commandments, and that belief in God Most High which is necessary for everyone. To be sure, we who are oppressed by the heavy mass of the body stand in great need of things that can move us to awaken the sleepy soul. Just as a noble horse, tired from a long journey, is roused to strength when the trumpet sounds—it cannot stand still, its ears twitch—and just as an elephant, sluggish with torpor, rises up in boldness when shown a flame; so too is our virtue weakened by worldly affairs. It requires external and bodily incitements, whether of voices or of figures, so that the vigor of our soul may more robustly pursue spiritual work, and so our contemplation may be driven into the heights with even greater sharpness, the more we were previously struck dumb with astonishment.

For this purpose, merciful <term>angels</term><note>The author views angels as intermediaries who provide humans with the "technology" of ritual—symbols and names—to bridge the gap between matter and spirit.</note> have often discovered figures, characters, forms, and voices, and have set them before us mortals. These are both unknown and astonishing, signifying nothing according to the common use of language, but leading us through our reason's greatest admiration into a diligent investigation of intelligible things, and finally into the veneration and love of those very things. For they do not signify according to the institution or pleasure of man, but according to the pleasure of God.

For this reason, that most learned man of your age and sect, the Count of Mirandola <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494), a famous Renaissance philosopher who sought to synthesize Kabbalah and Christianity.</note>, brought this point to you when he says in his *Nine Hundred Conclusions*: "Meaningless words have more power in magic than meaningful ones." For any word has power in magic insofar as it is formed by the voice of God, because that in which nature first exercises magic is the voice of God—these are the words of Pico.

Then Philolaus said: "Such names would move us men, who are sleepy and snoring, with a greater arousal if they moved more of our senses and not just one; so that they might not only appear to our sight through figures and characters, but also strike our ears at the same time with an articulate voice. Therefore, I greatly desire, if it were possible, not only to see these things painted, but also to hear them spoken."

Then Simon said: "In my opinion, they should be considered very sluggish—and if I may be permitted to say so with your pardon, very dull indeed—who require an external movement. And yet we are born such that one thing always affects one person more than another, and not the same thing affects everyone equally."

To this, the most learned Simon, I agree that you speak the truth, said Marranus. For our people also affirm that <margin>Q</margin> angels appear to men in different ways according to the condition and nature of the seer. Concerning this, Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407), an important Early Church Father.</note> writes extensively in his commentary on Matthew, saying these words about Joseph: <note>original Greek: "κατ’ ὄναρ φαίνεται ὁ ἄγγελος καὶ οὐχὶ γυμνὴ Φανερῶς καθὼς τοῖς ποιμέσι καὶ τῷ Ζαχαρίᾳ καὶ τῇ παρθένω. σφόδρα πιστὸς ἦν ὁ ἀνὴρ. καὶ οὐκ ἔδει τῆς ὄψεως ταύτης"</note> "The angel appears in a dream, and not openly and visibly as he did to the shepherds, to Zechariah, and to the Virgin. That man [Joseph] was exceedingly faithful, and did not stand in need of such a vision." That is to say: the angel appears through a dream, and why not manifest? Just as he did to the shepherds, Zechariah, and the Virgin. That man was vehemently believing, and did not need that [physical] vision.

<meta>This page continues the dialogue led by Simon, the Kabbalist, who is explaining to his companions how divine power manifests through symbols and names. # ON THE KABBALISTIC ART

To which Simon replied: And you are quite right in this; indeed, the Kabbalists <note>Practitioners of Kabbalah, a school of Jewish mysticism that seeks to understand the relationship between the eternal, mysterious Infinite and the finite universe.</note> feel no differently. They say that the visual power in Abraham was stronger than in Lot, and for that reason, men appeared to Abraham, whereas angels appeared to Lot. But perhaps we shall speak of these things in another place. Now, as it concerns our current cause, there is, as you well know, a great diversity among men. Some are quite grateful and perhaps content to have seen angels in human form; others in the form of fire, others in the form of wind and air, others in the form of a river and water, others in the form of birds, others in the form of gems or minerals or precious stones, others in the energy of prophecy, others in a certain spirit dwelling within themselves, others in the shape of letters and characters, others in the sound of a voice—and so it is with many types of visions found in Holy Scripture. 

However, since these characters of the seventy names <note>A reference to the 72-fold name of God (Shem HaMephorash), a central concept in practical Kabbalah derived from verses in Exodus.</note> will seem by no means sufficient to you, I will demonstrate the straight path—not only regarding the characters already mentioned but also those to be mentioned later—showing how a word that can be articulated and pronounced is formed from the shapes of the letters. We have God Himself as the author of this art. For we read in the twenty-third chapter of Exodus:

> Behold, I send my angel before you, to guard you on the way and to lead you into the place I have prepared. Be attentive to his presence and listen to his voice; do not provoke him, for he will not forgive your crimes, because my name is in him.

By this, we recognize that the name of an angel must, by the highest rite, sometimes contain the name of God. Therefore, when the Kabbalists were unable to meaningfully pronounce the name of any angel, they were accustomed to utter the whole thing at once by the aid of some name of God which they joined to it. For just as they see these three characters—<term>Mi-cha</term> <note>original Hebrew: מיד. Likely a transcription error in the OCR for מיכ, the root of Michael.</note>, or <term>Gabri</term> <note>original Hebrew: גברי</note>, or <term>Rapha</term> <note>original Hebrew: רפא</note>—used improperly to signify the name of an angel unless the name of God, <term>El</term>, is added (resulting in Michael, Gabriel, and Raphael), so they also, in attempting to imitate Holy Scripture with other angelic names, say Raziel, Jophiel, Zadkiel, Peliel, Malthiel, Uriel, and others in a similar fashion. 

Indeed, just as the Romans name their Capitoline God "Best and Greatest"—"Best" on account of his benefits and "Greatest" on account of his power, according to the testimony of Cicero in his speech to the Priests for his house <note>Cicero, *De Domo Sua*. Reuchlin often uses classical Roman parallels to make Jewish concepts more approachable for his Renaissance audience.</note>—so the nation of the Jews calls their God **Iah** <note>A shortened form of the Tetragrammaton (YHWH).</note> on account of His benefits, and calls Him **El** on account of His force and virtue. For so the Kabbalists say regarding the words of King David when he says:

> If you, **Iah**, should mark iniquities, Lord, who shall stand?

They say: <term>Iah, which is the world of mercy; Adonai, which is the world of judgment</term> <note>original: יה שהוא עולם הרחמים אדני שהוא עולם הדין</note>. This is found in the eighth chapter of the *Gates of Light* <note>original: *Portae Lucis*. This refers to the *Sha'are Orah*, a fundamental Kabbalistic text by Joseph Gikatilla (13th century).</note>. Regarding **El**, however, you read thus in the sixteenth chapter of Numbers:

> Most powerful **El**, God of the spirits of all flesh, shall your anger rage against everyone when only one man sins?

Therefore, God is "Best" to us because He is most merciful, and "Greatest" because He is most powerful.

<summary>Simon explains that angelic names are often unpronounceable until combined with names of God like "El," and he equates Jewish titles for God (Iah and El) with the Roman "Best and Greatest" to illustrate God's mercy and power.</summary>

### THIRD BOOK

...let us be aware that these two divine names represent Iah and El. If you join either of these to any of the seventy-two names, you will certainly create a notable word with an oxytone <note>A word with the grammatical accent or stress on the last syllable.</note> stress. In this manner, they should always be pronounced so that the words become trisyllabic <note>Consisting of three syllables.</note>. The aspirations written with this unique mark "**h**" should come forth from the depths of the chest with a strong breath, like a double breathing of the Latin letter "**h**," and everywhere "Iah" should be pronounced uniquely using the consonant "**i**" <note>Pronounced as a "y" sound, as in "Yah."</note>. Similarly with "El," for both of these words, even when used in the composition of names, are spoken as monosyllables, and the accent falls upon them.

There are, therefore, 72 sacred names, which collectively are called the one <term>Semhamaphores</term> <note>Original: "Shem HaMephorash," Hebrew for "The Explicit Name." In Kabbalistic tradition, this is a 72-fold name of God derived from Exodus 14:19-21.</note>, that is, the explanatory name of the most holy <term>Tetragrammaton</term> <note>The four-letter Hebrew name of God, YHWH, often considered too sacred to pronounce.</note>. These names are to be spoken through the invocations of angels by men dedicated to God and the most devout, with fear and trembling, as follows:

->Vehuiah, Ieliel, Sitael, Elemiah, Mahasiah, Ielahel, Achaiah, Cahethel, Haziel, Aladiah, Lauiah, Hahaiah, Iezalel, Mebahel, Hariel, Hakamiah, Lauiah, Caliel, Leuuiah, Pahaliah, Nelchael, Ieiaiel, Melahel, Haiuiah, Nithhaiah, Haaiah, Ierathel, Seehiah, Reiaiel, Omael, Lecabel, Vasariah, Iehuiah, Lehahiah, Chauakiah, Manadel, Aniel, Haamiah, Rehael, Ieiazel, Hahahel, Michael, Veualiah, Ielahiah, Sealiah, Ariel, Asaliah, Mihael, Vehuel, Daniel, Hahasiah, Imamiah, Nanael, Nithael, Mebahiah, Poiel, Nemamiah, Ieiaiel, Harahel, Mizrael, Umabel, Iahhael, Anauel, Mehiel, Damabiah, Mauakel, Eiael, Habuiah, Roehel, Iabamiah, Haiaiel, Mumiah.<-

Now these are ready at hand, excellent men, with whom you may not only whisper secret conversations from the innermost depths of your heart, but also mingle clearly expressed voices. You may invoke each one by their symbolic name, for although they are the overseers of individual regions, they hold nothing that is not shared. For although they dwell in the super-celestial world, they nonetheless care for these lower things. 

If it happens that natural influences dwell in the heavens and simultaneously govern earthly things, how much more are such offices granted to the more noble and simple virtues of the higher world? They penetrate our affairs, and in turn are penetrated by ours. To this end, I shall use the assertion of your <term>Plotinus</term> <note>A major Neoplatonic philosopher (c. 204–270 AD) whose ideas deeply influenced Renaissance thought.</note> in his book *On Intellect, Ideas, and Being*, who says: "This sensible world is determined by only one place, but the intelligible world is everywhere." It is as if he were to say that the higher world surrounds, orders, preserves, and penetrates this world of ours. 

Notice what worthy thing the wise ones among the <term>Cabalistarum</term> <note>Kabbalists; practitioners of Jewish mysticism.</note> bring forward here, saying:

> <note>Original Hebrew: "אין לך כל עשב ועשב למטה שאין לו מזל ברקיע שמכה אותו ואומר לו גדל"</note>
> There is not a single herb or plant below that does not have a star in the firmament which strikes it and says to it: "Grow."

They themselves have come to this opinion.

# ON THE ART OF THE KABBALAH

...fortified by sacred scripture, as we read in Job chapter 38: *Do you know the laws of the heavens, or have you established their rule* <note>Original: "praefectum, seu praesidem, uel executorem" — literally a prefect, president, or executor.</note> *upon the earth?* Therefore, let not the vast distractions of the world or the cares of lower things—to which the aforementioned angels are assigned by the creator’s dispensation—hold you back from recognizing them within the nine choirs of the super-celestial hierarchies. Since an angel represents **alterity** <note>The state of being "other" or different; in this philosophy, God is perfect "Identity" (1), and the first step toward creation is "Otherness" (2).</note>, just as God represents **identity**, and the first alterity is the <term>Binary</term> <note>The number two.</note>, we rightly believe that the number of angels arises from the multiplication of the binary. The cubical multiplication of the binary is done thus: two times two times two, which equals eight—the first cube. If you distribute these eight [units] into the nine choirs, there will be seventy-two, for nine times eight is seventy-two.

Return now, if you wish, through the choirs to the cube; through the cube to your <term>Tetractys</term> <note>A Pythagorean symbol of ten points arranged in a triangle, representing the organization of the universe.</note> (which we call the **Tetragrammaton**, and the Romans call the "four-foldness"); from that to the binary signifying the angelic nature; and from there to the unity of God, the Best and Greatest. You will surely experience, if we apply our study to the angels, that we are joined to God through the angels by the ineffable Tetragrammaton: **Iod, He, Vav, He** <note>The letters of the name YHWH: יהוה.</note>, in which the most noble nature of those angels first shines forth.

For if you take these four letters **יהוה** and set down the letter **Iod** four times, and then descending, the letter **He** three times, **Vav** twice, and **He** once, the sum of seventy-two will soon arise for you <note>This is a Kabbalistic calculation: (4x10) + (3x5) + (2x6) + (1x5) = 72.</note>. This is the explanatory sum of the unspeakable and incomprehensible Name of God, to which all sacred names refer. While there is a vast abundance of such names, they are all merely descriptive; this name alone is God's own and appropriated, which is why it is called **Meyuchad** <note>Hebrew: מיוחד — meaning "Unique" or "Singular."</note>. These seventy-two are called a single "symbolic name" because their intention is to signify the one God, the Best and Greatest, even if they do so through many and various accounts of angels—just as we recognize a prince through his courtiers or an emperor by his army.

The Masters of the <term>Kabbalah</term> certainly venerate and cherish these names most highly, through which devoted men perform wonders—even more marvelous than it is permitted for me to speak of. However, I will cite a most learned man as a witness in this matter, **Racanat** <note>Menahem Recanati, a 13th-14th century Italian Kabbalist known for his commentary on the Torah.</note>, in his commentaries on Exodus 14. He affirms that these characters and these letters are <gloss>characters flying above in the foundation of the spiritual Chariot, and they are administrative spirits or prefects appointed to perform every task through them, and their operations are known to the Kabbalists.</gloss> <note>Original Hebrew: אותיות פורחות למעלה בעיקר המרכבה והם ממונים לעשות כל דבר בהם ופעול ותיהם ידועים למקובלים. Reuchlin translates "Merkavah" (Chariot) here as "spiritual wisdom."</note> Thus far the words of Rabbi Menahem Recanat. And according to **Rabbi Akiba**, they proceed from the throne of God's glory. But let no one, led by vain superstition, think that all things are conferred upon human mortality from heaven by the angels alone, and not rather that all things are done by the majesty of God himself *through* the angels and *in* the angels, as seen in Daniel...

<meta>catchword: Nabuchad (referring to Nebuchadnezzar in the following page's reference to the Book of Daniel).</meta>

-># ON THE KABBALISTIC ART<-

<meta>catchword: Nabuchad</meta>

fortified by sacred scripture, as it is read in Job chapter 38: *Do you know the laws of the heavens, if you can establish its authority, or governor, or its executor upon the earth?* <note>Job 38:33; Reuchlin uses this to justify the influence of heavenly beings on the terrestrial world.</note> Therefore, let not such great anxieties of the world or the cares of lower things—to which the aforementioned angels are assigned by the dispensation of the Creator—hold you back from also relating them to the nine choirs of the supercelestial hierarchies. For since the angel is **alterity** <note>The state of being "other" or "different"; in Neoplatonic thought, God is pure Unity, while the first step away from God into creation is "otherness."</note>, just as God is **identity** <note>The state of being one and the same; absolute simplicity.</note>, and the first alterity is the **binary** <term>binarius: the number two, representing the first departure from unity into plurality</term>, we shall rightly suppose that the number of angels arises from the multiplication of the binary. Now, the cubic multiplication of the binary is done thus: twice two, twice <note>i.e., $2 \times 2 \times 2$</note>, and they will be eight, the first cube. If you then distribute these eight angels into nine choirs, there will be seventy-two, for that is how many nine times eight makes. 

Return now, if you wish, through the choirs to the cube, through the cube to your **Tetractys** <note>The Pythagorean "four-fold" number ($1+2+3+4=10$), which Reuchlin equates to the four letters of God's name.</note>, which we call the **Tetragrammaton** and the Romans call the "four-foldness"; from that, return to the binary signifying the angelic nature, and from there to the Unity—God, the Best and Greatest. You will certainly experience that if we apply our study to the angels, we are also joined to God through the angels by the ineffable Tetragrammaton: *Yod, He, Vau, He* <note>The Hebrew letters יהוה</note>, in which the most noble nature of those angels first shines forth. For if, from these four letters יהוה, you place *Yod* four times, and thus descending, *He* three times, *Vau* twice, and *He* once, the sum of seventy-two will soon arise for you <note>This is a Kabbalistic calculation: $(10 \times 4) + (5 \times 3) + (6 \times 2) + (5 \times 1) = 72$.</note>. This is the expository sum of the unutterable and incomprehensible name of God, to which all sacred names are referred. Of these names there is a vast abundance, yet each is a descriptive title; this alone is God’s proper and appropriated name, for which reason it is surnamed the **Unique** <note>original: מיוחד (*Meyuchad*)</note>. 

However, these seventy-two are called "one symbolic name," because their intention is to signify the one God, the Best and Greatest, albeit through the many and various accounts of the angels—just as we recognize a prince through his courtiers and an emperor through his army. And the Masters of the Kabbalah greatly venerate and cherish these names; through them, devoted men perform miraculous works, even more marvelous than is lawful for me to speak of. I shall, however, cite as a witness in this matter a most learned man, **Recanati**, in his commentaries on Exodus 14. He affirms that these characters and these letters are *letters flying on high at the foundation of the Chariot, and they are administrative spirits or prefects appointed to do every thing through them, and their operations are known to the Kabbalists* <note>Original: אותיות פורחות למעלה בעיקר המרכבה והם ממונים לעשות כל דבר בהם ופעול ותיהם ידועים למקובלים. "Chariot" refers to the Merkavah, the mystical vision of God's throne-chariot.</note>; thus far says Rabbi Menahem Recanati. And according to Rabbi Akiba, they proceed from the throne of God’s glory. But let no one, led by vain superstition, think that all things are conferred upon human mortality from heaven by the angels themselves, and not rather that all things are done by the majesty of God through the angels—and even in the angels—as in Daniel...

Then Marranus said: "Are we to suffer you to wander so far while laboring on this one single thing? For we hasten with all our desire toward the art of Cabala itself, if such a thing exists." And Philolaus replied: "I do not believe it is a single thing that Simon has discussed, but rather three or four times more—indeed, many, many things. For he has instructed us with a clear voice about the Sabbath of Sabbaths, which is eternal rest and the end of Cabala; and then about the steps by which we ascend to it, through both the gates of understanding and the paths of wisdom <note>References to the '50 Gates of Understanding' and '32 Paths of Wisdom' in Cabalistic tradition.</note>; and about the angels who explain the four-letter Name <term>Tetragrammaton: the four-letter Hebrew name of God, YHWH</term> and the *Shem HaMephorash* <term>Shem HaMephorash: the 'Divided Name' of 72 parts</term>." To this Simon responded: "If you remember well, I have already touched on something concerning that worthy religion of the ten Cabalistic enumerations <term>Sefirot: the ten channels through which God reveals Himself</term>, and perhaps I promised that I would speak of them. I shall do so by means of a catalog, if you will listen to me attentively." Then both said eagerly, "We are listening; therefore, proceed without delay." 

Soon Simon said: "The ten enumerations, called by the Cabalists 
<margin>V</margin>
the *Ten Sefirot* <note>original Hebrew: עשר ספירות</note>, are treated by many of us in manifold ways. Some treat them in the manner of a tree; others in the form of a man, so that mention is often made of the root, trunk, branches, and bark; but often also of the head, shoulders, legs, feet, and the right and left sides. These are the ten divine names which we mortals conceive of God—whether essential, personal, notional, or common—and they are named as follows: 

1. **Keter** <note>כתר</note>, that is, the **Crown**; 
2. **Chochmah** <note>חכמה</note>, that is, **Wisdom**; 
3. **Binah** <note>בינה</note>, that is, **Prudence** or **Intelligence**; 
4. **Chesed** <note>חסד</note>, that is, **Clemency** or **Goodness**; 
5. **Gevurah** <note>גבורה</note>, that is, **Gravity** or **Severity**; 
6. **Tiferet** <note>תפארת</note>, that is, **Beauty** or **Ornament**; 
7. **Netzach** <note>נצח</note>, that is, **Triumph**; 
8. **Hod** <note>הוד</note>, that is, **Confession of Praise**; 
9. **Yesod** <note>יסוד</note>, that is, **Foundation**; 
10. **Malkhut** <note>מלכות</note>, that is, **Kingdom**. 

But above the Crown is placed **Ein Sof** <note>אין סוף</note>, that is, **Infinity**."

<meta>This page continues the transition from the discussion of the seventy-two names of God to the foundational structure of the ten Sefirot, or divine emanations. # ON THE ART OF THE KABBALAH

And it is an abyss; should I speak or remain silent? <note>original Latin: "Eloquar an sileā"</note> The matter is surely one of profound speculation and a kind of immense sea, in which all our contemplation is submerged, and once submerged, is swallowed up by a gaping void. Do you not remember how much the new "divinely-taught" teachers <note>original Latin: "theodidascali"</note> of almost all nations now toil day and night, sweating almost solely over the concepts of divine attributes? Some call these "perfections in the divine," others "attributes"—some negative, some affirmative, some absolute, and others relative or connotative. You can easily learn of these now, I believe, from the Kabbalistic book called the *Gates of Light* <note>original Latin: "Portæ lucis"</note>, which Paulus Ricius—an exceptionally learned man, formerly one of our own people and now a Christian—collected from a certain Rabbi from Castile, and from the *Introductions* <note>original Latin: "Isagogis"</note> which he wrote on the Kabbalah. Likewise, regarding this matter, that great Master of the Kabbalah, Rabbi Joseph son of Gikatilla <note>original Latin: "Carnitolis"</note> wrote the book **Gates of Justice** <note>original Hebrew: "שערי צדק" (Sha’arei Tzedek)</note>. Many commentators have written much concerning the **Tree of the Ten Numerations** <note>The Sefirot, the ten attributes or emanations through which the Infinite reveals itself</note>, unfolding this involved cause and reducing almost all the sacred Scripture of the Old Testament into these ten numerations. Through these, they lead back to the ten names of God themselves, and through those, to the single name of the Tetragrammaton <note>The four-letter name of God, YHWH</note>. They affirm that the **Infinite** <note>original Hebrew: "Ensoph" (Ein Sof)</note> is the Alpha and the Omega <note>The beginning and the end</note>, who said: "I am the first and I am the last." And that **Crown** <note>original Hebrew: "כתר" (Kether)</note>, which is the "Crown of the kingdom of all ages," is a bottomless fountain and the **Father of Mercies** <note>original Hebrew: "אב הרחמים" (Av HaRachamim)</note>. The mystery of this is that *Ehieh* (I Am) is sealed by *Emeth* (Truth)—that is, Essence is sealed by Truth. As that noble dictator Eliezer Haklir says: **Truth is His seal** <note>original Hebrew: "אמת חותמו" (Emeth chotamo)</note>. Arithmetical reasoning proves this; following it, if we multiply *Ehieh* by *Ehieh*, four hundred and forty-one arises, which together equals **Truth** <note>original Hebrew: "אמת" (Emeth). In Gematria, Ehieh (1+5+10+5) equals 21. 21 squared is 441. Emeth (1+40+400) also equals 441.</note>, just as **The Lord is Peace** <note>original Hebrew: "אד ני שלום" (Adonai Shalom)</note>. They reduce many things to this, such as the "Great Aleph," the "Fear of the Lord," "Inaccessible Light," and the "Days of Eternity," as in the verse: "His going forth is from the beginning, from the days of eternity." Thus writes the distinguished Kabbalist Todros <note>original Latin: "Tedacus"</note> Levi in his book on the ten numerations. To the second numeration, however, which is **Wisdom** <note>The Sefirah of Chokmah</note>, they refer these attributes or properties: primogeniture, *Yes* <note>original Hebrew: "יש", meaning "Existence" or "Is-ness"</note>, the Primitive Law, the letter *Yod* (the first letter of the Tetragrammaton), the Land of the Living, the thirty-two paths, the seventy species of the Law, war, judgment, Amen, book, holy, will, beginning, and other things of that kind. And perhaps it is strange that the second numeration should be called "the Beginning." For one reads in Recanati, an excellent Master of the Kabbalah, concerning the start of Genesis, in this manner: **And perhaps you will ask, since Wisdom is the second numeration, why is it called the Beginning?** <note>original Hebrew: "ואולי תשאל שהחכמה היא ספירה השנייה למה קראת ראשית"</note> For it is written in the book *Bahir*: **There is no "Beginning" except Wisdom.** <note>original Hebrew: "אין ראשית אלא חכמה" (Ein Reshith ella Chokmah)</note> To this I seem to respond correctly: the infinity itself of the three highest numerations of the Kabbalistic tree—which you are accustomed to call the three Persons in the divine—is most absolute...

<summary>Simon introduces the Sefirot (the ten divine numerations) and explains how Kabbalists use them to interpret Scripture and the nature of God. He specifically focuses on the first two Sefirot—Kether (Crown) and Chokmah (Wisdom)—and uses mathematical Gematria to link the divine name "I Am" with "Truth."</summary>

# BOOK THREE

->M iiii<-

The most absolute essence, since it is withdrawn in an abyss of darkness and remains inward and idle—or, as they say, looking toward nothing—is therefore called *Ayin* <note>Hebrew: אין</note>, that is, "Nothing," or "non-being," and "without end," which is *Ayin Sof* <note>Hebrew: אין סוף; the Infinite</note>. This is because we, punished with such a meager poverty of intellect regarding divine matters, judge those things which do not appear in the same way we judge things that do not exist. But when it shows itself in such a way that it is something and truly subsists, then the dark *Aleph* <note>The first letter of the Hebrew alphabet, representing the first movement of the Divine</note> is converted into a luminous *Aleph*. For it is written: *As is its darkness, so also is its light.* It is then called the "Great Aleph" when it desires to go forth and appear as the cause of all things through *Beth*, the letter following immediately after. 

Regarding this, Menahem Recanati <note>A 14th-century Italian Kabbalist</note> writes: **"Therefore you will find this letter [Beth] effecting all things."** For this reason, *Aleph* receives that same letter as its closest and most fertile companion, and it is named *Ab* <note>Hebrew: אב; Father</note>, the father of all generation and production. Then, having taken up *Beth*, it sends it out again into the universe of beings, desiring to reach its fulfillment from the infinite *Ayin*. By joining the final letter *Nun* to *Beth*, it generates *Ben* <note>Hebrew: בן; Son</note>, that is, the "Son." This is the first production within the Godhead and the principle of "otherness" <note>The first distinction between the Creator and the Created</note>, whence it is called *Reshit* <note>Hebrew: ראשית; Beginning</note>. Even though it is the second emanation from infinity—that is, the second Kabbalistic numeration <note>term: Sefirah (plural Sefirot); the ten channels of divine energy</note>—it is the one through which all things were made. For it is written: *In wisdom you have made them all.* In this way, the first efflux becomes the second numeration, because the goal of generation is the son.

Thirdly, there remains the middle between *Aleph* and *Nun*, which is *Iod*, the sign of the holy name *Yah* <note>Hebrew: יה; a shortened form of the Tetragrammaton</note>. If you interweave both characters of that name alternately into the name *Ben* <note>I.e., B-I-N-H</note>, it will be *Binah* <note>Hebrew: בינה; Understanding</note>: "understanding," "prudence," or "providence." This is the third emanation in divine matters, to which is attributed: *Adonai* <note>The Lord</note>, spirit, soul, vow, the mystery of faith, the mother of sons, the king sitting on the throne of mercies, the great Jubilee, the great Sabbath, the foundation of spirits, the wondrous light, the supreme day, the fifty gates, the Day of Atonement, the inner voice, and the river flowing out of Paradise. It is also the second letter of the *Tetragrammaton* <note>The four-letter name of God, YHWH</note>, repentance, deep waters, "my sister," "the daughter of my father," and other titles. 

Thus far we have noted the three numerations which are called by the Kabbalists—as Rabbi Isaac testifies in his commentaries on the *Book of Formation* <note>term: Sefer Yetzirah; one of the foundational texts of Kabbalah</note>—**"the three highest and supreme numerations are one throne,"** upon which sits the Holy, Holy, Holy Lord God of Hosts.

To "Goodness" or "Clemency," which is the fourth numeration, and associated with the divine name *El*, these attributes are assigned: grace, mercy, the right arm, the innocent, the third day, white fire, the face of the lion, the first foot, and Abraham the Elder. Also: the East, the upper waters, the silver of God, Michael, the priest, the angel in the form of the amber-like *Chashmal* <note>A mysterious "glowing metal" or "electrum" mentioned in the visions of Ezekiel</note>, white garments, the south wind, and others. In the fifth numeration of "Severity"...

# ON THE ART OF THE KABBALAH

->M iiii<-

<meta>catchword: elis</meta>

The divine name is **Elohim** <note>Meaning "God," but specifically associated here with the attribute of Judgment</note> and to it are applied fear, the property of rigor or severity, the negative precepts of the law, the left arm, and fire emerging from the waters, as described in the *Book of Creation* <note>The *Sefer Yetzirah*, an ancient foundational text of Jewish mysticism</note>. Likewise the fourth day, the West, Gabriel. Isaac the Elder <note>The Patriarch Isaac, traditionally associated with "Fear" and "Judgment"</note>, night, strength, the golden altar, the second foot, sanctification, and thick darkness. Metatron <note>The highest of angels</note>, the North, and the dark-brown color. To the sixth is applied **Eloha** <note>A singular form of the divine name</note>, illuminating contemplation, the Tree of Life, delight, the middle line, the written law, the high priest, the rising of the sun, and the color purple. And Tedacus Levi <note>Likely Todros ben Joseph Abulafia, a 13th-century Kabbalist</note> writes that from this place the seventy nations of the earth are explained; its seal is **Emeth Adonai** <note>The Truth of the Lord</note>; it is called "Peace," and its form is figured in the moon. Its mystery is the third letter of the **Tetragrammaton** <note>The sacred four-letter name of God, YHWH</note>, and this mystery is "Our Father who is in heaven," the Supernal Man or celestial **Adam** <note>The archetype of humanity in the divine realm</note>, judgment, and sentence. Michael. Israel the Elder. The God of Jacob. To the seventh are referred **Adonai Sabbaoth** <note>Lord of Hosts</note>, the leg, the foot, the right column, the great wheel, the vision of prophecy, Moses, etc. To the eighth belongs **Elohe Sabbaoth** <note>God of Hosts</note>. The mystery of the column and the left foot, and **Boaz** <note>One of the two pillars of the Temple of Solomon</note>; and from here is drawn the ancient serpent, the discipline of the Lord, the branch, Aaron, the Cherub, the sons of the king, the grinding mills, and other things. To the ninth is appropriated **Shaddai** <note>The Almighty</note>, the foundation of the world, Zion, the fountain of pools, the righteous one, the Living God. The complete Sabbath. The middle between "Keep" and "Remember" <note>Referring to the two versions of the Sabbath commandment in Exodus and Deuteronomy</note>. The fiftieth day of Leviathan, Aries, Joseph the Just, Solomon, justice, strength, the Tree of Knowledge of Good and Evil, the Covenant of the Lord, the bow of testimony, the glory of the Lord, the foundation of David’s prophecy, Redemption, and the World of Souls. They are also traced back to the tenth numeration <note>the final Sephirah, Malkuth or "Kingdom"</note>: **Adonai** <note>Lord</note>, sovereignty, life, the second cherub. Contemplation that does not illuminate. The back parts. The End. The Assembly of Israel, the Bride in the Song of Songs. The Queen of Heaven. The Virgin of Israel. The mystery of the Law given by the mouth <note>The Oral Torah/tradition</note>. The Eagle, the fourth letter of the **Tetragrammaton**. The Kingdom of the house of David. The King’s temple, the door of God, the Ark of the Covenant, and the two tablets within it. The Lord of the whole earth. 

You have heard a brief account of the ten properties, notions, or divine attributes, which the Kabbalists call **Belimah** <note>original: בלימה</note>. Some understand this as **Beli** <note>original: בלי; meaning "without"</note>, and **Mah** <note>original: מה; meaning "what"</note>, as if one were to say "ten beyond 'what'"—that is, excluding the "whatness" <note>the essential essence</note> of God. Whence they are accustomed to interpret *Belimah* as that which is beyond what is ineffable; others derive it from "restrain your mouth and your tongue from speaking" <note>original: בלום פיך ולשונך מלדבר</note>, that is, by restricting or binding your tongue so that you do not speak, as these are sacred words that should not be published to the common people. It would now be time to speak of the angelic princes and the demonic prefects, whom the Kabbalists place on the sides of mercy and severity—a matter certainly requiring many words, were we not already past midday and heading toward evening. For who could explain such great things in so little time? Who could describe the thirty-five princes of purity and the seventy princes of Ishmael...

->BOOK THREE<-

<meta>The catchword 'elis' at the end of the previous page completes the word 'himself' (ipse) in the opening sentence.</meta>

...[him]-self, how could I finish so quickly on the side of the fourth numeration? Who likewise, in the fifth numeration—characterized by gravity and fear alike—could sufficiently explain the thirty-five princes of guilt and the seventy princes of Esau <note>In Kabbalah, the "Princes of Esau" represent the spiritual overseers of the seventy gentile nations, often associated with the attribute of Judgment or Rigor</note> so briefly and perfunctorily? These indeed demand their own volumes, and quite extensive ones at that; therefore, having set these aside for the present, let us proceed to the art itself.

<margin>X</margin>
The happiness, I say, of the most contemplative men—following their choice and the manner of meditation on the law (that is, the twenty-four books which we call *Ephraim Varba* <note>A Latinized corruption of the Hebrew *Esrim ve-Arba*, meaning "Twenty-Four," the traditional number of books in the Hebrew Bible</note>)—is found to depend on the sacred letters, both by day and by night. For it is written, "Blessed is the man," among other things, "who will meditate on His law day and night" <note>Psalm 1:1-2</note>. It does not say "he who reads," nor "he who writes," nor "he who speaks." But he who *meditates*, lest perhaps the writing of the law or the reading, being eventually finished and ceasing, should also compel happiness to cease and end. But he at last, who gathers the thoughts in his heart to that place so that, having dismissed carnal things, he meditates on the spiritual matters of the law—he, I say, he is blessed, when with a pure heart he shall see God. For in my judgment, there was no need for such great diligence regarding the histories of Holy Scripture, which are as open to the Hebrews as Titus Livius <note>Livy, the famous Roman historian</note> is to the Latins. Likewise for the mandates and precepts, which have a specific number, and then for the religious rites and ceremonies, which are often performed even by the unrefined and unlearned common folk—often not without fault and sin—wherefore they do not deserve such great happiness, consisting as they do in bodily senses, that such assiduous, continuous, and diligent meditation by day and night should be required for them. But a far greater happiness is shown to be found in the higher levels of theory <note>From the Greek *theoria*, meaning contemplation or mystical insight</note>, which tends toward the Kabbalistic understanding of the law to such an extent that it imbues our minds with spiritual meditation and forms them, as it were, into its own likeness.

<margin>Y</margin>
We conjecture this to be the meditation on the law which was finally delivered from the mouth of God to Moses after the law was given in fire, and after the stone tablets were broken and then restored. For first, as the Kabbalists assert, God wrote His law in a sphere of fire, using dark fire upon white fire. For Ramban of Gerona <note>Rabbi Moses ben Nahman, or Nachmanides, a foundational 13th-century Spanish Kabbalist</note> says: **"That which appears to us through Kabbalah is that the writing was in black fire upon the back of white fire"** <note>original Hebrew: שבא לנו בקבלה שהיתה כתובה באש שחורה על גבי אש לבנה</note>. Whence that passage of Deuteronomy 33 stands out: "From His right hand a fiery law for them." And the letters then were, as they say, confused and massed together; those who were most studious, looking upon them with contemplative insight and considering them diligently while led by the Holy Spirit, could easily choose, read, collect, and form them into any words whatsoever—from here and there, up and down, to and fro, forward and backward—forming a sentence: a good one for the good, and a bad one for the wicked. But Moses, having been instructed by God, reduced them all into order to be published to the people, so that all might know and observe the things of the law; and from there the law was divided into books and placed in the ark, just as he [himself]...

# BOOK THREE

...on the side of the fourth numeration so quickly finish? <margin>X</margin> **Art.** The blessedness, I say, of the most contemplative men is found to depend—according to the manner of their choice—upon meditation on the Law; that is, on the twenty-four books which we call the *Essrim Varba* <note>original: "Essrim Varba," a transliteration of the Hebrew "Esrim V’Arba," meaning "Twenty-Four," the traditional number of books in the Hebrew Bible or Tanakh</note>, day and night, as gathered from the sacred letters. For it is written: *Blessed is the man*, among other things, *who shall meditate on His law day and night* [Psalm 1:1-2]. This is lest the writing or reading of the Law, being eventually finished and ceasing, should also compel blessedness to cease and end. Likewise regarding the mandates and precepts, which have a set number <note>The 613 Mitzvot</note>, or the religious rites and ceremonies, which are performed by the rough and unlearned common people—often not without fault or sin—whence they do not deserve such great blessedness, consisting as they do in bodily senses, that they should require such assiduous, continuous, and diligent meditation day and night. But a far greater blessedness is shown to be found in the higher degrees of theory <note>In this context, "theory" refers to "theoria" or divine contemplation</note>, which tends toward the Kabbalistic understanding of the Law to such an extent that it imbues our minds with spiritual meditation and forms them, as it were, into its own likeness.

<margin>Y</margin> This, we conjecture, is the meditation on the Law which was finally delivered by the mouth of God to Moses after the Law was given in fire, and after the stone tablets had been broken and then restored. For first, as the Kabbalists assert, God wrote His Law in a fiery sphere by means of dark fire upon white fire. For Ramban of Gerona <note>Rabbi Moses ben Nahman, also known as Nachmanides, a 13th-century Sephardic scholar</note> says: שבא לנו בקבלה שהיתה בתורה באש שחורה על גבי אש לבנה <note>original Hebrew: "She-ba lanu ba-kabbalah she-hayetah ba-Torah be-esh shechorah al gabbei esh levanah"</note>, that is: "What appears to us through Kabbalah is that the writing was in dark fire upon the back of white fire." Whence that passage of Deuteronomy 33 exists: *From His right hand came a fiery law for them.*

Any of the most studious men, looking upon them speculatively and considering them diligently while led by the Holy Spirit, could easily choose, read, collect, and form them into any words whatsoever—up and down, this way and that, forwards and backwards—forming sentences signifying good things for the good, and evil things for the evil. But Moses, having been taught by God, reduced them all into the order to be published to the people, so that all might know and observe the things that belonged to the Law; and from there the Law was divided into books and placed in the Ark, just as he himself...

<meta>This page continues the transition from the previous discussion on the Sefirot (the ten divine emanations) to the specific methodologies of Kabbalistic study. # ON THE KABBALISTIC ART

->received from the Lord.<- However, the art of ordering and varying letters and of most sweetly interpreting the sacred scripture for the elevation of the mind—having been received then from the divine majesty—he <note>Referring to Moses</note> did not reveal to the common people, as it was a most divine matter imperceptible to the unrefined. Instead, he delivered it "mouth to mouth" only to the chosen ones, Joshua and the seventy elders. From them, the chosen ones thereafter always received something, and that reception, as you have heard before, is named Kabbalah. <margin><unclear>How this Kabbalah</unclear></margin> Even the most wise of the Christian doctors agree somewhat on this; though I am a Jew, I have gladly read many of them, creeping into their camps like a scout. For concerning our Moses, Gregory Nazianzus—that Greek nicknamed "the Great Theologian"—says this in his book *On the State of Bishops*: "He receives the law: for the many, in the letter; but for those above the many, in the spirit." <note>original Greek: "δέχεται νόμον, τοῖς μὲν πολλοῖς, ἐν τῷ γράμματι· τοῖς δὲ ὑπὲρ τοὺς πολλοὺς, ἐν τῷ πνεύματι"</note> And in the first book of his *Theology*, he says: "He wishes it to be written thus on solid and stone tablets, and on both sides of them, on account of that which is manifest in the law and that which is hidden; the former for the many who remain below, the latter for the few who reach the heights." <note>original Greek: "βούλεται οὗτος πλάξι στερραῖς καὶ λιθίναις ἐγγράφεσθαι... διά τε τὸ φαινόμενον τοῦ νόμου καὶ τὸ κρυπτόμενον. ὃ μὲν τοῖς πολλοῖς ἢ κάτω μενοῦσι, ὃ δὲ τοῖς ὀλίγοις καὶ ἄνω φθάνουσι"</note> <margin>z</margin> From these words, it appears even to your own highly learned men that Moses delivered the text of the law to the common people, but reserved the mysteries, parables, and symbols for himself and the more excellent men. 

We have learned that this Kabbalistic art was divided into three ways, according to the testimony of Solomon, who says in the 22nd chapter of Proverbs: *Have I not written to you in a threefold way, with counsel and knowledge, that I might make known to you the certainty of the words of truth?* [Proverbs 22:20-21]. For our people are accustomed to speak this way when Kabbalah must be mentioned, calling it the <term>Words of Truth</term> <note>original Hebrew: "אמרי אמת" (*imrei emet*)</note>, written specifically <term>According to the Way of Truth</term> <note>original Hebrew: "על דרך האמת" (*al derekh ha-emet*)</note>, which is the way of Kabbalah. This custom was frequent for the Egyptian <note>likely Maimonides</note>, the Gerundese <note>Nahmanides</note>, and others. Others, however, have presented five parts of Kabbalah, such as Rabbi Hamai in the *Book of Speculation* <note>The *Sefer ha-Iyun*</note>, which he names as: <term>Arrangement</term>, <term>Combination</term>, <term>Discourse</term>, <term>Generalization</term>, and <term>Calculation</term>. <note>original Hebrew: "תיקון וצירוף ומאמר ומכלל וחשבון" (*tikkun, tziruf, ma'amar, mikhlal, heshbon*)</note> 

Your Pico della Mirandola wrote in his *900 Conclusions* in these words: "Whatever other Kabbalists may say, I would distinguish the science of Kabbalah in its primary division into the science of <term>Sefirot</term> and <term>Names</term> <note>original: "Sephiroth & Semoth," referring to the divine emanations and the mystical names of God</note>, as if into practical and speculative branches."
