### ON THE KABBALISTIC ART ###

<margin><image-desc>A small marginal sigil consisting of a cross with an 'X' shape through the center and small circles or dots at the ends of the horizontal and vertical arms.</image-desc></margin>
In a short time, enough can be said; these matters are so great, so deep, so innumerable, and so full of peril, that whoever is eager and studious for this cause must strive with the greatest powers of his intellect. One must look around not only with what industry it must be learned, but also with what danger it must be moderated and practiced. For since this is a science both of spiritual things and is itself spiritual, and a man cannot easily assert judgment concerning spirits—even one to whom the power of judging between angels and demons has been granted—any such discrete weighing, even if balanced by an exact rule, is certainly not done without much dread. Unless one’s character is first purified, one cannot rightly apply oneself to this faculty and exercise, lest we suffer the fate of the prophet Balaam <note>original: *Balam*; a biblical figure who attempted to curse Israel but was thwarted by divine intervention</note>, lest we imitate the mother of the living <note>original: *viventium matrem*; a reference to Eve, whose curiosity led to the Fall</note>, or lest we follow darkness under the guise of light. Be fearful of those spirits cast down by lightning—our most savage enemies—and believe me: just as angels do, so too the devils carry their own banners among us mortals.

In the army of God, there are four commanders: Michael, Gabriel, Uriel, and Raphael <note>original: מיכאל גבריאל אוריאל רפאל</note>. They are like the four elements, according to four locations or according to four spiritual numberings. Just as the children of Israel set out under four banners in the second chapter of the book of Numbers: Judah to the east, Reuben to the south, Ephraim to the west, and Dan to the north. Likewise, in the army of Satan, the avenging standard-bearers carry very wide veils: Samael, Azazel, Azael, and Mahazael <note>original: סמא"ל עזאז"ל עזא"ל מחזא"ל</note>. Concerning these, Menahem Recanati <note>An Italian Kabbalist (1250–1310) whose commentary on the Pentateuch was a primary source for Reuchlin</note> treats the discourse in his commentary on Leviticus 16 and in the first book of the Pentateuch; in that place, he himself also cites Targum Jonathan <note>An ancient Aramaic translation and interpretation of the Hebrew Bible</note> regarding the book of Genesis. Furthermore, there are still great, swelling crowds of demons and legions of fugitives from the abyss <note>original: *tartari*—Tartarus, or Hell</note>, all having their portion in the scapegoat <note>original: *capro emissario*; referring to the ritual in Leviticus where a goat is sent into the wilderness for Azazel</note>. Because of their filth and horror, I shall omit reciting them here, although a great part of them are included in the Holy Scriptures.

But with a proverb of the Kabbalists, I now make an end of speaking: "The prudent shall understand" <note>original: המשכיל יבין — *ha-maskil yavin*; a common phrase in mystical literature implying that deeper secrets are reserved for the enlightened</note>. I will also add this: just as Michael is the High Priest <note>original: הוא הכהן הגדול — *hu ha-kohen ha-gadol*</note> sacrificing in the upper world, who presents the spotless souls of men to the Blessed God, yet sends the impure and those burdened with vices to the devil; so too the high priest in the lower world (as it is written in Leviticus) is commanded to offer clean and innocent animals to God, but to hand over those burdened with crimes and a mass of guilt to Satan. The Kabbalists diligently approve of this, saying: "For all lower matters are representations of higher ones, and as it is done below, so it is done above" <note>original: כי כל העניינים התחתונים הם דוגמת לעליונים וכפי העשות למטה כך נעשה למעלה</note>. These things portend something owed to both virtues and vices, so that each person must be careful in what manner he lives and in what manner he dies. For this is the whole of our philosophy:

# BOOK THREE #

It is so that by living well, we may die well, lest by chance we become the portion of Tartarus <note>original: *tartaro*; the deepest pit of the underworld in Greek mythology, here used for Hell</note> and the avenging Furies, with all hope frustrated, and so that it does not turn out badly for the wicked. Now, because it is quite distressing, I think we must depart, since from morning until night I have been chatting with you more loquaciously than was proper. For as I make a kindly guess about myself, so I judge not unworthily of you, that sleep urges us to go to rest. Then they said: "We are torn away from you with such regret, Simon, for we wish to hear you forever; therefore, do not say a word about 'too much talk.' But since you so command, we will do as you wish and depart, returning to you tomorrow, unless it is inconvenient for you." To this Simon said, "I cannot hide from you, my friends, what I have decided for myself. Tomorrow I shall migrate to distant parts, having been called away for a wedding, because my uncle has taken a wife at Regensburg <note>original: *Ratispontę*</note>; may the matter turn out well." Then Philolaus said: "I would urge you with all my strength to stay, were it not unjust; for we are not born, I confess, for ourselves alone, but we yield a part of ourselves to our friends by their own right. Therefore, giving you thanks, we pray for a prosperous journey for you and yours." At this, Marranus, touched by sadness, said: "Go, with favorable omens <note>original: *sinistris auibus*; literally 'with left-hand birds,' which in Roman augury could mean favorable or unfavorable depending on the context, but here Simon’s friend wishes him well</note>, prosperously and happily, my dearest friend Simon, best of men. Meanwhile, we are forced to wait for the end of the Frankfurt fairs <note>original: *nundinarum Francofordiẽsium*; the Frankfurt Fair was the most important trade and book fair in Europe</note>, so that we might return more safely to our own countries from this marketplace along with our local merchants." Then Simon said, according to the custom of his people: "Peace be with you." To which both of them replied: "Farewell. Go, our glory, go!" <note>original: *I decus, I nostrum*; a quote from Virgil’s Aeneid</note>

***

You have here, most holy LEO THE TENTH <note>Giovanni de' Medici (1475–1521), the reigning Pope at the time of publication</note>, from Capnio <note>Reuchlin's Greek pseudonym, meaning 'smoky,' a translation of his German name</note>, your humble servant, the opinions and sentences of the ancients regarding the symbolic philosophy of Pythagoras and the wisdom of the Kabbalah, recounted in a brief compendium. Though they are few in number, they may provide to studious men a much wider handle for thinking and investigating. Concerning these matters, I, a man of mediocre talent and small prudence, would dare to judge nothing, nor indeed shall I judge. Instead, I submit this entire book to your authority, to whose judgment the censorship of the whole world has been committed, so that you may reject what displeases you; and then I shall rejoice that the rest has pleased. I trust that this effort of mine—which you can consider me to have undertaken for the sake of our people and the Republic—will not seem entirely improper to you, both because the works of others are opened to our people through my labor, and because during this half-year of reading them, I have striven to lighten, if it could not be avoided entirely, that five-year war <note>original: *quinquenne bellum*; Reuchlin refers to his long legal and intellectual battle against the inquisitor Jakob van Hoogstraten and the theologians of Cologne</note> which my enemies have been waging against me with your knowledge. Finally, it was so that there might be something of mine in your possession, by which your memory of me might be more benevolent whenever enemies strive to break and turn away your paternal spirit from me. For I know they do not cease daily to test your pious ears with whispers, now through hired agents, now through letters—such as the one I recently read, sent to you from Cologne <note>original: *Agrippina Colonia*</note> on the 14th of the Kalends of October <note>September 18th</note>, whose title lies about the author even as it delivers a false accusation. For it is not the worshipful Cologne, nor its venerable University, but a particular faction and a certain...

# XIX ❧ ON THE CABALISTIC ART ❧ XX #

...by a singular collection of enemies, and the smallest—and more insane—part of the city, committed this crime, so that they might affirm to your Holiness things which are not true, and this against Apostolic Inhibitions and against the peace commanded by the Emperor. You see also with what audacity in those same letters they presume to prescribe **Solonian laws** <note>original: *Solonianas leges*; referring to Solon, the famous Athenian lawmaker, implying these men are arrogantly trying to rewrite the law for the Pope</note> to you, and teach the very source of justice: by what path the judgment ought to proceed according to their whim and will, so that they might more easily overwhelm me with their filth—as if my innocence were not already held as a certainty by almost the entire world.

Whence I cannot be led to suspect that you have faith in those men who, having despised the Apostolic Inhibition and held your censures in contempt, burned my little book <note>The *Augenspiegel* (Mirror of the Eyes), Reuchlin’s defense of Jewish books, which his enemies burned in public</note> while the lawsuit was still pending, having observed the path of the law not at all. You will instead believe the weightier men of Upper Germany, who are beyond all exception, that I have set forth no scandal and provided no occasion for ruin before any of the German people. These people are joined to me by the fellowship of the same language, in which language—unknown to those **Belgians** <note>original: *Belgis*; here Reuchlin refers to the theologians of Cologne and the Low Countries who opposed him</note>—I published that **Chamber Counsel** <note>original: *Consilium illud Camerarium*; Reuchlin’s legal opinion written for the Emperor regarding the confiscation of Jewish books</note> of mine with its plain declaration in a single text, as was proper. Indeed, you can believe this securely, and all the more firmly because you have been made certain of my innocence, piety, faith, and integrity by many most illustrious rulers of the widest lands of our nation, by magistrates, by the German people, and by the most holy Bishops of our dioceses, through sealed and trustworthy letters nearly three years ago.

There exist in your possession the testimonies offered three and four times over for my innocence by the most invincible elected Roman Emperor, **Maximilian**, and by the most reverend Cardinal, my lord of **Gurk**. After the Bishops, the most illustrious governors of the provinces and dukes born of the noblest blood also gave their testimony: the Electors of the Empire, **Frederick of Saxony** and **Louis of Bavaria**, the Imperial Vicar; the **Duke of Württemberg**, the **Marquis of Baden**, and the most strenuous **Master of the Teutonic Order**. And on the other side of these are the reverend and God-beloved prelates of Germany: the **Bishop of Worms**, the **Bishop of Strasbourg**, the **Bishop of Constance** (who acknowledges me as a sheep of his own pasture), and the **Bishop of Speyer**, that judge given to this lawsuit by your Holiness, who, exercising your authority and by the counsel of experts, brought forth a definitive sentence for my innocence and that of my writings.

With those men, fifty-three towns of **Swabia**—all most dutiful, brave, and upright men—likewise gave letters of recommendation and letters as witnesses of my correct faith, probity, and harmlessness. To their testimony, they add strength and weight through the distinguished learning and gravity of the prelates of the Church, whom you joined as senatorial assessors—lights of the world—to the most reverend judges of our cause, Cardinals **Grimani** and **Ancona**, the pillars of the orthodox faith. Archbishops, Bishops,

<meta>This page concludes Johann Reuchlin’s dedicatory epistle to Pope Leo X for "De Arte Cabalistica." Reuchlin summarizes the legal support he received in Rome during the controversy over his Hebrew studies and highlights his legacy as the scholar who reintroduced Greek and Hebrew to Germany and the wider Church.</meta>

# BOOK THREE XC #

The Generals of the Religious Orders and their Proctors, the Magistrates of the **Roman Wisdom** <note>original: *Sapientiæ Romanæ*; referring to the Sapienza University of Rome</note>, the Penitentiaries, and other most select Doctors of theology and law—who are to be named in the history of my times according to their individual dignities—were present for so many public sessions held in your Majesty’s domestic sanctuary which they call the **Papal Chapel**. My case was always handled by that most faithful and highly skilled legal orator, **Johannes Vanderbicus** <note>original: *Ioanne Vanderbico*; Jan van der Beeck, a Dutch jurist and nobleman who served as Reuchlin’s legal representative in Rome</note>, a man as noble in his equestrian rank as he is a sharp debater in the advocacy of causes. Finally, in the last session, after the case was fully examined, they decreed through written sentences that I should be freed and acquitted from this injurious persecution. There is no doubt that a definitive sentence of equal authority from the most reverend Judges would have followed as it ought, had the accusers not then obtained from you a mandate to suspend the proceedings, as they claimed. If you recall the testimonies and votes of all those we have cited, and if you take care to have the acts of the trials read before you, you will clearly find me entirely innocent of every accusation made by my detractors. Almost the entire city of Rome leaps to support my purity, as do the most learned men of every nation. I daily receive letters of decree from them, even from the ends of the earth, confirming that I have never been a cause of scandal to any man through my writings; rather, they say I build up the Church daily and plant it in various languages for the Holy Spirit, who gathered the nations into the unity of faith through the diversity of all tongues.

They surely notice that I was the first of all to bring back **Greek** studies to Germany, and the first of all to bestow and hand down the art and study of the **Hebrew** language to the universal Church. Therefore, I hope that I do not hope in vain that the future generations of the Church will not be ungrateful for my merits. I hope that you, most blessed **LEO**, Supreme Pontiff—a judge of deeds rather than words—will justly restore peace and tranquility of mind to me in exchange for so many and such difficult labors contributed as a benefit to the orthodox faith. But if you truly wish for me to remain perpetually subject to the persecution of evil men in this life, I shall greatly rejoice to appear

->worthy to suffer such great<-
->wrongs for our<-
->Christ.<-

---

->At Haguenau, by Johann Setzer,<-
->In the year 1530.<-

<meta>This page concludes the introductory or defensive material of Johannes Reuchlin’s work. The previous page detailed his legal struggles in Rome regarding his Hebrew studies; here, he reflects on his role as a pioneer of language study in Germany and asserts his innocence against his detractors before the final publication details.</meta>

# BOOK THREE XC #

The Proctors of the Spanish Order and all the Roman Magistrates seem to me like those who, by the students of theology and sacred letters, are named as belonging to the household of **Martin Luther** <note>original: *Martini Lutheri*; Reuchlin is likely referencing the contemporary religious tensions and how his own scholarly "linguist" movement was being grouped with the burgeoning Reformation</note> because of their support for the study of languages. These men, who were the only ones who did not hold certain private councils regarding this public matter, always seemed to act in my favor. Within that same spirit of **Johannes Reuchlin of Pforzheim** <note>original: *Ioannis Reuchlin Phorcensis*; the author referring to himself in the third person</note>, and in that same noble rank, they wished to cast aside the impudence of the heart and that final choice of the soul; clearly, in this published writing, they have removed any appearance of this persecution. I have no doubt that on the day of the trial, the judge saw this opinion as a divine oracle and removed me from the "white list" <note>original: *albo*; likely referring to a list of the accused or those under suspicion</note> of those standing trial. As we have already said, through their testimony and voice, I have been judged in all other matters as well, finding my supporters despite the detraction, insults, and reproaches of others.

But if any think that there will be no letters from the city of Rome in my name, let them know that all the most learned men support me. Since an exception is made for me regarding any merit, I should be held as one by no men in the continents of the world—judging by my writings—except that I am daily received into the Church of the **Spouse** <note>The Church as the Bride of Christ</note> in various languages. For the sake of the holy, uncorrupted tongue, there is grace if the understanding is appropriate. They will surely have noticed that I was the **first of all in Germany** who—in the memory of Christ and for the universal Church—established and handed down the study of the **Hebrew language** <note>original: *sermonis Hebraici*</note>. Therefore, it was not for me that posterity should read of my ecclesiastical merits, but rather that I should not be ungrateful for these blessed things. I have applied my care to God, the Greatest and Best. 

Furthermore, I have produced these works not so much for my own sake, but so that my labors, gathered in an orthodox place, might provide evidence of my faith, which I believe will be most useful for me and for souls. If it pleases them to continue to pursue me through this harassment of evils, I greatly rejoice to be seen as **worthy to sing for Christ against the enemies of the Father**.

***

-> Haguenau, at the house of Johann Secer, <-
-> In the Year 1530. <-
